title: Clinical Shift foundations and rotation practice
reviewStatus: Source and consistency checks are recorded with each encounter. Independent clinician review remains pending for all 84 encounters.

rotations.name: Emergency Medicine
rotations.description: Sort out what is urgent and decide what happens next.

rotations.name: Cardiology
rotations.description: Connect symptoms, exam findings and tests to a decision.

rotations.name: Neurology
rotations.description: Work out where the problem is and catch the dangerous misses.

rotations.name: Neurosurgery
rotations.description: Recognize pressure on the brain or spinal cord, and act in time.

rotations.name: General Surgery
rotations.description: Decide who needs an operation, and what has to happen first.

rotations.name: Pediatrics
rotations.description: Children are not small adults. Learn what changes, and what cannot wait.

rotations.name: OB/GYN
rotations.description: Pregnancy changes the rules. Learn the emergencies that cannot wait.

rotations.name: Internal Medicine
rotations.description: The body’s chemistry goes wrong quietly. Read the numbers, and act on them.

rotations.name: Pulmonology
rotations.description: What fills a lung, what squeezes it, and what hides in it quietly.

rotations.name: Gastroenterology
rotations.description: From the gallbladder to the gut: find the bleed, the blockage or the inflammation.

rotations.name: Infectious Disease
rotations.description: Some infections can wait for a culture. Learn the ones that cannot.

rotations.name: Family Medicine
rotations.description: The clinic sees everything first. Sort the common from the dangerous.

rotations.name: Nephrology
rotations.description: Read the kidneys through blood and urine, and find what is blocking or poisoning them.

rotations.name: Endocrinology
rotations.description: Hormones run the body from a distance. Trace the signal, and replace what is missing.

rotations.name: Hematology & Oncology
rotations.description: White cells that cannot fight, blood that will not clot, and a transfusion gone wrong.

rotations.name: Rheumatology
rotations.description: A hot joint, or a fever that will not break. Inflammation leaves damage when it is missed.

rotations.name: Orthopedics
rotations.description: Bones break in patterns. Learn the ones that threaten a limb, a hip or the years ahead.

rotations.name: Urology
rotations.description: From a simple bladder infection to a kidney that cannot be saved. Learn where the line is.

rotations.name: Otolaryngology (ENT)
rotations.description: A nosebleed that will not stop, a swallowed battery and a voice that keeps giving out.

rotations.name: Vascular Neurology
rotations.description: A stroke, something that only looks like one, and the warning that comes before one.

rotations.name: Neuro-Oncology
rotations.description: Tumors of the brain, the spine and the pituitary gland, and the hours when treatment still changes the outcome.

rotations.name: Pediatric Neurology
rotations.description: A seizure that will not stop, a baby with a tense soft spot and a teenager who falls asleep mid-sentence.

rotations.name: Dermatology
rotations.description: The skin can be the first sign of trouble inside, or the whole problem. Learn to tell which.

rotations.name: Ophthalmology
rotations.description: Three red or failing eyes. One could be lost within days, and one is a warning from behind the eye.

rotations.name: Physical Medicine & Rehab
rotations.description: Weak muscles, a curving spine and a hip that is turning to bone. This specialty treats what a person can do.

em-016.assessment: 32-year-old hemodynamically stable woman with abrupt recurrent regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 188 bpm without visible P waves, terminated by adenosine, consistent with AVNRT. Post-conversion ECG, electrolytes, and TSH are normal, with no pre-excitation or ischemic changes.
em-016.plan: Acute episode managed per the stable-SVT pathway: modified Valsalva failed, and rapid IV adenosine (6 mg, then 12 mg) converted her to sinus rhythm on continuous monitoring. After observation, discharge with return precautions, caffeine reduction, instruction in vagal maneuvers, and outpatient cardiology follow-up; discuss elective ablation if episodes become frequent or poorly tolerated.

em-018.assessment: 50-year-old man on warfarin with delayed headache, confusion, gait instability, and focal right-sided findings after head trauma. CT shows a 12-mm left crescentic mixed-density extra-axial collection crossing sutures with 6-mm midline shift, consistent with an acute-on-subacute subdural hematoma with mass effect; INR 3.8.
em-018.plan: Hold warfarin and urgently reverse anticoagulation with four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K, rechecking INR after infusion to confirm correction. Obtain immediate neurosurgical consultation for operative evacuation, admit to an ICU for close neurologic and intracranial-pressure monitoring with repeat imaging, and avoid restarting anticoagulation until neurosurgery determines it is safe.

em-015.assessment: 78-year-old man with recurrent abrupt syncope and symptomatic bradycardia. ECG shows complete AV dissociation with atrial rate 88, ventricular escape 38, and wide QRS, confirming third-degree AV block.
em-015.plan: Stop AV-nodal-blocking medication, place the patient on continuous monitoring with pacing pads, and begin transcutaneous pacing with analgesia/sedation, confirming both electrical and mechanical capture, while preparing for urgent transvenous pacing (epinephrine or dopamine infusion as backup if capture fails). Obtain cardiology or electrophysiology consultation and arrange permanent pacemaker implantation; evaluate reversible contributors (trend the pending troponin to exclude acute ischemia; check potassium and magnesium) and admit to a monitored CCU bed, but do not delay pacing in this symptomatic patient.

em-020.assessment: 59-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes and septic physiology, rapidly progressive perineal pain out of proportion, necrosis, crepitus, and CT-demonstrated soft-tissue gas. Findings are consistent with Fournier gangrene and sepsis with hypoperfusion (hypotension, lactate 4.2 mmol/L) and acute kidney injury.
em-020.plan: Activate surgery immediately for debridement while starting broad IV antibiotics, cultures, and resuscitation. Use balanced crystalloid with frequent assessment of perfusion and fluid tolerance; add norepinephrine when hypotension persists or shock severity warrants concurrent support. One empiric option is vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam, with toxin-suppressing therapy when indicated. Adjust to renal function and microbiology. ICU care, repeat operative assessment, glucose management, and wound reconstruction follow source control.

em-033.assessment: 29-year-old woman at approximately 7 weeks' gestation with acute abdominal pain, shock, hemoglobin 8.1, positive hCG, empty uterus, left adnexal mass, and intraperitoneal free fluid, consistent with ruptured ectopic pregnancy and hemorrhagic shock. Blood type O negative.
em-033.plan: Stabilize airway, breathing, and circulation; place large-bore IV access, type and cross, and activate blood-product resuscitation with O-negative packed red cells as needed. Obtain immediate obstetric and gynecologic surgical intervention by laparoscopy or laparotomy, admit postoperatively to a monitored bed for ongoing hemodynamic and transfusion surveillance, trend CBC, coagulation, and hemodynamics, and administer Rho(D) immune globulin.

cd-001.assessment: 61-year-old man with reproducible exertional substernal pressure relieved by rest, unchanged over three months. Exercise ECG reproduced symptoms with 1.5-mm horizontal ST depression in V4-V6, supporting chronic stable angina with suspected obstructive coronary disease; coronary anatomy has not yet been demonstrated; no resting or unstable features are present.
cd-001.plan: Begin a beta-blocker such as metoprolol succinate for symptom control and prescribe sublingual nitroglycerin with use and emergency instructions. Start aspirin 81 mg daily and high-intensity atorvastatin with adherence counseling, plus smoking cessation, blood-pressure control, and close cardiology follow-up; escalate anatomic evaluation if symptoms persist or risk increases.

cd-006.assessment: 68-year-old man with new symptomatic atrial fibrillation and rapid ventricular response at 138-152 bpm, hemodynamically stable, likely precipitated by an alcohol binge. Troponin, electrolytes, TSH, and chest radiograph show no alternate acute trigger; CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3.
cd-006.plan: Use IV diltiazem for acute rate control with telemetry. Start long-term anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban after bleeding-risk review, counsel alcohol reduction, obtain echocardiographic and cardiology follow-up, and reassess rhythm-control options based on duration, symptoms, and anticoagulation status.

cd-055.assessment: 17-year-old athlete with exertional syncope, exertional chest tightness, family history of sudden death, and a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva. ECG and echocardiography show asymmetric septal hypertrophy, systolic anterior motion, mitral regurgitation, and a resting LVOT gradient of 60 mmHg, confirming obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with high-risk syncope.
cd-055.plan: Pause intense competitive sports pending specialist evaluation and start a nonvasodilating beta-blocker. Refer urgently to a hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy and electrophysiology center for sudden-death risk stratification — including ambulatory ECG monitoring and cardiac MRI — and ICD evaluation, counsel hydration and avoidance of preload-reducing drugs, use shared decision-making about later exercise participation, and screen all first-degree relatives with ECG and echocardiography with genetic counseling as appropriate.

cd-061.assessment: 26-year-old man who injects drugs with 10 days of fever, a tricuspid regurgitation murmur, leukocytosis, and bilateral peripheral cavitary pulmonary nodules, highly concerning for Staphylococcus aureus tricuspid-valve infective endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli.
cd-061.plan: Admit for respiratory support, prompt cultures, IV antibiotics, and complication assessment. Include MRSA coverage while choosing the full empiric regimen with infectious disease input; narrow to an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam for confirmed MSSA when tolerated. Obtain TTE promptly, using TEE when indicated. Repeat cultures to establish clearance and individualize antibiotic duration and surgical assessment to the organism, valve findings, response, and complications. Follow pending HIV and hepatitis testing, and offer addiction treatment and harm-reduction support.

cd-019.assessment: 39-year-old woman three weeks postpartum with inferior STEMI and angiographic RCA dissection. Initially preserved coronary flow allowed monitored conservative management, but later recurrent ischemia and hypotension indicate deterioration requiring urgent reassessment.
cd-019.plan: Activate urgent repeat coronary assessment and revascularization planning with interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery because ischemia and hypotension have recurred. Continue monitored supportive care and avoid thrombolysis for known SCAD. After stabilization, individualize antiplatelet and other treatment to the intervention and clinical course; arrange rehabilitation, extracoronary vascular assessment, and specialist counseling about recurrence, breastfeeding-compatible medications, and future pregnancy.

nr-011.assessment: 58-year-old woman with brief position-triggered vertigo and no auditory or focal neurologic symptoms. Right Dix-Hallpike testing produces delayed, transient, fatigable upbeating-torsional nystagmus, confirming right posterior-canal BPPV.
nr-011.plan: Repeat an appropriate Epley maneuver for the documented recurrence of right posterior-canal BPPV, after checking mobility and neck limitations. Avoid routine scheduled vestibular suppressants. Give fall advice and suitable home instructions, and reassess within one month; persistent, atypical, or central findings require further evaluation.

nr-025.assessment: 24-year-old man with a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure, postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury, and incontinence. Glucose, electrolytes, toxicology, CT, MRI, and EEG are normal, supporting a first unprovoked seizure without an identified structural lesion.
nr-025.plan: Discuss recurrence risk, benefits and adverse effects of medication, occupation, and the patient’s preferences with prompt neurology follow-up. Deferring medication is one reasonable option; normal tests do not eliminate recurrence risk. Give practical seizure precautions and applicable driving guidance, and clear return instructions for another or prolonged event.

nr-012.assessment: 45-year-old man with 18 hours of continuous acute vestibular syndrome. HINTS by a trained examiner favors a peripheral pattern, with an abnormal right head impulse, unidirectional left-beating nystagmus, and no skew; hearing is intact and no focal deficits are present, consistent with right vestibular neuritis.
nr-012.plan: Provide brief symptom relief and early vestibular rehabilitation. Discuss uncertain steroid benefit. Reassess promptly for new neurologic or auditory findings, severe gait impairment, or other atypical evolution; activate stroke assessment when concern persists.

nr-016.assessment: 22-year-old man after temporal head trauma with a lucid interval followed by rapid neurologic decline, left pupillary dilation, and right weakness. CT shows a 22-mm left biconvex epidural hematoma with temporal fracture, 9-mm midline shift, and early uncal herniation, consistent with middle meningeal artery injury.
nr-016.plan: Secure the airway and ventilation as needed and activate neurosurgery for immediate craniotomy and evacuation. While moving to the operating room, elevate the head 30 degrees with the neck midline, give hypertonic saline or mannitol, use only brief controlled hyperventilation for active herniation, prevent hypoxia and hypotension, maintain cervical spine precautions until cleared, and start 7-day post-traumatic seizure prophylaxis (levetiracetam).

nr-008.assessment: 38-year-old man with right neck and facial pain after cervical manipulation, painful partial Horner syndrome, and transient contralateral sensory symptoms. CTA shows flame-shaped right internal-carotid narrowing with intramural hematoma, confirming internal carotid artery dissection without established infarct.
nr-008.plan: Admit to a monitored stroke unit for serial neurologic checks, begin antithrombotic therapy with an antiplatelet agent or anticoagulation after contraindication review, obtain stroke and neurology consultation, and monitor for cerebral or retinal ischemia. Avoid further neck manipulation, arrange follow-up vascular imaging, and reserve endovascular treatment for recurrent ischemia or selected refractory disease.

em-101.assessment: A brief event during a characteristic trigger with prodrome, pallor and rapid recovery is most consistent with a vasovagal faint. Brief jerks are part of the witness account; they do not independently establish epilepsy. Current assessment identifies no cardiac red flag.
em-101.plan: Explain the working interpretation, document the patient and witness accounts plus ECG assessment, discuss trigger avoidance and what to do if symptoms recur, and arrange follow-up. Reassess a recurrent or changed event. Exertional collapse or a concerning family history would change urgency; neither belongs to this original presentation.

cd-101.assessment: A symptomatic fall from 148/82 lying to 112/64 after one minute standing supports postural hypotension. Recent medication and intake changes are possible contributors. Persistence after initial measures leaves the cause incompletely resolved.
cd-101.plan: Document the posture measurements and symptoms; review medication and volume status with individualized management and fall-risk advice. Recheck standing pressure. Persistent symptoms call for reassessment and consideration of specialist evaluation. New acute features would require a separate urgency decision.

nr-101.assessment: The witnessed convulsive episode, post-event confusion and lateral tongue injury support a first suspected epileptic seizure. Onset and cause remain unclassified. Initial ECG and metabolic evaluation are reassuring but not exhaustive. The later normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy.
nr-101.plan: Complete a first-seizure specialist assessment, using the cited NICE urgent referral pathway as the course example. Provide individual interim safety advice and a contact plan if another event occurs. Arrange further testing and any treatment according to the specialist assessment; do not select a permanent regimen or withdraw precautions solely because the routine EEG is normal.

ns-006.assessment: 35-year-old woman with bilateral sciatica, saddle anesthesia, reduced anal tone, and painless urinary retention (post-void residual 650 mL). MRI shows a large central L4-L5 disc herniation compressing the cauda equina, confirming cauda equina syndrome.
ns-006.plan: Catheterize the bladder, keep her nil by mouth, and obtain emergent spine-surgery review for urgent decompression (laminectomy and discectomy). Do not delay for steroids or outpatient treatment. Document baseline perianal sensation, anal tone, and strength, and counsel that earlier decompression improves the chance of bladder, bowel, and motor recovery.

ns-030.assessment: 7-year-old boy with a VP shunt presenting with headache, vomiting, lethargy, sunsetting eyes, papilledema, hypertension, and relative bradycardia. CT shows ventricles enlarged from baseline and the shunt series shows catheter discontinuity at the clavicle, confirming mechanical shunt malfunction with raised intracranial pressure; he then develops a dilated pupil and worsening bradycardia.
ns-030.plan: Emergent CSF drainage by shunt tap or ventricular access, with immediate neurosurgical shunt revision. Elevate the head, avoid lumbar puncture, give hyperosmolar therapy as a bridge, send CSF for culture, and monitor in intensive care after surgery.

ns-010.assessment: 58-year-old man with untreated hypertension and sudden right hemiplegia, dysarthria, headache, and vomiting; BP 214/118 mmHg. CT shows a 25-mL acute left putaminal hemorrhage without significant midline shift or hydrocephalus, and coagulation is normal, consistent with hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.
ns-010.plan: No thrombolysis or antithrombotics. Lower the systolic blood pressure in a controlled way toward 130-140 mmHg with a titratable IV agent, avoiding precipitous drops. Monitor airway and neurologic status in a stroke or neurocritical care unit, repeat imaging for any deterioration, manage glucose and temperature, and consult neurosurgery, with surgery reserved for selected cases.

gs-023.assessment: 66-year-old man with a prior laparotomy and 8 hours of constant severe abdominal pain, obstipation, fever, tachycardia, peritoneal signs, and a rising lactate. CT shows a C-shaped closed loop with a whirl sign and reduced bowel-wall enhancement: closed-loop small bowel obstruction with strangulation.
gs-023.plan: Resuscitate with IV fluids, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, and take him for immediate exploratory laparotomy. No nonoperative trial and no contrast challenge. Release the band, assess viability, resect nonviable bowel, and plan a second look if viability is marginal.

gs-058.assessment: 57-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and recent diverticulitis, with five days of fever, rigors, and right-upper-quadrant pain, leukocytosis, and cholestatic liver tests. CT shows a 6 cm rim-enhancing multiloculated right-lobe collection: pyogenic liver abscess with sepsis.
gs-058.plan: Draw blood cultures, start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric gram-negatives, streptococci, and anaerobes, and arrange image-guided percutaneous drainage with cultures to narrow therapy. Control glucose. Look for the source, and with monomicrobial Klebsiella evaluate the colon and watch for metastatic infection such as endophthalmitis.

gs-052.assessment: 46-year-old man with paroxysmal headache, palpitations, and sweating, resistant hypertension, and a 4.5 cm lipid-poor right adrenal mass. Plasma and urinary metanephrines are markedly elevated with normal cortisol suppression and aldosterone-renin ratio: pheochromocytoma, with a family history suggesting MEN2.
gs-052.plan: Alpha-blockade for 7-14 days before surgery with liberal salt and fluids, adding a beta-blocker only after alpha-blockade is established. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy with early adrenal vein ligation, minimal tumor handling, and close communication with anesthesia. No biopsy. Refer for genetic counseling and germline testing (RET, VHL, SDHx) and screen for associated tumors.

pd-027.assessment: 9-year-old girl with weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss, now vomiting and drowsy with Kussmaul breathing. Glucose 512 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 9 mEq/L, anion gap 24, and large ketones with HbA1c 11.6%: new-onset type 1 diabetes in diabetic ketoacidosis.
pd-027.plan: Isotonic IV fluids first, then a continuous low-dose insulin infusion without a bolus once potassium is known; add potassium to fluids and monitor glucose, electrolytes, and neurologic status hourly. No routine bicarbonate. Watch for cerebral edema (headache, altered mental status, bradycardia with hypertension) and treat at once with hypertonic saline or mannitol, head elevation, and a reduced fluid rate.

pd-064.assessment: 5-day-old term boy with abrupt bilious emesis, poor perfusion, and blood per rectum. The upper GI series shows the duodenum failing to cross the midline with a corkscrew configuration and a right-sided ligament of Treitz; lactate is 4.2 mmol/L: malrotation with midgut volvulus and evolving bowel ischemia.
pd-064.plan: Nothing by mouth, nasogastric decompression, IV access and isotonic fluid resuscitation, and emergent pediatric surgery consultation. Emergent laparotomy with detorsion and a Ladd procedure, assessing bowel viability. Counsel the family about short bowel syndrome if extensive resection is needed.

pd-081.assessment: Well-appearing 4-year-old boy with 48 hours of petechiae, bruising, and minor epistaxis two weeks after a viral illness. Platelets are 11 ×10³/µL with normal hemoglobin, white count, smear morphology, and coagulation, and there is no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy: immune thrombocytopenia.
pd-081.plan: Observation, because bleeding is limited to the skin and brief epistaxis. Counsel the parents: avoid contact sports, NSAIDs, and aspirin, and seek emergency care for headache, vomiting, or altered mental status. Recheck the count. Reserve IVIG, anti-D, or corticosteroids for significant bleeding, and platelet transfusion for life-threatening hemorrhage.

ob-001.assessment: 31-year-old G2P1 at 34 weeks 2 days with new severe-range hypertension (168/112 mmHg), headache, visual symptoms, hyperreflexia with clonus, and a urine protein/creatinine ratio of 0.6, with normal platelets, creatinine, and transaminases: preeclampsia with severe features.
ob-001.plan: Admit. Treat the severe-range blood pressure promptly with IV labetalol (or hydralazine or immediate-release nifedipine) and give IV magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, monitoring reflexes, respiration, and urine output. Give betamethasone, continue fetal monitoring, and proceed toward delivery after maternal stabilization; the route is individualized.

ob-010.assessment: 26-year-old G2P1 about 7 weeks from her last period with right lower abdominal pain, spotting, and risk factors (prior PID, pelvic surgery, smoking). Beta-hCG is 3,200 mIU/mL with an empty uterus and a 3 cm right adnexal mass with a tubal ring: ectopic pregnancy, which then ruptures with hemorrhagic shock.
ob-010.plan: While stable and unruptured she meets criteria for methotrexate with serial hCG follow-up. With rupture and instability: large-bore IV access, blood products, and emergent surgery (laparoscopy or laparotomy, usually salpingectomy). Give anti-D immune globulin because she is Rh-negative.

ob-064.assessment: 22-year-old woman with three hours of sudden severe colicky right pelvic pain and vomiting and a known right ovarian cyst. Pregnancy test negative. Ultrasound shows a 6.5 cm edematous right ovary with peripherally displaced follicles, a 5 cm cyst, and absent Doppler flow: ovarian torsion.
ob-064.plan: Emergent diagnostic laparoscopy with detorsion. Conserve the ovary even if it appears dusky, and remove the cyst (cystectomy); reserve oophorectomy for frankly necrotic or suspicious tissue. Analgesia and antiemetics before surgery. Routine oophoropexy is not required.

im-034.assessment: 38-year-old man with autoimmune hypothyroidism and vitiligo, weeks of fatigue, weight loss, salt craving, and hyperpigmentation, now hypotensive after a vomiting illness. Sodium 126, potassium 6.1 with peaked T waves, glucose 62, cortisol 2.8 µg/dL with markedly elevated ACTH: primary adrenal insufficiency in adrenal crisis.
im-034.plan: Draw cortisol and ACTH, then give IV isotonic saline (with dextrose) and IV hydrocortisone at once without waiting for confirmatory testing. Give IV calcium gluconate for the ECG changes; the hyperkalemia corrects with fluids and steroid. Long term: lifelong hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, sick-day dosing, an emergency injection kit, and a medical alert.

im-024.assessment: 62-year-old woman with a new lung mass and two days of confusion. Sodium 118 mEq/L, serum osmolality 248, urine osmolality 540, urine sodium 58, clinically euvolemic with normal thyroid and cortisol: symptomatic hypotonic hyponatremia from SIADH, likely paraneoplastic.
im-024.plan: Cautious 3% hypertonic saline to raise sodium about 4-6 mEq/L over the first hours, checking sodium every 2-4 hours. Limit correction to about 6-8 mEq/L in 24 hours and re-lower with free water or desmopressin if exceeded. Then fluid restriction and treatment of the underlying tumor, with salt tablets or a vasopressin antagonist if restriction is inadequate.

im-019.assessment: 36-year-old man found down after at least 12 hours of immobilization, with muscle pain and tea-colored urine. CK 38,000 U/L, creatinine 2.6 mg/dL from a baseline near 0.9, potassium 6.1 with peaked T waves, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and a dipstick positive for blood without red cells: rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury.
im-019.plan: Early aggressive IV isotonic fluids titrated to urine output; no early diuretics. IV calcium gluconate now for the ECG changes, then insulin with glucose and other measures to shift and remove potassium. Monitor potassium, CK, kidney function, urine output, and limb compartments; dialysis for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, or volume overload.

pm-018.assessment: 50-year-old man with diabetes and heavy alcohol use, febrile on day 6 of antibiotics for pneumonia, with a right pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yields frank pus (pH 6.9, glucose 28 mg/dL, LDH 2,400 IU/L, mixed organisms), and CT shows a loculated collection with the split-pleura sign: empyema.
pm-018.plan: Continue IV antibiotics with anaerobic coverage and place a chest tube for source control, adding intrapleural tPA and DNase when loculations limit drainage. If sepsis and loculated collections persist with trapped lung, refer for VATS debridement and decortication.

pm-028.assessment: 78-year-old woman 5 days after an ischemic stroke with dysphagia, now with fever, productive cough, hypoxemia, leukocytosis, a failed swallow screen, and right lower-lobe consolidation: aspiration pneumonia from post-stroke dysphagia.
pm-028.plan: Nothing by mouth pending a formal swallow evaluation, supplemental oxygen, and empiric antibiotics such as ampicillin-sulbactam chosen by severity and local resistance; routine added anaerobic coverage is not needed. Then speech-language assessment, texture and liquid modification, upright positioning, and oral care to prevent recurrence.

pm-023.assessment: Asymptomatic 28-year-old nurse with a positive IGRA on pre-employment screening, a normal examination, a clear chest radiograph, negative HIV testing, normal transaminases, and a negative pregnancy test: latent tuberculosis infection.
pm-023.plan: Active disease is excluded by symptom review and chest radiograph. Offer a short rifamycin-based regimen such as 12 weeks of once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine, with pyridoxine. Counsel about hepatitis symptoms, alcohol, harmless orange discoloration of body fluids from rifapentine, and drug interactions.

gi-004.assessment: 48-year-old woman with 8 hours of constant right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal, fever, a positive Murphy sign, and leukocytosis. Ultrasound shows gallstones, a 5 mm gallbladder wall, pericholecystic fluid, and a normal-caliber common bile duct with normal bilirubin and liver enzymes: acute calculous cholecystitis.
gi-004.plan: Admit; IV fluids, analgesia, and IV antibiotics, with early laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission. No ERCP, because there is no evidence of a common duct stone. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is reserved for patients unfit for surgery.

gi-014.assessment: 64-year-old man in the ICU with sudden massive painless hematemesis and hemorrhagic shock (BP 84/52 mmHg, HR 126); hemoglobin 7.1 g/dL from 12.8, with normal INR and liver tests. Endoscopy shows a 5 mm mucosal defect on the lesser curve with a protruding, spurting artery and no ulcer: Dieulafoy lesion.
gi-014.plan: Resuscitate first: two large-bore IVs, crystalloid and blood products, crossmatch, and massive-transfusion readiness; protect the airway before endoscopy. IV PPI and urgent EGD with mechanical hemostasis (clip or band), with or without thermal therapy, and tattoo the site. For rebleeding, repeat endoscopy, then angiographic embolization, with surgery last.

gi-065.assessment: 38-year-old man with a 3 cm fluctuant perianal abscess and fever, on a background of months of bloody diarrhea, weight loss, oral ulcers, and arthralgias. After drainage a fistulous opening persists; hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL with microcytosis and raised CRP and ESR: perianal abscess with fistula as the presentation of Crohn disease.
gi-065.plan: Incision and drainage now. Then ileocolonoscopy with biopsies to confirm Crohn disease and pelvic MRI to map the fistula. For a complex fistula in active disease: seton placement for drainage with anti-TNF therapy such as infliximab, with antibiotics as a bridge; avoid wide fistulotomy.

inf-048.assessment: 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes, two days of leg pain out of proportion after a puncture wound, hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, skin anesthesia, and septic shock. WBC 24.5, sodium 128, creatinine 2.1, lactate 4.8, and fascial gas on plain film (LRINEC 9): necrotizing fasciitis.
inf-048.plan: Fluid resuscitation and vasopressors as needed, broad empiric antibiotics (vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin), and immediate operative exploration and debridement without waiting for further imaging. Planned re-exploration every 24-48 hours until no necrosis remains; continue antibiotics and narrow to cultures.

inf-093.assessment: 45-year-old landscaper in North Carolina with five days of fever and severe headache, a rash that began on the wrists and ankles and involves the palms and soles, and a tick bite a week ago. Sodium 129, platelets 88, AST 96, creatinine 1.6, and mild lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis: Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
inf-093.plan: Start doxycycline immediately on clinical suspicion and send serology, which is usually negative in the first week. Admit for fluids and monitoring. Doxycycline is first-line at any age; sulfonamides are contraindicated. Continue for at least 3 days after the fever resolves.

inf-032.assessment: 32-year-old woman with three days of dysuria followed by fever, rigors, right flank pain, and vomiting, with marked costovertebral angle tenderness. WBC 16.8, pyuria with white cell casts, positive nitrites, and gram-negative rods on urine stain; pregnancy test negative: acute pyelonephritis.
inf-032.plan: Urine and blood cultures before antibiotics. Admit because she cannot keep down fluids or tablets; IV fluids and IV ceftriaxone (or a fluoroquinolone), narrowed to culture results, then an oral agent to complete the course. Image the kidneys if she is not improving after 48-72 hours.

fm-095.assessment: 59-year-old woman with a week of brief vertigo triggered by head position, a normal neurologic examination at rest, and a right Dix-Hallpike test producing latent, fatigable, upbeating-torsional nystagmus with reproduction of her vertigo: right posterior-canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
fm-095.plan: Epley canalith repositioning maneuver in clinic, repeated if needed. Avoid long-term vestibular suppressants. No imaging, because the history and Dix-Hallpike are typical and there are no central signs. Advise return for vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, gait ataxia, or any new neurologic symptom.

fm-076.assessment: 18-year-old woman with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, and a rash after amoxicillin. Monospot positive, lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, mildly elevated transaminases, and a negative rapid strep test: infectious mononucleosis from Epstein-Barr virus.
fm-076.plan: Supportive care: rest, fluids, and analgesics; stop the amoxicillin. No contact sports or heavy lifting for at least 3-4 weeks, and longer if the spleen remains enlarged. Explain that the aminopenicillin rash is usually not a true allergy; consider allergy evaluation later. Return for severe abdominal pain, difficulty swallowing or breathing, or jaundice.

fm-023.assessment: 34-year-old woman with four months of fatigue, pica, pallor, and koilonychia and two years of heavy menstrual bleeding. Hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, MCV 71 fL, RDW 17%, ferritin 6 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation 8%: iron deficiency anemia from menorrhagia.
fm-023.plan: Oral iron such as ferrous sulfate, taken with vitamin C and away from calcium, antacids, and tea. Evaluate and treat the heavy menstrual bleeding. Recheck hemoglobin in 2-4 weeks, and continue iron for 3-6 months after it normalizes to replete stores. IV iron if oral iron fails or is not tolerated.

nph-067.assessment: 76-year-old man with two years of obstructive urinary symptoms and 18 hours of acute retention after starting a pseudoephedrine-diphenhydramine cold remedy. Palpable bladder; 1,400 mL drained on catheterization; creatinine 2.6 mg/dL from 1.0 with bilateral hydronephrosis: acute urinary retention with post-renal AKI from benign prostatic hyperplasia.
nph-067.plan: Immediate urethral catheterization. Stop the cold remedy. Monitor urine output, electrolytes, and creatinine for post-obstructive diuresis and recovery. Start an alpha-blocker such as tamsulosin before a voiding trial; avoid anticholinergics. Urology follow-up.

nph-076.assessment: 36-year-old man found confused beside an empty antifreeze container, with Kussmaul breathing. pH 7.18, bicarbonate 8, anion gap 30, osmolar gap 35, undetectable ethanol, rising creatinine, hypocalcemia, and calcium oxalate crystalluria: ethylene glycol poisoning.
nph-076.plan: Fomepizole immediately to block alcohol dehydrogenase, IV fluids, and urgent hemodialysis for severe acidosis and kidney injury, with bicarbonate for the acidosis. Replace calcium only for symptomatic hypocalcemia. Give thiamine and pyridoxine as cofactors. Psychiatric evaluation and safety planning once he is medically stable.

nph-063.assessment: 66-year-old woman with heavy smoking, weight loss, and a 5 cm right hilar mass, with two weeks of confusion, polyuria, and constipation. Corrected calcium 14.6 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 from 0.9, PTH suppressed below 5 pg/mL, and PTHrP markedly elevated: humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy with AKI.
nph-063.plan: Aggressive isotonic saline; stop hydrochlorothiazide and the calcium-vitamin D supplement. Then an IV bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid (dose adjusted for kidney function), with calcitonin for faster short-term effect if needed; denosumab is an alternative. Loop diuretics only for volume overload after rehydration. Tissue diagnosis and oncology referral.

endo-046.assessment: 50-year-old man with a thunderclap headache, right third nerve palsy, reduced right visual acuity, and hypotension. Sodium 130, glucose 64, pre-treatment cortisol 1.8 µg/dL; MRI shows hemorrhage into a pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm and extending toward the right cavernous sinus: pituitary apoplexy with acute secondary adrenal insufficiency.
endo-046.plan: Empiric stress-dose IV hydrocortisone immediately after drawing cortisol, with IV fluids and glucose. Urgent neurosurgical consultation for transsphenoidal decompression because vision and eye movements are deteriorating. Assess the remaining pituitary axes; lifelong endocrine follow-up with replacement of deficient hormones.

endo-042.assessment: 30-year-old man four days after a basilar skull fracture with more than 6 L/day of dilute urine and intense thirst. Sodium 152, serum osmolality 312, urine osmolality 110, normal glucose, and loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot; urine osmolality rises to 480 after desmopressin: post-traumatic central diabetes insipidus.
endo-042.plan: Desmopressin on a schedule, free access to water, and gradual correction of the free-water deficit, with serum sodium and urine output monitored closely. Reassess regularly, because post-traumatic central DI may be transient or follow a triphasic course. Evaluate the anterior pituitary axes.

endo-001.assessment: 54-year-old man with obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a family history of diabetes, with three months of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss and acanthosis nigricans. HbA1c 9.2%, fasting glucose 214 mg/dL, glucosuria without ketones, and normal kidney function: new type 2 diabetes mellitus.
endo-001.plan: Lifestyle counseling and metformin, titrated as tolerated. Dilated retinal examination and comprehensive foot examination now, with annual urine albumin and kidney function. Address blood pressure and LDL cholesterol, and review the choice of additional agents by cardiovascular and kidney risk. Recheck HbA1c in three months.

ho-064.assessment: 52-year-old woman 10 days after dose-dense chemotherapy for breast cancer with a temperature of 38.7 °C, tachycardia, and no localizing source. WBC 0.8, absolute neutrophil count 180 cells/µL, lactate 1.8, clear chest radiograph: febrile neutropenia.
ho-064.plan: Blood cultures from a peripheral vein and the port, then an empiric antipseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam) within one hour of arrival. Add vancomycin only for specific indications. Admit for IV antibiotics and monitoring given profound neutropenia with an expected prolonged nadir.

ho-016.assessment: 55-year-old man who develops rigors, flank pain, hypotension, fever, and hemoglobinuria 10 minutes into a red cell transfusion. Positive direct antiglobulin test, pink plasma, undetectable haptoglobin, rising creatinine, falling fibrinogen; clerical check shows a group A unit given to a group O patient: acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility.
ho-016.plan: Stop the transfusion at once, keep the line open with saline through new tubing, and notify the blood bank, returning the unit and tubing with fresh samples. Aggressive IV fluids to support blood pressure and maintain brisk urine output; monitor for kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and DIC. Report the event; prevention is bedside identity checking before every transfusion.

ho-048.assessment: 39-year-old woman with days of mucocutaneous and vaginal bleeding, pancytopenia (platelets 18), PT 22 s, aPTT 48 s, fibrinogen 90 mg/dL, and markedly elevated D-dimer. Smear shows hypergranular promyelocytes with bundled Auer rods; PML-RARA positive: acute promyelocytic leukemia with DIC.
ho-048.plan: Start all-trans retinoic acid immediately on morphologic suspicion, with aggressive product support (platelets, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen, plasma) to set targets. Add arsenic trioxide or chemotherapy by risk group. Watch for differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnea, hypoxia, infiltrates, weight gain) and treat at once with dexamethasone.

rh-008.assessment: 60-year-old man with diabetes and a recent intra-articular steroid injection, with two days of a hot, swollen right knee, fever, and inability to bear weight. Synovial WBC 78,000/µL with 90% neutrophils, gram-positive cocci in clusters, and no crystals: septic arthritis, most likely Staphylococcus aureus.
rh-008.plan: Arthrocentesis and blood cultures, then IV antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA, narrowed to cultures. Urgent joint drainage by arthroscopic or open washout or serial aspiration, with orthopedic consultation. No intra-articular steroids. Optimize glycemic control.

rh-003.assessment: 52-year-old man on hydrochlorothiazide with abrupt nocturnal pain, swelling, and erythema of the right first MTP joint after a weekend of meat and beer, and two prior milder attacks. Synovial fluid shows 28,000 WBC/µL with needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals and a negative Gram stain: acute gout.
rh-003.plan: Anti-inflammatory treatment for the flare: an NSAID, colchicine, or a short corticosteroid course, chosen by comorbidity. Do not start high-dose allopurinol alone during the flare. Afterward: replace hydrochlorothiazide, counsel on alcohol, red meat, and fructose, and offer urate-lowering therapy titrated to a serum urate below 6 mg/dL with flare prophylaxis.

rh-035.assessment: 3-year-old boy with five days of high fever, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, fissured lips and strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, extremity changes with periungual desquamation, and a 1.8 cm cervical node. Platelets 620, ESR 78, CRP 12.4, sterile pyuria, and coronary artery dilation on echocardiography: Kawasaki disease.
rh-035.plan: High-dose IVIG (2 g/kg) with aspirin, given promptly and within 10 days of fever onset. Serial echocardiography at diagnosis, 1-2 weeks, and 4-6 weeks, with low-dose aspirin continued and cardiology follow-up; escalate therapy for persistent fever after IVIG.

orth-034.assessment: 27-year-old man with a closed, completely displaced mid-shaft tibial fracture and fibular fracture after a motorcycle crash, with pain out of proportion unrelieved by opioids, tense compartments, severe pain on passive toe stretch, and early first web space numbness: acute compartment syndrome of the leg.
orth-034.plan: Keep the leg at heart level, remove any constricting dressing, and call orthopedics at once. Compartment pressures support the diagnosis but must not delay emergent four-compartment fasciotomy. Stabilize the fracture, with intramedullary nailing as definitive fixation. Monitor for rhabdomyolysis.

orth-045.assessment: 13-year-old boy with obesity and three weeks of left groin and knee pain with a limp, limited internal rotation of the left hip, and obligate external rotation on flexion. Radiographs show posteroinferior displacement of the left femoral epiphysis with a positive Klein line: slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
orth-045.plan: Strict non-weight-bearing immediately and urgent orthopedic consultation for in situ screw fixation. No forceful reduction. Follow the contralateral hip, and consider endocrine evaluation given his age and stature. Counsel about avascular necrosis and chondrolysis.

orth-009.assessment: 68-year-old right-handed woman with osteoporosis who fell on an outstretched hand, with a dinner-fork deformity and intact neurovascular status. Radiographs show an extra-articular distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation, displacement, and shortening and an ulnar styloid avulsion: Colles fracture, a fragility fracture.
orth-009.plan: Analgesia, closed reduction under a hematoma block or sedation, and a well-molded below-elbow splint, with post-reduction radiographs and repeat neurovascular checks. Orthopedic follow-up within a week to confirm alignment; surgery if the reduction is lost. Review osteoporosis treatment, adherence, and fall risk.

ur-001.assessment: 24-year-old nonpregnant woman with two days of dysuria, frequency, and urgency, no fever or flank pain, mild suprapubic tenderness, and a urinalysis positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites with pyuria: acute uncomplicated cystitis. Sulfa allergy.
ur-001.plan: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is avoided because of her sulfa allergy, and fluoroquinolones are reserved. No culture is required for a first uncomplicated episode. Counsel on hydration and on the diaphragm-spermicide method as a risk factor; return for fever, flank pain, or persistent symptoms.

ur-059.assessment: 23-year-old man with severe right scrotal pain and a tense, ecchymotic hemiscrotum two hours after a kick. Doppler ultrasound shows disruption of the tunica albuginea with extruded seminiferous tubules, a large hematocele, and reduced flow in part of the testis: testicular rupture.
ur-059.plan: Analgesia, antiemetic, nothing by mouth, and emergent urologic exploration with evacuation of the hematocele, debridement of nonviable tubules, and repair of the tunica albuginea. Early surgery gives the best chance of salvage and of preserved hormonal and reproductive function.

ur-049.assessment: 61-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c 12.0%) and septic shock after three days of fever and right flank pain unresponsive to oral antibiotics. WBC 21.8, glucose 468, lactate 4.6, creatinine 3.2, platelets 96; CT shows gas within the right renal parenchyma extending into the collecting system: emphysematous pyelonephritis.
ur-049.plan: Resuscitation with IV fluids and vasopressors, broad IV antibiotics, an insulin infusion, and percutaneous drainage of the kidney. Repeat imaging if she does not improve; refractory shock with extensive parenchymal destruction requires emergency nephrectomy.

ent-042.assessment: 70-year-old man on apixaban with poorly controlled hypertension and 75 minutes of brisk epistaxis. No anterior source is seen, blood streams down the posterior pharynx, and bleeding continues despite bilateral anterior packing; hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL: posterior epistaxis.
ent-042.plan: IV access, CBC, type and screen, and continuous monitoring. Posterior nasal pack (balloon catheter) with anterior packing, then admission with continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring. Hold apixaban and discuss with the prescriber; treat blood pressure once volume status is addressed. If packing fails, endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolization.

ent-011.assessment: 18-month-old girl with three hours of drooling and refusal to swallow after access to loose button batteries. Radiographs show a 20 mm disc in the proximal esophagus with a double-ring sign on the AP view and a step-off on the lateral view: esophageal button battery.
ent-011.plan: Nothing else by mouth except honey 10 mL every 10 minutes (up to 6 doses) while the team is mobilized, without delaying removal. Emergent endoscopic removal in the operating room, ideally within 2 hours, with inspection of the mucosa. Admit, and watch for delayed complications over the following weeks: perforation, tracheoesophageal fistula, stricture, and aortoesophageal fistula.

ent-069.assessment: 38-year-old teacher and choir leader, a nonsmoker, with months of use-related hoarseness and vocal fatigue. Laryngoscopy shows symmetric bilateral thickenings at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of fully mobile vocal folds, with an hourglass glottic gap: vocal fold nodules.
ent-069.plan: Voice therapy with a speech-language pathologist and vocal hygiene: hydration, amplification in the classroom, avoiding shouting and throat clearing, and rest breaks. Treat reflux if it contributes. Surgery is reserved for nodules that persist after therapy.

vn-001.assessment: 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, off apixaban for three months, last known well at 07:40, with global aphasia, right face, arm and leg weakness, left gaze deviation, and NIHSS 14. CT shows no hemorrhage and a hyperdense left MCA sign; glucose 112, INR 1.0: acute left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke, likely cardioembolic, within the thrombolysis window.
vn-001.plan: Lower blood pressure to below 185/110 mmHg, then give IV alteplase or tenecteplase; obtain vessel imaging to assess for thrombectomy without delaying the lytic. Admit to a stroke unit or ICU with neurologic checks and blood pressure below 180/105 for 24 hours; no antithrombotics until a 24-hour CT excludes hemorrhage.

vn-072.assessment: 63-year-old woman with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes who took mealtime insulin and skipped lunch, with 30 minutes of confusion, diaphoresis, tremor, and left face and arm weakness. Fingerstick glucose 38 mg/dL; CT normal. Complete resolution ten minutes after IV dextrose: hypoglycemia presenting as a stroke mimic.
vn-072.plan: 25 g of IV dextrose, then recheck glucose and the neurologic exam. Observe for several hours because long-acting insulin is still active, give a carbohydrate meal, and review insulin dosing against her new diet and exercise, with diabetes education before discharge. No thrombolysis or antithrombotics.

vn-018.assessment: 64-year-old smoker with untreated hypertension and four stereotyped, increasingly frequent episodes of right arm weakness and aphasia in 24 hours, a left carotid bruit, and a normal exam between spells. MRI shows a punctate left frontal cortical infarct, and CTA shows an 85% ulcerated left internal carotid stenosis: crescendo TIA from artery-to-artery embolism.
vn-018.plan: Urgent admission. Dual antiplatelet therapy and a high-intensity statin; avoid aggressive blood pressure lowering while the stenosis limits flow. Early carotid revascularization, ideally within about two weeks of symptom onset. Smoking cessation and long-term risk factor control.

no-001.assessment: 62-year-old man with six weeks of morning-predominant headaches with vomiting and two weeks of progressive right-hand weakness. MRI shows a 4.2 cm thick-walled, ring-enhancing left frontal mass with central necrosis crossing the corpus callosum, extensive vasogenic edema, and 8 mm of midline shift: probable glioblastoma.
no-001.plan: Dexamethasone for vasogenic edema and urgent neurosurgical consultation. Maximal safe resection, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is unsafe, with histopathology and molecular analysis (IDH status, MGMT promoter methylation). No lumbar puncture. Radiotherapy with temozolomide follows a tissue diagnosis.

no-042.assessment: 67-year-old man with prostate cancer and a rising PSA, two weeks of nocturnal thoracic back pain, two days of bilateral leg weakness with a T10 sensory level, hyperreflexia, and urinary retention. MRI shows a T9–T10 epidural mass with vertebral marrow replacement compressing the cord: metastatic epidural spinal cord compression.
no-042.plan: Dexamethasone immediately on suspicion, bladder catheter, and emergent whole-spine MRI. For a fit patient with a single compressive level, surgical decompression and stabilization followed by postoperative radiotherapy. Treat hypercalcemia. Neurologic status when treatment starts is the main determinant of walking afterward.

no-032.assessment: 48-year-old man with thunderclap headache, a right third-nerve palsy, bitemporal field loss, and hypotension, after a year of fatigue, low libido, and cold intolerance. Cortisol 2 µg/dL, free T4 0.5 ng/dL, sodium 129, glucose 58; MRI shows hemorrhage into a pituitary macroadenoma displacing the optic chiasm: pituitary apoplexy with acute hypopituitarism.
no-032.plan: IV fluids and stress-dose IV hydrocortisone immediately, without waiting for results. Urgent neurosurgical evaluation for transsphenoidal decompression given progressive visual loss and ophthalmoplegia. Replace glucocorticoid before or with thyroid hormone; fludrocortisone is not needed in secondary adrenal insufficiency.

pn-014.assessment: 3-year-old boy with known epilepsy, missed levetiracetam doses, and a febrile viral illness, in a generalized convulsion for over 20 minutes despite intramuscular midazolam. Glucose and electrolytes normal, levetiracetam level subtherapeutic, head CT normal: convulsive status epilepticus precipitated by a subtherapeutic drug level and fever.
pn-014.plan: Airway, oxygen, and IV access; a second benzodiazepine dose (IV lorazepam), then a second-line IV load of levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate. Admit for monitoring, resume levetiracetam (IV while vomiting), treat the febrile illness, and give the family a rescue-medication plan and adherence counseling.

pn-017.assessment: 11-month-old under-immunized boy with one day of high fever, lethargy, vomiting, a tense fontanelle, nuchal rigidity, paradoxical irritability, and poor perfusion. CSF shows 3,200 white cells (90% neutrophils), glucose 22 mg/dL, protein 180 mg/dL, and gram-positive diplococci: bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae.
pn-017.plan: Fluid resuscitation, blood cultures, and immediate empiric IV antibiotics (a third-generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin) without waiting for lumbar puncture or imaging. Consider adjunctive dexamethasone with or just before the first antibiotic dose. Admit to intensive care; formal audiology before or soon after discharge, and catch-up immunizations.

pn-016.assessment: 16-year-old boy with six months of severe daytime sleepiness despite adequate sleep, laughter-triggered cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations. MSLT mean sleep latency 4 minutes with three sleep-onset REM periods; CSF hypocretin-1 low: narcolepsy type 1.
pn-016.plan: Scheduled short naps and regular sleep hours, with a wake-promoting agent such as modafinil or a stimulant for sleepiness; add treatment for cataplexy if it remains troublesome. No driving until sleepiness is controlled. School accommodations and follow-up in sleep clinic.

dm-061.assessment: 45-year-old man with stage 3 chronic kidney disease, six weeks into allopurinol 300 mg daily, with a morbilliform eruption over 60% of the body surface, facial edema, fever, and lymphadenopathy. Eosinophils 2.4 ×10³/µL with atypical lymphocytes, AST 188, ALT 224, creatinine 1.9 (baseline 1.6): DRESS syndrome due to allopurinol.
dm-061.plan: Stop allopurinol immediately and record it as an allergy. Start systemic corticosteroids with a slow taper given hepatic and renal involvement; monitor liver and kidney function and blood counts. Do not substitute another urate-lowering drug during the reaction. Monitor thyroid function for several months for autoimmune sequelae.

dm-074.assessment: 63-year-old man with long-standing plaque psoriasis and two weeks of erythema and scale over 90% of the body surface after abrupt withdrawal of oral prednisone. Hypothermic (35.4 °C), tachycardic, and hypotensive, with sodium 132, potassium 3.4, albumin 2.6, creatinine 1.4, and a hyperdynamic heart on echo: erythrodermic psoriasis.
dm-074.plan: Admit. Warm environment, IV fluids with electrolyte repletion, nutritional support, bland emollients with wet wraps, and cardiac monitoring. Start psoriasis-directed systemic therapy such as cyclosporine or a biologic; avoid systemic corticosteroids. Watch for secondary infection and high-output heart failure.

dm-025.assessment: 21-year-old athlete in a warm, humid climate with recurrent, finely scaly hypopigmented macules on the upper trunk that do not tan. KOH preparation shows short hyphae with clusters of yeast, and Wood’s lamp shows pale yellow-green fluorescence: tinea (pityriasis) versicolor due to Malassezia.
dm-025.plan: Topical antifungal such as selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo applied to the trunk, or zinc pyrithione. Counsel that color returns over weeks to months after the yeast is cleared, that recurrence is common, and that periodic preventive washes can help. Oral terbinafine is not effective.

oph-027.assessment: 23-year-old soft contact lens wearer who sleeps and swims in her lenses, with two days of a rapidly worsening painful red right eye, acuity 20/100, a 3 mm central corneal ulcer with stromal infiltrate and melting edges, and a hypopyon. Scrapings grow Pseudomonas aeruginosa: contact-lens-related bacterial keratitis.
oph-027.plan: Corneal scrapings for Gram stain and culture, then intensive topical antibiotics at once: an hourly fluoroquinolone around the clock or fortified tobramycin with a cephalosporin, with daily review. No patching and no initial corticosteroid. No lens wear until healed; counsel on lens hygiene.

oph-032.assessment: 34-year-old man with three days of aching left eye pain, photophobia, ciliary flush, and a miotic pupil, plus two prior episodes and months of inflammatory back pain. Slit lamp shows 3+ cells and 2+ flare, keratic precipitates, and early posterior synechiae with normal pressure: acute anterior uveitis, likely HLA-B27-associated.
oph-032.plan: Topical corticosteroid (prednisolone acetate) with a cycloplegic to relieve ciliary spasm and prevent posterior synechiae; review within days and taper slowly. Test for HLA-B27 and refer to rheumatology for suspected ankylosing spondylitis.

oph-037.assessment: 31-year-old woman with obesity, recent weight gain, and isotretinoin use, with six weeks of positional headaches, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, bilateral papilledema, and a left sixth-nerve palsy. MRI and MR venography show no mass or thrombosis; opening pressure 32 cm H2O with normal CSF: idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
oph-037.plan: Acetazolamide and weight-loss support; stop isotretinoin. Serial visual fields and acuity with ophthalmology. Escalate to surgery (optic nerve sheath fenestration or shunting) if vision is threatened despite medical therapy.

pmr-099.assessment: 48-year-old woman with three months of symmetric proximal weakness, no rash, no sensory loss, and no fatigability. Creatine kinase 4,200 U/L, irritable myopathy on EMG, and symmetric proximal muscle edema on MRI: polymyositis.
pmr-099.plan: High-dose corticosteroids with an early steroid-sparing agent such as methotrexate or azathioprine. Supervised, progressive exercise beginning with range of motion and submaximal strengthening. Age-appropriate cancer screening, and monitoring for dysphagia and lung involvement.

pmr-095.assessment: 13-year-old girl, six months after menarche, with a painless right thoracic curve found on screening and a normal neurologic examination. Standing radiographs show a Cobb angle of 28° with Risser grade 1: adolescent idiopathic scoliosis with substantial growth remaining and a meaningful risk of progression.
pmr-095.plan: Thoracolumbosacral brace worn as many hours a day as prescribed, with repeat radiographs every four to six months until skeletal maturity. Continue sports. Surgery is considered if the curve passes about 45 to 50 degrees.

pmr-073.assessment: 31-year-old man 40 days after severe traumatic brain injury with a week of progressive loss of right hip motion and a deep, firm, warm periarticular mass. Alkaline phosphatase 412 U/L, a three-phase bone scan positive in all phases, faint immature ossification on radiograph, and no DVT on duplex: heterotopic ossification of the right hip.
pmr-073.plan: Bisphosphonate (etidronate) or an NSAID to limit progression, with gentle, pain-limited range-of-motion exercises and positioning. No forceful manipulation. Consider surgical resection only after the bone has matured and activity has quieted, if function remains limited.

interview.prompt: Ask about the fainting episodes and recovery
interview.finding: He had three abrupt syncopal episodes in two days without warning, followed by quick recovery and no postictal confusion, tongue injury, or head trauma.

interview.prompt: Ask about symptoms between episodes
interview.finding: Between events he feels fatigued, dizzy, and short of breath with minimal exertion. He has noticed a very slow pulse at home.

interview.prompt: Review cardiac history and medications
interview.finding: History includes prior anterior MI, hypertension, and diabetes. Medications include metoprolol 50 mg daily; there were no recent medication changes or illnesses.

exam.prompt: Assess mental status and perfusion
exam.finding: He is alert but pale and fatigued, mildly hypotensive and bradycardic, with mildly delayed capillary refill.

exam.prompt: Examine the heart and neck veins
exam.finding: The rhythm is slow and regular with varying S1 intensity and occasional cannon A waves. There is no murmur or gallop.

exam.prompt: Perform a focused neurologic and pulmonary exam
exam.finding: The neurologic exam is nonfocal, lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema.

interview.prompt: Characterize the palpitations
interview.finding: The fast, regular pounding began abruptly 40 minutes ago at rest. Several similar episodes over the past year ended spontaneously within minutes.

interview.prompt: Ask about instability or cardiopulmonary symptoms
interview.finding: She has mild lightheadedness and throat fluttering but denies chest pain, syncope, or significant dyspnea.

interview.prompt: Ask about triggers and arrhythmia risks
interview.finding: She drinks two to three coffees daily and had extra caffeine today. She has no cardiac history, recent illness, thyroid symptoms, recreational stimulant or sympathomimetic drug use, or family history of sudden death.

exam.prompt: Assess hemodynamic stability and perfusion
exam.finding: She is alert, mildly anxious, normally mentating, and well perfused without respiratory distress.

exam.prompt: Auscultate the heart and check the pulse
exam.finding: There is a rapid, regular tachycardia with normal heart sounds, no murmur, and rapid regular peripheral pulses of good volume.

exam.prompt: Look for heart-failure or thyroid findings
exam.finding: Lungs are clear, there is no JVD or edema, and the neck has no thyromegaly.

interview.prompt: Ask about the injury and symptom timeline
interview.finding: He struck his head on tile 10 days ago. After only a brief initial headache, he developed three days of worsening headache, drowsiness, confusion, gait difficulty, and vomiting.

interview.prompt: Review bleeding risk and medications
interview.finding: He has atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin and believes his recent INR was a little high. He also drinks alcohol regularly.

interview.prompt: Ask about new focal or infectious symptoms
interview.finding: His wife reports new word-finding difficulty and right-hand clumsiness. He has had no fever, neck stiffness, or seizures.

exam.prompt: Assess consciousness and orientation
exam.finding: He is drowsy but arousable and oriented to person and place, but not date.

exam.prompt: Perform a focused neurologic exam
exam.finding: There is right pronator drift, subtle right-hand clumsiness, mild word-finding hesitancy, and a wide-based unsteady gait.

exam.prompt: Look for trauma and raised-pressure clues
exam.finding: There is left parietal scalp tenderness without laceration. Pupils are equal and reactive, and no papilledema or neck rigidity is seen.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain and skin progression
interview.finding: Perineal and scrotal pain, swelling, and discoloration worsened rapidly over 24 hours, with pain far out of proportion and a crackling sensation.

interview.prompt: Ask about infection source and risk factors
interview.finding: He has poorly controlled diabetes, obesity, tobacco use, and a perianal abscess drained two weeks ago. He now reports foul-smelling discharge.

interview.prompt: Ask about systemic symptoms
interview.finding: He has fever, chills, malaise, nausea, poor intake, and orthostatic lightheadedness.

exam.prompt: Inspect the perineum and scrotum
exam.finding: Dusky erythematous-to-violaceous skin, tense edema, areas of necrosis, and foul serosanguinous discharge are present.

exam.prompt: Palpate for extent, tenderness, and crepitus
exam.finding: Tenderness extends beyond the erythema with palpable crepitus, patchy anesthesia, and pain out of proportion extending toward the lower abdominal wall.

exam.prompt: Assess systemic toxicity and perfusion
exam.finding: He is toxic, diaphoretic, tachycardic, and hypotensive with delayed capillary refill.

interview.prompt: Ask about pregnancy possibility and bleeding
interview.finding: Her last menstrual period was about seven weeks ago. She has had two days of light vaginal spotting and uses condoms inconsistently.

interview.prompt: Characterize the pain and collapse
interview.finding: Sudden severe left lower-quadrant pain became diffuse, followed by near-syncope, increasing weakness, feeling cold, and new right shoulder discomfort.

interview.prompt: Ask about ectopic-pregnancy risks
interview.finding: She has a prior medically managed ectopic pregnancy and a history of chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease.

exam.prompt: Assess appearance, mentation, and perfusion
exam.finding: She is pale, diaphoretic, cool, clammy, and slow to respond, with delayed capillary refill.

exam.prompt: Examine the abdomen
exam.finding: The abdomen is diffusely tender, worst in the left lower quadrant, with guarding, rebound, and mild distension.

exam.prompt: Perform a focused pelvic examination
exam.finding: There is scant dark blood at the cervical os, marked cervical-motion tenderness, and severe left adnexal tenderness with fullness.

interview.prompt: Characterize the chest discomfort
interview.finding: He describes a tight substernal band radiating to the left shoulder, lasting three to five minutes and resolving completely with rest.

interview.prompt: Ask about pattern and unstable features
interview.finding: Symptoms occur reliably after two uphill blocks or two flights of stairs and have not changed for three months. There is no rest or nocturnal pain.

interview.prompt: Review vascular risks and medications
interview.finding: He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, a 30 pack-year smoking history, and paternal MI at 58. He often misses atorvastatin doses.

exam.prompt: Examine the heart, lungs, and neck veins
exam.finding: Heart sounds and rhythm are normal without murmur, rub, or gallop; lungs are clear and JVP is not elevated.

exam.prompt: Assess pulses, bruits, and volume status
exam.finding: Pulses are symmetric, no carotid or femoral bruits are heard, and there is no edema or abdominal pulsatile mass.

exam.prompt: Try to reproduce the pain mechanically
exam.finding: The chest wall is nontender, and pain is not reproduced by palpation, arm movement, or deep inspiration.

interview.prompt: Ask about onset and concerning symptoms
