exam.finding: No discrete anterior septal bleeding point, mass or telangiectasia. Blood wells up from deep within the nasal cavity.

exam.prompt: Inspect the oropharynx
exam.finding: A steady stream of fresh blood runs down the posterior pharyngeal wall.

exam.prompt: Assess general appearance, heart and lungs
exam.finding: Anxious and pale, with blood-stained clothing. Irregularly irregular rhythm; lungs clear. No facial deformity or signs of trauma.

interview.prompt: Establish what happened and when
interview.finding: Found crying and drooling about three hours ago after playing unsupervised near a table with a TV remote and loose hearing-aid and watch batteries. The battery compartment of a small remote was open and empty. Ingestion window estimated at under four hours.

interview.prompt: Ask about swallowing, breathing and vomiting
interview.finding: Refuses her bottle and solids, gags when she tries to swallow and points to her chest. No vomiting, fever or respiratory distress.

interview.prompt: Review past history
interview.finding: Previously healthy, developing normally, immunizations up to date, no medications and no known allergies. No prior choking episodes.

exam.prompt: Observe swallowing and general appearance
exam.finding: Alert, fussy and consolable. Drooling pooled saliva and gagging with attempts to swallow. Well perfused, with no cyanosis.

exam.prompt: Assess the airway and lungs
exam.finding: No stridor, retractions or wheeze. Air entry is symmetric, and the lungs are clear.

exam.prompt: Inspect the mouth, and palpate the neck and abdomen
exam.finding: No visible foreign body, burns or erythema in the oropharynx. No neck swelling, crepitus or tenderness. Abdomen soft and non-tender.

interview.prompt: Characterize the voice change
interview.finding: Several months of progressive hoarseness and vocal fatigue. Her voice gives out by the end of a teaching day, is worse with heavy use and improves after weekends. Symptoms have plateaued.

interview.prompt: Ask about voice use
interview.finding: Elementary school teacher and part-time choir leader who often raises her voice over a noisy classroom, rarely uses amplification and drinks little water during the day.

interview.prompt: Screen for red flags and contributing factors
interview.finding: No pain, dysphagia, hemoptysis, weight loss or neck mass. Never smoked, and rarely drinks alcohol. Mild intermittent heartburn.

exam.prompt: Listen to the voice
exam.finding: Breathy, slightly rough voice with reduced projection and visible strain on sustained phonation. No stridor.

exam.prompt: Palpate the neck
exam.finding: Supple, with no masses or lymphadenopathy, a normal thyroid and no laryngeal tenderness.

exam.prompt: Examine the mouth, throat and cranial nerves
exam.finding: No oral or oropharyngeal lesions; mild posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning. Normal gag and palatal elevation.

interview.prompt: Establish the time last known well
interview.finding: Seen normal at 07:40 pouring his coffee and found slumped at the table at 08:00 with a facial droop and unable to answer. No headache, seizure activity or loss of consciousness.

interview.prompt: Review history and anticoagulant use
interview.finding: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia and atrial fibrillation. Prescribed apixaban but stopped it three months ago because of cost. Takes amlodipine and atorvastatin.

interview.prompt: Screen for contraindications to thrombolysis
interview.finding: No recent surgery, trauma or bleeding, and no prior intracranial hemorrhage. No known drug allergies.

exam.prompt: Assess language
exam.finding: Alert but globally aphasic, with minimal verbal output and poor comprehension.

exam.prompt: Test face, arm and leg strength
exam.finding: Right facial droop sparing the forehead. The right arm drifts and falls within five seconds, and the right leg drifts.

exam.prompt: Check gaze, visual fields and attention
exam.finding: Eyes deviated to the left, a partial right visual field cut and right-sided sensory inattention. NIHSS 14. Pulse irregularly irregular.

interview.prompt: Establish onset and associated symptoms
interview.finding: Sudden confusion, diaphoresis and inability to use the left arm while preparing dinner; completely normal 30 minutes earlier. No headache, seizure, chest pain or trauma.

interview.prompt: Review diabetes treatment and today’s meals
interview.finding: Type 2 diabetes for 15 years on insulin glargine 24 units at night and insulin aspart with meals. She has started exercising and eating less, and probably took her mealtime insulin today and then skipped lunch.

interview.prompt: Review other history and bleeding risk
interview.finding: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia, on lisinopril and atorvastatin. No recent surgery, bleeding or anticoagulant use. A brother had a stroke at 60.

exam.prompt: Assess mental status and skin
exam.finding: Drowsy and confused, oriented only to person, with cool diaphoretic skin and a fine tremor.

exam.prompt: Test face, arm and leg strength and speech
exam.finding: Left facial droop, left arm drift with 3/5 strength and left leg 4/5. Mildly slurred speech. NIHSS about 6.

exam.prompt: Check pupils, visual fields and for signs of seizure
exam.finding: Pupils equal and reactive, with no visual field cut. No tongue laceration or incontinence. Regular tachycardia.

interview.prompt: Characterize the episodes
interview.finding: Four discrete, stereotyped episodes in 24 hours of sudden right arm weakness and word-finding difficulty, each lasting 5 to 15 minutes and resolving completely. They are becoming more frequent; the most recent was two hours ago.

interview.prompt: Review vascular risk factors and medications
interview.finding: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia with poor adherence to hydrochlorothiazide and simvastatin. A 35 pack-year smoker who still smokes. On no antiplatelet agent. Father had a stroke at 60.

interview.prompt: Screen for other causes
interview.finding: No prior stroke, known atrial fibrillation, recent illness or trauma. He feels entirely normal between episodes and has not seen a physician in two years.

exam.prompt: Perform a neurologic examination
exam.finding: Alert and fully oriented with fluent speech. Cranial nerves intact, strength 5/5 throughout with no pronator drift, intact sensation, symmetric reflexes, and normal coordination and gait.

exam.prompt: Auscultate the carotid arteries
exam.finding: A bruit is heard over the left carotid artery.

exam.prompt: Examine the heart
exam.finding: Regular rhythm, with no murmur.

interview.prompt: Characterize the headache
interview.finding: Six weeks of dull, holocephalic headaches that are worse in the early morning and occasionally wake him, with two episodes of vomiting without nausea. No fever, neck stiffness, trauma or visual loss.

interview.prompt: Ask about focal symptoms
interview.finding: Two weeks of dropping objects with the right hand and illegible handwriting, a brief episode of word-finding difficulty this morning and several days of feeling foggy.

interview.prompt: Review history and systemic symptoms
interview.finding: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia, on lisinopril and atorvastatin; a 30 pack-year smoker. No anticoagulants. No weight loss, night sweats or hemoptysis, and no family history of cancer.

exam.prompt: Assess mental status and the optic discs
exam.finding: Alert and oriented but mildly inattentive. Pupils equal and reactive; no papilledema on bedside fundoscopy.

exam.prompt: Test strength and pronator drift
exam.finding: Right upper extremity 4/5 with a subtle pronator drift and a weak grip. Left side and both legs 5/5.

exam.prompt: Test coordination, handwriting and gait
exam.finding: Mild right-hand dysgraphia and mild right dysmetria on finger-to-nose. Steady gait. Reflexes symmetric with flexor plantar responses.

interview.prompt: Characterize the back pain
interview.finding: Two weeks of progressively severe, constant mid-thoracic back pain that is worse at night and when lying flat and is unrelieved by acetaminophen. No trauma, fever or prior back surgery.

interview.prompt: Ask about leg, sensory and bladder symptoms
interview.finding: Two days of weak, heavy legs, numbness from the umbilicus downward and inability to urinate for 12 hours with a feeling of abdominal fullness. Fully ambulatory until this week.

interview.prompt: Review the cancer history
interview.finding: Prostate cancer diagnosed three years ago and treated with radiation, with a recently rising PSA; on leuprolide and tamsulosin. A 5 kg unintentional weight loss over two months.

exam.prompt: Test leg strength, tone and reflexes
exam.finding: Symmetric 3/5 weakness at the hips, knees and ankles, with increased tone, brisk patellar reflexes and bilateral upgoing toes. Arms and cranial nerves normal.

exam.prompt: Map sensation to pinprick
exam.finding: A sensory level at T10.

exam.prompt: Palpate the spine and the bladder
exam.finding: Focal tenderness over the lower thoracic spinous processes. The bladder is palpable and distended, with a 700 mL post-void residual, and rectal tone is reduced.

interview.prompt: Characterize the headache
interview.finding: Sudden severe retro-orbital and bifrontal headache four hours ago that peaked within seconds, the worst of his life, followed by nausea, two episodes of vomiting and horizontal diplopia. No trauma, neck stiffness or fever.

interview.prompt: Ask about symptoms over the preceding months
interview.finding: A year of fatigue and reduced libido, with cold intolerance, less frequent shaving, occasional mild headaches and reduced peripheral vision noticed when driving.

interview.prompt: Ask about lightheadedness, medications and history
interview.finding: Lightheaded with near-syncope on standing. Untreated hypertension, on no regular medications and no anticoagulants. Drinks two to three beers nightly.

exam.prompt: Examine the eyes and eye movements
exam.finding: The right eye is deviated down and out with ptosis, and the right pupil is dilated and sluggish. Left eye movements are intact.

exam.prompt: Test visual fields by confrontation
exam.finding: A bitemporal field deficit.

exam.prompt: Assess perfusion, the neck and the limbs
exam.finding: Ill-appearing and diaphoretic, with cool clammy skin, dry mucous membranes and a regular tachycardia. No nuchal rigidity and no limb weakness.

interview.prompt: Establish the timeline and treatment so far
interview.finding: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure that began at home about 22 minutes ago and has not stopped. Paramedics gave one dose of intramuscular midazolam eight minutes ago without effect; their point-of-care glucose was 84 mg/dL.

interview.prompt: Review the epilepsy history and adherence
interview.finding: Epilepsy diagnosed at age two, on levetiracetam. Yesterday’s doses were missed because he was vomiting. His usual seizures last under two minutes, and none has been this long.

interview.prompt: Ask about the current illness and other causes
interview.finding: Two days of fever, runny nose and poor oral intake. No head trauma, toxic ingestion or shunt, and immunizations are up to date. A sibling had febrile seizures.

exam.prompt: Assess responsiveness and movements
exam.finding: Unresponsive, with ongoing rhythmic clonic jerking of all four limbs, eye deviation and oral secretions. No focal asymmetry.

exam.prompt: Assess airway, breathing and circulation
exam.finding: Transmitted upper-airway sounds with adequate air entry on positioning and oxygen. Capillary refill under two seconds, with strong pulses.

exam.prompt: Check pupils, the neck and the skin
exam.finding: Pupils 4 mm and reactive. No nuchal rigidity appreciated, no signs of trauma, and warm flushed skin without petechiae or purpura.

interview.prompt: Characterize the illness
interview.finding: One day of high fever and worsening fussiness after two days of mild upper respiratory symptoms. Poor feeding, two episodes of vomiting, and increasing lethargy; he became harder to rouse on the way in.

interview.prompt: Ask how he responds to handling
interview.finding: He arches his back and cries inconsolably when picked up. No seizures, and no rash noticed by his parents.

interview.prompt: Review immunizations and exposures
interview.finding: Immunizations are delayed: he has not received the Haemophilus influenzae type b or pneumococcal conjugate series. Attends daycare. Born at term; no known immunodeficiency, trauma or travel.

exam.prompt: Palpate the fontanelle and flex the neck
exam.finding: The anterior fontanelle is full and tense. Nuchal rigidity is present, he resists neck flexion and Brudzinski sign appears positive.

exam.prompt: Assess alertness and consolability
exam.finding: Ill-appearing and lethargic, difficult to console and more irritable when picked up. Pupils equal and reactive; he moves all extremities.

exam.prompt: Inspect the skin and assess perfusion
exam.finding: A few faint non-blanching petechiae on the trunk. Capillary refill three seconds with cool extremities. Lungs clear; tachycardic without murmur.

interview.prompt: Characterize the sleepiness
interview.finding: Six months of irresistible daytime sleepiness despite 8 to 9 hours of sleep at night. He falls asleep in class, while texting and mid-sentence; brief naps refresh him for an hour or two.

interview.prompt: Ask about episodes of weakness and their triggers
interview.finding: With hard laughter or surprise his head nods, his jaw slackens and his knees buckle. He once slumped to the floor but stayed fully aware and recovered within seconds.

interview.prompt: Ask about sleep-onset phenomena, breathing and consequences
interview.finding: Vivid dream-like images and an inability to move as he falls asleep. No snoring or witnessed apneas. Falling grades and a near-miss car accident from drowsiness. No medications or drug use.

exam.prompt: Assess alertness
exam.finding: Alert and oriented but visibly drowsy, yawning frequently. Mood appropriate.

exam.prompt: Examine strength, reflexes, coordination and gait
exam.finding: Strength 5/5 with normal tone, symmetric reflexes, full eye movements without ptosis, and normal coordination and gait.

exam.prompt: Observe a provoked episode, and examine the airway
exam.finding: A hearty laugh triggers transient head droop and jaw slackening with preserved awareness, resolving in seconds. No tonsillar hypertrophy or retrognathia.

interview.prompt: Characterize the rash and its course
interview.finding: Four days of pink spots that began on the trunk and spread to the limbs and face, with pruritus, malaise, low-grade fevers and swelling around the eyes and cheeks. No mucosal pain, blistering or sloughing.

interview.prompt: Take a full medication history with start dates
interview.finding: Allopurinol 300 mg daily started six weeks ago for recurrent gout. Long-term lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. IV cefazolin started two days ago for cellulitis. No known drug allergies.

interview.prompt: Review past history and systemic symptoms
interview.finding: Gout, hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Fatigue and mild right-upper-quadrant discomfort; no sore throat, eye pain or joint swelling.

exam.prompt: Inspect the skin and the face
exam.finding: Confluent morbilliform erythematous macules and papules over more than 60% of the body surface, accentuated in the flexures, with marked periorbital and facial edema. No pustules.

exam.prompt: Examine the mucosae and test for skin fragility
exam.finding: Oral, ocular and genital mucosae are spared. No targetoid lesions, no Nikolsky sign and no epidermal detachment.

exam.prompt: Palpate lymph nodes and the abdomen
exam.finding: Tender, firm cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Mild hepatomegaly with right-upper-quadrant tenderness.

interview.prompt: Characterize the eruption
interview.finding: Two weeks of progressive generalized redness and scaling that began on the trunk and now covers nearly the entire body, with intense pruritus, skin tightness and heavy shedding of scale.

interview.prompt: Review skin history and recent treatment
interview.finding: Plaque psoriasis for 20 years, controlled on topical therapy until he ran out a month ago. An urgent-care clinician then gave a course of oral prednisone for a flare, and it was stopped abruptly. Takes lisinopril and atorvastatin.

interview.prompt: Ask about systemic symptoms
interview.finding: Feels cold despite blankets, with chills and rigors, malaise, poor oral intake and lightheadedness on standing. Lives alone.

exam.prompt: Inspect the skin, nails, palms and soles
exam.finding: Confluent erythema over about 90% of the body surface with diffuse fine scale and tight, edematous skin. Thickened palms and soles; nail pitting and onycholysis. Mucous membranes spared; no bullae and no Nikolsky sign.

exam.prompt: Assess temperature and perfusion
exam.finding: Shivering and ill-appearing. The trunk is warm, and the hands and feet are cool.

exam.prompt: Examine lymph nodes, legs, heart and lungs
exam.finding: Diffuse non-tender cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Pitting edema of the lower extremities. Regular tachycardia, mildly elevated jugular venous pressure and clear lungs.

interview.prompt: Characterize the patches
interview.finding: Multiple light-colored patches on the upper chest, shoulders and back, noticed after a summer outdoors when the surrounding skin tanned. Mildly itchy with sweating and occasionally slightly scaly.

interview.prompt: Ask about previous episodes and symptoms
interview.finding: Similar patches in previous summers that faded in cooler months. No pain, numbness or systemic symptoms.

interview.prompt: Review history, medications and environment
interview.finding: Healthy college athlete on no regular medications. Lives in a warm, humid climate, sweats heavily every day and shares a locker room. Worried about vitiligo.

exam.prompt: Inspect the distribution and borders
exam.finding: Numerous well-demarcated hypopigmented macules and patches, 0.5 to 1.5 cm, coalescing over the upper trunk, shoulders and upper back. A few are faintly salmon-tan. Face, palms, soles and mucosae are spared.

exam.prompt: Scrape a patch lightly
exam.finding: Light scraping produces a fine, branny scale. No induration, vesicles or surrounding erythema.

exam.prompt: Test sensation over the patches
exam.finding: Sensation is fully intact, and no nerves are thickened.

interview.prompt: Characterize the eye symptoms
interview.finding: Two days of rapidly worsening right eye pain, redness, marked photophobia, blurred vision and thick discharge, with a foreign-body sensation. A white spot on the eye has grown since yesterday. No trauma.

interview.prompt: Take a contact lens history
interview.finding: Daily soft contact lens wearer who frequently sleeps and swims in her lenses and tops off old solution. She napped in her lenses two nights ago and has worn glasses since.

interview.prompt: Review history and systemic symptoms
interview.finding: Myopia, otherwise healthy, on an oral contraceptive. No fever, joint pains or oral ulcers, and no symptoms in the left eye.

exam.prompt: Measure visual acuity and inspect both eyes
exam.finding: Right eye 20/100 with marked conjunctival injection, ciliary flush and copious mucopurulent discharge. Left eye 20/20, white and quiet.

exam.prompt: Examine the right cornea at the slit lamp
exam.finding: A 3 mm central round epithelial defect over a dense stromal infiltrate with indistinct, melting edges and surrounding corneal haze.

exam.prompt: Examine the anterior chamber, pupil and eye movements
exam.finding: A 1.2 mm hypopyon with significant cell and flare. The pupil is reactive. Normal intraocular pressure, full painless eye movements and no preauricular node.

interview.prompt: Characterize the eye symptoms
interview.finding: Three days of dull, aching left eye pain with severe photophobia, tearing and mildly blurred vision. Redness forms a ring around the iris. No purulent discharge, itching, trauma, contact lens use or foreign-body sensation.

interview.prompt: Ask about previous episodes
interview.finding: Two similar but milder episodes in the past, each resolving over a couple of weeks.

interview.prompt: Review systems and family history
interview.finding: Several months of low-back pain with morning stiffness lasting over an hour that improves with exercise. Father with chronic back stiffness; a maternal uncle with inflammatory bowel disease. No urinary symptoms, diarrhea or joint swelling.

exam.prompt: Measure acuity and inspect the pattern of redness
exam.finding: Acuity 20/20 right and 20/30 left. Ciliary injection of the left eye, most intense at the limbus, with no discharge and normal lids. The right eye is normal.

exam.prompt: Examine the pupils and test for consensual photophobia
exam.finding: The left pupil is smaller than the right and sluggish. Light shone in the right eye causes pain in the left.

exam.prompt: Stain the cornea, and examine the spine
exam.finding: Clear cornea with no fluorescein uptake. Reduced lumbar flexion and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints.

interview.prompt: Characterize the headache
interview.finding: Six weeks of daily dull headaches that are worse in the morning and on lying down, bending or straining. No fever, neck stiffness, trauma, weakness, numbness or speech difficulty.

interview.prompt: Ask about visual and auditory symptoms
interview.finding: Brief episodes lasting seconds in which vision in both eyes grays or blacks out, often on standing, and now more frequent. A pulsatile whooshing in the ears, intermittent horizontal diplopia and a sense that her side vision has narrowed.

interview.prompt: Review weight change and medications
interview.finding: Obesity, with about 14 kg gained over the past year. Oral isotretinoin for acne started three months ago; takes a combined oral contraceptive.

exam.prompt: Examine the optic discs
exam.finding: Bilateral optic disc swelling with blurred margins and obscured vessels at the disc. No hemorrhages.

exam.prompt: Test acuity, pupils and visual fields
exam.finding: Acuity 20/20 in both eyes, with equal reactive pupils and no relative afferent pupillary defect. Enlarged blind spots bilaterally with early nasal constriction.

exam.prompt: Test eye movements, and examine the neck
exam.finding: A mild left abducens palsy with limited left lateral gaze and horizontal diplopia. The neck is supple. No other focal deficit. BMI 36 kg/m².

interview.prompt: Characterize the weakness
interview.finding: Three months of gradually worsening, symmetric weakness of the shoulders and hips: difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a low chair, lifting groceries to a shelf and washing her hair. Muscles are mildly achy, but pain is not the main problem.

interview.prompt: Screen for ocular, bulbar, sensory and fatigable symptoms
interview.finding: No ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia or dyspnea. No numbness, tingling or bowel or bladder change. The weakness does not worsen toward the end of the day.

interview.prompt: Review history, medications and systemic symptoms
interview.finding: Hypothyroidism on stable levothyroxine with a recent normal TSH; no statin. No rash, fever, weight loss or Raynaud phenomenon. A sister has rheumatoid arthritis.

exam.prompt: Test proximal and distal strength
exam.finding: Deltoids and hip flexors 4-/5 and neck flexors 4/5, symmetric. Distal strength 5/5 with preserved grip. She uses her arms to rise from a chair.

exam.prompt: Examine reflexes, sensation and muscle bulk
exam.finding: Reflexes 2+ and symmetric, with intact sensation. No atrophy, fasciculations or significant muscle tenderness.

exam.prompt: Inspect the skin, and test for fatigability
exam.finding: No heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign or mechanic’s hands. No ptosis, and no fatigable weakness on sustained upgaze. Lungs clear.

interview.prompt: Establish how the curve was noticed and screen for red flags
interview.finding: Flagged at a school scoliosis screening. Her mother has noticed a prominent shoulder blade and clothing that hangs unevenly. No back pain, night pain, leg weakness, numbness or bowel or bladder change.

interview.prompt: Assess growth and maturity
interview.finding: Menarche six months ago, with a recent growth spurt and changing shoe size.

interview.prompt: Review history, activity and family history
interview.finding: Healthy, on no medications, and active in volleyball. A maternal aunt wore a back brace as a teenager. No developmental delay or foot deformity.

exam.prompt: Inspect standing posture, and perform the forward-bend test
exam.finding: Right shoulder slightly elevated, right scapular prominence and asymmetric waist creases. The Adams forward-bend test shows a right thoracic rib hump. Leg lengths equal and pelvis level.

exam.prompt: Inspect the skin over the spine
exam.finding: No café-au-lait macules, midline hair tuft, sacral dimple or lipoma.

exam.prompt: Perform a neurologic examination
exam.finding: Strength 5/5 throughout, intact sensation, symmetric reflexes including abdominal reflexes, flexor plantar responses, no clonus and normal gait.

interview.prompt: Establish the course of the hip problem
interview.finding: Day 40 of rehabilitation after a severe traumatic brain injury. Over the past week the right hip has progressively lost range of motion, and he grimaces and becomes agitated with flexion and abduction. New warmth and a firm, deep swelling of the proximal thigh.

interview.prompt: Review the hospital course and medications
interview.finding: Motorcycle collision with a prolonged ICU stay and mechanical ventilation. On levetiracetam, prophylactic enoxaparin, famotidine and acetaminophen. No documented fever spikes.

interview.prompt: Assess function
interview.finding: Speaks in simple words and follows one-step commands. Needs maximal assistance for mobility; the hip now limits sitting tolerance and transfer training.

exam.prompt: Examine the right hip
exam.finding: Markedly reduced passive range of motion with a firm end-feel: flexion to about 70 degrees, with abduction and rotation severely restricted and painful. The left hip moves more freely.

exam.prompt: Palpate around the joint, and inspect the skin
exam.finding: A deep, firm, warm fullness anterior and lateral to the joint that feels continuous with deep tissue. No erythema, fluctuance or skin breakdown.

exam.prompt: Examine the calves, pulses and tone
exam.finding: No calf tenderness or cord, with equal calf circumferences and intact distal pulses. Spasticity in both lower limbs with brisk reflexes.

nr-101.alternativesAndLimits: This patient is recovered and stable. An ongoing or recurrent acute seizure requires a different immediate pathway. Referral timing is drawn from NICE in the UK; local systems differ. No jurisdiction-specific driving rule is asserted.

sources.title: NICE NG217 · Diagnosis and assessment of epilepsy (updated 2025)
NICE CG109 · Initial assessment and causes of transient loss of consciousness

reviewQuestions: Check the interpretation against every finding available at each stage.
Check whether the distractors or written plan exclude a legitimate alternative.
Verify the follow-up and any regional guidance before public use.

ns-006.objective: Recognize cauda equina red flags and act on the time-critical need for imaging and decompression.
ns-006.alternativesAndLimits: Exact timing thresholds for surgery are debated; the case teaches that decompression should not be delayed once compression is confirmed. Outcome also depends on the deficit at presentation.

sources.title: Ahn et al. (Spine 2000): cauda equina syndrome secondary to lumbar disc herniation, a meta-analysis of surgical outcomes
Lavy et al. (BMJ 2009): cauda equina syndrome

ns-030.objective: Recognize raised intracranial pressure from shunt failure and escalate to emergent CSF diversion.
ns-030.alternativesAndLimits: A shunt tap is performed by clinicians trained to do it. Infection and malfunction can coexist, so CSF is sampled at the tap or revision. The choice between CT and rapid-sequence MRI depends on local availability.

sources.title: Hanak et al. (Pediatr Neurosurg 2017): cerebrospinal fluid shunting complications in children
Yue et al. (J Neurosurg Pediatr 2015): test characteristics of quick brain MRI for shunt evaluation in children

ns-010.objective: Image before treating an acute focal deficit, and manage a deep hypertensive hemorrhage medically.
ns-010.alternativesAndLimits: Blood-pressure targets follow current guideline ranges and are individualized. Minimally invasive evacuation is an evolving area and may be considered for selected patients at experienced centers.

INTERACT2 trial (NEJM 2013): rapid blood-pressure lowering in acute intracerebral hemorrhage
STICH II trial (Lancet 2013): early surgery versus initial conservative treatment in lobar intracerebral hematomas

gs-023.objective: Tell a strangulated obstruction from a simple one, and recognize that it needs an operation now.
gs-023.alternativesAndLimits: Most adhesive obstructions without ischemia are managed without surgery at first; this case teaches the exception. Viability is judged by the operating surgeon.

sources.title: Ten Broek et al. (World J Emerg Surg 2018): Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction
Maung et al. (J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2012): evaluation and management of small-bowel obstruction, an EAST practice management guideline

gs-058.objective: Recognize a pyogenic liver abscess and pair antibiotics with drainage.
gs-058.alternativesAndLimits: Small single abscesses can sometimes be treated with antibiotics alone; size thresholds vary between sources. The colorectal evaluation after a Klebsiella abscess rests on observational studies.

sources.title: Lardière-Deguelte et al. (J Visc Surg 2015): hepatic abscess, diagnosis and management
Siu et al. (Lancet Infect Dis 2012): Klebsiella pneumoniae liver abscess, a new invasive syndrome

gs-052.objective: Confirm a pheochromocytoma biochemically and prepare safely for its removal.
gs-052.alternativesAndLimits: The choice of alpha-blocker and the length of preparation vary between centers. The clinic crisis after a first beta-blocker dose is written for teaching; its timing and size differ between patients.

sources.title: Lenders et al. (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014): pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline
Neumann, Young and Eng (N Engl J Med 2019): pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma

pd-027.objective: Recognize diabetic ketoacidosis in a child, treat it in the right order and catch cerebral edema.
pd-027.alternativesAndLimits: Fluid rates and insulin timing follow current pediatric consensus guidance and differ from adult protocols. Clinically apparent cerebral edema is uncommon; it is written into this patient for teaching.

Kuppermann et al. (N Engl J Med 2018): clinical trial of fluid infusion rates for pediatric diabetic ketoacidosis

pd-064.objective: Treat bilious vomiting in a newborn as midgut volvulus and get the baby to surgery quickly.

sources.title: Langer (Surg Clin North Am 2017): intestinal rotation abnormalities and midgut volvulus
Applegate (Pediatr Radiol 2009): evidence-based diagnosis of malrotation and volvulus

pd-081.objective: Recognize childhood immune thrombocytopenia and manage by bleeding, not by the platelet count.
pd-081.alternativesAndLimits: Some families and clinicians choose a short course of treatment even for mild bleeding; observation is the guideline-preferred default. Findings that suggest another diagnosis call for further testing.

Provan et al. (Blood Adv 2019): updated international consensus report on the investigation and management of primary immune thrombocytopenia

ob-001.objective: Recognize preeclampsia with severe features, treat the blood pressure, prevent seizures and plan delivery.
ob-001.alternativesAndLimits: The choice among first-line antihypertensives varies by unit, and the timing of delivery relative to the steroid course is individualized.

sources.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (Obstet Gynecol 2020): gestational hypertension and preeclampsia
Magpie Trial (Lancet 2002): do women with pre-eclampsia, and their babies, benefit from magnesium sulphate?

ob-010.objective: Locate an early pregnancy, recognize an ectopic and act at once when it ruptures.
ob-010.alternativesAndLimits: Thresholds for the discriminatory zone and for methotrexate vary by institution. Rupture while awaiting treatment is uncommon; it is written into this patient for teaching.

sources.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 193 (Obstet Gynecol 2018): tubal ectopic pregnancy
Barnhart (N Engl J Med 2009): ectopic pregnancy

ob-064.objective: Exclude pregnancy, recognize ovarian torsion and treat it as a surgical emergency that spares the ovary.
ob-064.alternativesAndLimits: Doppler flow can be present in early or intermittent torsion, so the decision to operate is clinical. How long an ovary survives without blood flow varies and cannot be predicted for one patient.

Huchon and Fauconnier (Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol 2010): adnexal torsion, a literature review

im-034.objective: Recognize adrenal crisis and treat it before the diagnosis is confirmed.
im-034.alternativesAndLimits: Hydrocortisone doses and fluid volumes follow local protocols. Dexamethasone is an alternative when a stimulation test is planned at once.

sources.title: Bornstein et al. (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016): diagnosis and treatment of primary adrenal insufficiency, an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline
Rushworth, Torpy and Falhammar (N Engl J Med 2019): adrenal crisis

im-024.objective: Work up hyponatremia in order, treat symptoms promptly and avoid correcting too fast.

sources.title: Verbalis et al. (Am J Med 2013): diagnosis, evaluation, and treatment of hyponatremia, expert panel recommendations
Spasovski et al. (Eur J Endocrinol 2014): clinical practice guideline on diagnosis and treatment of hyponatraemia

im-019.objective: Recognize rhabdomyolysis from the urine and the story, protect the kidneys with fluids and treat the potassium.

Chavez et al. (Crit Care 2016): beyond muscle destruction, a systematic review of rhabdomyolysis for clinical practice

pm-018.objective: Sample an effusion that persists despite antibiotics, recognize empyema and drain it.
pm-018.alternativesAndLimits: Tube size, the timing of fibrinolytics and the threshold for early surgery vary between centers.

Shen et al. (J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2017): AATS consensus guidelines for the management of empyema

pm-028.objective: Recognize aspiration pneumonia after a stroke, treat it and prevent the next episode.

sources.title: Mandell and Niederman (N Engl J Med 2019): aspiration pneumonia
Metlay et al. (Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019): diagnosis and treatment of adults with community-acquired pneumonia, an ATS/IDSA guideline

pm-023.objective: Tell latent tuberculosis infection from active disease and choose a short preventive regimen.

Sterling et al. (N Engl J Med 2011): three months of rifapentine and isoniazid for latent tuberculosis infection

gi-004.objective: Recognize acute cholecystitis, image it correctly and plan early surgery.

Present et al. (N Engl J Med 1999): infliximab for the treatment of fistulas in patients with Crohn’s disease

inf-048.objective: Recognize a necrotizing soft-tissue infection and get the patient to surgery without delay.

Stevens et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2014): practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections, 2014 update by the IDSA

inf-093.objective: Treat suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever at once, without waiting for confirmation.

sources.title: Gupta et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2011): international clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of acute uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women
Johnson and Russo (N Engl J Med 2018): acute pyelonephritis in adults

fm-095.objective: Confirm positional vertigo at the bedside, treat it with a repositioning maneuver and know the signs of a central cause.

Kim and Zee (N Engl J Med 2014): benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

Ebell et al. (JAMA 2016): does this patient have infectious mononucleosis? The rational clinical examination systematic review

sources.title: Camaschella (N Engl J Med 2015): iron-deficiency anemia
Pasricha et al. (Lancet 2021): iron deficiency

nph-067.objective: Relieve acute urinary retention at once and recognize obstruction as a reversible cause of kidney injury.

Selius and Subedi (Am Fam Physician 2008): urinary retention in adults, diagnosis and initial management

Kraut and Mullins (N Engl J Med 2018): toxic alcohols

El-Hajj Fuleihan et al. (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023): treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy in adults, an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline

endo-046.objective: Recognize pituitary apoplexy, give hydrocortisone before confirmation and refer for decompression when vision is threatened.

Briet et al. (Endocr Rev 2015): pituitary apoplexy

Refardt, Winzeler and Christ-Crain (Endocrinol Metab Clin North Am 2020): diabetes insipidus, an update

Panch, Montemayor-Garcia and Klein (N Engl J Med 2019): hemolytic transfusion reactions

Lo-Coco et al. (N Engl J Med 2013): retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide for acute promyelocytic leukemia

Margaretten et al. (JAMA 2007): does this adult patient have septic arthritis?

Mauck and Swigler (Orthop Clin North Am 2018): evidence-based review of distal radius fractures

oph-032.objective: Tell inflammation inside the eye from conjunctivitis, treat it with steroid and dilating drops and look for a linked disease.
oph-032.alternativesAndLimits: Steroid drops for uveitis are prescribed after a slit-lamp examination, because they can worsen an infection of the cornea.

sources.title: Jabs et al. (Am J Ophthalmol 2005): standardization of uveitis nomenclature for reporting clinical data
Agrawal et al. (Indian J Ophthalmol 2010): current approach in diagnosis and management of anterior uveitis

oph-037.objective: Recognize swollen optic nerves as raised pressure in the skull, image before a spinal tap and treat to protect vision.
oph-037.alternativesAndLimits: The diagnosis is one of exclusion. Rapid visual loss needs urgent surgical treatment, not tablets alone.

sources.title: Friedman, Liu and Digre (Neurology 2013): revised diagnostic criteria for the pseudotumor cerebri syndrome in adults and children
Wall et al., NORDIC Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Study Group (JAMA 2014): effect of acetazolamide on visual function in patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and mild visual loss

pmr-099.objective: Work up symmetric weakness of the shoulders and hips, recognize an inflammatory muscle disease and pair drug treatment with graded exercise.
pmr-099.alternativesAndLimits: A muscle biopsy is often used to confirm the diagnosis and to exclude conditions that look similar. Antibody results refine it.

sources.title: Dalakas (N Engl J Med 2015): inflammatory muscle diseases
Alexanderson (Curr Rheumatol Rep 2012): exercise in inflammatory myopathies, including inclusion body myositis

pmr-095.objective: Measure a spinal curve, judge how much growth remains and choose between watching, bracing and surgery.
pmr-095.alternativesAndLimits: Thresholds are approximate. A curve with pain, an abnormal neurologic exam or an unusual pattern needs an MRI.

sources.title: Weinstein et al. (N Engl J Med 2013): effects of bracing in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis
Hresko (N Engl J Med 2013): idiopathic scoliosis in adolescents

pmr-073.objective: Recognize new bone forming around a joint after brain injury, confirm it early and protect movement without forcing the joint.
pmr-073.alternativesAndLimits: Evidence for drug treatment is limited, and practice varies. A clot and a joint infection must be excluded first.

sources.title: Cipriano et al. (J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2009): heterotopic ossification following traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury
Ranganathan et al. (J Bone Joint Surg Am 2015): heterotopic ossification, basic-science principles and clinical correlates

em-016.title: A heartbeat that suddenly _took off._

start.alarm: Very fast heart rate

em-016.handoff: A 32-year-old woman was sitting at her desk 40 minutes ago when her heart began to pound. It is fast and steady, and it has not stopped.

interview.prompt: Ask how the pounding started and whether it has happened before
interview.finding: It began all at once 40 minutes ago, while she was sitting still. It is fast and regular. She has had a few spells like it this past year, and each one stopped on its own within minutes.

interview.prompt: Ask about chest pain, fainting and trouble breathing
interview.finding: She feels a little lightheaded, with a fluttering in her throat. No chest pain, no fainting, and no real trouble breathing.

interview.prompt: Ask about caffeine, drugs and her family’s heart history
interview.finding: She drinks two or three coffees a day and had an extra one this morning. She has no heart problems, no recent illness and no signs of a thyroid problem. She takes no stimulant drugs or medicines. No one in her family has died suddenly.

exam.prompt: Check how she looks and whether enough blood is reaching her brain and skin
exam.finding: Awake, a little anxious and thinking clearly. Her skin is warm, with good blood flow. She is breathing comfortably.

exam.prompt: Listen to her heart and feel her pulse
exam.finding: Very fast and perfectly regular. Her heart sounds are normal, with nothing extra. The pulse at her wrist is fast, regular and strong.

exam.prompt: Check her lungs, her neck and her legs
exam.finding: Her lungs are clear. The veins in her neck are not swollen, and her thyroid gland is not enlarged. Her legs are not swollen.

2.label: Heart tracing after the medicine
2.content:
After the second dose of adenosine (12 mg), the fast rhythm stopped all at once.
Heart tracing (ECG) now: a normal rhythm at 78 beats a minute.
Signals cross from the upper to the lower chambers in a normal time, with no sign of an extra pathway (no “delta wave”).
No sign of strain on the heart muscle, and a normal reset time between beats (QT).
Blood salts and thyroid test: normal.

0.resident: The monitor shows a fast, regular rhythm at 188 with narrow beats. Her blood pressure is fine and she is thinking clearly.
0.question: What do we try first?
options: Shock her heart back to a normal rhythm right away
Coach her through a bearing-down maneuver while watching the monitor
Give amiodarone, a strong rhythm medicine, through a vein
Give procainamide, another rhythm medicine, through a vein

terms.meaning: On the heart tracing each beat is a thin spike. That means the signal starts above the heart’s lower chambers.
Blowing hard against resistance for about 15 seconds, then lying back with the legs lifted. It sets off a nerve reflex that can slow the heart’s signals.
A timed electric shock that resets the heart’s rhythm. The patient is sedated for it.

outcomes.story: You ask for the shock pads and sedation. The resident stops the cart before anyone opens it.
outcomes.reply: A shock is for a patient who is crashing: low blood pressure, chest pain, confusion. She has none of those. We start with the gentlest thing that can work.

outcomes.story: She blows hard into a syringe for 15 seconds. Then you lay her back and lift her legs. The monitor does not change: still 188. She is no worse.
outcomes.reply: Right first step. It stops this rhythm in about 4 of every 10 people, and it costs almost nothing to try. It did not work this time, so we move on.

outcomes.story: You write the order for amiodarone. The pharmacist calls before it is mixed.
outcomes.reply: Amiodarone is a heavy medicine that can drop the blood pressure. For this rhythm there are simpler, safer steps to try first.

outcomes.story: You write the order for procainamide. The nurse checks with the resident before drawing it up.
outcomes.reply: Procainamide has to run in slowly and can drop the blood pressure. We keep it for other rhythm problems. This one has a simpler first step.

1.resident: The maneuver did not work. She is still at 188, and her blood pressure is holding.
1.question: Which medicine do we give next?
options: Adenosine, pushed fast into a vein
Digoxin, run slowly into a vein
Flecainide, as a tablet
Magnesium, through a vein

terms.meaning: A medicine that blocks the heart’s relay station for a few seconds. The body clears it within seconds, so it is pushed in fast and chased with salt water.
The one normal electrical link between the heart’s upper and lower chambers.
An old heart medicine that slows the relay station. It can take hours to reach its full effect.

outcomes.story: You warn her that she will feel awful for a few seconds. The first dose changes nothing. The second, larger dose goes in: the monitor pauses for a moment, then shows a normal rhythm at 78. She says her chest has gone quiet.
outcomes.reply: That pause was the medicine working. It breaks the loop for a moment, and the heart’s own pacemaker takes over again.

outcomes.story: The digoxin runs in slowly. Forty-five minutes later her heart is still at 188. She is more lightheaded, and her blood pressure has started to drift down.
outcomes.reply: Digoxin can take hours to work. She has now spent most of an hour at 188. Her pressure is still good enough for the fast medicine, so we give adenosine now.
outcomes.alarm: Still 188 beats a minute · more lightheaded

outcomes.story: You ask for a flecainide tablet. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: A tablet has to be absorbed first, and flecainide is a long-term medicine for preventing these spells. She needs something that works in seconds.

outcomes.story: You write the order for magnesium. The pharmacist calls to ask what rhythm it is for.
outcomes.reply: Magnesium treats a different, dangerous rhythm called torsades. It is not the medicine that stops this one.

4.resident: She feels fine, and her heart tracing is normal now.
4.question: What is the plan from here?
options: Admit her for a procedure tonight to burn away the short circuit
Send her home with a plan and a heart clinic visit
Start amiodarone, to be taken for life
Put in a permanent pacemaker
4.fix: Send her home with a plan

terms.meaning: A procedure that passes a thin wire into the heart and destroys the tiny patch of tissue behind the short circuit.
A small implanted device that speeds up a heart that beats too slowly.
The specialists who follow heart rhythm problems and decide whether anything more is needed.

outcomes.story: You call to book the procedure for tonight. The resident takes the phone.
outcomes.reply: Ablation can cure this, but it is a planned procedure, not an emergency one. It is worth discussing if the spells keep coming back. That is a conversation for the heart clinic.

outcomes.story: You watch her on the monitor a little longer, and her rhythm stays normal. You teach her the maneuver, talk about cutting back on caffeine and book the heart clinic. She knows when to come back.
outcomes.reply: That is the whole plan. One spell that stopped cleanly, a normal tracing, and a patient who knows what to do next time.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for amiodarone. The pharmacist calls before it is filled.
outcomes.reply: Amiodarone taken for years can damage the thyroid, the lungs and the liver. That is far too much risk for a healthy 32-year-old with a few short spells a year.

outcomes.story: You ask about booking a pacemaker. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A pacemaker speeds up a slow heart. Hers was too fast, and it is normal now. A pacemaker would do nothing for her.

differential.resident: The second dose of adenosine worked, and her heart is back in a normal rhythm. The new heart tracing is in her chart.
differential.question: What was this rhythm?
options: Atrial fibrillation: the upper chambers quiver, so the pulse is irregular
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT): a short circuit near the relay station, fast and regular
Multifocal atrial tachycardia: many spots in the upper chambers fire, so the pulse is irregular
Ventricular tachycardia: a fast rhythm that starts in the lower chambers, with wide beats
differential.reveal: It was supraventricular tachycardia, or SVT. It began all at once, it was fast, regular and narrow, and it stopped the moment adenosine blocked the relay station. That points to a loop running through the relay. Her full set of tracings will show the exact type.

terms.meaning: Above the ventricles, the heart’s two lower chambers.
A heart rate over 100 beats a minute.

ending.better: Going home with her heart in a normal rhythm
ending.stable: Going home with her heart in a normal rhythm
ending.worse: Still on the monitor in the emergency department

em-016.plainDiagnosis: A fast heart rhythm caused by a short circuit in the heart’s wiring (supraventricular tachycardia, or SVT).

science.title: Why her heart suddenly ran at 188
science.text: A signal should cross the heart’s relay station once per beat. Hers most likely has two paths side by side. A signal went down one and back up the other, and the loop fired her heart again on every lap.

science.title: How adenosine stopped it in seconds
science.text: Adenosine opens potassium channels in the cells of the relay station. Potassium flows out of the cells, and for a few seconds they are much harder to fire. The loop has nowhere to go, so it stops.

science.title: Why a racing heart made her lightheaded
science.text: The heart fills between beats. At 188 beats a minute there is little time to fill, so each beat pushes out less blood. Less flow means less pressure to carry blood up to the brain.

sources.title: REVERT trial (Lancet 2015): modified Valsalva maneuver for supraventricular tachycardia
2015 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline: management of adults with supraventricular tachycardia
AHA guidelines: adult advanced life support (2025)
StatPearls: adenosine
StatPearls: amiodarone

em-018.title: Headache and confusion _after a fall._
em-018.handoff: A 50-year-old man fell and hit his head ten days ago. His wife says he has been getting sleepier and more confused for three days.

interview.prompt: Ask what happened and when it started
interview.finding: He hit his head on a tile floor 10 days ago and felt fine at first. For three days his headache, sleepiness and confusion have been getting worse, and he vomited once.

interview.prompt: Ask about his medicines and bleeding risk
interview.finding: He takes warfarin, a blood thinner, for an irregular heartbeat. His last clotting test was “a little high”. He also drinks alcohol regularly.

interview.prompt: Ask about new weakness, speech trouble or fever
interview.finding: His wife says he is struggling to find words and his right hand is clumsy today. No fever, no stiff neck, no seizures.

exam.prompt: Check how awake and aware he is
exam.finding: Drowsy, but he wakes when you speak. He knows who he is and where he is, but not the date.

exam.prompt: Test his strength, speech and walking
exam.finding: His right arm drifts down when he holds both arms out. He is slow to find words and walks with his feet wide apart.

exam.prompt: Look at his head, eyes and neck
exam.finding: The left side of his scalp is tender, with no cut. Both pupils are the same size and react to light. His neck moves freely.

1.label: Scan and blood tests
1.content:
CT scan of the head: a crescent of blood over the left side of the brain. It crosses the seams of the skull, is about 12 mm thick, and pushes the brain 6 mm off center.
Clotting test (INR): 3.8. About 1 is normal, so his blood is very slow to clot.
Platelets, blood sugar and salts: normal.

0.resident: He hit his head ten days ago, he takes a blood thinner, and he is getting drowsier.
0.question: What do we do first?
options: Tell him it is from the altitude and send him home
Get a CT scan of his head now
Do a spinal tap to check for infection
Book an MRI for next week and let him go

terms.meaning: A medicine that slows clotting. His is called warfarin.
A fast X-ray scan that shows bleeding within minutes.
A needle in the lower back that samples the fluid around the brain and spine.

outcomes.story: You tell him the mountain trip is the likely cause and start his discharge. Before he leaves, the nurse calls you back: he is hard to wake and has vomited again.
outcomes.reply: A head injury on a blood thinner is a bleed until a scan says otherwise. We are getting a CT now.
outcomes.alarm: Harder to wake · blood pressure rising

outcomes.story: The scan is done within minutes. It shows a crescent of blood between his skull and his brain, pushing the brain 6 mm to one side.
outcomes.reply: Good call. That is blood pressing on his brain. The full report is in his chart.

outcomes.story: You start setting up for the spinal tap. The resident sees the tray and stops you before anything happens.
outcomes.reply: Not with possible bleeding inside the skull. Draining fluid from below can let the brain shift downward. We scan first.

outcomes.story: You book the MRI and start his discharge papers. Before he leaves, his wife says he can no longer find his words.
outcomes.reply: He cannot wait a week. Speech that is getting worse means the pressure is building. CT now.

3.resident: His clotting test is back. His INR is 3.8, and normal is about 1, so his blood is very slow to clot. The surgeon is on the way.
3.question: What do we do about his blood?
options: Keep the warfarin going and watch him closely
Reverse the blood thinner now with clotting factors and vitamin K
Give aspirin to stop new clots forming
Start heparin, another blood thinner, for his irregular heartbeat

terms.meaning: A blood test of how long clotting takes. About 1 is normal; higher means slower clotting.
Proteins in blood that build a clot. Warfarin lowers them; a concentrate puts them back within minutes.
The liver needs it to make clotting factors. It keeps the reversal going after the concentrate wears off.

outcomes.story: You keep the warfarin on his chart and watch. Half an hour later his right arm is weaker and he is harder to wake.
outcomes.reply: Watching does not stop a bleed. His blood still cannot clot, so the bleed keeps growing. We reverse it now.
outcomes.alarm: Right arm weaker · harder to wake

outcomes.story: The clotting factors go in through his vein, with vitamin K to make the effect last. A repeat test shows his INR is down to 1.3.
outcomes.reply: Now his blood can clot. That slows the bleeding and makes surgery safer.

outcomes.story: You write the order for aspirin. The pharmacist calls before anyone gives it.
outcomes.reply: Aspirin stops platelets from sticking together, so it makes bleeding worse. He needs help clotting, not less of it.

outcomes.story: You write the order for heparin. The nurse stops at the bedside and asks the resident to check it.
outcomes.reply: Heparin is another blood thinner. With blood already in his skull it would make the bleed far worse. His heartbeat can wait; the bleed cannot.

4.resident: The bleed is 12 mm thick and has pushed his brain 6 mm off center. His clotting is fixed.
4.question: What is the plan for the bleed itself?
options: Watch him closely with repeated checks, and no surgery
Surgery now to drain the blood
A medicine to lower the pressure in his skull, and nothing else
Restart a blood thinner once he looks stable

terms.meaning: How far the bleed has pushed the brain off center. More than 5 mm is a sign surgeons act on.
A surgeon who operates on the brain and spine.
The surgeon opens the skull and removes the clot, so the brain has room again.

outcomes.story: You order checks every hour. At the first one his left pupil is larger than the right, and he no longer follows commands.
outcomes.reply: That pupil means his brain is being squeezed downward. He goes to the operating room now.
outcomes.alarm: Left pupil enlarged · slow heart rate · uneven breathing

outcomes.story: The neurosurgeon looks at the scan and agrees. The operating room is called and he is taken straight up.
outcomes.reply: A bleed this thick, with this much shift, comes out. You do not wait for him to get worse.

outcomes.story: The medicine eases the pressure for a while. Half an hour later he is drowsier again. The blood is still there.
outcomes.reply: That medicine buys time. It does not remove the clot. He needs surgery.

outcomes.story: You suggest restarting a blood thinner. The neurosurgeon overhears.
outcomes.reply: Not with fresh blood in his head. That decision comes later, with the surgical team.

differential.resident: The scan report is in his chart. Read it, then tell me what kind of problem this is.
differential.question: What is going on inside his skull?
options: Epidural hematoma: bleeding from an artery, just under the skull
Subdural hematoma: bleeding from torn veins, over the surface of the brain
Subarachnoid hemorrhage: blood in the fluid spaces around the brain
Ischemic stroke: a blocked artery, with no bleeding
differential.reveal: It is a subdural hematoma: a crescent of blood that crosses the skull’s seams, from torn veins over the surface of the brain. An epidural bleed bulges like a lens and stops at the seams.

terms.meaning: A collection of blood outside the blood vessels.
A subdural bleed spreads in a thin crescent and crosses the skull’s seams. An epidural bleed bulges like a lens and stops at them.

ending.stable: In the operating room, stable
ending.worse: In the operating room, after getting worse
ending.critical: In the operating room, in critical condition

em-018.plainDiagnosis: Bleeding around the brain (a subdural hematoma) in a man on a blood thinner.

science.title: Why a blood thinner turns a bump into a bleed
science.text: Warfarin blocks an enzyme the liver needs to recycle vitamin K. Without it, the liver makes fewer working clotting factors, so a small torn vein keeps leaking.

science.title: Why pressure inside the skull is dangerous
science.text: The skull is a closed box. Blood that collects has nowhere to go, so the pressure climbs and squeezes the brain.

science.title: Why his blood pressure climbs as he gets worse
science.text: Blood reaches the brain only if the pressure pushing it in beats the pressure inside the skull. As that inside pressure rises, the body raises blood pressure to keep blood flowing.

sources.title: Brain Trauma Foundation: surgical management of traumatic brain injury (acute subdural hematoma)
Neurocritical Care Society and SCCM guideline, full text: reversal of antithrombotics in intracranial hemorrhage
NICE guideline NG232: head injury, assessment and early management
Merck Manual Professional: how to do lumbar puncture (contraindications)
StatPearls: Cushing reflex
StatPearls: transtentorial herniation
StatPearls: intracranial hypertension
StatPearls: warfarin

em-015.title: He keeps passing out, _and his pulse is slow._

start.alarm: Very slow heart rate · low blood pressure

em-015.handoff: A 78-year-old man has passed out three times in two days, each time with no warning. He says his pulse feels very slow.

interview.prompt: Ask what happens when he passes out
interview.finding: He has passed out three times in two days, each time with no warning. He comes round quickly and is not confused afterward. He has not bitten his tongue or hit his head.

interview.prompt: Ask how he feels between the episodes
interview.finding: Tired and dizzy, and short of breath after very little effort. When he checks his pulse at home, it feels very slow.

interview.prompt: Ask about his heart history and his medicines
interview.finding: He had a heart attack six years ago. He has high blood pressure and diabetes. One of his daily medicines is metoprolol, which slows the heart. None of his medicines has changed lately, and he has not been ill.

exam.prompt: Check how awake he is and how well blood is reaching his skin
exam.finding: Awake and making sense, but pale and tired. His blood pressure is a little low and his pulse is slow. When you press on a fingernail, the color is a little slow to come back.

exam.prompt: Listen to his heart and watch the veins in his neck
exam.finding: Slow and regular. The first heart sound is loud on some beats and soft on others. Now and then a vein in his neck gives a big jump. There are no extra heart sounds.

exam.prompt: Check his strength, his speech and his lungs
exam.finding: His strength and speech are normal, with no sign of a stroke. His lungs are clear. His legs are not swollen.

1.label: Heart tracing (ECG)
1.content:
Upper chambers: beating about 88 times a minute.
Lower chambers: beating about 38 times a minute.
The two are completely out of step. Each keeps its own steady beat, and neither follows the other.
The beats of the lower chambers are wide. A slow backup pacemaker low in the heart is driving them.
The tracing also shows the scar of his earlier heart attack.
Blood test for new heart damage (troponin): not back yet.

0.resident: He keeps passing out with no warning, and his pulse is 38.
0.question: What do we do first?
options: A heart tracing (ECG) now, and keep him on a heart monitor
A CT scan of his head
A tilt-table test, to see whether being upright makes him faint
An ultrasound of his heart before any other test

terms.meaning: A tracing of the heart’s electrical signals, taken with stickers on the chest. It takes a few minutes at the bedside.
A test that straps a patient to a table and tilts them upright, to bring on a simple faint while they are watched.
Moving pictures of the heart’s walls and valves. It shows the pump, not the wiring.

outcomes.story: The tracing is done at his bedside within minutes, and he stays on the monitor. While it prints, he says he feels faint again. His blood pressure now reads 84/50.
outcomes.reply: Good call. The tracing is in his chart. That drop in pressure is the slow heart, not anything you did, and it is why he stays on a monitor.

outcomes.story: You send him down the hall for a head scan. On the scanner table he passes out again for a few seconds. The scan itself is normal.
outcomes.reply: His brain is not why he faints. His heart is. With a pulse of 38 he should not leave a heart monitor. We get the tracing now.
outcomes.alarm: Passed out again · blood pressure falling

outcomes.story: You ask for a tilt-table test. The resident cancels the request before it is sent.
outcomes.reply: That test is for simple faints, and it works by making the patient faint. With a pulse of 38 that is not safe, and it would not show us his heart rhythm.

outcomes.story: You order the heart ultrasound first. It takes forty minutes to arrive. In that time nobody has looked at his heart rhythm, and he is dizzier.
outcomes.reply: The ultrasound shows the pump. His problem is the timing. A tracing takes five minutes and answers the question, so we do it now.

3.resident: He feels faint again. His blood pressure is 84/50 and his pulse is still 38.
3.question: What do we do right now?
options: Hold his home medicines and watch the monitor
Pace his heart now, through pads on his chest
Give fluid through a vein and check him again in an hour
Give metoprolol through a vein to steady the rhythm

terms.meaning: Sticky pads on the chest and back deliver small timed pulses that make the heart beat. It is uncomfortable, so the patient is given pain relief and sedation.
A thin wire passed through a vein into the heart. It paces more reliably and more comfortably than pads.
A beta blocker. It slows the heart and its electrical signals.

outcomes.story: You hold his home medicines, the metoprolol among them, and watch. Twenty minutes later the monitor shows several seconds with no heartbeat at all. He slumps over, then comes round.
outcomes.reply: Stopping the metoprolol is right, but it takes many hours to wear off. A backup rhythm this slow can simply stop. We pace him now.
outcomes.alarm: Pause on the monitor · passed out again

outcomes.story: Sticky pads go on his chest and back. He gets medicine for pain and to make him drowsy, because each pulse makes his chest muscles jump. The pacer is set to 70, and you can feel a pulse with every beat.
outcomes.reply: Now the machine is doing the timing that his own wiring cannot. A pulse you can feel with each beat shows the heart is really pumping. This is a bridge until the heart team places a pacing wire.

outcomes.story: The fluid runs in and you come back in an hour. His pulse is still 38 and his blood pressure is lower. He is confused, and his hands are cold.
outcomes.reply: Fluid cannot fix this. His tank is not empty. His heart is beating too slowly to move what is in it. We pace him now.
outcomes.alarm: Confused · cold hands · blood pressure very low

outcomes.story: You write the order for metoprolol. The nurse reads it twice and calls the resident before giving it.
outcomes.reply: Metoprolol slows the heart’s signals even more. In a heart that depends on a slow backup rhythm, it could stop that rhythm altogether.

4.resident: The pacer is working. His pulse is 70 and his blood pressure is back up. We are checking for causes we can reverse: his medicines, his blood salts and a new heart attack.
4.question: If the block stays, what is the lasting fix?
options: A permanent pacemaker, placed under the skin
Atropine, a medicine that speeds the heart, for life
Bypass surgery to bring more blood to his heart muscle
Flecainide, a daily rhythm medicine

terms.meaning: A small battery-powered device placed under the skin of the chest, with a wire into the heart. It sends a signal whenever the heart’s own wiring fails to.
A medicine given through a vein that briefly speeds the heart by blocking the nerve that slows it.
An operation that reroutes blood around blocked heart arteries.

outcomes.story: The heart-rhythm team sees him. They agree: unless a cause they can reverse turns up, he gets a permanent pacemaker. He goes to the cardiac unit on a monitor, with the pacer still running.
outcomes.reply: That is the lasting fix. A pacemaker does for good what the pads are doing now.

outcomes.story: You suggest atropine for life. The resident stops you before it goes into the plan.
outcomes.reply: Atropine is a short-acting medicine given through a vein. It cannot be a lifelong treatment, and for a block this low in the wiring it often does nothing at all.

outcomes.story: You suggest bypass surgery. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Bypass brings blood to the heart muscle. His problem is the wiring between the chambers, and new plumbing does not reliably repair old wiring.

outcomes.story: You write flecainide into the plan. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: Flecainide slows the electrical signals in the heart. That would make a heart block worse, not better.

differential.resident: The tracing is in his chart. Look at how the upper and the lower chambers are beating.
differential.question: What kind of block is this?
options: Second-degree block: signals slow more and more until one beat is dropped
First-degree block: every signal gets through, just slowly
Third-degree (complete) block: no signal gets through at all
Sinus bradycardia: a slow heartbeat with the wiring working normally
differential.reveal: It is a complete heart block. The upper chambers beat at 88 and the lower at 38, each one steady and neither following the other. In the lesser blocks at least some signals still get through.

terms.meaning: A fault in the wiring that carries each heartbeat signal from the upper chambers to the lower ones.
When no signal arrives from above, cells in the lower heart fire on their own. They are slow, and they can stop without warning.

ending.stable: In the cardiac unit on a temporary pacer, waiting for a permanent pacemaker
ending.worse: In the cardiac unit on a temporary pacer, after getting worse
ending.critical: In the cardiac unit on a temporary pacer, in critical condition

em-015.plainDiagnosis: A complete break in the heart’s wiring, so the upper and lower chambers beat on their own (complete heart block).

science.title: Why one break stops every signal
science.text: In a circuit with a single path, one break stops the current everywhere past it. His heart has one electrical link between the upper and lower chambers, and it has failed. No signal arrives from above, so the lower chambers run on a slow backup of their own.

science.title: Why a slow heart drops his blood pressure
science.text: The blood his heart moves each minute is the amount per beat times the beats per minute. At 38 beats a minute too little blood flows, and with less flow through the same vessels the pressure falls. A pacer set to 70 brings the flow back.

sources.title: AHA 2025 adult bradycardia algorithm
AHA guidelines: adult advanced life support (2025)
2018 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline: evaluation and management of bradycardia and cardiac conduction delay
StatPearls: third-degree atrioventricular block
Review: transcutaneous cardiac pacing, indications and technique

em-020.title: Pain far worse _than the skin looks._

start.alarm: High fever · fast heart rate · low blood pressure

em-020.handoff: A 59-year-old man with diabetes has pain and swelling between his legs that became much worse in one day. He has a fever and looks very unwell.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain and how the skin has changed
interview.finding: The pain, swelling and dark color between his legs and over his scrotum became much worse within 24 hours. The pain is far worse than the skin looks, and he says the skin feels as if it is crackling.

interview.prompt: Ask what could have let an infection in
interview.finding: His diabetes is poorly controlled. He has obesity and he smokes. Two weeks ago an abscess beside his anus was drained. Now a foul-smelling fluid is leaking from the area.

interview.prompt: Ask how the rest of his body feels
interview.finding: He has fever and chills. He feels weak and sick to his stomach, has eaten little, and gets lightheaded when he stands.

exam.prompt: Look at the skin between his legs and over his scrotum
exam.finding: The skin is dusky red to purple and tightly swollen. Some patches are dead. A foul, blood-tinged fluid is leaking out.

exam.prompt: Press gently to find how far it has spread
exam.finding: It is tender well beyond the edge of the red skin, up toward his lower belly, and the pain is far more than the skin would explain. The tissue crackles under your fingers, as if there is gas in it. Some patches of skin have no feeling at all.

exam.prompt: Check how sick he looks and how well blood is reaching his skin
exam.finding: He looks very ill and is drenched in sweat. His heart is racing and his blood pressure is low. When you press on a fingernail, the color is slow to come back.

1.label: Blood tests and scan
1.content:
The surgical team has been called, and treatment is starting. A scan that was already done is below. Treatment does not wait for more pictures.
White blood cells: 22.4, about twice the upper limit, with many young cells. His body is fighting a severe infection.
Sodium: 128 (low). Blood sugar: 412 (very high).
Kidney test (creatinine): 1.9, up from his usual 1.1. His kidneys are under strain.
Inflammation marker (CRP): 320 (very high).
Lactate: 4.2 (high). Parts of his body are not getting enough blood flow.
X-ray and CT scan of the pelvis: gas under the skin, tracking through the tissue between his legs and into the scrotum.

0.resident: Look at the skin, and then look at him. A simple skin infection and a deep one that kills tissue are treated very differently.
0.question: Which picture is his?
options: A simple skin infection: mild redness with clear edges and no body-wide illness
A deep infection killing tissue: pain beyond what shows, crackling, dead skin
Harmless swelling: warmth and puffiness that settle when the area is raised
A skin rash: an itchy, raised patch of skin with sharp, clear edges
0.fix: Treat it as a deep infection

terms.meaning: A common infection of the skin. It causes redness and warmth and is usually treated with antibiotics alone.
An infection that kills the tissue under the skin and spreads fast along the layers that wrap the muscles.
Gas made by bacteria and trapped in the tissue. It should never be there.

outcomes.story: You call it a simple skin infection. He gets one antibiotic and a plan to check on him later. An hour on, the dark skin has spread past the line the nurse drew around it, and he is drowsy.
outcomes.reply: This was never a simple skin infection. Pain far beyond what the skin shows, crackling, dead patches and a patient this sick mean the tissue underneath is dying. We call the surgeons now.

outcomes.story: You name it: a deep infection that is killing tissue. The resident nods and phones the surgical team. Blood tests are sent, and fluids are started through a vein.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Pain far worse than the skin looks, crackling, dead and numb patches, and a very sick patient. Any one of those is a warning. Together they mean we move now.

outcomes.story: You suggest it is swelling that will settle if the area is raised. The resident stops you before the plan is written.
outcomes.reply: Harmless swelling does not come with a fever, a racing heart and dead skin. Look at the whole patient, not only the swelling.

outcomes.story: You suggest it is an itchy skin rash. The resident stops you before the plan is written.
outcomes.reply: A rash itches. It does not crackle, kill skin or make a patient this sick. This is far deeper than the skin.

3.resident: The surgical team is here. He is getting fluids, and his blood pressure is still low.
3.question: What does he need most?
options: Strong antibiotics through a vein, and no surgery
Surgery now to cut away all the dead tissue
A session in a high-pressure oxygen chamber first, then decide
A small cut at the bedside to let the pus out

terms.meaning: Surgery that cuts away dead and infected tissue until only healthy, bleeding tissue is left.
Breathing pure oxygen in a pressurized chamber. Some centers add it after surgery. It never replaces surgery.
Removing the place an infection is coming from. Antibiotics work far better once that is done.

outcomes.story: The antibiotics run in, and you wait for them to work. Ninety minutes later the dark, crackling area has reached his lower belly. His blood pressure is lower and he is breathing fast.
outcomes.reply: Antibiotics travel in the blood, and dead tissue has no blood flow, so they cannot reach the bacteria living in it. The longer surgery waits, the lower his chance of living. He goes to the operating room now.
outcomes.alarm: Spreading to the belly · blood pressure falling

outcomes.story: The surgeon examines him and agrees. The operating room is called, and the team starts getting him ready.
outcomes.reply: Right. Antibiotics and fluids help, but only surgery removes the dead tissue the infection is feeding on. The sooner it is done, the better his chances.

outcomes.story: You call to book the oxygen chamber. The surgeon overhears and stops the call.
outcomes.reply: Some centers use the chamber as an extra, after surgery. It must never hold surgery up. Time in a chamber is time the infection keeps spreading.

outcomes.story: You open a small procedure kit at the bedside. The surgeon stops you before you start.
outcomes.reply: A small cut drains one pocket of pus. This infection runs along whole layers of tissue, far past what you can see. It needs a full operation, with him asleep.

4.resident: The operating room will be ready in a few minutes. He needs antibiotics before he goes.
4.question: Which antibiotics?
options: One mild antibiotic as a tablet, the kind used for ordinary skin infections
Broad antibiotics through a vein, plus one that blocks toxins
An antifungal medicine through a vein, and no antibiotics
No antibiotics yet: wait for the lab to test samples taken in surgery

terms.meaning: A mix that covers many kinds of bacteria at once. It is used when several kinds are likely and there is no time to find out which.
Poisons that some bacteria release. They damage tissue and drive shock.
Samples grown in the lab to find out which bacteria are present. Results take a day or more.

outcomes.story: You order one antibiotic tablet. The pharmacist calls before it leaves the pharmacy.
outcomes.reply: One mild antibiotic covers only a few kinds of bacteria. This infection is usually several kinds at once, and he is far too sick for tablets. He needs broad antibiotics through a vein.

outcomes.story: The antibiotics are running within minutes, and he goes to the operating room with them still going in. The surgeons cut away the dead tissue. About ninety minutes later he is in intensive care.
outcomes.reply: Good. The mix covers the many kinds of bacteria this infection usually involves. The extra one cuts down the toxins that some of those bacteria make.

outcomes.story: You order an antifungal on its own. The pharmacist calls to question it.
outcomes.reply: This infection is caused mainly by bacteria. An antifungal alone leaves them untouched.

outcomes.story: You hold the antibiotics so that the samples will be clean. Getting him into the operating room takes another hour, and in that hour nothing is fighting the infection. His fever climbs and his blood pressure falls further.
outcomes.reply: In shock from an infection, antibiotics go in within the hour. Samples can be taken first if that causes no delay, but treatment never waits for their results.

5.resident: He is out of the first operation and in intensive care. The surgeons removed all the dead tissue they could find.
5.question: What does he need now?
options: One more wash of the wound, then home once the fever is gone
Intensive care, with more operations until the infection stops spreading
Wound care at a clinic, with antibiotic tablets
An operation to reroute his urine for good, before anything else

terms.meaning: A planned return to the operating room, usually within a day or so, to find and remove any tissue that has died since.
A unit with constant monitoring and a nurse for every one or two patients, for people whose organs need support.
Later surgery, such as skin grafts, to close and rebuild the area once the infection is gone.

outcomes.story: You write a plan for one more wash and a discharge once his fever settles. The surgeon reads it and crosses it out.
outcomes.reply: This infection often keeps spreading after the first operation. He will go back to the operating room, usually within a day or so, and again until no dead tissue is left.

outcomes.story: The plan is set with the intensive care team: antibiotics, fluids and careful control of his blood sugar. The surgeons book a second look for tomorrow. Rebuilding the area comes much later.
outcomes.reply: That is the plan. Beating this takes repeated surgery and days of close support, not one operation.

outcomes.story: You suggest clinic visits and antibiotic tablets. The intensive care doctor stops you.
outcomes.reply: He is still dangerously ill and needs support that only intensive care can give. Tablets and a clinic are for much later.

outcomes.story: You ask about an operation to reroute his urine for good. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Not first, and not for good. Sometimes a temporary tube or bag is used later to keep urine or stool off the wound. Removing dead tissue always comes first.
