differential.resident: The blood tests and the scan are in his chart. The scan shows gas in the tissue.
differential.question: What is this?
options: An infection of the testicle and of the coiled tube behind it
Fournier gangrene: a tissue-killing infection of the groin
A trapped hernia: a loop of bowel stuck in the groin
A simple abscess: one pocket of pus in the scrotum
differential.reveal: It is Fournier gangrene: a fast-spreading infection that kills the tissue under the skin of the groin and genitals. Gas in the tissue, dead skin and a patient this sick do not fit an infected testicle, a trapped hernia or a single pocket of pus.

terms.meaning: Tissue that has died. Here infection has cut off its blood supply.
The body’s response to an infection has started to damage its own organs. Low blood pressure and a high lactate are signs of it.

ending.stable: In intensive care after surgery, with another operation planned
ending.unstable: In intensive care after surgery, with another operation planned
ending.worse: In intensive care after surgery, sicker than when he arrived
ending.critical: In intensive care after surgery, in critical condition

em-020.plainDiagnosis: A fast-spreading infection that kills the tissue under the skin of the groin and genitals (Fournier gangrene).

science.title: Why antibiotics alone cannot cure this
science.text: A medicine reaches tissue only in flowing blood. This infection clots the small vessels, so flow into the dying tissue falls to nothing and the antibiotics never arrive. Surgery removes what blood can no longer reach.

science.title: How one antibiotic switches off the toxins
science.text: Bacterial toxins are proteins, built on the bacteria’s ribosomes from their own genes. Clindamycin and linezolid jam the bacterial ribosome, so fewer toxins are made while the other antibiotics do the killing.
science.lessonTitle: Follow a gene into a protein

science.title: Why his lactate is high
science.text: A cell that is short of oxygen makes its energy by glycolysis alone, and turns pyruvate into lactate to keep glycolysis running. His lactate of 4.2 is one sign that parts of his body are not getting enough blood flow.

sources.title: IDSA practice guidelines for skin and soft tissue infections (2014)
2018 WSES/SIS-E consensus conference: management of skin and soft-tissue infections
Systematic review and meta-analysis (2020): timing of surgery in necrotizing soft tissue infections
Surviving Sepsis Campaign: international guidelines for sepsis and septic shock 2021
StatPearls: Fournier gangrene

em-033.title: Sudden belly pain, _then she nearly fainted._

start.alarm: Low blood pressure · fast heart rate

em-033.handoff: A 29-year-old woman had sudden, severe pain low in her belly an hour ago and then nearly passed out. She is pale and sweating.

interview.prompt: Ask whether she could be pregnant
interview.finding: Her last period was about seven weeks ago. She has had light bleeding from the vagina for two days. She does not always use condoms.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain and the near-faint
interview.finding: The pain came on suddenly, low on the left side of her belly, and has spread across it. Then she nearly passed out. She feels weaker and cold, and her right shoulder has started to ache.

interview.prompt: Ask about earlier pregnancies and pelvic infections
interview.finding: She had one earlier pregnancy that grew outside the womb (an ectopic pregnancy), which was treated with medicine. She has also had a pelvic infection caused by chlamydia.

exam.prompt: Check how she looks and how well blood is reaching her skin
exam.finding: Pale and sweating, with cool, clammy skin. She is slow to answer. When you press on a fingernail, the color is slow to come back.

exam.prompt: Press gently on her belly
exam.finding: Her whole belly is tender, worst low on the left, and a little swollen. Her muscles tense when you press, and it hurts more when you let go.

exam.prompt: Do a pelvic exam
exam.finding: There is a little dark blood at the opening of the womb. Moving the cervix is very painful. The area beside the womb on the left is very tender and feels full.

1.label: Bedside tests
1.content:
Urine pregnancy test: positive.
Pregnancy hormone in her blood (hCG): 4,800.
Hemoglobin, the oxygen carrier in blood: 8.1. Hers is usually 13, so she has lost a lot of blood.
Bedside ultrasound of her belly: free fluid beside the liver and in the pelvis. Free fluid there is most likely blood.
Ultrasound through the vagina: the womb is empty. There is a mass beside it on the left, and a moderate amount of fluid behind it.
Blood type: O negative.

0.resident: Her blood pressure is 84/52 and her heart rate is 126. She is pale, cold and slow to answer.
0.question: What do we do first?
options: Send her for a CT scan of her belly and pelvis to find where she is bleeding
Large IV lines, blood and the surgeon called, and a bedside pregnancy test
Start antibiotics through a vein for a suspected pelvic infection
Give methotrexate, the medicine used for a pregnancy outside the womb
0.fix: Start IV lines and call for blood

terms.meaning: Blood pressure too low to supply the organs. A fast heart, cold clammy skin and slow answers are signs of it.
A wide tube placed in a vein. Blood and fluid can run through it quickly.
A lab test that matches donor blood to the patient before a transfusion.

outcomes.story: You send her to the scanner. On the table her blood pressure drops further and she nearly passes out again. The scan has to be stopped.
outcomes.reply: A patient in shock does not leave for a scanner. Whatever is bleeding, she needs IV lines, blood and a surgeon first. A bedside ultrasound can look for blood without moving her.
outcomes.alarm: Blood pressure falling · nearly passed out

outcomes.story: Two large IV lines are in. Blood has been sent for matching, and the gynecology surgeon is on the way. The bedside tests are done, and the results are in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Good. You treated the shock and looked for the cause at the same time. In a patient this sick, neither one waits for the other.

outcomes.story: You start antibiotics for a pelvic infection and wait to see whether she improves. Twenty minutes later she is paler, and her blood pressure has dropped again.
outcomes.reply: Sudden pain, a near-faint and a missed period mean bleeding from a pregnancy in the wrong place until a test says otherwise. IV lines, blood and a pregnancy test, now.

outcomes.story: You write the order for methotrexate. The pharmacist calls before it is drawn up.
outcomes.reply: We have not even confirmed that she is pregnant. And methotrexate works over days, in a patient who is stable. She is in shock now.

3.resident: The gynecology surgeon has seen the ultrasound. She is bleeding into her belly from a burst tube.
3.question: What will stop the bleeding?
options: Methotrexate by injection, with repeat blood tests
Watch and wait, with another ultrasound in two days
Emergency surgery to remove the bleeding tube
A procedure to empty the womb (a D&C)

terms.meaning: A medicine that stops pregnancy tissue growing. It works over days and is only for an ectopic pregnancy that has not burst, in a stable patient.
Surgery to remove a fallopian tube. It stops the bleeding at its source.
A procedure that empties the inside of the womb.

outcomes.story: You write the order for methotrexate. The surgeon stops it before it is sent.
outcomes.reply: Methotrexate takes days to work and is only for an ectopic pregnancy that has not burst. Hers has, and she is bleeding now. No medicine closes a torn tube.

outcomes.story: You plan to watch her and scan again in two days. Half an hour later her blood pressure falls again, and she can barely answer you.
outcomes.reply: Watching is only ever for a stable patient whose pregnancy hormone is low and falling. She is bleeding into her belly. She goes to the operating room now.

outcomes.story: The surgeon agrees and books the operating room. It will be ready in a few minutes.
outcomes.reply: Right. Surgery finds the torn tube and removes it. That is the only thing that stops this bleeding.

outcomes.story: You ask for a D&C. The surgeon stops you.
outcomes.reply: A D&C empties the womb, and her womb is already empty. The pregnancy is in the tube, and that is where she is bleeding.

4.resident: The operating room needs a few more minutes. She is still bleeding, and her blood pressure is still low.
4.question: What do we give her while we wait?
options: More salt-water fluid, bag after bag, up to 4 liters
O-negative blood now, with more blood products ready
A medicine drip that squeezes blood vessels to raise her pressure
Tranexamic acid on its own, and check her again in 30 minutes

terms.meaning: The blood type that can be given to almost anyone in an emergency, before matching is finished. It is also her own type.
A hospital plan that sends red cells, plasma and platelets together, fast, for a patient who is bleeding heavily.
A medicine that keeps blood clots from breaking down. It can help, but it does not replace lost blood.

outcomes.story: Bag after bag of salt water runs in. Her blood pressure will not hold, and she is cold and shivering.
outcomes.reply: Salt water carries no oxygen and has nothing in it to form clots. Too much of it thins her blood and chills her, and both make bleeding worse. She needs blood.

outcomes.story: O-negative blood is running within minutes, and the blood bank sends more. She goes to the operating room with it still running. The surgeons remove the torn tube, and the bleeding stops. About an hour later she is in the recovery room.
outcomes.reply: Good. She was losing blood, so we gave her blood. It carries oxygen and helps her clot. Then surgery stopped the loss at its source.

outcomes.story: You ask for a drip to raise her blood pressure. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: That medicine squeezes the blood vessels. Her problem is that she is running out of blood to fill them. A better number on the monitor would hide the bleeding, not treat it.

outcomes.story: The tranexamic acid goes in, and you wait. Half an hour later she is barely awake, and her heart is racing even faster.
outcomes.reply: Tranexamic acid can help a clot hold, alongside blood. It cannot replace the blood she has lost, and it cannot close a torn tube. She needs blood now.

5.resident: She is out of surgery. The torn tube has been removed and the bleeding has stopped. Her blood type is O negative.
5.question: What else does she need?
options: Nothing more. The surgery fixed the problem
An injection of anti-D
Iron tablets, and home later today
Antibiotics for two weeks, to prevent infection

terms.meaning: Red blood cells either carry a protein called Rh (D) or they do not. Hers do not, which is the “negative” in O negative.
Ready-made antibodies, given by injection. They clear away any Rh-positive cells before her body learns to attack them.
When the immune system has learned to attack Rh-positive blood. It can harm a baby in a later pregnancy.

outcomes.story: You write “no further treatment” in the plan. The resident points to her blood type before it is signed.
outcomes.reply: One thing is left. Her blood is Rh negative, and a US guideline still advises anti-D after an ectopic pregnancy, to protect a later pregnancy. UK guidance changed in 2026 and no longer gives it this early, so the rule depends on where she is treated. Here, she is offered it.

outcomes.story: The anti-D is ordered and given as an injection, well inside the 72 hours allowed for it.
outcomes.reply: Good. Her blood is Rh negative. If the pregnancy’s blood was Rh positive, her immune system could learn to attack it, and that can harm a later pregnancy. Anti-D prevents that. A US guideline still advises it after an ectopic pregnancy. UK guidance changed in 2026 and no longer gives it this early, so the rule depends on where she is treated.

outcomes.story: You plan iron tablets and a discharge for this afternoon. The nurse asks the resident to look at the plan.
outcomes.reply: She lost a lot of blood and had emergency surgery today. She needs to be watched, with her blood count checked again. And iron does nothing about her Rh-negative blood.

outcomes.story: You write for two weeks of antibiotics. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: This was bleeding, not an infection. The antibiotic given around the operation is enough. Two weeks more would bring side effects and no benefit.

differential.resident: The bedside tests are in her chart. Put them together with her pain and her blood pressure.
differential.question: What explains all of this?
options: A normal pregnancy in the womb, with a harmless cyst on the ovary
A pregnancy in a fallopian tube that has burst and is bleeding
A pregnancy in the womb that is at risk of miscarriage
A bleeding cyst on the ovary that has nothing to do with pregnancy
differential.reveal: It is a pregnancy in a fallopian tube that has burst, called a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. No single test proves it. A positive pregnancy test, an empty womb, a mass beside it, fluid in the belly and shock together make it the emergency to act on.

terms.meaning: A pregnancy that implants outside the womb, most often in a fallopian tube. The tube cannot stretch, so it can tear and bleed.
The tube that carries an egg from the ovary to the womb.

ending.better: In the recovery room after surgery, with the bleeding stopped
ending.stable: In the recovery room after surgery, with the bleeding stopped
ending.worse: In intensive care after surgery
ending.critical: In intensive care after surgery, in critical condition

em-033.plainDiagnosis: A pregnancy growing in a fallopian tube that burst and bled into her belly (a ruptured ectopic pregnancy).

science.title: Why the IV lines have to be wide
science.text: In the simple model of smooth flow, the flow through a tube rises with the fourth power of its radius. A line twice as wide can carry about sixteen times as much at the same pressure, and that is how blood gets into her fast enough.

science.title: Why salt water cannot stand in for blood
science.text: Almost all the oxygen in blood rides on hemoglobin. Hers fell from 13 to 8.1, so each liter of her blood carries far less oxygen, even though the monitor reads 98%. That number shows how full each hemoglobin is, not how much hemoglobin is left.

science.title: Why her blood type still matters after surgery
science.text: Rh negative is a recessive trait: she has no working copy of the Rh (D) gene. A pregnancy gets one copy from each parent, so with a working copy from the other parent its red cells are Rh positive. Her immune system can treat those cells as foreign.

sources.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 193: tubal ectopic pregnancy
MSD Manual Professional: ectopic pregnancy
Damage control resuscitation (Military Medicine, 2018)
Review: resuscitation of hemorrhagic shock with blood products rather than crystalloid
ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 181: prevention of Rh D alloimmunization
ACOG Clinical Practice Update (2024): Rh D immune globulin after abortion or pregnancy loss before 12 weeks
NICE guideline NG126: anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis (updated June 2026)

em-101.title: She went down _at the blood draw._
em-101.setting: Emergency department, after a collapse in a clinic
em-101.handoff: A 22-year-old woman passed out for about 20 seconds while watching a friend have blood drawn. She is awake now and feels well.

interview.prompt: Ask the nurse who saw it what happened
interview.finding: She had been standing for a long time at the blood draw. She felt hot and sweaty, then went down. She looked pale, her arms and legs jerked three times, and she woke within about 20 seconds, knowing where she was.

interview.prompt: Ask about exercise, her heart and her family
interview.finding: She was not exercising. She felt no pounding heartbeat and no chest pain. She has no known heart disease, and no one in her family has died suddenly at a young age.

interview.prompt: Ask whether she was hurt and how she feels now
interview.finding: The nurse caught her and lowered her to the floor. She did not hit her head or bite her tongue. She feels back to normal.

exam.prompt: Check how alert she is and look for injuries
exam.finding: Wide awake and clear-headed. Her strength and speech are normal, and she has no injuries.

exam.prompt: Listen to her heart and feel her pulse
exam.finding: Her pulse is regular. Her heart sounds are normal, with no whooshing sounds. Her vital signs are steady.

exam.prompt: Help her stand up and see how she feels
exam.finding: With someone beside her, she stands without feeling faint.

1.label: First checks
1.content:
The nurse’s account: a warm, sweaty feeling while standing for a long time at the blood draw, then a pale collapse, and a clear head as soon as she woke.
Heart tracing (ECG): a normal rhythm with normal timing. Nothing abnormal is reported.
No warning sign of a heart or brain problem was found in this assessment.

0.resident: She is awake, comfortable and back to normal. We still need to know what kind of collapse this was.
0.question: How do we start?
options: Book a brain-wave test (EEG) and a first-seizure clinic visit
Go over what the nurse saw, examine her, and get a heart tracing (ECG)
Get a CT scan of her head and watch her for a few hours
Get a heart ultrasound and book an exercise test
0.fix: Start with the story, the exam and an ECG

terms.meaning: A tracing of the heart’s electrical signals. It takes a few minutes and can show a dangerous rhythm problem.
A recording of the brain’s electrical activity, used when a seizure disorder is suspected.
What someone saw before, during and after a collapse. It is often the most useful clue there is.

outcomes.story: You start the referral to the seizure clinic. The resident reads it over your shoulder.
outcomes.reply: A few jerks do not make it a seizure. Jerking is common in a simple faint. We need the whole story first: what came before, during and after.

outcomes.story: The nurse walks you through it from start to finish. You examine her, and the heart tracing is done at the bedside. All of it is in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Good. The order of events tells us more than any scan. And everyone who blacks out gets a heart tracing, because the heart is the cause we cannot afford to miss.

outcomes.story: You fill in the request for a head CT. The resident stops it before it is sent.
outcomes.reply: She did not hit her head, and her exam is normal. A scan would give her radiation and no answer. The story and a heart tracing come first.

outcomes.story: You request a heart ultrasound and an exercise test. The resident holds the forms.
outcomes.reply: Those are for when the story, the exam or the heart tracing points to the heart. We have not done those yet. We start there.

3.resident: Everything so far points to a simple faint, and she feels well.
3.question: What is the right plan?
options: Explain what happened, how to head off the next one, and when to come back
Send her for seizure testing first, then decide on follow-up
Do a tilt-table test to prove the cause before giving any advice
Fit a heart monitor to wear at home, and hold the advice until the results are in

terms.meaning: What sets off the reflex. For her it was watching a blood draw while standing for a long time.
Feeling hot, sweaty or sick just before a faint. They are the cue to sit or lie down.
A test that tilts a patient upright, while they are watched, to bring on a faint. It is for cases where the cause is unclear.

outcomes.story: You sit down with her and explain the reflex, her triggers and the warning signs. If she feels hot and sweaty again, she should lie down, or sit and tense her legs and hands. A follow-up visit is booked, and she knows that a second collapse, or one that is different, needs a fresh look.
outcomes.reply: That is the right size of plan. One normal heart tracing is reassuring. It is not a promise about every future event, so we tell her that too.

outcomes.story: You start the seizure clinic referral. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: Nothing in her story points to a seizure, so this would be a test with no question to answer. A clear faint is managed with an explanation and follow-up.

outcomes.story: You request a tilt-table test and plan to hold the advice until it is done. The resident cancels the request.
outcomes.reply: That test is for when the cause is unclear. Hers is clear from the story. And she needs the advice today, before her next blood draw.

outcomes.story: You ask for a take-home heart monitor and plan to say nothing until the results are back. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Her story, her exam and her heart tracing gave no sign of a heart cause. A monitor is for when one of them does. Either way, she should not leave without knowing what to do if it happens again.

4.resident: Last step. Her discharge sheet should name the kind of collapse that is not a simple faint and needs an urgent heart check.
4.question: Which one do we write down?
options: A collapse that comes after feeling warm and sweaty for a few moments
A collapse where she turns pale and looks unwell to people nearby
A collapse she wakes from within seconds, knowing where she is
A collapse during exercise, or a sudden early death in the family

terms.meaning: A blackout in the middle of hard effort. It can mean a heart rhythm problem, and it needs an urgent heart check.
A close relative who died suddenly and without explanation at a young age can point to a heart condition that runs in families.

outcomes.story: You start to write “come back if you feel warm before a collapse”. The resident reads it before it is printed.
outcomes.reply: That warm feeling is the usual warning of a simple faint. It is reassuring. The warning to write down is a collapse during exercise, or a close relative who died suddenly when young.

outcomes.story: You start to write “come back if you turn pale”. The resident reads it before it is printed.
outcomes.reply: Turning pale is what a simple faint looks like. It does not point to the heart. The one that does is a collapse during exercise, or a close relative who died suddenly when young.

outcomes.story: You start to write “come back if you wake up quickly”. The resident reads it before it is printed.
outcomes.reply: Waking fast with a clear head is typical of a simple faint. The warning that matters is a collapse during exercise, or a close relative who died suddenly when young.

outcomes.story: You write it on her discharge sheet and go through it with her. She reads it back to you.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. Either of those changes the picture, even when the collapse itself looks just like today’s. Neither was true for her today.

differential.resident: The nurse’s account and the heart tracing are in her chart. Put the whole story together.
differential.question: What best explains her collapse?
options: A first seizure: a burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain
A heart rhythm problem that briefly stopped blood reaching the brain
A simple faint: a reflex that briefly drops her blood pressure
A drop in blood pressure on standing, from being low on fluid
differential.reveal: It fits a simple faint best. There was a trigger, a warning of warmth and sweating, a pale collapse and a clear head within seconds. A few jerks can happen in a faint. This is a working diagnosis, not a certainty.

terms.meaning: A reflex set off by things like the sight of blood, pain or long standing. The heart slows and the blood vessels widen, so the brain is briefly short of blood.
The best explanation for now. It is changed if new facts do not fit.

ending.stable: Going home with a plan for next time
ending.worse: Kept in the emergency department for more checks

em-101.plainDiagnosis: A simple faint (vasovagal syncope), set off by watching a blood draw while standing.

science.title: What the reflex did to her blood pressure
science.text: Blood pressure comes from blood flow pushing against the resistance of the vessels. The faint reflex slowed her heart, which cut the flow, and widened her vessels, which cut the resistance. Both at once dropped the pressure.

science.title: Why lying flat woke her up
science.text: While she stood, her brain was well above her heart, and blood had to be pushed up that height against gravity. On the floor her brain was level with her heart, so even a low pressure was enough to supply it.

sources.title: NICE guideline CG109: transient loss of consciousness (“blackouts”) in over 16s, recommendations
2018 ESC guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope
StatPearls: vasovagal episode

cd-001.title: A tight chest _on every hill._
cd-001.handoff: A 61-year-old man gets a tight band across his chest whenever he walks uphill. It goes away within minutes of stopping. It has been the same for three months.

interview.prompt: Ask him to describe the chest discomfort
interview.finding: It feels like a tight band behind his breastbone that spreads to his left shoulder. It lasts three to five minutes and is gone within minutes of resting.

interview.prompt: Ask what brings it on, and whether it is changing
interview.finding: It comes on every time after about two blocks uphill or two flights of stairs. It has not changed in three months. He has never had it at rest or at night.

interview.prompt: Ask about his risks and his medicines
interview.finding: He has high blood pressure and high cholesterol. He smokes half a pack a day and has smoked for decades. His father had a heart attack at 58. He often forgets his cholesterol tablet.

exam.prompt: Listen to his heart and lungs, and look at his neck veins
exam.finding: His heartbeat is regular, with normal sounds and nothing extra. His lungs are clear, and the veins in his neck are not swollen.

exam.prompt: Feel his pulses and check for swelling
exam.finding: His pulses are strong and equal on both sides. There is no whooshing sound over the arteries in his neck or groin, no swelling in his legs and no pulsing lump in his belly.

exam.prompt: Press on his chest and move his arm, to see if that brings on the pain
exam.finding: Pressing on his chest does not hurt. Moving his arm or taking a deep breath does not bring the pain on.

1.label: Heart tracing and blood tests
1.content:
Heart tracing (ECG) at rest: a normal rhythm at 74 beats a minute, with no sign of an old heart attack and no sign of strain.
Red blood cell level (hemoglobin): normal, so he is not anemic.
Kidney function: normal.
Blood sugar: slightly above normal, below the diabetes range (HbA1c 5.8%).
“Bad” cholesterol (LDL): 128 mg/dL, higher than it should be for someone with his risks.
Thyroid test: normal.

3.label: Treadmill test
3.content:
He walked on the treadmill for 7 minutes and reached a moderate workload (8.5 METs).
At peak effort his usual chest pressure came on. At the same time the heart tracing showed a pattern of strain (the ST segment dipped 1.5 mm) in the leads over the front and side of the heart.
Both the pressure and the tracing went back to normal within 3 minutes of rest.
His blood pressure rose as it should. No dangerous rhythm appeared.
Overall risk on the test’s score: intermediate.

0.resident: His story is steady and predictable, and he is comfortable right now. We start simple.
0.question: Which test do we get first, here in the clinic?
options: Dye pictures of his heart arteries through a thin tube (angiogram)
A heart tracing at rest (ECG)
A CT scan that measures the calcium in his heart arteries
An urgent blood test for heart damage and a trip to the emergency department
An ultrasound of his heart (echocardiogram)

terms.meaning: A tracing of the heart’s electrical signals. It takes a few minutes and cannot hurt the patient.
X-ray pictures of the heart’s arteries, taken by passing a thin tube up from the wrist or groin and injecting dye. It is an invasive test, with small but real risks.
A protein that leaks into the blood when heart muscle is damaged. It is the blood test for a heart attack.

outcomes.story: You start the referral for an angiogram. The resident reads it before it is sent.
outcomes.reply: That is a tube inside his heart arteries, with real risks. He is stable, so we begin with tests that cannot hurt him and see what they show.

outcomes.story: The nurse runs the tracing in the clinic room. It takes a few minutes. Blood is drawn for some basic tests while he is here, and the results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Good. It is quick and harmless. It can show an old heart attack, and it tells us whether a simple treadmill test will be readable.

outcomes.story: You fill in the request for a calcium scan. The resident holds the form.
outcomes.reply: A calcium scan shows how much hardened plaque he has. It cannot show whether a narrowing is choking off blood flow when he walks, and that is the question his symptoms are asking.

outcomes.story: You start to arrange an ambulance to the emergency department. The resident stops you at the desk.
outcomes.reply: That is the right call for chest pain at rest, or pain that is getting worse or more frequent. His comes only with effort, goes with rest and has not changed in three months. He can be worked up here.

outcomes.story: You request a heart ultrasound. The resident sets the request aside.
outcomes.reply: An ultrasound is the test when we suspect a weak heart or a faulty valve: breathlessness, swollen legs, a murmur. He has none of those. The tracing comes first.

2.resident: His tracing at rest is normal, and he walks every day with no trouble from his joints.
2.question: How do we test his heart under strain?
options: A treadmill test with a heart tracing, and no scan
A scan using adenosine, a drug that stands in for exercise
A heart ultrasound using dobutamine, a drug that makes the heart work harder
Dye pictures of his heart arteries through a thin tube (angiogram)
A heart monitor worn at home for 48 hours

terms.meaning: A test that makes the heart work hard, by exercise or by a drug, while the team watches for signs that part of it is short of blood.
Heart muscle that is not getting enough blood for the work it is doing.
A small recorder worn for a day or two that tracks the heart’s rhythm.

outcomes.story: The clinic’s exercise lab fits him in. He walks on the treadmill while the slope and speed go up every three minutes, with a tracing running the whole time. The report goes in his chart.
outcomes.reply: He can exercise and his resting tracing is easy to read, so a plain treadmill test is a reasonable choice. A scan-based test would also have been acceptable. This shows whether effort leaves his heart short of blood. It does not show the arteries themselves.

outcomes.story: You request the adenosine scan. The resident reads the form.
outcomes.reply: A drug stands in for exercise when a patient cannot walk on a treadmill. He can. Exercise also shows us how much he can do and what brings the pain on.

outcomes.story: You request the dobutamine ultrasound. The resident reads the form.
outcomes.reply: Dobutamine is for people who cannot exercise. He walks every day. We let his own legs do the work.

outcomes.story: You start a referral for an angiogram. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Too soon. He is stable, and we have not yet shown that effort leaves his heart short of blood. An invasive test waits until there is a reason for it.

outcomes.story: You ask for a 48-hour heart monitor. The resident sets it aside.
outcomes.reply: That monitor looks for rhythm problems, like skipped or racing beats. His problem is pain with effort. A monitor would not tell us whether his heart muscle is short of blood.

5.resident: The treadmill test brought on his usual pressure, and the tracing showed strain at the same moment. He needs a medicine plan, along with work on his risks.
5.question: Which plan eases his angina day to day and also gives him something for an attack?
options: Ranolazine every day
A long-acting nitrate every day, and nothing else
Metoprolol every day, plus a nitroglycerin tablet under the tongue when pain starts
Send him now for a stent to open the artery
Diltiazem and verapamil together
5.fix: Start metoprolol and give him nitroglycerin

terms.meaning: Chest pain or pressure that comes when the heart muscle needs more blood than its arteries can deliver.
A medicine that slows the heart and softens each beat, so the heart needs less oxygen.
A tablet or spray under the tongue that relaxes blood vessels within minutes and eases an attack.
A tiny mesh tube placed inside a narrowed artery to hold it open.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for ranolazine alone. The pharmacist calls the clinic before filling it.
outcomes.reply: Ranolazine is an add-on for people whose pain continues on the first medicines. It does not slow the heart, and it gives him nothing to take when the pain comes on.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for a long-acting nitrate on its own. The resident reads it before he leaves.
outcomes.reply: A long-acting nitrate can ease angina through the day, but it does not slow the heart, and it works too slowly to stop an attack that has started. He would have nothing to take on the hill.

outcomes.story: You go through it with him: metoprolol every morning, and a nitroglycerin tablet under the tongue if the pressure comes on. If it has not eased five minutes after one tablet, he calls an ambulance. His cholesterol medicine is stepped up, a low-dose aspirin is added, and you talk about stopping smoking. A follow-up visit is booked.
outcomes.reply: That covers both jobs: fewer attacks, and a way to stop one. A calcium channel blocker would also have been a fair first choice. And if the pain ever comes at rest, or more often, that is an emergency visit and not a clinic one.

outcomes.story: You start an urgent referral for a stent. The resident takes the form.
outcomes.reply: For stable angina like his, a large trial found that starting with medicines prevented heart attacks and deaths about as well as going straight to a procedure. A stent is for pain that persists on good medicines, or for high-risk findings. We start with medicines.

outcomes.story: You write for diltiazem and verapamil together. The pharmacist calls before filling it.
outcomes.reply: Those two are the same kind of medicine, and both slow the heart’s electrical signals. Together they can slow the heart dangerously. He would also still have nothing for an attack.

differential.resident: The treadmill report is in his chart. Put it together with his story.
differential.question: What is this chest pressure?
options: Unstable angina: heart pain that is new, getting worse or coming at rest
Artery spasm (vasospastic angina): a heart artery clamps down, usually at rest or at night
Acid reflux: stomach acid rising into the food pipe
Stable angina: predictable heart pain with effort, most likely from a narrowed artery
A badly narrowed heart valve (aortic stenosis) straining the heart
differential.reveal: It is stable angina. The pressure comes at the same level of effort every time, goes with rest and has not changed in three months, and the treadmill test brought it on together with signs of strain. A narrowed heart artery is the likely cause, but no one has seen the artery yet. Pain at rest, or a pattern that is getting worse, would make it unstable and urgent.

terms.meaning: The same trigger, the same pain and the same relief, week after week.
The arteries that feed the heart muscle itself.

ending.stable: Going home with a medicine plan and a follow-up visit
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department for more tests

cd-001.plainDiagnosis: Predictable chest pain with effort (stable angina), most likely from a narrowed heart artery.

science.title: Why the pressure only comes on hills
science.text: If one of his heart arteries is narrowed, as the test suggests, enough blood still gets past it at rest. On a hill his heart needs several times more, and flow through a narrow tube cannot rise to match. The muscle downstream runs short, and that is the pressure he feels.

science.title: Why heart muscle cannot wait for oxygen
science.text: Heart muscle makes almost all of its ATP using oxygen, and it stores very little. When the oxygen supply falls behind the work, the muscle signals trouble within moments. When he stops walking, the demand drops and the pain fades.

science.title: How his two medicines help
science.text: Metoprolol slows his heart and softens each beat, so the muscle needs less oxygen. Nitroglycerin relaxes his veins, so less blood returns to the heart. A less full heart does less work with each beat.

sources.title: 2023 AHA/ACC guideline: management of patients with chronic coronary disease
2021 AHA/ACC guideline: evaluation and diagnosis of chest pain
ISCHEMIA trial (NEJM 2020): initial invasive or conservative strategy for stable coronary disease

cd-006.title: A heartbeat that _lost its rhythm._

start.alarm: Fast, irregular heart rate

cd-006.handoff: A 68-year-old man has felt his heart pounding and fluttering since breakfast, six hours ago. He gets a little short of breath when he walks. He drank much more than usual at a wedding last night.

interview.prompt: Ask when it started and what else he feels
interview.finding: It began all at once six hours ago. He is a little short of breath when he walks, and tired. No chest pain, no fainting, no fever and no cough.

interview.prompt: Ask what might have set it off
interview.finding: He had five or six drinks at a wedding last night, far more than his usual one or two. He takes no cold remedies or stimulants.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health and his risk of stroke
interview.finding: He is 68, with high blood pressure and diabetes. He has never had a stroke, heart failure or blocked arteries.

exam.prompt: Listen to his heart and feel his pulse
exam.finding: Fast and completely irregular, with no pattern to it. Some beats are too weak to reach his wrist, so the pulse there is slower than the heartbeat you hear.

exam.prompt: Check that enough blood is reaching his body, and look for fluid backing up
exam.finding: He is alert, with warm hands and feet. His lungs are clear, the veins in his neck are not swollen and his legs are not swollen.

exam.prompt: Check his thyroid gland and look for a tremor
exam.finding: His thyroid gland is a normal size, with no lumps. His hands are steady.

1.label: Heart tracing and tests
1.content:
Heart tracing (ECG): a completely irregular rhythm at 138 to 152 beats a minute. The small wave that should come before each beat (the P wave) is missing, and the baseline quivers instead. The beats themselves are narrow, and there is no sign of strain on the heart muscle.
Blood test for heart damage (troponin): normal.
Blood salts, kidney function and thyroid test: normal.
Blood sugar: 162, raised, as expected with his diabetes.
Blood count: normal.
Chest X-ray: a normal-sized heart and clear lungs.
Heart ultrasound on file: a normal squeeze (60%), with no badly narrowed valve and no artificial valve.

0.resident: He is awake and talking in full sentences. His blood pressure is fine, and his pulse is fast and uneven.
0.question: What do we do first?
options: Shock his heart back to a normal rhythm right away
Get a 12-lead heart tracing (ECG)
Push adenosine into a vein
Send him for a CT scan to look for a clot in his lungs
Press on the artery in his neck to slow the heart

terms.meaning: A tracing of the heart’s electrical signals. It takes a few minutes and cannot hurt the patient.
A timed electric shock that resets the heart’s rhythm. The patient is sedated for it.
Blood pressure holding, thinking clearly, no chest pain and no fluid in the lungs. A stable patient gives the team time to find out what the rhythm is.

outcomes.story: You ask for the shock pads and sedation. The resident stops the cart before anyone opens it.
outcomes.reply: A shock is for a patient who is crashing: low blood pressure, chest pain, confusion, fluid in the lungs. He has none of those. And we do not yet know what rhythm we would be shocking.

outcomes.story: The tracing is run at the bedside in a couple of minutes, and blood is drawn at the same time. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Name the rhythm before you treat it. The tracing also checks for a heart attack, and for wiring problems that would change which medicines are safe.

outcomes.story: You ask the nurse to draw up adenosine. The resident stops the syringe.
outcomes.reply: Adenosine stops rhythms that run in a loop through the heart’s relay station, and those are regular. His pulse is completely irregular. We need the tracing before any rhythm medicine.

outcomes.story: He is wheeled to the scanner for a CT of his lungs. It shows no clot. Forty minutes later he is back in his bay with his heart still racing, and he is more breathless than when he left.
outcomes.reply: Nothing in his story pointed to a lung clot: no sharp pain on breathing in, no low oxygen, no swollen leg. He has spent forty more minutes with a racing heart and no one knowing his rhythm. The tracing takes two minutes. We do it now.
outcomes.alarm: Still racing · more short of breath

outcomes.story: You reach for his neck. The resident catches your hand.
outcomes.reply: That maneuver is for fast rhythms that are regular. His is plainly irregular, so it would tell us nothing. In an older patient, pressing on a neck artery can also, rarely, cause a stroke.

3.resident: The tracing shows atrial fibrillation at about 145. His blood pressure is holding, his heart’s squeeze is normal, and there is no sign of an extra electrical pathway.
3.question: How do we treat him right now?
options: Diltiazem through a vein, to slow the heart rate
Shock his heart back to a normal rhythm right away
Adenosine, pushed fast into a vein
Amiodarone, a strong rhythm medicine, through a vein
Digoxin tablets, starting with a large first dose

terms.meaning: Slowing how often the lower chambers beat, without trying to fix the rhythm itself. It eases symptoms and takes strain off the heart.
A medicine that blocks calcium channels in the heart’s relay station, so fewer signals get through to the lower chambers.
The one normal electrical link between the heart’s upper and lower chambers.
An old heart medicine that slows the relay station. It can take an hour or more to start working.

outcomes.story: The diltiazem goes in over two minutes, with the monitor running. Within a quarter of an hour his rate settles to 92. The rhythm is still irregular, but he says the pounding has eased and he can breathe more easily.
outcomes.reply: That is the goal for now: a slower rate. His heart is still in atrial fibrillation. Whether to reset the rhythm is a decision for later, once his stroke risk has been dealt with.

outcomes.story: You ask for the shock pads. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He is stable, so there is no need to shock him now. A shock also carries a stroke risk if a clot has formed in the heart, so the team plans it with blood thinning in mind. First we slow the rate.

outcomes.story: You ask for adenosine. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: Adenosine blocks the relay station for a few seconds and then wears off. It does not stop atrial fibrillation, so his heart would be racing again before the syringe was put down.

outcomes.story: You write the order for amiodarone. The pharmacist calls before it is mixed.
outcomes.reply: Amiodarone is kept for patients who are very sick or whose heart is failing. It can also flip the rhythm back to normal without warning, before his stroke risk has been dealt with. He has a simpler, faster choice.

outcomes.story: He swallows the first digoxin tablets. An hour later his heart is still racing at over 140. He is more tired and more breathless, and his blood pressure has started to slip.
outcomes.reply: Digoxin by mouth takes hours to slow the heart, and it works poorly when the body is revved up. He has now spent another hour racing. His pressure is still good enough for diltiazem, so we give it now.

4.resident: His rate is down to 92 and he feels better. Atrial fibrillation lets blood pool in the heart’s upper chambers, where clots can form and travel to the brain. He is 68, with high blood pressure and diabetes.
4.question: How do we protect him from a stroke?
options: A low-dose aspirin every day
Nothing, because the episode has lasted less than 48 hours
Warfarin, but only if the rate medicine stops working
Start a blood thinner such as apixaban
Aspirin plus clopidogrel

terms.meaning: A medicine that slows the clotting proteins in the blood. It does not actually thin it.
One of the newer blood thinners (a DOAC). It needs no regular blood test, unlike warfarin.
A points score built from age, blood pressure, diabetes and other conditions. He scores 3: one each for his age, his blood pressure and his diabetes.
Medicines that make platelets less sticky. They act on a different part of clotting than a blood thinner does.

outcomes.story: You write for a daily aspirin. The pharmacist calls to check.
outcomes.reply: Aspirin does little to stop the kind of clot that forms in a fibrillating heart, and it still causes bleeding. For someone at his level of risk, the guidelines advise against using it in place of a blood thinner.

outcomes.story: You tell him he needs nothing more, since it has only been six hours. The resident steps back into the room.
outcomes.reply: The 48-hour mark matters when planning a shock. It says nothing about his long-term risk. Atrial fibrillation often comes back, and his age, blood pressure and diabetes put him in the group that benefits from a blood thinner.

outcomes.story: You plan to hold off unless the rate medicine fails. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Stroke risk does not depend on how well the rate is controlled. A slow, comfortable heart in atrial fibrillation can still form a clot. The decision rests on his risk score.

outcomes.story: You check his kidney function and his bleeding risk, and ask about anything that would rule a blood thinner out. Then you go through apixaban with him: twice a day, no skipped doses, and what bleeding to watch for. He is asked to cut back on alcohol, and a heart clinic visit is booked.
outcomes.reply: Good. His risk score drives the decision, not the length of this episode. Apixaban fits because he has no artificial valve and no badly narrowed mitral valve.

outcomes.story: You write for aspirin with clopidogrel. The pharmacist calls before filling it.
outcomes.reply: The guidelines advise against that pair too. Two platelet medicines add bleeding risk and protect him less than a blood thinner would. A blood thinner is the right tool for this kind of clot.

differential.resident: The heart tracing is in his chart. Look at the rhythm, then tell me what it is.
differential.question: What rhythm is this?
options: Multifocal atrial tachycardia: several spots in the upper chambers fire in turn, mostly in people with severe lung disease
Atrial flutter: the upper chambers beat in a fast, regular loop, giving a steady pulse near 150
Atrial fibrillation: the upper chambers quiver, so the pulse is fast and completely irregular
A short circuit near the relay station (AVNRT): fast and perfectly regular
A fast but normal rhythm with frequent early beats
differential.reveal: It is atrial fibrillation with a fast heart rate. The rhythm has no pattern at all, and the small wave that should come before each beat is missing because the upper chambers are quivering instead of squeezing. A night of heavy drinking is a well-known trigger, sometimes called “holiday heart”.

terms.meaning: To do with the atria, the heart’s two upper chambers.
Fast, disorganized quivering in place of a coordinated beat.

ending.better: Heart rate controlled and on a blood thinner, with a heart clinic visit booked
ending.stable: Heart rate controlled and on a blood thinner, with a heart clinic visit booked
ending.worse: Still on the monitor in the emergency department

cd-006.plainDiagnosis: A fast, irregular heart rhythm from quivering upper chambers (atrial fibrillation), most likely set off by heavy drinking.

science.title: Why his pulse had no pattern
science.text: Normally one spot in the upper chambers fires and the signal spreads in order. In atrial fibrillation, signals swirl through the upper chambers hundreds of times a minute. The relay station lets only some of them through, at uneven intervals, so his pulse was fast and irregular.

science.title: How diltiazem slowed him down
science.text: The cells of the relay station fire by letting calcium flow in through channels in their membranes. Diltiazem blocks those channels. Each cell takes longer to be ready to fire again, so fewer signals reach the lower chambers.

science.title: How apixaban lowers his stroke risk
science.text: Blood that pools in a quivering upper chamber can clot. Clotting is a chain of enzymes, each switching on the next. Apixaban sits in the active site of one of them, factor Xa, and competes with its normal target, so the chain slows down.

sources.title: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline: diagnosis and management of atrial fibrillation
2023 atrial fibrillation guideline: recommendations for acute rate control
AVERROES trial (NEJM 2011): apixaban versus aspirin in atrial fibrillation
2015 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline: management of adults with supraventricular tachycardia
AHA guidelines: adult advanced life support (2025)
StatPearls: adenosine
StatPearls: amiodarone

cd-055.title: Down on the court, _mid-sprint._
cd-055.handoff: A 17-year-old basketball player collapsed during a game yesterday while sprinting. He was out for about 20 seconds and woke up clear-headed. He feels fine today.

interview.prompt: Ask exactly what happened when he went down and when he woke
interview.finding: He fell with no warning in the middle of a sprint. His coach says he was out for about 20 seconds. He woke knowing where he was, with no confusion, no bitten tongue and no loss of bladder control.

interview.prompt: Ask whether anything like this has happened before during exercise
interview.finding: Twice this season he felt lightheaded during sprints. He sometimes gets a tight chest when he pushes hard. He put it down to being out of shape and told no one.

interview.prompt: Ask about heart problems in his family
interview.finding: His father’s brother died suddenly at 38 while swimming. It was called a heart attack, and no autopsy was done. His father was once told he has “thick heart walls” and never followed it up.

exam.prompt: Listen to his heart while he bears down, stands, squats and grips
exam.finding: There is a harsh whooshing sound (a murmur) with each beat, low on the left side of his breastbone. It gets louder when he bears down or stands up, and softer when he squats or squeezes his fists.

exam.prompt: Feel his heartbeat on his chest and the pulse in his neck
exam.finding: The heartbeat against his chest wall is forceful but in the normal place. There is an extra heart sound just before each beat. The pulse in his neck rises fast and has a double tap.

exam.prompt: Check his nervous system and look for fluid backing up
exam.finding: His strength, sensation, balance and reflexes are normal. The veins in his neck are not swollen, his lungs are clear and his legs are not swollen.

1.label: Heart tracing and ultrasound
1.content:
Heart tracing (ECG): a normal rhythm, but with the tall signals of a thickened heart and abnormal patterns (deep Q waves and flipped T waves) in the leads over the left side.
Heart ultrasound (echo): the wall between the two lower chambers is 21 mm thick, about twice normal. The back wall is a normal 9 mm.
With each beat, a flap of the mitral valve is pulled toward that thick wall and partly blocks the way out of the heart. Some blood also leaks backward through the valve.
Pressure drop across the blockage: 60 mmHg at rest, rising to 95 when he bears down. Normally there is almost none.
The heart squeezes strongly (70%). The valve that leads out of the heart is normal.
Blood test for heart damage, blood count and thyroid test: normal.

0.resident: A blackout in the middle of hard exercise, with no warning, is never brushed off. And there is that murmur.
0.question: What do we do next?
options: Put him on a treadmill today, to see if exercise brings it on again
A heart tracing (ECG) and a heart ultrasound
A tilt-table test, looking for a simple faint
A brain-wave test (EEG) and a visit to the nerve specialists, in case it was a seizure
Tell the family that fainting is common in teenagers, and send him home
0.fix: Get the heart tracing and the ultrasound

terms.meaning: Moving pictures of the heart made with sound waves. It shows how thick the walls are and how blood flows through.
A reflex that briefly drops the blood pressure. It usually happens while standing still, after a warning of warmth, sweating or nausea.
A test that tilts a patient upright, while they are watched, to bring on a faint. It is for cases where the cause is unclear.

outcomes.story: He starts on the treadmill with a tracing running. A few minutes in, as the slope steepens, he turns pale and says the room is going gray. His blood pressure has fallen when it should be climbing. The test is stopped and he is laid flat. He feels normal again within a minute.
outcomes.reply: Exercise is what made him black out yesterday, and we have not looked at his heart yet. An exercise test can be useful later, at a heart center, with the right team watching. Not today. Now we get the tracing and the ultrasound.
outcomes.alarm: Nearly passed out on the treadmill · blood pressure fell with exercise

outcomes.story: The tracing takes a few minutes. The ultrasound is done down the hall, and he lies still for it. The reports go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. When a young athlete blacks out during exercise, you look at the heart first: its electrical pattern and its structure. Everything else waits.

outcomes.story: You request a tilt-table test. The resident sets the form aside.
outcomes.reply: A tilt test is for repeated faints once the heart has been cleared. A simple faint comes on while standing still, with a warning. He went down mid-sprint with none. The heart comes first.

outcomes.story: You start the referral for a brain-wave test. The resident reads it over your shoulder.
outcomes.reply: Nothing here looks like a seizure. He had no warning feeling and no bitten tongue, and he woke clear-headed. A blackout during hard exercise points to the heart.

outcomes.story: You begin to tell his mother it was a simple faint. The resident steps in before she picks up her bag.
outcomes.reply: This is the one kind of faint we never wave through. A blackout during exercise with no warning, a murmur, and a relative who died suddenly at 38: each is a red flag for a dangerous heart condition. He does not leave without a heart check.

3.resident: The ultrasound shows a very thick heart wall that partly blocks the way out with every beat. The blockage gets worse when his heart is less full.
3.question: What is the plan now?
options: Start lisinopril, to relax his arteries and shrink the muscle
Start furosemide, a water tablet, to lower the pressure across the blockage
Start verapamil, with nitroglycerin under the tongue for chest tightness
Start a beta-blocker, and send him urgently to heart specialists to be assessed for an implanted defibrillator
3.fix: Start a beta-blocker and refer him

terms.meaning: A medicine that slows the heart and softens each beat. A slower heart has longer to fill, and a fuller heart is less blocked.
A small device under the skin that watches the heart’s rhythm and gives a shock if a deadly rhythm starts.
A medicine that relaxes blood vessels. Lisinopril and nitroglycerin are two.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for lisinopril. The resident reads it before it is printed.
outcomes.reply: Lisinopril relaxes the arteries. With less to push against, his heart empties faster and more completely, and the thick wall and the valve flap close in on each other. The blockage gets worse. And it has not been shown to shrink this kind of muscle.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for furosemide. The pharmacist calls the clinic before filling it.
outcomes.reply: A water tablet drains fluid, so his heart fills less. In this condition a less full heart is a more blocked heart. He needs to stay well filled, and well hydrated.

outcomes.story: You write for verapamil and nitroglycerin. The resident stops at the second line.
outcomes.reply: Nitroglycerin relaxes the veins, so less blood returns to the heart and the blockage tightens. It could make him black out. Verapamil has a place in this condition, but it is the second choice, for when a beta-blocker does not work or cannot be taken.

outcomes.story: You explain the medicine to him and his mother. The resident calls the heart center, and he is given an urgent appointment for a full risk assessment, including a monitor to wear and an MRI of his heart. He is told to stay well hydrated.
outcomes.reply: The beta-blocker eases the blockage. It does not protect him from a dangerous rhythm. That is what the specialists will weigh up, and why they will discuss a defibrillator with him and his family.

4.resident: One more conversation before they leave. This condition usually runs in families, and he wants to know about Friday’s game.
4.question: What do we tell them about sports and about his relatives?
options: He can keep playing if he drinks plenty of water and takes his beta-blocker
His relatives need checking only if they get symptoms
No hard competitive sport until the specialists have assessed him, and his parents and any brothers or sisters all need a heart check
No family checks are needed, because his uncle died of a heart attack
4.fix: Pause competitive sport and check the family

terms.meaning: Parents, brothers, sisters and children. This condition is usually passed on so that each child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it.
Checking people who feel well, here with a heart tracing and a heart ultrasound, to find a condition before it causes harm.
A choice made by the patient, the family and the specialists together, once the risks are understood.

outcomes.story: You start to tell him Friday’s game is fine. The resident cuts in.
outcomes.reply: Not yet. He blacked out during a sprint yesterday, and no one has sized up his risk. Some people with this condition do go back to sport, but that is decided with the specialists after a full assessment, not before it.

outcomes.story: You tell his mother the rest of the family can wait and see. The resident steps in.
outcomes.reply: In this condition the first symptom can be a sudden death. That is why relatives are checked while they feel well. Waiting for symptoms throws away the chance to protect them.

outcomes.story: You explain it to them both. He is unhappy about missing Friday’s game, and his mother has a lot of questions. She starts arranging heart checks for the family, beginning with his father.
outcomes.reply: That is the right message. Sitting out is a pause, not a verdict: the specialists will decide with him what he can return to. His father’s “thick heart walls” and his uncle’s death may well be the same condition, which makes the family checks urgent.

outcomes.story: You tell them the uncle’s heart attack is a separate matter. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A 38-year-old dying suddenly while swimming, with no autopsy, is how this condition often hides in a family. “Heart attack” was a guess. It makes checking the family more important, not less.

differential.resident: The heart tracing and the ultrasound are in his chart. Read them, then tell me what he has.
differential.question: What explains his blackout and his murmur?
options: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with obstruction: an inherited thickening of the heart muscle that blocks the way out
Athlete’s heart: normal, even thickening from years of training
A thin shelf of tissue below the valve that leads out of the heart, causing a fixed blockage
A narrowed valve where blood leaves the heart (aortic stenosis)
differential.reveal: It is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with obstruction. One wall of his heart is 21 mm thick while the other is normal, and a valve flap is pulled into the path of the blood with each beat. Training thickens the heart evenly, and rarely past 13 to 15 mm. The murmur that gets louder when he bears down was the clue at the bedside: the heart fills less, and the blockage tightens.

terms.meaning: Overgrown. The muscle cells are larger than normal.
A disease of the heart muscle itself.
A blockage. Here the thick wall and a valve flap narrow the way out of the heart.

ending.stable: Home with his family, off the court for now, with an urgent heart center visit booked
ending.unstable: Seen by the heart specialists the same day, after a scare on the treadmill
ending.worse: Kept in hospital for heart monitoring

cd-055.plainDiagnosis: An inherited thickening of the heart muscle that blocks blood leaving the heart (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with obstruction).

science.title: Why a thick wall becomes a blockage
science.text: Blood leaving his heart has to pass between the thick wall and the mitral valve. In a narrow channel the same flow has to move faster, and the pressure at its edges drops. That drop pulls the valve flap toward the wall, and the channel narrows further.

science.title: Why bearing down made the murmur louder
science.text: Bearing down squeezes the chest, and less blood returns to the heart. A less full heart is smaller, so the wall and the valve flap sit closer together and the blockage tightens. Squatting does the opposite: it pushes blood back to the heart, and his murmur softened.

science.title: Why his whole family needs a heart check
science.text: This condition is usually passed on by a single changed copy of a gene, so each child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it. His father’s thick heart walls and his uncle’s sudden death fit that pattern. His own gene test has not been done yet.

sources.title: 2024 AHA/ACC guideline: management of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Frenneaux et al. (Circulation 1990): abnormal blood pressure response during exercise in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Conway et al. (Circulation 2023): exercise test abnormalities and outcomes in childhood hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
2017 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline: evaluation and management of patients with syncope

cd-061.title: Ten days of fever, _and now his breathing._

start.alarm: High fever · fast heart rate · low oxygen

cd-061.handoff: A 26-year-old man has had fevers and drenching sweats for ten days. For the last three days he has been short of breath, with chest pain when he breathes in. He injects heroin several times a day.

interview.prompt: Ask about the fevers and how he has been overall
interview.finding: Ten days of fever, drenching night sweats and exhaustion. He has no appetite and has lost about 4 kg without trying.

interview.prompt: Ask how he injects and what he may have been exposed to
interview.finding: He injects heroin several times a day and reuses needles. He has no stable place to live. He has never been tested for HIV.

interview.prompt: Ask about his chest and his breathing
interview.finding: For three days it has hurt to take a deep breath, and he has been getting more breathless. He coughs up phlegm that is sometimes streaked with blood.

exam.prompt: Listen to his heart and look at his neck veins
exam.finding: A soft whooshing sound (a murmur) runs through each beat, low on the left side of his breastbone. It gets louder when he breathes in. The veins in his neck are a little swollen.

exam.prompt: Listen to his lungs and watch his breathing
exam.finding: He is working a little harder than normal to breathe. There are crackling sounds scattered through both lungs.

exam.prompt: Look at his injection sites, and at his hands, feet and eyes
exam.finding: There are fresh and healed needle marks inside both elbows, with no skin infection around them. His nails, fingers, toes and the lining of his eyes show none of the small spots that a heart valve infection can cause.

1.label: Blood tests and chest X-ray
1.content:
White blood cells: 18.6, well above normal. That is a sign the body is fighting an infection.
Red blood cell level (hemoglobin): 10.4, mildly low.
Platelets and kidney function: normal.
Lactate: 2.4, slightly raised. It rises when the body is under strain from an infection.
Blood cultures (3 sets): still growing. No result yet.
Chest X-ray: many round patches near the edges of both lungs. Several have a hollow center.
Heart tracing (ECG): a fast but normal rhythm, with normal timing between the upper and lower chambers.
HIV test: not back yet.

0.resident: He looks sick. He has a fever of 39.1, a murmur and low oxygen. We need antibiotics in him soon, and one thing has to happen first.
0.question: What do we do before the first dose?
options: Start vancomycin now, and take blood cultures once his fever has gone
Draw at least three sets of blood cultures, each from a different vein
Send one blood culture and a urine culture
Start antibiotic tablets and book a heart ultrasound as an outpatient
0.fix: Draw three sets of blood cultures

terms.meaning: A sample of blood kept warm in a bottle of broth, to see whether bacteria grow. One “set” is two bottles filled from one needle stick.
Antibiotics chosen as a best guess, before the lab has named the bacteria.
A strong antibiotic given through a vein. It covers staph, including the resistant kind called MRSA.

outcomes.story: You ask the nurse to hang the vancomycin. The nurse is holding the culture bottles, and checks with the resident first.
outcomes.reply: Once an antibiotic is in his blood, the cultures may grow nothing, and we would be treating blind for weeks. Drawing them takes minutes. Cultures first, then the antibiotic straight after.

outcomes.story: Three sets are drawn from three separate veins, a few minutes apart. While that is done, the nurse starts oxygen through a small tube at his nose, and a chest X-ray and basic blood tests are sent. His oxygen level comes up.
outcomes.reply: Good. Three sets from separate sites give the lab the best chance of naming the bacteria. They also show whether it is in his blood all the time, which is the mark of an infection inside the heart or a blood vessel. The antibiotic follows as soon as the bottles are filled.

outcomes.story: You send one blood culture and a urine sample. The resident sees the single set on the trolley.
outcomes.reply: One set is not enough. If it grows a skin germ, we cannot tell contamination from real infection, and if it grows nothing we have learned little. Nothing points to his urine, either. Three sets, from three veins.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for antibiotic tablets and start his discharge papers. Half an hour later he is still waiting on the ward, breathing room air. His oxygen has dropped, and he cannot finish a sentence without stopping for breath.
outcomes.reply: He cannot go home. A fever, a murmur, low oxygen and failing breath mean an infection that is treated in hospital, with antibiotics through a vein and close watching. Oxygen on, cultures now, then the first dose.

3.resident: The picture is a heart valve infection that is sending infected clots to his lungs. The cultures are drawn. In someone who injects drugs, staph is the most likely germ, and it may be the resistant kind.
3.question: Which antibiotic has to be in the first treatment?
options: Vancomycin through a vein, to cover resistant staph (MRSA)
Ceftriaxone through a vein, on its own
Linezolid tablets
Ampicillin plus gentamicin through a vein

terms.meaning: A common skin bacterium. It is the usual cause of heart valve infection in people who inject drugs.
Staph that has become resistant to the penicillin family of antibiotics.
Switching from a broad antibiotic to the one that best fits the germ, once the lab has named it and tested it.

outcomes.story: The pharmacy sends the vancomycin up and the first dose is started. The infection specialists are called to help choose the rest of his treatment. He stays on oxygen and on the monitor.
outcomes.reply: Right. Until the lab says otherwise, we assume the staph may be resistant, and vancomycin covers that. When the cultures name the germ and show what kills it, the team will narrow to the antibiotic that fits best.

outcomes.story: You write the order for ceftriaxone alone. The pharmacist calls the ward.
outcomes.reply: Ceftriaxone does not kill resistant staph, and that is a real possibility for him. If we guess wrong, he gets days of the wrong drug while the infection damages his valve. The first treatment has to cover MRSA.

outcomes.story: You ask for linezolid tablets. The pharmacist calls before sending them.
outcomes.reply: Linezolid only holds staph back. It does not kill it outright. An infection on a heart valve is started on a drug that kills, given through a vein. He is also too sick to rely on tablets.

outcomes.story: You write the order for ampicillin with gentamicin. The pharmacist calls the ward.
outcomes.reply: That pair is aimed at other valve germs, such as enterococci. It misses resistant staph, and gentamicin can harm the kidneys. For him, staph cover comes first.

4.resident: The vancomycin is running. Now we need to look at the valve itself.
4.question: Which scan of his heart do we ask for first?
options: An ultrasound from inside the food pipe (TEE), skipping the one through the chest wall
An ultrasound through the chest wall (TTE)
An MRI of his heart
A CT scan of his chest in a week, to follow the patches in his lungs
4.fix: Ask for the ultrasound through the chest wall

terms.meaning: A clump of bacteria and clot stuck to a heart valve. Pieces can break off and travel in the blood.
Transthoracic echocardiogram: an ultrasound probe on the chest. It is quick and painless, and needs no sedation.
Transesophageal echocardiogram: a probe passed down the food pipe under sedation. It gives sharper pictures, and is used when the first scan is not enough.
The valve on the right side of the heart, between its upper and lower chambers. Blood from the veins passes through it on the way to the lungs.

outcomes.story: You request the scan through the food pipe. The heart ultrasound team calls back.
outcomes.reply: That scan needs sedation and a probe down the throat of a man who is short of breath. The scan through the chest wall is quick and safe, and it often shows the tricuspid valve well. We go on to the other one if the first is unclear, or if we still suspect more.

outcomes.story: The ultrasound team brings the machine to his bedside. He lies on his left side while they scan. The heart specialists will read it and decide whether a closer look from the food pipe is needed.
outcomes.reply: Good. We ask for it early. We do not wait for the lab to finish naming the germ. And a clear scan through the chest wall would not rule the infection out.

outcomes.story: You request a heart MRI. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: An MRI is slow, and he would have to lie flat in a tunnel while breathless. It is also not the test for finding clumps on a valve. Ultrasound is.

outcomes.story: You plan a chest CT for next week. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: The patches in his lungs came from somewhere. A lung scan next week tells us nothing about the valve they are breaking off from, and a week is a long time for a valve infection. We look at the heart now.

differential.resident: His blood tests and chest X-ray are in the chart. Put them together with the murmur and with how he got sick.
differential.question: What ties all of this together?
options: Pneumonia with fluid around the lung
Tuberculosis that has become active again
An infection on a right-sided heart valve, sending infected clots to the lungs
A blood clot in the lungs that has killed a patch of lung
differential.reveal: It is an infection on a heart valve on the right side of the heart. The murmur gets louder when he breathes in, which points to the tricuspid valve. Clumps break off that valve and are carried straight to the lungs, where they form the round, hollow patches on his X-ray. Pneumonia would not explain the murmur, or patches scattered through both lungs.

terms.meaning: An infection of the heart’s inner lining, usually on a valve.
Infected clumps that break off and lodge in blood vessels further on.
The side that receives blood from the veins and pumps it to the lungs. Whatever breaks off there goes to the lungs.

ending.stable: On the ward, on oxygen and antibiotics through a vein
ending.unstable: On the ward, on oxygen and antibiotics through a vein, being watched closely
ending.worse: On the ward, on oxygen and antibiotics, after getting worse while he waited

cd-061.plainDiagnosis: A staph infection on a heart valve on the right side of the heart (infective endocarditis), with infected clots carried to the lungs.

science.title: Why the infection landed in his lungs
science.text: Blood from his veins enters the right side of the heart, passes through the tricuspid valve and is pumped straight to the lungs. Bacteria injected into a vein reach that valve first, and anything that breaks off it is caught in the fine vessels of the lungs.

science.title: Why his oxygen was 91%
science.text: Each infected clump blocks and inflames a patch of lung. Oxygen crosses from air to blood only where the two meet across a thin, healthy wall, and he has fewer such places working. Less oxygen reaches his blood with every breath.

science.title: Why the team assumed resistant staph
science.text: Staph can carry a gene that makes the whole penicillin family useless against it, and bacteria can pass such genes to one another. Resistant staph is common enough that his first antibiotic had to cover it until the lab had tested his own.

sources.title: AHA scientific statement (2015): infective endocarditis in adults
AHA scientific statement (2022): management of infective endocarditis in people who inject drugs
2023 ESC guidelines: management of endocarditis

cd-019.title: Crushing chest pain, _three weeks after giving birth._

start.alarm: Severe chest pain · sweating

cd-019.handoff: A 39-year-old woman had her first baby three weeks ago. An hour ago, while she was resting, a crushing pain started in her chest and spread to her left arm. She is sweating and feels sick.

interview.prompt: Ask her to describe the chest pain
interview.finding: A heavy, crushing pressure behind her breastbone that spreads to her left arm. It started suddenly an hour ago while she was resting, with sweating and nausea, and it has not let up.

interview.prompt: Ask about the birth and the weeks since
interview.finding: Her first baby was born three weeks ago. The delivery was straightforward, and she is breastfeeding.

interview.prompt: Ask about her risks for heart and artery disease
interview.finding: She has no diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol. She has never smoked and does not use cocaine. No one in her family had early heart disease. An old kidney scan noted a mild irregularity in her artery walls (fibromuscular features).

exam.prompt: Check how she looks, and whether enough blood is reaching her body
exam.finding: She is frightened, sweating and still in pain. Her blood pressure is holding, and her hands and feet are warm.

exam.prompt: Listen to her heart and lungs
exam.finding: Her heartbeat is regular, with normal sounds and nothing extra. Her lungs are clear. There is no sign of fluid backing up.

exam.prompt: Feel the pulses on both sides and check her legs for a clot
exam.finding: Her pulses are equal on both sides. There is no whooshing sound over her arteries. Her legs are not swollen and her calves are not tender.

1.label: Heart tracing, blood tests and bedside scan
1.content:
Heart tracing (ECG): the pattern of a heart attack in progress (ST elevation) in the leads that look at the underside of the heart.
Blood test for heart damage (troponin): raised, and rising.
Red blood cell level and kidney function: normal.
Pregnancy test: negative.
Bedside heart ultrasound: the underside of the heart is not squeezing as it should. The overall squeeze is at the low end of normal (50%). There is no fluid around the heart.
She is taken straight to the catheter lab for dye pictures of her heart arteries (an angiogram).

0.resident: She is young and fit, with none of the usual risks. She also has crushing chest pain and she is drenched in sweat.
0.question: What happens in the next ten minutes?
options: Tell her a heart attack is unlikely at her age, and send her home
Send her for a CT scan first, to rule out a clot in her lungs
Give a clot-busting drug right away, before any tests
Get a heart tracing (ECG) and a blood test for heart damage now, and give aspirin
0.fix: Get the tracing, the blood test and aspirin

terms.meaning: Heart muscle dying because its blood supply has been cut off.
A tracing of the heart’s electrical signals. It takes a few minutes and cannot hurt the patient.
A protein that leaks into the blood when heart muscle is damaged. It is the blood test for a heart attack.
A medicine that dissolves blood clots. It also raises the risk of bleeding anywhere in the body.

outcomes.story: You start to tell her it is probably not her heart. The resident is already wheeling in the tracing machine.
outcomes.reply: Young women have heart attacks too, and the weeks after childbirth carry risks of their own. Crushing pain with sweating gets a heart tracing within ten minutes, at any age.

outcomes.story: She is taken to the scanner. Her lungs are clear of clots. Forty minutes later she is back, gray and sweating, with the pain worse than before. No one has yet looked at her heart.
outcomes.reply: A lung clot was worth a thought so soon after a birth. But her pain is a classic heart pain, and the tracing takes two minutes. Her heart has gone forty more minutes without help. Tracing, blood test and aspirin, now.
outcomes.alarm: Pain getting worse · no heart tracing yet

outcomes.story: You ask for a clot-busting drug. The pharmacist will not release it without a heart tracing.
outcomes.reply: We never give that drug blind. We do not know yet that this is a heart attack, or what kind. In some heart attacks the problem is a tear in the artery wall, and a clot-buster can make a tear bleed and spread.

outcomes.story: The tracing is run at the bedside within minutes, blood is drawn and she chews an aspirin. The tracing shows a heart attack in progress. The heart team is called, and she is taken to the catheter lab for dye pictures of her arteries.
outcomes.reply: That is the right first move for anyone with chest pain like this. The tracing gave the answer in minutes, and the artery pictures will show us why it is happening.

3.resident: The pictures show a tear in the wall of her right heart artery, with blood trapped inside the wall. Blood is still flowing down the artery, her blood pressure is steady and her pain is easing.
3.question: How do we treat the torn artery?
options: Put stents along the whole torn section
Emergency bypass surgery, as for every torn heart artery
Medicines and close monitoring, keeping a procedure in reserve in case the blood flow fails
