A simple collection beside a pneumonia is thin and clear and settles with antibiotics alone.

terms.meaning: Pus in the space between the lung and the chest wall.
The thin lining that covers the lung and the inside of the chest wall.

ending.stable: On the ward with a chest drain, booked for keyhole surgery to clear the infection
ending.unstable: On the ward with a chest drain, booked for keyhole surgery to clear the infection
ending.worse: On the ward with a chest drain, sicker than he needed to be, booked for surgery

pm-018.plainDiagnosis: Pus in the space around the lung, after a pneumonia (empyema).

science.title: Why infected fluid is acidic and low in sugar
science.text: Bacteria and white blood cells packed into a closed space burn glucose fast, with little oxygen, and turn it into acid. So the sugar in the fluid falls and its pH drops. Those two numbers measure how hard the fight is going.

science.title: Why fluid around a lung lowers oxygen
science.text: Oxygen enters the blood across the thin walls of air sacs. Fluid pressing on the lung squashes those sacs flat. Blood still flows past them but picks up no oxygen, and it mixes back in and pulls the oxygen level down.

sources.title: Rahman et al. (N Engl J Med 2011): intrapleural use of tissue plasminogen activator and DNase in pleural infection (MIST2)
Shen et al. (J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg 2017): AATS consensus guidelines for the management of empyema

pm-028.title: Five days after a stroke, _coughing at every meal._

start.alarm: Fever · oxygen 91% · more confused

pm-028.handoff: A 78-year-old woman had a stroke five days ago. Today she has a fever, a wet cough and is more confused. The nurses say she coughs whenever she eats.

interview.prompt: Ask what is new today
interview.finding: A fever, a cough that brings up phlegm, and more confusion than yesterday.

interview.prompt: Ask the nurses about her meals
interview.finding: She coughs during meals and holds food in her cheek. She was put back on normal food before anyone had formally tested her swallowing.

interview.prompt: Check what the stroke left her with, and her medicines
interview.finding: The stroke left her right side weak and her speech slurred. She has an irregular heartbeat and takes a blood thinner for it, with tablets for blood pressure and cholesterol.

exam.prompt: Listen to her lungs and tap on her chest
exam.finding: At the bottom of her right lung, at the back, the breath sounds are harsh and crackly, and the chest sounds dull when tapped.

exam.prompt: Look in her mouth, and watch her sip water
exam.finding: Saliva is pooling in her mouth, and her teeth are in poor condition. When she sips water she gives a wet, gurgling cough.

exam.prompt: Check her pulse and how alert she is
exam.finding: Her pulse is irregular. She is sleepier than she was yesterday. Her right arm and leg are weak, as before.

1.label: Chest X-ray, blood tests and swallow test
1.content:
Chest X-ray: a solid white patch at the bottom of the right lung.
White blood cells: 15.8, high.
Lactate: 1.8, normal.
Bedside swallow test: failed. She coughs and splutters on sips of water.
Blood cultures: sent, results pending.

0.resident: She coughs when she eats, and now she has a fever. I think food or saliva has gone down into her lungs. Before the X-ray comes back, tell me where you expect it to show.
0.question: Why the bottom of the right lung?
options: The right middle lobe is the lowest point when a person is upright
The airway to the right lung is straighter and wider, so what goes down the wrong way tends to end up there
The heart protects the left lower lobe
Aspiration always lands in the same small part of the left lung

terms.meaning: Food, drink, saliva or vomit going down the windpipe into the lungs.
One of the two main airways that branch from the windpipe, one to each lung.
Difficulty swallowing.

outcomes.story: You pick the right middle lobe. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It is not the lowest part. Material falls into the lower lobe, and it goes right because that airway is straighter and wider.

outcomes.story: You answer, and the resident nods. Her meals are stopped and she is given oxygen. A chest X-ray and bloods are done, and a nurse tests her swallow at the bedside. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The windpipe runs almost straight into the right main airway, so that is the easy path. In someone propped up in bed, gravity takes it to the bottom.

outcomes.story: You say the heart protects the left side. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The heart does not shield the airway. The left airway branches off at a sharper angle, and that is the reason less ends up there.

outcomes.story: You say it always lands in the left lung. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It usually goes right, and where it settles depends on how the person was lying at the time.

3.resident: The X-ray shows pneumonia at the bottom of her right lung, and she failed her swallow test. She has a fever and a high white count.
3.question: What about antibiotics?
options: None. This is only irritation from stomach contents
Ampicillin-sulbactam into a vein, or a similar choice fitted to how sick she is and to local resistance
Add extra cover against anaerobic bacteria, as a routine for everyone who aspirates
Azithromycin tablets, at home

terms.meaning: Inflammation of the lung from something irritating, such as stomach acid. It often settles without antibiotics.
Infection of the lung. It needs antibiotics.

outcomes.story: No antibiotics are given. Four hours later her temperature is higher, she is breathing faster and her oxygen level has dropped despite the oxygen.
outcomes.reply: Irritation alone settles within a day or two. Fever, a rising white count and a solid patch on the X-ray mean infection, and she has gone four hours without treatment. Start the antibiotics.

outcomes.story: The first dose goes in through her drip. She stays on oxygen, with nothing by mouth for now.
outcomes.reply: Yes. She has a true infection, so she needs antibiotics, and through a vein because she cannot swallow safely.

outcomes.story: You add extra anaerobic cover. The resident takes it off.
outcomes.reply: That used to be routine and no longer is. It is kept for lung abscesses, pus around the lung or badly infected gums. Her antibiotic already covers what she needs.

outcomes.story: You write for tablets and a discharge. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: She needs oxygen, and she cannot swallow safely. Tablets at home are the one thing she must not have.

4.resident: The antibiotics will treat this infection. Unless something changes, the next meal will cause another.
4.question: What matters most for preventing the next one?
options: A formal swallowing assessment, with a plan for safe eating
Preventive antibiotics, indefinitely
Strict bed rest, lying flat
An acid-reducing tablet, and nothing else

terms.meaning: A specialist who assesses swallowing and teaches safe ways to eat and drink.
Drinks made thicker so that they move slowly and are easier to control when swallowing.

outcomes.story: You request the assessment. Until it is done she stays off food and drink, sits upright, and has her mouth cleaned regularly.
outcomes.reply: Right. The therapist finds out what she can swallow safely. Thicker drinks, softer food, sitting upright and a clean mouth all cut the risk.

outcomes.story: You suggest long-term antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: They do not stop food going down the wrong way. They breed resistant bacteria and cause gut infections.

outcomes.story: You suggest lying flat. The nurse raises the head of her bed.
outcomes.reply: Flat is the worst position. It lets whatever is in her mouth and stomach run toward her lungs. She should be propped upright.

outcomes.story: You suggest an acid-reducing tablet alone. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That changes how acidic the stomach contents are. It does nothing about her swallowing.

differential.resident: The X-ray, blood tests and swallow test are in her chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A blood clot in the lung
Aspiration pneumonia: food or saliva went down the wrong way after her stroke and infected the lung
Heart failure
Tuberculosis
differential.reveal: It is aspiration pneumonia. The stroke weakened her swallowing, so food and saliva have been slipping into her airway, carrying bacteria from her mouth. The patch sits at the bottom of the right lung, where swallowed material ends up. A clot would not cause a solid patch with fever and phlegm, and heart failure shows fluid in both lungs.

terms.meaning: Lung that has filled with pus and fluid, so it looks solid white on an X-ray.
A quick bedside test with sips of water, to see whether swallowing is safe.

ending.stable: On the ward on antibiotics and oxygen, with a plan for safe swallowing
ending.unstable: On the ward on antibiotics and oxygen, with a plan for safe swallowing
ending.worse: On the ward on antibiotics and more oxygen, after hours without treatment
ending.critical: In intensive care on a breathing machine

pm-028.plainDiagnosis: A lung infection from food or saliva going down the wrong way after a stroke (aspiration pneumonia).

science.title: Why it went to the right lung
science.text: Anything moving down a tube follows the straighter, wider branch. The right main airway leaves the windpipe at a gentle angle and is wider than the left, which turns off sharply. So most of what is inhaled by accident goes right.

science.title: Why her oxygen was low
science.text: Oxygen crosses from air into blood through the walls of tiny air sacs. In pneumonia those sacs fill with pus. Blood flowing past them meets no air, picks up no oxygen, and lowers the level in the blood leaving the lungs.

sources.title: Mandell and Niederman (N Engl J Med 2019): aspiration pneumonia
Metlay et al. (Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019): diagnosis and treatment of adults with community-acquired pneumonia, an ATS/IDSA guideline

pm-023.title: A positive test _in a nurse who feels fine._

start.alarm: Positive tuberculosis blood test · feels well

pm-023.handoff: A 28-year-old nurse had a routine blood test for tuberculosis before starting a new job, and it came back positive. She feels completely well.

interview.prompt: Ask about symptoms
interview.finding: She feels well. No cough, no fever, no night sweats, no coughing up blood and no weight loss. Her breathing is normal.

interview.prompt: Ask how she might have been exposed
interview.finding: She once volunteered in a country where tuberculosis is common. She has never injected drugs.

interview.prompt: Ask about her health and her medicines
interview.finding: She has no medical problems. She takes a contraceptive pill and a multivitamin, and has a drink or two a month.

exam.prompt: Listen to her lungs
exam.finding: Clear on both sides.

exam.prompt: Feel for swollen glands
exam.finding: None in her neck, above her collarbones, in her armpits or in her groin.

exam.prompt: Feel her belly, and look at her skin and fingers
exam.finding: Her belly is soft, and her liver and spleen are not enlarged. Her skin and fingertips look normal.

1.label: Chest X-ray and blood tests
1.content:
Chest X-ray: clear. No shadows, no cavities and no swollen glands.
HIV test: negative.
Liver tests: normal.
Pregnancy test: negative.

0.resident: A positive blood test tells us tuberculosis bacteria have been in her body at some point. It does not tell us whether they are active now.
0.question: What has to happen before any treatment?
options: A chest X-ray, to rule out active tuberculosis
Start isoniazid straight away
Repeat the blood test, to be sure it is really positive
Collect three phlegm samples, whether or not she has symptoms

terms.meaning: A blood test for tuberculosis infection. It checks whether her immune cells react to tuberculosis proteins.
Tuberculosis bacteria that are multiplying and causing illness. It can spread to others.

outcomes.story: She has a chest X-ray and a few blood tests that are needed before treatment. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Active disease needs four drugs. Latent infection needs one or two. Treating active disease as if it were latent breeds resistant bacteria, so we rule it out first.

outcomes.story: You write for isoniazid. The resident holds the prescription.
outcomes.reply: Not until we know it is not active disease. One drug against active tuberculosis is how resistance starts.

outcomes.story: You ask to repeat the test. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: This test is very specific, and she has a believable exposure. A repeat only delays the X-ray she needs.

outcomes.story: You ask for phlegm samples. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: She has no cough and nothing to bring up. Phlegm tests are for people with symptoms or an abnormal X-ray.

3.resident: She has latent infection. Treating it now makes it much less likely to wake up later.
3.question: Which treatment is recommended?
options: Four drugs for six months
Rifampin alone for two months
Isoniazid with rifapentine once a week for 12 weeks
Isoniazid alone for two months

terms.meaning: An antibiotic that kills tuberculosis bacteria.
A long-acting antibiotic in the same family as rifampin. It turns urine and tears orange.

outcomes.story: You suggest four drugs. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is the treatment for active tuberculosis. For sleeping bacteria it is far more than she needs.

outcomes.story: You suggest two months of rifampin. The resident corrects the length.
outcomes.reply: Rifampin alone is a good option, but it takes four months. Two is too short to clear the bacteria.

outcomes.story: You go through the course with her: one dose a week for twelve weeks, with a check-in each month.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Short courses are the ones people actually finish, and this one works as well as nine months of the older treatment.

outcomes.story: You suggest two months of isoniazid. The resident corrects the length.
outcomes.reply: Isoniazid alone takes six to nine months. Two would leave her unprotected.

4.resident: Her course includes isoniazid, which has one side effect that a simple supplement prevents.
4.question: What do we tell her?
options: Take vitamin B6, to protect her nerves
Avoid all dairy products
Expect harmless orange tears, from the isoniazid
Take high-dose acetaminophen for any muscle aches

terms.meaning: Damage to the nerves of the hands and feet, felt as numbness, tingling or burning.
Vitamin B6.

outcomes.story: You add vitamin B6 to her prescription and tell her why.
outcomes.reply: Right. Isoniazid uses up vitamin B6, and nerves suffer without it. One small tablet prevents the problem.

outcomes.story: You tell her to avoid dairy. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Dairy makes no difference to these medicines. The advice she needs is vitamin B6.

outcomes.story: You blame orange tears on isoniazid. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: The orange color is real and harmless, but it comes from the rifapentine. What isoniazid needs is vitamin B6.

outcomes.story: You suggest high-dose acetaminophen. The resident says no.
outcomes.reply: Isoniazid can strain the liver, and so can large doses of acetaminophen. She should tell us about aches, not treat them heavily.

differential.resident: Her X-ray and blood tests are in the chart.
differential.question: What does she have?
options: Active tuberculosis of the lungs
Latent tuberculosis infection: the bacteria are in her body, walled off and asleep
A false-positive test in someone who was never infected
A positive result caused by an old BCG vaccination
differential.reveal: She has latent tuberculosis infection. Her immune system has met the bacteria and walled them off. They are alive but not multiplying, so she has no symptoms, a clear X-ray and cannot infect anyone. The blood test is not affected by BCG vaccination, and with her exposure a false positive is unlikely.

terms.meaning: Present but inactive.
A tuberculosis vaccine given in many countries. It can make the older skin test positive, but not this blood test.

ending.stable: Cleared to start work, with a 12-week course of treatment
ending.worse: Admitted for observation

pm-023.plainDiagnosis: Tuberculosis bacteria that are present but asleep (latent tuberculosis infection).

science.title: What a positive test did and did not show
science.text: The test shows that her immune cells recognize tuberculosis proteins, which proves her body has met the bacteria. It cannot show whether they are multiplying. Answering that took different evidence: her symptoms and an X-ray.

science.title: Why isoniazid can hurt nerves
science.text: Many enzymes only work with a small helper molecule attached. Nerve cells depend on enzymes whose helper is made from vitamin B6. Isoniazid binds B6 and carries it out in the urine, so those enzymes slow down unless the vitamin is topped up.

sources.title: Sterling et al. (MMWR Recomm Rep 2020): guidelines for the treatment of latent tuberculosis infection, recommendations from the NTCA and CDC
Sterling et al. (N Engl J Med 2011): three months of rifapentine and isoniazid for latent tuberculosis infection

gi-004.title: Pain under the ribs _after a fried dinner._

start.alarm: Severe pain under the right ribs · fever

gi-004.handoff: A 48-year-old woman has had severe, constant pain under her right ribs for eight hours. It started an hour after a fried chicken dinner. She has vomited twice and feels feverish.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain
interview.finding: It started an hour after a fried meal, eight hours ago. It is severe and constant, under her right ribs, and it spreads to her right shoulder blade. She feels sick and has vomited twice.

interview.prompt: Ask whether this has happened before
interview.finding: Several times in the past few months, after fatty meals, but milder. Each time it passed within an hour. This time it has not let up.

interview.prompt: Ask about her health and her medicines
interview.finding: She has two children and takes a combined contraceptive pill. She is otherwise well. She feels hot and shivery now.

exam.prompt: Press under her right ribs while she breathes in
exam.finding: The area is very tender. As she breathes in against your hand, she suddenly stops and catches her breath with pain.

exam.prompt: Look at her eyes and skin for yellowing
exam.finding: The whites of her eyes are white. Her skin is not yellow.

exam.prompt: Press on the rest of her belly, and tap over her kidneys
exam.finding: The rest of her belly is soft, and no lump can be felt. Tapping over her kidneys does not hurt.

1.label: Blood tests and ultrasound
1.content:
White blood cells: 13.8, high.
Bilirubin and liver tests: normal.
Lipase, a test of the pancreas: normal.
Ultrasound: several gallstones. The gallbladder wall is thickened to 5 mm (normal is under 3), with a rim of fluid around it. Pressing the probe over the gallbladder brings on her pain. The main bile duct is a normal width.

0.resident: Pain under the right ribs after a fatty meal, a fever, and she catches her breath when I press there. I am thinking about her gallbladder.
0.question: Which scan do we get first?
options: An ultrasound of the upper right belly
A CT scan without contrast
A nuclear scan of the gallbladder (HIDA scan)
An MRI of the bile ducts (MRCP)
A set of plain X-rays

terms.meaning: A small bag under the liver that stores bile and squeezes it into the gut after a meal.
Hard lumps, usually of cholesterol, that form in the gallbladder.
Catching the breath with pain when the examiner presses under the right ribs during a breath in.

outcomes.story: The ultrasound is done at the bedside while her blood is sent. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Ultrasound is the best first look at the gallbladder. It is quick, uses no radiation, and shows stones, a swollen wall and fluid.

outcomes.story: You request a CT. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: CT misses many gallstones. It is for when we suspect something else or a complication.

outcomes.story: You request a HIDA scan. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: That is the back-up test, for when the ultrasound is unclear. It takes hours. Ultrasound first.

outcomes.story: You request an MRI of the bile ducts. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: That looks for stones in the ducts, once we have a reason to suspect one. We do not yet.

outcomes.story: You request plain X-rays. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: Most gallstones do not show on an X-ray, and an inflamed gallbladder never does.

3.resident: She has an inflamed gallbladder, blocked by a stone. Her bile duct and her liver tests are normal.
3.question: What is the right treatment?
options: Send her home on antibiotic tablets, and see her in clinic
An urgent camera procedure on the bile duct (ERCP)
A drain through the skin into the gallbladder, as the first choice
Fluids, pain relief and antibiotics through a vein, and keyhole surgery to remove the gallbladder during this admission
Tablets that slowly dissolve gallstones

terms.meaning: An operation to remove the gallbladder, usually by keyhole surgery.
A camera passed through the mouth to the opening of the bile duct, used to remove stones from the duct.

outcomes.story: She goes home with tablets. Twelve hours later she comes back by ambulance. Her fever is higher, her heart is racing, and the whole upper part of her belly is rigid.
outcomes.reply: An inflamed, blocked gallbladder does not settle on tablets. Part of its wall has started to die, and the operation is now harder. She is admitted, as she should have been.

outcomes.story: You suggest an urgent ERCP. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That removes stones from the bile duct. Her duct is a normal width, and her liver tests are normal. The stone is in the gallbladder’s own outlet.

outcomes.story: You suggest a drain into the gallbladder. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A drain is for people too frail for an operation. She is fit, and surgery fixes the problem for good.

outcomes.story: A drip is started with fluids, pain relief and antibiotics. The surgeon sees her and books keyhole surgery for the morning. Her pain eases.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Settle her, then take the gallbladder out within a day or two. Early surgery means fewer complications and a shorter stay than waiting weeks.

outcomes.story: You suggest dissolving tablets. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those take months and work only on some stones. They do nothing for a gallbladder that is inflamed tonight.

4.resident: While she waits for surgery she asks why she got gallstones. Her own history holds most of the answer.
4.question: Which features raise the risk of gallstones?
options: Being male, young and thin
Smoking and heavy drinking
A vegetarian diet with plenty of fiber
Regular anti-inflammatory painkillers and a stomach infection
Being female, around 40, heavier, having had children, and taking estrogen

terms.meaning: A hormone that raises the amount of cholesterol the liver puts into bile.
A fluid made by the liver that helps digest fat.

outcomes.story: You pick young thin men. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is nearly the reverse. Gallstones are commonest in women around 40 who carry extra weight and have had children.

outcomes.story: You pick smoking and drinking. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Neither is a main cause of cholesterol stones. Think about what raises cholesterol in bile.

outcomes.story: You pick a high-fiber diet. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: If anything that protects. The risks are female sex, age, weight, pregnancies and estrogen.

outcomes.story: You pick painkillers and a stomach infection. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those cause stomach ulcers, not gallstones.

outcomes.story: You explain it to her. She nods: it describes her closely.
outcomes.reply: Right. Estrogen, from pregnancies and from the pill, pushes more cholesterol into bile, and extra weight does the same. Too much cholesterol in bile hardens into stones.

differential.resident: Her blood tests and ultrasound are in the chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A gallstone stuck in the main bile duct
An infection of the bile ducts (cholangitis)
Acute cholecystitis: an inflamed gallbladder, blocked by a stone
Pancreatitis
Gallstone pain that passes without inflammation (biliary colic)
differential.reveal: It is acute cholecystitis. A stone has blocked the gallbladder’s outlet, and the trapped gallbladder has become inflamed: hence the fever, the high white count, the thick wall and the fluid around it. Her bile duct is a normal width and her liver tests are normal, so no stone is stuck in the duct. Her earlier attacks were the same stone blocking briefly and then moving.

terms.meaning: Inflammation of the gallbladder.
Pain from a gallstone briefly blocking the gallbladder’s outlet. It passes within hours and causes no fever.

ending.stable: Admitted, with keyhole surgery to remove her gallbladder booked for the morning
ending.worse: Admitted for a harder operation, after coming back sicker

gi-004.plainDiagnosis: A gallbladder inflamed because a stone is blocking its outlet (acute cholecystitis).

science.title: Why the pain followed a fatty meal
science.text: Fat arriving in the gut makes its lining release a hormone that tells the gallbladder to squeeze out bile. Hers squeezed hard against a stone wedged in its outlet. With nowhere for the bile to go, pressure built and the wall became inflamed.

science.title: Why she felt it in her shoulder blade
science.text: Pain nerves from the gallbladder enter the spinal cord alongside nerves from the skin over the right shoulder blade. The brain is far more used to signals from skin, so it places some of the pain there.

sources.title: Okamoto et al. (J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Sci 2018): Tokyo Guidelines 2018, flowchart for the management of acute cholecystitis
Gutt et al. (Ann Surg 2013): acute cholecystitis, early versus delayed cholecystectomy, a multicenter randomized trial

gi-014.title: Without warning, _he vomits bright red blood._

start.alarm: Vomiting blood · blood pressure 84 over 52

gi-014.handoff: A 64-year-old man has been in intensive care for two days with pneumonia. A few minutes ago he suddenly vomited a large amount of bright red blood. He had no pain beforehand. He is now pale, clammy and lightheaded.

interview.prompt: Ask about the bleeding
interview.finding: It came out of nowhere: a large amount of bright red blood with clots. He had no stomach pain, no heartburn and no retching first. Within minutes he felt faint and sweaty.

interview.prompt: Ask about past bleeding, ulcers and his liver
interview.finding: He has never bled like this and has never had an ulcer. He used to drink and stopped five years ago.

interview.prompt: Check why he is in hospital, and his medicines
interview.finding: He came in two days ago with pneumonia. He has high blood pressure and long-term lung disease. In hospital he has been getting small injections of a blood thinner to prevent clots.

exam.prompt: Check his circulation
exam.finding: He is pale, sweaty and anxious. His hands and feet are cool, his mouth is dry, and a pressed fingertip takes three to four seconds to turn pink again.

exam.prompt: Feel his belly, and look for signs of liver disease
exam.finding: His belly is soft and does not hurt. His liver and spleen are not enlarged, and he has none of the skin signs of long-term liver disease.

exam.prompt: Examine his rectum
exam.finding: The stool is black and tarry, which means blood has passed through his gut.

2.label: Blood tests
2.content:
Hemoglobin: 7.1, down from 12.8 two days ago. He has lost close to half of his red cells.
Platelets and clotting test: normal.
Lactate: 3.6, raised.
Urea: 38, raised, as it is when blood is digested in the gut.
Liver tests: normal.
Blood bank: 4 units of red cells are ready.

4.label: Camera test of the stomach
4.content:
High on the inner curve of the stomach there is a pit about 5 mm across, with an artery sticking out of it and pumping blood.
There is no ulcer, no swollen veins and no tear. The rest of the stomach lining is normal.
The spot has been marked with ink, so it can be found again.

0.resident: He is bleeding fast from somewhere in his stomach or gullet, and his blood pressure is 84 over 52. He needs a camera test to find the source.
0.question: What comes before the camera test?
options: Nothing. Rush him straight to the camera test
Two large drips, fluids and blood, a cross-match, and the transfusion team warned
A CT scan of the blood vessels first, to find the bleed
Activated charcoal by mouth, to bind the blood

terms.meaning: Vomiting blood.
Testing a patient’s blood against donor blood so that a transfusion is safe.
A camera on a flexible tube passed through the mouth into the stomach.

outcomes.story: You call for the camera team at once. The anesthetist refuses to start.
outcomes.reply: He is in shock. Sedating him for a procedure now could stop his heart, and he could breathe in blood. Fill him up first.

outcomes.story: Two large drips go in. Fluid runs fast, blood is cross-matched, and the first unit is hung. His blood pressure comes up a little.
outcomes.reply: Right. Blood and fluid first. A camera test is safer and works better once his circulation has been refilled.

outcomes.story: He is wheeled to the scanner with a single small drip. On the table he vomits blood again. His blood pressure drops further, and he is barely responding.
outcomes.reply: A scan can wait, and the camera will find the source anyway. He has lost half an hour and more blood with almost nothing going back in. Resuscitate him now.
outcomes.alarm: Vomiting blood again · blood pressure 72 over 42

outcomes.story: You ask for charcoal. The nurse looks at the resident.
outcomes.reply: Charcoal is for swallowed poisons. It does nothing for bleeding, and it would black out the camera’s view.

1.resident: Blood and fluids are running. He is awake, but he is still vomiting blood, and the camera test means lying flat under sedation.
1.question: What else should be done around the camera test?
options: Pass a balloon tube into his gullet to press on the bleed
Consider a breathing tube first, to keep blood out of his lungs
Give barium by mouth to outline the bleeding point
Give ceftriaxone, as the most important step

terms.meaning: Placing a breathing tube in the windpipe. A cuff around it seals the lungs off from the throat.
A medicine that switches off stomach acid. Clots hold better when the stomach is less acidic.

outcomes.story: You ask for a balloon tube. The resident says no.
outcomes.reply: That is a last resort for bleeding from swollen veins in liver disease. He has no liver disease, and the tube can tear the gullet.

outcomes.story: The anesthetist places a breathing tube, so blood cannot run into his lungs. An acid-suppressing drip is started. His blood results go in the chart, and the camera team sets up.
outcomes.reply: Yes. A man vomiting this much blood, sedated and flat, can drown in it. The tube makes the procedure safe.

outcomes.story: You ask for barium. The resident says no.
outcomes.reply: Barium coats the stomach white and hides everything the camera needs to see.

outcomes.story: You ask for ceftriaxone first. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Antibiotics matter in bleeding from liver disease, which he does not have. His airway is the priority.

5.resident: The camera has found the source: an artery poking through a tiny pit in the stomach lining, spurting blood.
5.question: How should it be stopped?
options: An injection of adrenaline around it, and nothing else
A metal clip or a rubber band on the vessel, often with heat sealing as well
An operation straight away, without trying through the camera
An octreotide drip as the only treatment

terms.meaning: Stopping bleeding.
A tiny metal clip, placed through the camera, that pinches a bleeding vessel shut.

outcomes.story: You suggest adrenaline alone. The specialist adds a clip.
outcomes.reply: Adrenaline narrows the artery for a while, and then it wears off and the bleeding comes back. It needs something permanent with it.

outcomes.story: The specialist closes a clip across the artery and seals around it with heat. The spurting stops. His blood pressure settles as the transfusion catches up.
outcomes.reply: Right. An artery needs to be physically closed. Clips and bands hold far better than an injection.

outcomes.story: You suggest surgery now. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Surgery is for when the camera fails. Nearly all of these can be stopped without an operation.

outcomes.story: You suggest octreotide alone. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That drug lowers pressure in the veins of people with liver disease. This is an artery, and it needs closing.

6.resident: Twelve hours later he vomits a cupful of fresh blood, and his blood count has dropped again. His blood pressure is holding for now.
6.question: What now?
options: Remove his whole stomach
Repeat the camera test and treat the spot again. If that fails, block the artery through a catheter
Switch to acid-suppressing tablets and watch
Start an octreotide-type drug, and avoid any more camera tests

terms.meaning: Bleeding that starts again after it has been stopped.
Blocking a bleeding artery from the inside, with tiny coils passed through a catheter under X-ray.

outcomes.story: You suggest removing his stomach. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is an enormous operation for a 5 mm spot. There are two smaller steps to try first.

outcomes.story: The camera goes back in, and the ink mark leads straight to the spot. A second clip is placed and the bleeding stops. The X-ray team is on standby in case it starts again.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Go back and treat it again first. If that fails, the artery can be blocked from the inside. Surgery comes last.

outcomes.story: He is given tablets and watched. An hour later he vomits a large amount of blood, and his blood pressure collapses.
outcomes.reply: Tablets do not close an artery. He has had a second big bleed that we saw coming. Get the camera team now.

outcomes.story: You suggest avoiding more camera tests. The specialist disagrees.
outcomes.reply: The camera is exactly what he needs. We know where the spot is, and we can treat it again.

differential.resident: The camera shows a normal stomach lining apart from one tiny pit, with an artery sticking out of it and spurting. There is no ulcer around it.
differential.question: What is that?
options: A bleeding stomach ulcer
Swollen veins in the gullet (esophageal varices)
A Dieulafoy lesion: an oversized artery that has broken through the stomach lining
A tear at the bottom of the gullet from retching (Mallory-Weiss tear)
differential.reveal: It is a Dieulafoy lesion. Some people have an artery in the stomach wall that is much wider than it should be and runs just under the lining. It can wear through a pinpoint spot and bleed heavily, with no pain and no warning. An ulcer would show a crater, swollen veins come with liver disease, and a tear follows retching.

terms.meaning: The layer just beneath the lining of the gut, where its blood vessels run.
A crater eaten into the lining of the stomach, usually by acid.

ending.stable: In intensive care, with the bleeding artery clipped and no further bleeding
ending.unstable: In intensive care, with the bleeding artery clipped and no further bleeding
ending.worse: In intensive care with the bleeding stopped, after a slow start
ending.critical: In intensive care after a second large bleed that could have been prevented

gi-014.plainDiagnosis: An oversized artery that broke through the stomach lining and bled heavily (Dieulafoy lesion).

science.title: Why an artery bleeds so much faster than a vein
science.text: Flow through an opening depends on the pressure behind it. Arteries carry blood at many times the pressure of veins, so the same pinhole loses blood far faster. It is also why the bleeding came in spurts, in time with his pulse.

science.title: Why his oxygen reading stayed fair while his tissues starved
science.text: A finger probe reports what share of his hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. It says nothing about how much hemoglobin is left. With half his red cells gone, each liter of blood delivered half the oxygen, and his rising lactate showed it.

sources.title: Laine et al. (Am J Gastroenterol 2021): ACG clinical guideline, upper gastrointestinal and ulcer bleeding
Baxter and Aly (Ann R Coll Surg Engl 2010): Dieulafoy’s lesion, current trends in diagnosis and management

gi-065.title: A painful swelling, _and months of something more._

start.alarm: Painful swelling beside the anus · fever

gi-065.handoff: A 38-year-old man has had a throbbing, painful swelling beside his anus for three days, with fevers. He cannot sit comfortably.

interview.prompt: Ask about the swelling
interview.finding: It began three days ago, beside his anus, and has grown and throbbed more each day. He feels feverish and cannot sit on it.

interview.prompt: Ask about his bowels and his weight
interview.finding: For several months he has had loose stools, sometimes with blood, and crampy belly pain. He has lost 4 kg without trying and has had slight fevers. He put it down to stress.

interview.prompt: Ask about his mouth and his joints, and any past operations
interview.finding: He gets mouth ulcers that come and go, and his joints ache. He has never had an operation near his anus.

exam.prompt: Look at the area around his anus, and press on it gently
exam.finding: Beside the anus there is a red, hot swelling 3 cm across that feels as if it holds fluid. A little pus comes out when it is pressed. Nearby there is a skin tag and a pinpoint opening that weeps clear fluid.

exam.prompt: Examine his rectum with a finger
exam.finding: It is very tender, and one side feels full.

exam.prompt: Press on his belly
exam.finding: It is soft, and slightly tender low on the right.

1.label: Drainage and blood tests
1.content:
Drainage: about 15 mL of pus released, and the cavity packed with gauze.
Pus culture: a mix of gut bacteria.
White blood cells: 14.8, high.
Hemoglobin: 11.2, low, with small red cells.
Inflammation markers (CRP and ESR): both raised.
Once the abscess had emptied, a small opening remained that leaks stool-stained fluid.

0.resident: That swelling is hot, soft in the middle and leaking pus. It is an abscess.
0.question: What do we do about it now?
options: Antibiotic tablets alone, and see him in clinic
Open it and drain it
Warm baths and stool softeners only
An urgent CT scan before anything is done
Metronidazole cream, and send him home

terms.meaning: A walled-off pocket of pus.
Numbing the skin, cutting into an abscess and letting the pus out.

outcomes.story: He is sent home with tablets. He is back twelve hours later. The swelling has doubled, the redness has spread across his buttock, and his fever is higher.
outcomes.reply: Antibiotics cannot get into a pocket of pus, so the infection kept spreading. It should have been drained this morning. Drain it now.

outcomes.story: The area is numbed, and the surgeon opens the abscess and lets the pus out. The relief is immediate. Blood is sent, and the results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Pus has to come out. Draining it is the treatment, and it also stops the infection tracking deeper.

outcomes.story: You suggest warm baths. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Baths soothe, and they help after drainage. They do not empty an abscess.

outcomes.story: You request a CT first. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: We can see it and feel it. A scan would only delay the drainage. Scans are for abscesses that are deep or hidden.

outcomes.story: You suggest a cream. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A cream on the skin cannot reach pus underneath it. It has to be opened.

3.resident: The abscess is drained, but an opening is still leaking stool. Put that with his months of bloody diarrhea, weight loss, mouth ulcers and low blood count.
3.question: Which tests will confirm what is behind this?
options: A camera test of the colon and the end of the small bowel with tissue samples, and an MRI of the pelvis
Drain it again in a week
A stool test for parasites, and nothing else
Pressure testing of the anal muscles
Lifelong antibiotics, with no more tests

terms.meaning: An abnormal tunnel between two surfaces. Here it runs from inside the bowel to the skin.
A camera test of the whole colon. Small tissue samples can be taken through it.
A small sample of tissue, examined under a microscope.

outcomes.story: You book both tests. The gut specialist will see him as soon as the results are back.
outcomes.reply: Right. The camera shows the inflammation and lets us sample it. The MRI maps where the tunnel runs, which the surgeon needs before touching it.

outcomes.story: You plan to drain it again next week. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Draining treats the pus, not the cause. We need to find out why a tunnel formed.

outcomes.story: You request a parasite test only. The resident adds to it.
outcomes.reply: Worth ruling out infection, but a stool test cannot show the bowel wall. He needs the camera test.

outcomes.story: You request pressure testing. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: That measures how strong the anal muscles are. It says nothing about why he has a tunnel and bloody diarrhea.

outcomes.story: You suggest lifelong antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That treats a guess, forever, with a drug that has its own harms. He needs a diagnosis.

4.resident: A week later the results are back. He has Crohn disease, and the tunnel beside his anus branches and passes through the muscle that keeps him continent.
4.question: How should the tunnel be treated?
options: Cut the whole tunnel open widely, now
A soft thread through the tunnel to keep it draining, with a medicine that blocks TNF
Antibiotics alone, indefinitely
A stoma to divert the stool, as the first step
Watch it and do nothing
4.fix: Plan a seton and anti-TNF treatment

terms.meaning: A soft thread looped through a fistula. It keeps the tunnel open so pus drains out and no new abscess forms.
An antibody, such as infliximab, that blocks TNF, one of the signals driving the inflammation.
The ring of muscle that holds the anus closed.

outcomes.story: You suggest cutting it open. The surgeon says no.
outcomes.reply: This tunnel passes through the muscle that keeps him continent. Cutting it open could leave him unable to hold his stool, and inflamed tissue heals badly.

outcomes.story: The surgeon will place the thread, and the gut specialist starts the paperwork for infliximab. You explain the plan to him.
outcomes.reply: Yes. The thread keeps it draining so that no new abscess forms, and the medicine calms the disease so the tunnel can heal.

outcomes.story: You suggest antibiotics alone. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: They help for a few weeks as a bridge. They do not treat Crohn disease, and the tunnel comes back when they stop.

outcomes.story: You suggest a stoma. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is kept for severe disease that nothing else controls. It is not where we start.

outcomes.story: You suggest watching it. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: An untreated tunnel in active Crohn disease forms abscess after abscess. It needs draining and the disease needs treating.

differential.resident: The drainage findings and blood tests are in his chart.
differential.question: What underlying condition do they point to?
options: Ulcerative colitis
Crohn disease
Irritable bowel syndrome
Celiac disease
Diverticular disease
differential.reveal: They point to Crohn disease. It inflames the full thickness of the bowel wall, so it can burrow through and form tunnels and abscesses around the anus. The months of bloody diarrhea, weight loss, mouth ulcers, joint aches and a low blood count fit. Ulcerative colitis affects only the inner lining and does not tunnel. Irritable bowel causes no bleeding, fever or weight loss.

terms.meaning: A long-term inflammation that can affect any part of the gut, through the full thickness of its wall.
The family that Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis belong to.

ending.stable: Home with the abscess drained, and a treatment plan for Crohn disease
ending.worse: Home after a longer stay, with the abscess drained and a treatment plan for Crohn disease

gi-065.plainDiagnosis: An abscess and a tunnel beside the anus, caused by Crohn disease.

science.title: Why antibiotics cannot clear an abscess
science.text: Medicines travel in the blood, and the middle of an abscess has no blood vessels. The drug reaches the wall and goes no further, while the bacteria sit in the pus beyond its reach. Opening it removes them directly.

science.title: How an antibody medicine switches off a signal
science.text: TNF is a small protein that immune cells release to call in more inflammation. Infliximab is an antibody shaped to fit TNF exactly. Once bound, TNF can no longer dock on its receptor, and the signal stops.

sources.title: Lichtenstein et al. (Am J Gastroenterol 2018): ACG clinical guideline, management of Crohn’s disease in adults
Present et al. (N Engl J Med 1999): infliximab for the treatment of fistulas in patients with Crohn’s disease

inf-048.title: A small cut, _and pain far beyond what the skin shows._

start.alarm: Unbearable leg pain · blood pressure 88 over 52 · confused

inf-048.handoff: A 58-year-old man with diabetes pricked his left leg while gardening two days ago. The pain has become unbearable, the leg is swollen and discolored, and since this morning he has had a fever and is confused.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain
interview.finding: It began near a small puncture wound from working in his yard two days ago. It has grown quickly, and it is far worse than the look of the skin would explain.

interview.prompt: Ask his family about the last 12 hours
interview.finding: The leg has swollen and changed color. He has a fever, is drowsy and at times does not make sense.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health
interview.finding: He has type 2 diabetes, and it is poorly controlled.

exam.prompt: Look at the leg
exam.finding: The lower leg is very swollen. The skin is dusky and blotchy, with tight blisters full of dark, bloody fluid. A small wound leaks thin, gray, foul-smelling fluid. The edge of the redness can be seen creeping upward.

exam.prompt: Feel the leg, and test the skin with a light touch
exam.finding: Pressing on the leg gives a crackling feel, like bubble wrap under the skin. Some patches of skin are numb, even though he says the leg is agony. It is tender well beyond the red area.

exam.prompt: Check how he looks and how alert he is
exam.finding: He is sweaty and gray, and he drifts in and out of making sense.

1.label: Blood tests and X-ray
1.content:
White blood cells: 24.5, very high.
Sodium: 128, low. Blood sugar: 412, very high.
Kidney test (creatinine): 2.1, double his usual.
CRP, a marker of inflammation: 280, very high.
Lactate: 4.8, high.
Creatine kinase, which leaks from dying muscle: raised.
X-ray of the leg: gas bubbles tracking along the layers between the muscles.
Risk score for this kind of infection: 9 out of 13, high.

0.resident: Pain far beyond the look of the skin, blisters, crackling under the fingers and a falling blood pressure. Fluids are running. I am very worried about what is happening under that skin.
0.question: What is the most important thing to do now?
options: Call the surgeon urgently, to open and explore the leg
Get an MRI of the leg before anything else
Apply warm compresses and raise the leg
Start a blood thinner for a clot in the leg

terms.meaning: The sheet of tough tissue under the skin that wraps the muscles. Infection can race along it.
Cutting away dead and infected tissue.
A crackling feel under the skin, caused by gas that bacteria produce.

outcomes.story: The surgeon is called and is on the way. Blood is sent and a quick X-ray is taken at the bedside. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. If this is what it looks like, the only thing that saves him is a surgeon cutting out the dead tissue. Everything else supports that.

outcomes.story: He is sent for an MRI. Ninety minutes later the redness has climbed past his knee, and his blood pressure has fallen further.
outcomes.reply: This diagnosis is made at the bedside and in the operating room, not in a scanner. The infection moved several centimeters while he lay in it. Call the surgeon.
outcomes.alarm: Redness past the knee · blood pressure falling

outcomes.story: The leg is raised and wrapped in warm cloths. Two hours later the skin around the wound has turned black, and his blood pressure is lower still.
outcomes.reply: That is the treatment for a mild skin infection. This one is killing tissue by the hour, and two hours have gone. Call the surgeon.
outcomes.alarm: Skin turning black · blood pressure falling

outcomes.story: You write for a blood thinner. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: A clot does not cause blisters, gas under the skin or shock. And he is about to need surgery, which a blood thinner makes more dangerous.

3.resident: The operating room is being made ready. He needs antibiotics running before he gets there.
3.question: Which antibiotics?
options: Cephalexin tablets
Ceftriaxone alone
Metronidazole alone
Vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam and clindamycin together

terms.meaning: Covering many kinds of bacteria at once. It is used when the cause is unknown and the stakes are high.
An antibiotic that stops bacteria from making proteins, including the toxins that destroy tissue.

outcomes.story: You write for tablets. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: He is in shock, so nothing by mouth will be absorbed, and that tablet covers only a few of the bacteria this could be.

outcomes.story: You write for ceftriaxone alone. The resident adds to the order.
outcomes.reply: That leaves out resistant staph and the bacteria that live without oxygen, and it does nothing about toxins.

outcomes.story: You write for metronidazole alone. The resident adds to the order.
outcomes.reply: That covers only the bacteria that live without oxygen. These infections usually involve several kinds at once.

outcomes.story: All three are hung. The anesthetist arrives to take him to the operating room.
outcomes.reply: Right. One for resistant staph, one for gut bacteria and those that live without oxygen, and clindamycin to switch off the toxins. They help the surgeon. They do not replace one.

4.resident: The surgeon is held up in another operation. Someone suggests getting an MRI in the meantime, to confirm the diagnosis before operating.
4.question: What do we do?
options: Go to the operating room as soon as a surgeon is free. Do not wait for a scan
Wait for the MRI to confirm it before any surgery
Try 24 hours of antibiotics, and reassess
Send him home on antibiotic tablets with close follow-up
4.fix: Insist on surgery without a scan

terms.meaning: Death of tissue. Dead tissue has no blood supply, so neither antibiotics nor immune cells can reach it.
Dangerously low blood pressure caused by severe infection.

outcomes.story: A second surgeon is found. He is taken straight to the operating room, where the dead tissue is cut away back to healthy, bleeding edges. He returns on a breathing machine, with medicine supporting his blood pressure.
outcomes.reply: Yes. With gas on the X-ray, blisters and shock, a scan adds nothing. Every hour before surgery raises the chance that he dies.
outcomes.alarm: Back from surgery · dead tissue removed

outcomes.story: He waits for the scanner. Two hours later the leg is black to mid-thigh, and his blood pressure cannot be held with fluids.
outcomes.reply: We already knew what this was. Those two hours cost him tissue he will not get back. He goes to the operating room now.
outcomes.alarm: Leg black to mid-thigh · blood pressure 70 over 40

outcomes.story: The antibiotics run and he is watched. Three hours later his kidneys have stopped making urine, and the discoloration has reached his groin.
outcomes.reply: Antibiotics cannot get into dead tissue. Without surgery the infection keeps spreading whatever is in the drip. He goes to the operating room now.
outcomes.alarm: Discoloration at the groin · no urine

outcomes.story: You suggest sending him home. The resident stares.
outcomes.reply: He is in shock in intensive care with an infection that kills within hours. He is going to the operating room.

5.resident: He is back from the operating room. The surgeons removed all the dead tissue they could find.
5.question: What has to be part of the plan from here?
options: Nothing more. One operation is enough
Amputation of the leg, as in every case
A planned return to the operating room in 24 to 48 hours, to look again and remove any new dead tissue
Stopping the antibiotics now that surgery is done

terms.meaning: A planned repeat operation a day or two later, to check for and remove tissue that has died since the first.

outcomes.story: You say one operation is enough. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It almost never is. The infection often runs further than anyone can see on the first day.

outcomes.story: You say the leg must come off. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Sometimes it must, when the infection cannot be controlled or the limb cannot survive. It is not automatic.

outcomes.story: The second operation is booked for tomorrow. The antibiotics continue and will be narrowed once the lab names the bacteria.
outcomes.reply: Right. We go back every day or two until we find nothing left to remove.

outcomes.story: You suggest stopping the antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Surgery removes the dead tissue. The antibiotics protect the living tissue around it. He needs both.

differential.resident: The blood tests and the X-ray are in his chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: An ordinary skin infection (cellulitis)
A large clot in the leg veins
Necrotizing fasciitis: an infection destroying the tissue under the skin
A sharp-edged infection of the skin surface (erysipelas)
differential.reveal: It is necrotizing fasciitis. Bacteria got in through the puncture wound and are spreading along the sheet of tissue under the skin, killing it as they go. The gas on the X-ray, the blisters, the numb skin and the shock all say so. An ordinary skin infection does none of that. The surface looked mild at first because the damage starts underneath.

terms.meaning: Causing tissue to die.
A common infection of the skin and the fat beneath it. It is treated with antibiotics alone.

ending.stable: In intensive care after surgery, with a second operation planned
ending.unstable: In intensive care after surgery, with a second operation planned
ending.worse: In intensive care after surgery, having lost more tissue than he needed to
ending.critical: In intensive care on life support, after a late operation and the loss of his leg

inf-048.plainDiagnosis: A fast-spreading infection destroying the tissue under the skin of his leg (necrotizing fasciitis).

science.title: Why the skin was numb while the leg was agony
science.text: The fine nerves that carry touch run through the skin and the layer beneath it. As that layer dies, those nerves die with it, and the skin goes numb. Deeper nerves, still alive, are being flooded with pain signals from dying tissue.

science.title: Why clindamycin was added
science.text: The toxins that destroy tissue are proteins, built on the bacteria’s ribosomes. Clindamycin jams those ribosomes. Even before the bacteria die, they stop making toxin, which is why it is added to antibiotics that only kill.
science.lessonTitle: Follow a gene into a protein

sources.title: Stevens and Bryant (N Engl J Med 2017): necrotizing soft-tissue infections
Stevens et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2014): practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of skin and soft tissue infections, 2014 update by the IDSA

inf-093.title: Fever, a brutal headache _and spots on his wrists._

start.alarm: Fever 39.4 · spreading rash · confused at times

inf-093.handoff: A 45-year-old landscaper has had five days of high fever and a severe headache. Two days ago spots appeared on his wrists and ankles, and they are spreading. Today he has been confused at times.

interview.prompt: Ask about the fever, the headache and the rash
interview.finding: Five days of fever, a severe headache and aching all over. Two days ago spots came up on his wrists and ankles. They have spread to his palms and the soles of his feet and are moving toward his chest and belly.

interview.prompt: Ask about his work and any tick bites
interview.finding: He works outdoors in rural North Carolina. About a week ago he pulled a swollen tick off his calf while clearing brush. His dogs often carry ticks.

interview.prompt: Ask about today
interview.finding: He feels sick, and his wife says he has been confused on and off.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin, including his palms and soles
exam.finding: Flat red spots cover his wrists, ankles, palms and soles, and reach onto his forearms and lower belly. Some fade when pressed. Others are tiny purple dots that do not.

exam.prompt: Check how alert he is, and bend his neck
exam.finding: His attention drifts, but he wakes easily and knows who and where he is. Light hurts his eyes, which are red. His neck bends freely.

exam.prompt: Listen to his heart and lungs, and feel his belly
exam.finding: His heart is fast and regular. His lungs are clear. His belly is soft and slightly tender.

1.label: Blood tests and spinal fluid
1.content:
Sodium: 129, low.
Platelets: 88, low.
White blood cells: 7.8, normal.
Liver tests: about twice normal.
Kidney test (creatinine): 1.6, raised.
Spinal fluid, taken because of his confusion: a few extra white cells and a normal sugar.
Antibody test for Rocky Mountain spotted fever: sent, result pending.
Blood cultures: nothing growing at 24 hours.

0.resident: Fever, headache, a rash that started at the wrists and ankles and reached the palms and soles, and a tick bite a week ago. The test that would confirm what I suspect takes days.
0.question: What do we do right now?
options: Wait for the antibody test before starting any antibiotic
Start doxycycline now, and send the tests
Start ceftriaxone for a meningococcal infection, and hold the doxycycline
Take a skin biopsy, and hold antibiotics until it is back

terms.meaning: An antibiotic that works against the bacteria ticks carry.
Treatment started on strong suspicion, before tests confirm the cause.
A blood test that looks for antibodies the body has made against an infection.

outcomes.story: No antibiotic is given while the test is awaited. Six hours later he is more confused, and the spots are turning purple and running together.
outcomes.reply: That test is usually negative in the first week even when the disease is there. People die of this on the days spent waiting for it. Start doxycycline.

outcomes.story: The first dose of doxycycline is given within minutes. Blood is sent, and because of his confusion a spinal tap is done. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. This is treated on the story and the rash. Deaths rise sharply when treatment starts after the fifth day, and today is day five.

outcomes.story: Ceftriaxone runs in, and doxycycline is held. Six hours later his fever is no lower, he is more confused, and the rash is darker.
outcomes.reply: Covering for meningococcus is reasonable. Holding the doxycycline is not, because ceftriaxone does nothing to the bacteria ticks carry. Give it now.
outcomes.alarm: No better on ceftriaxone · more confused

outcomes.story: You ask for a biopsy before any antibiotic. The resident starts the antibiotic.
outcomes.reply: A biopsy can help, but it must not hold up treatment. Antibiotic first.

3.resident: His first dose is in. A question that comes up every summer: suppose he were a 5-year-old child with the same illness.
3.question: Which antibiotic would a child get?
options: Chloramphenicol, to spare the teeth
Amoxicillin
Doxycycline, the same as an adult
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole

terms.meaning: A side effect of older, related antibiotics given in long courses to young children. A short course of doxycycline has not been shown to cause it.

outcomes.story: You pick chloramphenicol. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It works less well and can harm the bone marrow. The worry about teeth came from older drugs given for months. A week of doxycycline does not stain them.

outcomes.story: You pick amoxicillin. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It does nothing to these bacteria. Children have died of this illness while taking it.

outcomes.story: You say doxycycline. The resident nods.
outcomes.reply: Right, at every age. Doctors once held it back from children out of fear for their teeth, and children died for that mistake.

outcomes.story: You pick a sulfa drug. The resident says never.
outcomes.reply: Sulfa drugs are linked to worse outcomes in this disease. They are the one group to avoid.

4.resident: His family asks why we treated before the test came back, and what happens if it comes back negative.
4.question: Which statement is true?
options: Sulfa drugs work just as well and can be swapped in
The antibiotic can stop once the rash fades
Treatment is optional, because this usually clears up without it
The antibody test is often negative in the first week, so treatment must not wait for it

terms.meaning: A protein the immune system makes to target one specific germ. It takes a week or more to appear in the blood.

outcomes.story: You say sulfa drugs can be swapped in. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: They make this disease worse. Doxycycline is the treatment.

outcomes.story: You say it can stop when the rash fades. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: The rash is not the guide. Treatment runs until at least three days after the fever has gone.

outcomes.story: You say treatment is optional. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Untreated, this disease kills a large share of the people who get it. It does not clear up by itself.

outcomes.story: You explain it to his family: the test looks for antibodies, and his body has not had time to make them yet.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. A negative test this early rules nothing out. We repeat it in a couple of weeks to confirm, long after the treatment has done its work.

differential.resident: His blood tests and spinal fluid results are in the chart.
differential.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rocky Mountain spotted fever
A meningococcal blood infection
Gonorrhea that has spread through the blood
Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)
differential.reveal: It is Rocky Mountain spotted fever, an infection carried by ticks. The bacteria invade the cells that line small blood vessels, which leak. That gives the rash, starting at the wrists and ankles and reaching the palms and soles, and it explains the low sodium, the low platelets and the strained liver. Meningococcal infection moves faster, and its rash is mostly on the trunk.

terms.meaning: The family of bacteria that causes this disease. They can only live inside the cells of an animal.
Inflammation of blood vessels, which makes them leak.

ending.stable: Admitted on doxycycline, with his fever starting to settle
ending.unstable: Admitted on doxycycline, with his fever starting to settle
ending.worse: In intensive care on doxycycline, after six hours without it
ending.critical: In intensive care on life support

inf-093.plainDiagnosis: An infection carried by ticks that attacks the lining of blood vessels (Rocky Mountain spotted fever).

science.title: A bacterium that lives like a virus
science.text: These bacteria are true cells, with their own ribosomes and their own membrane. But they can only grow inside our cells, as a virus does. That is why they do not show up in ordinary cultures, and why antibiotics that cannot get into cells, such as ceftriaxone, do not touch them.

science.title: Why a negative test did not mean no disease
science.text: The test detects antibodies, and the body needs a week or more to make them. Early on, a sick person and a healthy one give the same negative result. A test only counts as evidence at a time when it is able to turn positive.

sources.title: Biggs et al. (MMWR Recomm Rep 2016): diagnosis and management of tickborne rickettsial diseases, United States
Kirkland et al. (Clin Infect Dis 1995): therapeutic delay and mortality in cases of Rocky Mountain spotted fever

inf-032.title: It burned for three days. _Now the fever._

start.alarm: Fever 39.2 · pain in the right side

inf-032.handoff: A 32-year-old woman has had a high fever with shaking chills and a steady pain in her right side since yesterday. For three days before that it burned when she passed urine. She has vomited twice.

interview.prompt: Ask about the fever and the pain
interview.finding: Since yesterday: a fever up to 39.4 °C, shaking chills and a steady pain in her right side, at the back. She feels sick and has vomited twice.

interview.prompt: Ask about passing urine
interview.finding: For three days before the fever it burned when she passed urine, and she was going far more often than usual. She ignored it.

interview.prompt: Ask about pregnancy, discharge and past infections
interview.finding: Her last period was two weeks ago. She has no discharge or unusual bleeding. She has had one bladder infection before, never a kidney infection, and she does not have diabetes.

exam.prompt: Tap gently over each kidney, at the back
exam.finding: A light tap over her right kidney makes her flinch and cry out. The left side does not hurt.

exam.prompt: Press on her belly
exam.finding: It is soft, and slightly tender on the right. Nothing else is found.

exam.prompt: Do an internal exam
exam.finding: It is normal, with no discharge and no tenderness.

1.label: Urine and blood tests
1.content:
White blood cells: 16.8, high.
Kidney test (creatinine): normal. Lactate: normal.
Urine test strip: positive for white cells, and for nitrites, a chemical made by bacteria from the gut.
Urine under the microscope: many white cells, some packed into tube-shaped clumps called casts, which form only inside the kidney.
Urine stain: rod-shaped bacteria of the kind that live in the gut.
Blood cultures: sent, results pending.
Pregnancy test: negative.

0.resident: Burning urine, and now a fever and pain over one kidney. She looks ill.
0.question: Which tests do we send?
options: A urine test and culture, a blood count, blood salts and kidney tests, and blood cultures
A urine culture only, with no blood tests
A CT scan of her belly straight away, before any lab tests
No tests: reassure her and give nitrofurantoin to take at home

terms.meaning: Growing bacteria from a urine sample to identify them and test which antibiotics kill them.
The side of the body between the ribs and the hip, over the kidney.

outcomes.story: Urine and blood are collected before any antibiotic is given. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The urine shows where the infection is. The blood tests show how sick she is and whether bacteria have reached her bloodstream.

outcomes.story: You request a urine culture only. The resident adds the blood tests.
outcomes.reply: She has a high fever and a racing heart. We need to know whether her kidneys are coping and whether bacteria are in her blood.

outcomes.story: You request a CT first. The resident changes the order.
outcomes.reply: A scan is for when we suspect a blocked kidney or an abscess, or when treatment is not working. It does not come before a urine test.

outcomes.story: You write for nitrofurantoin and a discharge. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: She is too ill to go untested. And that antibiotic only works in the bladder, which matters more in a moment.

3.resident: She has a kidney infection. Her blood pressure, kidney tests and lactate are fine. But she has vomited twice and cannot keep fluids down.
3.question: Where should she be treated?
options: At home, on ciprofloxacin tablets, with a check in 48 hours
At home, on nitrofurantoin tablets
In hospital, with antibiotics and fluids through a vein, because she cannot keep anything down
At home with no antibiotics until the culture is back
3.fix: Admit her for treatment through a vein

terms.meaning: Staying in hospital. For a kidney infection the usual reasons are vomiting, low blood pressure, pregnancy or a blocked kidney.

outcomes.story: She goes home with tablets and vomits each one back up. Eight hours later she returns, shaking, with a higher fever and a low blood pressure.
outcomes.reply: Tablets only work if they stay down. For eight hours she has had no antibiotic at all, and the infection has reached her blood. She should have been admitted.
outcomes.alarm: Back in the department · blood pressure 88 over 50

outcomes.story: You write for nitrofurantoin at home. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: That drug collects in the urine and treats the bladder. It never reaches a useful level in the kidney. And she cannot keep tablets down.

outcomes.story: She is admitted. A drip is started, and fluids run in.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Plenty of women with a kidney infection can go home on tablets. One who vomits everything cannot.

outcomes.story: You suggest waiting for the culture. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Cultures take two days. A kidney infection is treated at once, and the antibiotic is adjusted when the result arrives.

4.resident: She is admitted, and her drip is running. Her urine shows gut bacteria.
4.question: Which antibiotic do we start?
options: Nitrofurantoin by mouth
Ceftriaxone into a vein, narrowed once the culture is back
Amoxicillin by mouth
Vancomycin into a vein, alone

terms.meaning: A once-a-day antibiotic given into a vein that covers most of the gut bacteria behind kidney infections.
Switching to a more targeted antibiotic once the lab has identified the bacteria.

outcomes.story: You write for nitrofurantoin. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: It treats the bladder, not the kidney. And she is vomiting.

outcomes.story: The first dose of ceftriaxone goes in with her fluids. Over the next hours her temperature starts to come down.
outcomes.reply: Right. It reaches the kidney, covers the likely bacteria and does not have to be swallowed. In two days the culture tells us whether to change it.

outcomes.story: You write for amoxicillin. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: Too many of these bacteria are resistant to it now, and it would have to be swallowed.

outcomes.story: You write for vancomycin alone. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: Vancomycin covers a different family of bacteria altogether. It would miss the gut bacteria seen in her urine.

differential.resident: Her urine and blood results are in the chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A simple bladder infection (cystitis)
A kidney infection (acute pyelonephritis)
A kidney stone
Pelvic inflammatory disease, an infection of the womb and tubes
differential.reveal: It is a kidney infection. Bacteria from a bladder infection climbed up to her right kidney. The fever, the pain over the kidney and the white-cell casts in her urine place the infection in the kidney itself. A bladder infection causes burning without fever or flank pain, and a stone causes pain in waves with blood in the urine.

terms.meaning: Infection of the kidney.
Tiny molds of the kidney’s tubules, washed out in the urine. White-cell casts mean inflammation inside the kidney.

ending.stable: On the ward on antibiotics through a vein, with her fever coming down
ending.worse: On the ward on antibiotics, after a night of sepsis that could have been avoided
ending.critical: In intensive care with septic shock

inf-032.plainDiagnosis: A kidney infection that climbed up from the bladder (acute pyelonephritis).

science.title: Why casts pointed to the kidney
science.text: Each kidney is built from about a million fine tubules. White cells fighting infection inside a tubule get stuck together in its shape, like jelly in a mold, and are then flushed out. Only the kidney has tubules, so only the kidney can make casts.

science.title: Why she shook with chills as her fever rose
science.text: Infection raised her brain’s temperature set point. Her body then read its normal temperature as too cold, so it shivered to make heat and tightened skin vessels to keep it. The shaking was her own body driving the fever up.

sources.title: Gupta et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2011): international clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of acute uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women
Johnson and Russo (N Engl J Med 2018): acute pyelonephritis in adults

fm-095.title: The room spins _every time she rolls over._

start.alarm: Spinning spells with head movement

fm-095.handoff: A 59-year-old woman has had a week of sudden spinning spells. They come on when she rolls over in bed or looks up at a high shelf, and each lasts less than a minute. A friend recently had a stroke, and she is afraid this is one.

interview.prompt: Ask about the spinning and what sets it off
interview.finding: The room spins when she rolls over in bed, looks up at a shelf or lies back at the hairdresser. Each spell lasts 20 to 40 seconds and makes her feel sick. It stops when she keeps her head still.

interview.prompt: Ask about her hearing, and about weakness or speech
interview.finding: Her hearing is normal, with no ringing or fullness in her ears. She has had no headache, double vision, slurred speech, weakness or trouble walking.

interview.prompt: Ask about recent illness and her medicines
interview.finding: She has not had a cold, a fever or ear pain. She takes one blood pressure tablet and nothing that causes drowsiness. She used to get migraines.

exam.prompt: Check her face, speech and eye movements while she sits still
exam.finding: Her face moves evenly and her speech is clear. Her eyes move fully in every direction and hold steady, with no flickering.

exam.prompt: Test her coordination and watch her walk
exam.finding: She touches her nose and your finger accurately. She walks steadily, even heel to toe, and stands firm with her feet together and eyes closed.

exam.prompt: Test her hearing, and take her blood pressure standing
exam.finding: She hears equally well in both ears. Her blood pressure does not fall when she stands.

1.label: Positional test
1.content:
Lying her back quickly with her head turned to the right: after about 3 seconds her eyes beat upward with a twist toward the right ear, and the spinning she knows comes on.
The eye movement fades and stops within 30 seconds.
The same test with her head turned to the left: nothing happens.
The eye movement never changes direction and does not persist.

0.resident: Short spinning spells set off by head position, with a normal exam in between. That pattern usually comes from the inner ear, and one bedside test can show it.
0.question: Which test?
options: Standing with her feet together and eyes closed (Romberg test)
Lying her back quickly with her head turned to one side (Dix-Hallpike test)
Running cold water into her ear in the office
A quick head turn while she fixes on your nose, and nothing else

terms.meaning: A false feeling that you or the room are spinning.
A rhythmic flicking of the eyes. Its direction and timing help show where a balance problem is.
Moving a patient quickly from sitting to lying with the head turned and hanging back slightly, while watching the eyes.

outcomes.story: You ask her to stand with her eyes closed. She stands firm.
outcomes.reply: That tests position sense in the legs. It was normal, and it cannot bring out a positional problem in the ear.

outcomes.story: You warn her that it may bring on the spinning, then lie her back quickly with her head turned to the right. You watch her eyes, then repeat it on the left. What you saw goes in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. This test puts the suspect canal of the inner ear in line with gravity. If loose crystals are in it, they move, and her eyes show it.

outcomes.story: You suggest cold water in her ear. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is a hospital test of a different part of the inner ear. It is unpleasant, and it does not answer this question.

outcomes.story: You do the quick head turn. Her eyes stay on your nose.
outcomes.reply: That test helps when dizziness is constant. Hers comes in short spells with position, and for that we need the lying-back test.

3.resident: The test brought on her spinning, with exactly the eye movement we expected. Loose crystals are sitting in the back canal of her right inner ear.
3.question: How do we treat it?
options: Meclizine every day, long term, to damp the symptoms
Move her head through a set sequence of positions to roll the crystals out (Epley maneuver)
An urgent MRI of her brain before any treatment
Refer her for surgery to block the canal

terms.meaning: A sequence of four head and body positions, each held for about 30 seconds, that rolls loose crystals out of the canal.
A tablet that dulls the sense of motion. It can ease nausea for a day or two and does not fix the cause.

outcomes.story: You write for daily meclizine. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: It blunts the spinning and leaves the crystals where they are. It also makes people drowsy and unsteady. We can fix the cause in five minutes.

outcomes.story: You guide her head through the four positions, holding each one. She feels one last spin on the second position. When she sits up, you repeat the lying-back test, and nothing happens.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Most people are cured by one or two treatments. You have moved the crystals back to where they belong.
outcomes.alarm: Spinning gone on the repeat test

outcomes.story: You request an urgent MRI. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Her story is typical, her exam is normal and the test was positive in the expected way. A scan would find nothing and delay the cure.

outcomes.story: You suggest surgery. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Surgery is for the rare person whom repeated maneuvers have failed. Nobody starts there.

4.resident: She is relieved, and she still asks how she would know if it ever were a stroke. It is a good question.
4.question: Which finding would send her for urgent brain tests?
options: Spinning that lasts about 30 seconds and weakens when the movement is repeated
Eye flicking that is purely up and down or changes direction, with unsteady walking
Symptoms that come only with a change of position
A short pause before the eye flicking starts

terms.meaning: A cause in the brain itself, such as a stroke at the back of the brain, as opposed to the inner ear.
Clumsy, unsteady movement or walking.

outcomes.story: You pick short, fading spells. The resident shakes their head.
