outcomes.reply: That describes what she has. Short spells that tire out with repetition are the mark of the harmless inner ear kind.

outcomes.story: You tell her which signs to act on: trouble walking, double vision, slurred speech, weakness, or dizziness that does not stop.
outcomes.reply: Right. Eye movements that go straight up and down or switch direction, with unsteady walking, point to the brain. Those need a scan the same day.

outcomes.story: You pick symptoms that come only with position. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is reassuring, not worrying. It is what the inner ear kind does.

outcomes.story: You pick the short pause. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The pause is typical of the harmless kind: the crystals take a moment to start moving. A brain cause tends to start at once.

differential.resident: The positional test is written up in her chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Vestibular neuritis, an inflamed balance nerve
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
Meniere disease
A stroke in the cerebellum
differential.reveal: It is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Tiny crystals that belong in one part of the inner ear have come loose and drifted into a canal that senses turning. When her head moves, they roll and send a false signal of spinning. An inflamed nerve causes constant dizziness for days, Meniere disease brings hearing loss and ringing, and a stroke would show on her exam.

terms.meaning: Not dangerous.
Coming in sudden, short attacks.

ending.better: Home, with the spinning gone after one treatment in clinic
ending.stable: Home, with the spinning gone after one treatment in clinic
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

fm-095.plainDiagnosis: Loose crystals in the inner ear that cause short spinning spells with head movement (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo).

science.title: How loose crystals fool the brain
science.text: The inner ear’s canals are filled with fluid. When the head turns, the fluid lags, bends sensory hairs, and the brain reads rotation. Crystals rolling through a canal drag the fluid the same way, so the brain is told the head is turning when it is still.

science.title: Why the treatment is done slowly, in a set order
science.text: The crystals are denser than the fluid around them, so gravity pulls them to the lowest point of the canal. Each position in the sequence makes a new part of the canal the lowest, and holding it gives them time to sink there, step by step, until they drop out.
science.lessonTitle: Choose a force or energy model

sources.title: Bhattacharyya et al. (Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017): clinical practice guideline, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (update)
Kim and Zee (N Engl J Med 2014): benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

fm-076.title: Two weeks of exhaustion _and a sore throat._

start.alarm: Exhausted for two weeks · rash after amoxicillin

fm-076.handoff: An 18-year-old college student has been exhausted for two weeks, with a sore throat, slight fevers and tender lumps at the back of her neck. Another clinic gave her amoxicillin four days ago, and she then came out in a rash.

interview.prompt: Ask about the tiredness and the throat
interview.finding: For about two weeks she has been exhausted however much she sleeps, with a sore throat, slight fevers and tender lumps at the back of her neck. She has little appetite and a feeling of fullness under her left ribs.

interview.prompt: Ask what treatment she has had
interview.finding: A clinic gave her amoxicillin four days ago for a presumed strep throat. Afterward a rash came up all over her body.

interview.prompt: Ask about college life and her medicines
interview.finding: She lives in a dorm, has a new partner and shares drinks with her roommates. Nobody around her has had strep. She takes a contraceptive pill.

exam.prompt: Look at her throat and feel her neck
exam.finding: Her throat is red, and her tonsils are large and coated with white patches. Tender glands can be felt on both sides, most of them at the back of the neck.

exam.prompt: Feel her belly
exam.finding: The tip of her spleen can be felt 2 cm below her left ribs, and it is slightly tender. Normally a spleen cannot be felt at all. Her liver is not enlarged.

exam.prompt: Look at her skin and eyes
exam.finding: A faint rash of flat and slightly raised pink spots covers her chest and back. Her eyes are not yellow.

1.label: Blood tests and throat swab
1.content:
Monospot, a quick antibody test for mononucleosis: positive.
White blood cells: 13.5, raised, and 62% of them are lymphocytes.
Blood film under the microscope: many large, unusual-looking lymphocytes.
Liver tests: about twice normal.
Rapid strep test on a throat swab: negative.

0.resident: A sore throat with white patches on the tonsils could be strep. Several things about her do not fit strep.
0.question: Which group of findings points to mononucleosis instead?
options: Glands at the front of the neck and white patches on the tonsils
Glands at the back of the neck, an enlarged spleen and deep tiredness, with a rash after amoxicillin
A sudden high fever with no swollen glands
A runny nose and a cough
0.fix: Name the pattern and send tests

terms.meaning: An infection, usually with Epstein-Barr virus, spread in saliva. It causes weeks of tiredness, a sore throat and swollen glands.
An organ under the left ribs that filters blood. It swells in mononucleosis.

outcomes.story: You point to the front glands and the white patches. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Strep causes exactly those too. They do not separate the two.

outcomes.story: You list them, and the resident nods. Blood is sent and her throat is swabbed. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Glands at the back of the neck, a spleen you can feel and tiredness that lasts weeks all point to mononucleosis. The amoxicillin rash is almost a signature.

outcomes.story: You pick fever without swollen glands. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Swollen glands are one of the main features of mononucleosis. Their absence would argue against it.

outcomes.story: You pick a runny nose and cough. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those suggest an ordinary cold. She has neither.

3.resident: She has mononucleosis, and her spleen is enlarged. She asks when she can get back to her usual activities.
3.question: What is the most important advice?
options: Go back to contact sports straight away, to keep fit
No contact sports or heavy lifting for at least three to four weeks, and longer if her spleen is still enlarged
Strict bed rest for six months
No limits at all

terms.meaning: A tear in the spleen that bleeds into the belly. It is rare in mononucleosis, and it can kill.

outcomes.story: You tell her sport is fine. The resident stops her at the door.
outcomes.reply: An enlarged spleen is soft and sticks out from under the ribs that normally shield it. One knock can tear it. No contact sports for now.

outcomes.story: You explain the risk and the time frame. Walking and light activity are fine once she feels up to it, and the antibiotic is stopped.
outcomes.reply: Yes. The spleen is at its most fragile in the first three to four weeks. She should come straight in if she gets sudden pain under her left ribs.

outcomes.story: You advise six months in bed. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Far too much. She should rest as she needs and build back up. Only contact sports and heavy lifting are off limits.

outcomes.story: You say there are no limits. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: There is one, and it matters: nothing that could hit or strain her spleen for at least three to four weeks.

4.resident: She asks why the amoxicillin gave her a rash, and whether she is now allergic to penicillin for life.
4.question: What do we tell her?
options: She has a true penicillin allergy and must avoid that whole family for life
The rash means the infection has turned bacterial and needs antibiotics through a vein
This rash is common when amoxicillin is taken during mononucleosis, and it does not by itself prove a lifelong allergy
She should take high-dose steroids, as everyone with mononucleosis does

terms.meaning: An immune reaction to a substance that can come back, sometimes more severely, each time the substance is met.
Treating symptoms with rest, fluids and pain relief while the body clears the infection.

outcomes.story: You tell her she is allergic for life. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Most people who get this rash can take penicillins safely later. Labeling her allergic for life would deny her useful antibiotics. An allergy clinic can test her properly.

outcomes.story: You say the infection has turned bacterial. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: It is a virus, and it is behaving as expected. Antibiotics do nothing against it. The rash came from the amoxicillin meeting the virus.

outcomes.story: You explain it, and she is relieved. A note goes in her chart that the rash happened during mononucleosis.
outcomes.reply: Right. The virus stirs up the immune system so that it reacts to the drug. Once she is well, that reaction usually does not happen again.

outcomes.story: You suggest steroids. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Steroids are kept for the rare case where swollen tonsils threaten to block the airway. For everyone else the treatment is rest and time.

differential.resident: Her blood tests and throat swab are in the chart.
differential.question: What is causing this?
options: Strep bacteria, with a rise in neutrophils
Cytomegalovirus, which always gives a positive Monospot
Epstein-Barr virus, with a rise in unusual-looking lymphocytes and mildly raised liver tests
A new HIV infection, with a positive Monospot
differential.reveal: It is Epstein-Barr virus, the usual cause of mononucleosis. Her Monospot is positive, most of her white cells are lymphocytes, many of them the large unusual kind made to fight this virus, and her liver tests are mildly raised. Strep raises a different kind of white cell, and her strep test is negative. Cytomegalovirus can look similar but usually gives a negative Monospot.

terms.meaning: A type of white blood cell that fights viruses.
A rapid blood test for antibodies that appear during mononucleosis.

ending.stable: Home to rest, with no contact sports for at least a month
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

fm-076.plainDiagnosis: Mononucleosis, a viral infection with an enlarged spleen (Epstein-Barr virus).

science.title: Why antibiotics could never have helped
science.text: Antibiotics attack things only bacteria have, such as their cell walls and their own kind of ribosome. A virus has neither. It is a set of genes in a protein coat that borrows our cells’ machinery, so there is nothing for the antibiotic to hit.

science.title: Why her spleen and glands swelled
science.text: This virus infects one kind of lymphocyte, and other lymphocytes multiply fast to kill the infected ones. The spleen and lymph glands are where that multiplying happens. They swell because they are packed with dividing cells.

sources.title: Luzuriaga and Sullivan (N Engl J Med 2010): infectious mononucleosis
Ebell et al. (JAMA 2016): does this patient have infectious mononucleosis? The rational clinical examination systematic review

fm-023.title: Tired for months, _and craving ice._

start.alarm: Tired for four months · pale

fm-023.handoff: A 34-year-old woman has felt more and more tired for four months. She gets lightheaded when she stands, is short of breath on the stairs, and has an odd craving to chew ice.

interview.prompt: Ask about the tiredness
interview.finding: It has built up over four months. She tires quickly, gets lightheaded when she stands, is slightly breathless on stairs and finds it hard to concentrate. She craves ice and chews it constantly.

interview.prompt: Ask about her periods
interview.finding: They have been heavy for two years. They last seven days, with clots, and on the worst days she soaks through a pad every two hours. Nobody has ever looked into it.

interview.prompt: Ask about other bleeding, her diet and her medicines
interview.finding: No black or bloody stools and no weight loss. She eats a varied diet that includes meat. She takes ibuprofen now and then for cramps. Her mother had low iron.

exam.prompt: Look at her eyelids, skin and nails
exam.finding: The insides of her lower eyelids are pale, and so are her nail beds. Several fingernails are slightly scooped, like a spoon. She is not yellow and has no bruises or red spots.

exam.prompt: Listen to her heart and lungs
exam.finding: There is a soft whooshing sound with each heartbeat, the kind heard when thin blood flows fast. Her lungs are clear.

exam.prompt: Feel her belly and her glands
exam.finding: Her belly is soft, with nothing enlarged. No swollen glands.

1.label: Blood tests
1.content:
Hemoglobin: 9.2, low (normal for a woman is about 12 to 16).
Red cell size (MCV): 71, small (normal is 80 to 100).
Red cell size variation: wide. New cells are smaller than older ones.
Ferritin, the measure of stored iron: 6, very low.
Iron in the blood: low. The proteins that carry iron are mostly empty.
Platelets: slightly high.

0.resident: Months of tiredness, pale eyelids, spoon-shaped nails and a craving for ice. I have a strong suspicion, and one cheap test starts to check it.
0.question: Which test comes first?
options: A full blood count, with the size of the red cells
A look at a blood film under the microscope, and nothing else
A bone marrow biopsy
Vitamin B12 and folate levels

terms.meaning: Too little hemoglobin in the blood, so less oxygen reaches the tissues.
The iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
A craving to eat things that are not food, such as ice or clay. It is a clue to iron deficiency.

outcomes.story: Blood is drawn in clinic, and iron studies are added. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The count shows whether she is anemic, and the size of her red cells points to the cause. Small cells suggest too little iron.

outcomes.story: You ask for a blood film only. The resident adds the count.
outcomes.reply: A film is useful later. The count comes first, because it gives the numbers everything else builds on.

outcomes.story: You ask for a bone marrow biopsy. The resident looks alarmed.
outcomes.reply: That is a needle into the hip bone. It is for unexplained problems in several kinds of blood cell, not a first test for tiredness.

outcomes.story: You ask for B12 and folate. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those cause anemia with large red cells. Start with the count, and let the cell size tell us which tests come next.

3.resident: She has iron deficiency anemia, and the cause is her heavy periods, which we will also have looked into. She is steady, with a hemoglobin of 9.2.
3.question: How do we treat the anemia?
options: A blood transfusion right away
Iron tablets, taken with vitamin C and not with calcium
Iron through a vein, as the first choice for everyone
Vitamin B12 injections, just in case

terms.meaning: The commonest iron tablet.
The protein that stores iron. A low level in the blood means the body’s iron stores are empty.

outcomes.story: You suggest a transfusion. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Transfusion is for severe anemia or a patient who is unstable. She walked in here. She needs iron, and her marrow will make the cells.

outcomes.story: You write for iron tablets and explain how to take them: with orange juice, on an empty stomach if she can manage it, and away from calcium, antacids and tea. You warn her about dark stools and constipation. She is referred for her heavy periods.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Tablets are cheap, and they work. Vitamin C helps iron get absorbed, and calcium and tea block it. Stopping the blood loss matters just as much.

outcomes.story: You suggest iron through a vein. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is for people who cannot absorb or tolerate tablets, or who keep losing blood faster than tablets can replace it. Tablets come first.

outcomes.story: You suggest B12 injections. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Her red cells are small and her iron stores are empty. B12 deficiency makes large cells. Treat what the tests show.

4.resident: She has her prescription. Iron works slowly, so we need a plan for checking that it is working and for when to stop.
4.question: What is the plan?
options: Stop the iron as soon as the hemoglobin is normal, with no more checks
Recheck the hemoglobin in two to four weeks, and continue iron for three to six months after it is normal
Repeat a bone marrow biopsy at three months
Iron every day for life, whatever happens
4.fix: Book the recheck and explain the course

terms.meaning: The reserve of iron kept in the liver and marrow. It refills only after the hemoglobin has recovered.

outcomes.story: You plan to stop when the hemoglobin is normal. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: At that point her blood looks normal, but her stores are still empty. One heavy period and she is back where she started. She needs months more.

outcomes.story: You book a blood test in three weeks and explain that she will take iron for several months after her count recovers.
outcomes.reply: Right. A rise in hemoglobin by then shows it is working. If it has not risen, we ask why: tablets not taken, not absorbed, or blood still being lost.

outcomes.story: You plan a bone marrow biopsy. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A blood test tells us everything we need. Nobody needs a biopsy to follow iron treatment.

outcomes.story: You plan lifelong iron. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Once her stores are full and her periods are under control, she can stop. Too much iron over years does its own harm.

differential.resident: Her blood results are in the chart.
differential.question: What kind of anemia is this?
options: Anemia of long-term illness
Beta-thalassemia trait, an inherited cause of small red cells
Iron deficiency anemia
Vitamin B12 deficiency
differential.reveal: It is iron deficiency anemia. Her red cells are small and her ferritin is 6, which means her iron stores are empty. Two years of heavy periods have used iron faster than her diet could replace it. Long-term illness gives a normal or high ferritin, thalassemia trait gives small cells with normal iron stores, and B12 deficiency gives large cells.

terms.meaning: Having red cells that are smaller than normal.
Heavy menstrual bleeding.

ending.stable: Home on iron tablets, with a blood test booked in three weeks and a referral for her heavy periods
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

fm-023.plainDiagnosis: Too little iron to make enough hemoglobin, because of heavy periods (iron deficiency anemia).

science.title: Why no iron means no hemoglobin
science.text: Each hemoglobin molecule is four protein chains, and each chain holds a heme group with one iron atom at its center. That iron is what binds oxygen. Without iron the heme cannot be finished, so less hemoglobin is made and each red cell comes out small and pale.

science.title: Why she was breathless with a normal oxygen reading
science.text: Her finger probe read 99% because the hemoglobin she has is fully loaded. But she has about a quarter less of it than she should. Each heartbeat delivers less oxygen, so on the stairs her heart and lungs have to work harder.

sources.title: Camaschella (N Engl J Med 2015): iron-deficiency anemia
Pasricha et al. (Lancet 2021): iron deficiency

nph-067.title: Eighteen hours _without passing a drop._

start.alarm: Cannot pass urine · swollen, painful lower belly

nph-067.handoff: A 76-year-old man has not been able to pass urine for 18 hours. His lower belly is swollen and painful. For two years his stream has been getting weaker, and three days ago he started a cold remedy from the pharmacy.

interview.prompt: Ask about not being able to pass urine
interview.finding: Nothing has come out for 18 hours, and his lower belly feels fuller and more painful by the hour. He has no fever, no burning and no blood in his urine.

interview.prompt: Ask how his urine flow has been over the years
interview.finding: For two years it has been slow to start and weak, and he gets up three or four times a night. He never feels he has emptied fully. It has never stopped completely before.

interview.prompt: Ask about his medicines
interview.finding: Three days ago he started a cold remedy that contains pseudoephedrine and diphenhydramine. Things got much worse after that. He also takes amlodipine for blood pressure.

exam.prompt: Feel and tap his lower belly
exam.finding: There is a tense, tender swelling that rises from his pubic bone almost to his navel. It sounds dull when tapped, like something full of fluid.

exam.prompt: Examine his prostate with a finger
exam.finding: His prostate is enlarged, smooth and firm on both sides, with no lumps. The muscle tone at his anus is normal, and feeling around it is normal.

exam.prompt: Tap over his kidneys, and test his legs
exam.finding: Tapping over his kidneys does not hurt. The strength, feeling and reflexes in his legs are normal.

1.label: Catheter, blood tests and ultrasound
1.content:
Catheter: 1,400 mL of urine drained at once (a full bladder normally holds about 400 to 500).
Kidney test (creatinine): 2.6, up from his usual 1.0.
Potassium: 4.8, at the top of normal.
Urine test: no infection.
Ultrasound: both kidneys are swollen with backed-up urine.
PSA, a prostate blood test: mildly raised.

0.resident: He cannot pass urine, and I can feel his bladder up near his navel.
0.question: What do we do first?
options: A CT scan of his belly before doing anything
Pass a catheter into his bladder to drain it now
Start an alpha-blocker tablet and send him home
Emergency dialysis

terms.meaning: Being unable to empty the bladder.
A soft tube passed through the urethra into the bladder to drain urine.
A gland that surrounds the urethra just below the bladder in men. It enlarges with age and can squeeze the urethra.

outcomes.story: He waits for a scanner and then for the report, which says what you could already feel: a huge bladder. Ninety minutes on he is in more pain, and still nothing has drained.
outcomes.reply: We could feel the diagnosis with one hand. Every hour of back-pressure hurts his kidneys, and he has just spent another ninety minutes in pain. Put the catheter in.
outcomes.alarm: In more pain · still no urine

outcomes.story: A catheter is passed, and urine pours out. His face relaxes within a minute. Blood is sent and an ultrasound is done, and the results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Draining the bladder treats the pain, proves the diagnosis and takes the pressure off his kidneys, all at once.

outcomes.story: You write for a tablet and a discharge. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: With a liter and a half trapped in his bladder? A tablet takes days to help. He needs draining first.

outcomes.story: You suggest dialysis. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His kidneys are being squeezed from below. Take the pressure off and they recover. Dialysis would not touch the cause.

3.resident: His prostate has been narrowing his flow for two years. Something tipped him into a complete blockage three days ago.
3.question: What was it?
options: The cold remedy, with pseudoephedrine and diphenhydramine
His amlodipine
Dehydration
A urine infection

terms.meaning: A decongestant. It tightens smooth muscle, including the muscle at the outlet of the bladder.
An older antihistamine. It blocks the nerve signal that makes the bladder squeeze.

outcomes.story: You name the cold remedy. It is stopped, and he is told which pharmacy medicines to avoid.
outcomes.reply: Right. One ingredient tightens the outlet, and the other weakens the bladder’s squeeze. In a man whose prostate is already in the way, that combination shuts the door.

outcomes.story: You blame the amlodipine. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He has taken that for years with no trouble, and it is not known for this. Look at what changed three days ago.

outcomes.story: You suggest dehydration. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A dry man makes less urine. He would not end up with a liter and a half trapped in his bladder.

outcomes.story: You suggest an infection. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His urine test shows no infection, and he has had no burning or fever.

4.resident: His bladder is drained, and his kidney test is already improving. In a few days the catheter will come out, to see whether he can pass urine by himself.
4.question: Which medicine gives that the best chance?
options: An anticholinergic, such as oxybutynin
An alpha-blocker, such as tamsulosin
A strong water tablet
None. Leave the catheter in long term

terms.meaning: A medicine that relaxes the smooth muscle of the prostate and the bladder outlet, so urine flows more easily.
Taking a catheter out to see whether the patient can pass urine without it.

outcomes.story: You write for oxybutynin. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: That weakens the bladder’s squeeze. It is the same effect that helped put him here. He needs the outlet relaxed.

outcomes.story: Tamsulosin is started tonight, and he is booked to see a urologist.
outcomes.reply: Yes. It relaxes the muscle around the outlet, and men who take it are more likely to pass urine when the catheter comes out.

outcomes.story: You write for a water tablet. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: Making more urine does not open a blocked outlet. It only fills the bladder faster.

outcomes.story: You suggest a long-term catheter. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A permanent catheter brings infections and discomfort. It is a last resort, and he has not yet had a fair try without one.

differential.resident: The catheter result, blood tests and ultrasound are in his chart.
differential.question: Why are his kidneys struggling?
options: Too little blood is reaching them (prerenal)
The kidney tissue itself is damaged (acute tubular necrosis)
Urine is blocked downstream and is backing up into them (post-renal, obstructive)
Their filters are inflamed (glomerulonephritis)
differential.reveal: His kidneys are being squeezed from below. The enlarged prostate blocked the outlet of his bladder, the bladder filled to nearly three times its normal size, and urine backed up into both kidneys. The ultrasound shows them swollen with it. Relieving the blockage usually lets the kidneys recover.

terms.meaning: A kidney swollen with urine that cannot drain.
A sudden drop in how well the kidneys work.

ending.stable: Admitted overnight with a catheter, his kidney tests already improving
ending.worse: Admitted with a catheter, after a longer wait than his kidneys needed

nph-067.plainDiagnosis: A bladder blocked by an enlarged prostate, with urine backing up into the kidneys (urinary retention with obstructive kidney injury).

science.title: Why a blocked bladder stops the kidneys
science.text: The kidney filters blood because pressure in its tiny blood vessels is higher than pressure in the tubules they empty into. When urine backs up, the pressure in the tubules climbs toward the pressure in the vessels, and filtering slows to a stop.

science.title: Why a slightly larger prostate matters so much
science.text: Flow through a tube depends very steeply on its width: halve the radius, and flow falls to about a sixteenth. The urethra runs through the middle of the prostate, so a little swelling or tightening there costs a great deal of flow.

sources.title: Lerner et al. (J Urol 2021): management of lower urinary tract symptoms attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia, AUA guideline part I
Selius and Subedi (Am Fam Physician 2008): urinary retention in adults, diagnosis and initial management

nph-076.title: He seems drunk, _but there is no alcohol in him._

start.alarm: Confused · breathing deep and fast

nph-076.handoff: A 36-year-old man was found by his roommate, confused and slurring his words, and has been getting sleepier for hours. He is breathing deep and fast. The roommate says he had no alcohol today, and found an empty container of car antifreeze beside him.

interview.prompt: Ask the roommate what he saw
interview.finding: Over several hours he became confused and unsteady, and slurred his words as if drunk, though he had no alcohol today. He has grown sleepier and is breathing hard. He has not had a seizure or a fall.

interview.prompt: Ask what was found near him
interview.finding: An empty container of car antifreeze was beside him in the garage. Nothing else seems to be missing, and nobody knows exactly when he drank it.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health
interview.finding: He has depression and may not have been taking his medicine. He has been very low since a breakup. He used to drink heavily.

exam.prompt: Check how alert he is, his speech and his balance
exam.finding: He is drowsy but wakes to your voice. His speech is slurred, his eyes flick from side to side, and he is unsteady when he moves. His breath does not smell of alcohol.

exam.prompt: Watch his breathing
exam.finding: His breaths are deep and fast. His lungs sound clear.

exam.prompt: Press on his belly and his sides
exam.finding: His belly is soft. He is slightly tender over both kidneys. He says his fingers and lips are tingling.

1.label: Blood and urine tests
1.content:
Blood acid level (pH): 7.18, acidic. Bicarbonate: 8, very low.
Anion gap: 30, high. An unmeasured acid is in his blood.
Blood sugar: normal. Lactate: only slightly raised, not enough to explain the acid.
Osmolar gap: 35, high. Something is dissolved in his blood that the standard tests do not measure.
Alcohol (ethanol) level: zero.
Kidney test (creatinine): 1.6, and rising. Calcium: low.
Urine: envelope-shaped and needle-shaped crystals of calcium oxalate. The urine glows under ultraviolet light.

0.resident: He looks drunk with no alcohol, he is breathing as if his blood were acidic, and there was antifreeze beside him.
0.question: Which tests will sort this out fastest?
options: A CT scan of his head only
A blood alcohol level only
A blood gas, blood salts, a measured blood concentration (osmolality) and a lactate
A urine drug screen only
0.fix: Send the blood gas, salts and osmolality

terms.meaning: A sum worked out from the blood salts. A high result means an extra acid is in the blood.
The difference between how concentrated the blood measures and how concentrated it should be from its known contents. A high gap means an unmeasured substance is present.

outcomes.story: He goes for a head scan, which is normal. Forty-five minutes have passed. He is harder to rouse and is breathing faster.
outcomes.reply: His brain is being poisoned, not injured. A scan cannot see that. While he lay there, his body turned more of the antifreeze into acid. Send the bloods.

outcomes.story: You request an alcohol level only. The resident adds to the order.
outcomes.reply: Worth having, and it will be zero. It cannot tell us what he did drink. We need the acid level and the two gaps.

outcomes.story: Blood is drawn, and urine is sent to be looked at under the microscope. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Those tests show an acid we cannot name and a substance we cannot see. Together they point to a toxic alcohol within minutes.

outcomes.story: You request a urine drug screen only. The resident adds to the order.
outcomes.reply: A drug screen does not look for antifreeze. It would come back clean while he gets worse.

3.resident: It is antifreeze. The antifreeze itself does little harm. His liver is turning it into acids that are destroying his kidneys.
3.question: What do we give first?
options: Fomepizole, which blocks the enzyme that makes the poisons
Sodium nitroprusside
High-dose insulin
Activated charcoal, and nothing else

terms.meaning: The main ingredient of most car antifreeze. It tastes sweet and causes drunkenness at first.
An antidote that blocks alcohol dehydrogenase, the liver enzyme that turns ethylene glycol into toxic acids.

outcomes.story: Fomepizole is given into a vein, with fluids. From this point his liver stops making new poison.
outcomes.reply: Right. Block the enzyme, and the antifreeze stays in its harmless form until it is cleared. The earlier it goes in, the more kidney is saved.

outcomes.story: You ask for nitroprusside. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: That lowers blood pressure, and his is normal. It has no place here.

outcomes.story: You ask for high-dose insulin. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is an antidote for overdoses of certain heart medicines. It does nothing for antifreeze.

outcomes.story: He is given charcoal to drink and nothing more. An hour later he is drowsier, and his kidney test has risen again.
outcomes.reply: Charcoal does not bind alcohols, and this one was absorbed hours ago. For an hour his liver has kept making acid. Give the fomepizole.

4.resident: The antidote stops new poison being made. He still has severe acid in his blood, and his kidneys are failing.
4.question: What else does he need?
options: All fluids stopped, to limit crystals forming
Dialysis, to clear the antifreeze and its acids and to correct his blood
Broad antibiotics
High-dose potassium chloride

terms.meaning: A machine that passes blood alongside a clean fluid, separated by a thin membrane, so that small unwanted molecules move out.

outcomes.story: You suggest stopping fluids. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His kidneys need a good flow of fluid to keep crystals moving through. Drying him out would make them settle.

outcomes.story: The kidney team places a dialysis line and starts the machine. Over the next hour his blood becomes less acidic and his breathing slows.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Dialysis takes out the antifreeze and the acids already made, and it does the work his kidneys cannot do right now.

outcomes.story: You suggest antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nothing here is an infection. He has no fever, and the cause is known.

outcomes.story: You ask for potassium chloride. The pharmacist calls at once.
outcomes.reply: His potassium is normal, and his kidneys are failing. A large dose could stop his heart.

5.resident: His calcium is low and his fingers tingle. Calcium has to be given carefully in this poisoning.
5.question: Why?
options: Calcium makes the osmolar gap worse
Calcium blocks fomepizole
Extra calcium can join with oxalate and form more crystals in his kidneys, so it is given mainly for symptoms
Low calcium here never causes symptoms and is never treated

terms.meaning: One of the acids made from ethylene glycol. It binds calcium into hard crystals that lodge in the kidneys.
Painful muscle spasms caused by low calcium.

outcomes.story: You say calcium worsens the gap. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Calcium has no effect on that. The worry is what it does when it meets oxalate.

outcomes.story: You say calcium blocks fomepizole. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The two do not interact. The worry is crystals.

outcomes.story: You explain it. His calcium is watched closely, with a dose ready if he develops spasms or a heart rhythm change.
outcomes.reply: Right. His calcium is low because oxalate has grabbed it. Pour in more and you make more crystals. So we treat symptoms, not the number.

outcomes.story: You say it is never treated. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Spasms, seizures or heart rhythm changes from low calcium must be treated. The point is to be careful, not to withhold it.

differential.resident: His blood and urine results are in the chart.
differential.question: Which poisoning is this?
options: Methanol poisoning
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Aspirin overdose
Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning
differential.reveal: It is ethylene glycol poisoning. The high anion gap shows an extra acid, and the high osmolar gap shows an unmeasured substance in his blood. The low calcium and the envelope-shaped crystals in his urine are calcium bound to oxalate, which only this poison makes. Methanol raises both gaps too, but it damages the eyes and forms no crystals.

terms.meaning: An alcohol other than the drinking kind, such as ethylene glycol or methanol, whose breakdown products are poisonous.
Blood made acidic by an acid the body has produced or taken in.

ending.stable: In intensive care on dialysis and waking up, with the psychiatry team asked to see him
ending.unstable: In intensive care on dialysis and waking up, with the psychiatry team asked to see him
ending.worse: In intensive care on dialysis, with more kidney damage than he needed to have
ending.critical: In intensive care on life support

nph-076.plainDiagnosis: Poisoning with car antifreeze, which the body turns into acids that injure the kidneys (ethylene glycol poisoning).

science.title: How the antidote works
science.text: Alcohol dehydrogenase has a pocket that ethylene glycol fits into, and that is where it gets converted. Fomepizole fits the same pocket and holds on far more tightly. With the pocket occupied, the antifreeze cannot be converted and leaves the body unchanged.

science.title: How dialysis pulls a poison out of blood
science.text: The dialysis membrane has pores that let small molecules through and hold back blood cells and proteins. Small molecules move from where they are concentrated, in the blood, to where they are not, in the clean fluid. Ethylene glycol and its acids are small enough to cross.

sources.title: Brent et al. (N Engl J Med 1999): fomepizole for the treatment of ethylene glycol poisoning
Kraut and Mullins (N Engl J Med 2018): toxic alcohols

nph-063.title: Confused, constipated _and always thirsty._

start.alarm: Confused · very thirsty · dry

nph-063.handoff: A 66-year-old woman has been getting more confused for two weeks. She is constipated, drinks constantly and passes a great deal of urine. She has smoked heavily for decades and was recently told there was a spot on her lung.

interview.prompt: Ask her family about the last two weeks
interview.finding: She has grown confused and exhausted. She is constipated, always thirsty and passing urine all the time. Her bones ache, she feels sick and she is hardly eating.

interview.prompt: Ask about her weight, her chest and smoking
interview.finding: She has lost 9 kg in three months. She has a long-standing cough and coughed up blood once last month. She smoked for 45 years. She was told recently about a spot on her lung and has not had it looked into.

interview.prompt: Check her medicines
interview.finding: A water tablet (hydrochlorothiazide) for blood pressure, and a calcium and vitamin D supplement for thin bones.

exam.prompt: Check how alert she is, and tap her reflexes
exam.finding: She is drowsy but wakes when spoken to. She knows her name and that she is in hospital, but not the date. Her reflexes are sluggish on both sides.

exam.prompt: Check whether she is dry
exam.finding: Her mouth is dry, and pinched skin is slow to flatten.

exam.prompt: Examine her chest, her neck and her belly
exam.finding: There is a fullness above her right collarbone. The bottom of her right lung sounds dull, with quiet breath sounds. Her belly is soft, with few bowel sounds.

1.label: Blood tests and chest X-ray
1.content:
Calcium: 14.6, very high (normal is about 8.5 to 10.5).
Phosphate: low.
Kidney test (creatinine): 2.1, up from her usual 0.9.
Parathyroid hormone (PTH): too low to measure. Her parathyroid glands have switched off, as they should when calcium is high.
PTHrP, a protein that mimics parathyroid hormone: very high.
Vitamin D: normal. Thyroid: normal.
Chest X-ray: a 5 cm mass at the root of the right lung, with fluid at the base.

0.resident: Confusion, constipation, thirst and passing a lot of urine, in someone who may have a lung tumor. One blood result would tie all of that together.
0.question: Which one?
options: A low sodium
A high calcium
A low blood sugar
A high potassium

terms.meaning: Too much calcium in the blood. It slows nerves, the gut and thinking, and it makes the kidneys lose water.
Passing an unusually large amount of urine.

outcomes.story: You suggest a low sodium. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Low sodium can cause confusion, but not thirst with floods of urine and constipation. One abnormality explains all four.

outcomes.story: Blood is sent for calcium and the tests that explain it, and a chest X-ray is done. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. High calcium dulls the brain, slows the bowel and stops the kidneys holding on to water. In a smoker with a lung mass, it is the first thing to check.

outcomes.story: You suggest a low blood sugar. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Low sugar comes on over minutes, with sweating and shaking. This has built up over two weeks.

outcomes.story: You suggest a high potassium. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: High potassium affects the heart and muscles. It does not cause thirst, constipation and confusion.

3.resident: Her calcium is 14.6, and her kidneys are struggling. She has been passing urine for days and is very dry.
3.question: What is the first treatment?
options: Plenty of salt-water fluid into a vein
A strong water tablet (furosemide) and nothing else
Phosphate by mouth
Dialysis

terms.meaning: Salt water at the same concentration as blood, used to refill the circulation.
A strong water tablet, such as furosemide, that makes the kidneys pass more urine.

outcomes.story: Fluid runs in steadily, and her water tablet and calcium supplement are stopped. Over the hour her pulse settles, and she starts to follow the conversation.
outcomes.reply: Right. The high calcium has drained her of water, and a dry kidney cannot get rid of calcium. Fluid breaks that circle.

outcomes.story: Furosemide is given with no fluids. She passes still more urine. Two hours later she is drier and more confused, and her blood pressure has dropped.
outcomes.reply: She was already dry. A water tablet took more fluid out, and her calcium is now more concentrated than before. Fluids first, always.

outcomes.story: You suggest phosphate. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It does very little here, and it can cause calcium to deposit in her tissues. She needs fluid.

outcomes.story: You suggest dialysis. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is for the rare patient whose kidneys cannot handle fluid at all. Hers should recover once she is refilled.

4.resident: After fluids her calcium is still 13.8. Fluids alone will not hold it down while the tumor keeps sending its signal.
4.question: Which medicine brings it down for longest?
options: Calcitriol by mouth
A bisphosphonate into a vein, such as zoledronic acid
A thiazide water tablet
Calcium gluconate

terms.meaning: A medicine that switches off the cells that dissolve bone, so less calcium is released into the blood.
A cell that breaks down bone.

outcomes.story: You write for calcitriol. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: That is active vitamin D. It makes the gut absorb more calcium, which is the last thing she needs.

outcomes.story: The infusion is given, at a dose adjusted for her kidneys. The cancer team is asked to see her about the lung mass.
outcomes.reply: Yes. It takes two or three days to work, and it lasts for weeks. The lasting answer is treating the cancer itself.

outcomes.story: You write for a thiazide. The resident points at her chart.
outcomes.reply: A thiazide makes the kidneys hold on to calcium. She was on one, and we stopped it this morning for that reason.

outcomes.story: You write for calcium gluconate. The pharmacist calls at once.
outcomes.reply: That is calcium. Her problem is too much of it.

differential.resident: Her blood tests and chest X-ray are in the chart. Look at the PTH beside the PTHrP.
differential.question: Why is her calcium high?
options: An overactive parathyroid gland
A cancer releasing a protein that acts like parathyroid hormone (humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy)
Too much vitamin D
Too much calcium and antacid by mouth (milk-alkali syndrome)
differential.reveal: A tumor is releasing PTHrP, a protein that imitates parathyroid hormone. It tells her bones to give up calcium and her kidneys to keep it. Her own parathyroid glands have shut down, which is why her PTH is unmeasurable. An overactive gland would show a high PTH, and vitamin D excess a high vitamin D level. The mass in her lung is the likely source.

terms.meaning: Parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium by acting on bone and kidney.
Parathyroid hormone-related protein. Some cancers make it, and the body responds as if it were PTH.

ending.stable: On the ward on fluids, more alert, with her calcium falling and the cancer team involved
ending.unstable: On the ward on fluids, more alert, with her calcium falling and the cancer team involved
ending.worse: On the ward on fluids, with her calcium falling after a harder start than she needed

nph-063.plainDiagnosis: A dangerously high blood calcium caused by a hormone-like protein from a tumor (hypercalcemia of malignancy).

science.title: Why her own parathyroid hormone was unmeasurable
science.text: Parathyroid glands sense calcium directly: when it rises, they stop releasing PTH. Hers did exactly that. The tumor’s look-alike protein answers to no such sensor, so it kept pushing calcium up after the body’s own control had switched off.

science.title: Why high calcium made her pass so much urine
science.text: The kidney saves water by drawing it out of the last part of the tubule, on a signal from ADH. High calcium blunts the tubule’s response to that signal. Water stays in the urine, she loses liters, and the thirst never catches up.

sources.title: Stewart (N Engl J Med 2005): hypercalcemia associated with cancer
El-Hajj Fuleihan et al. (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2023): treatment of hypercalcemia of malignancy in adults, an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline

endo-046.title: The worst headache of his life, _then double vision._

start.alarm: Worst headache of his life · blood pressure 92 over 58

endo-046.handoff: A 50-year-old man had a sudden, excruciating headache three hours ago. He is vomiting, sees double, and his right eyelid has drooped. His blood pressure is low.

interview.prompt: Ask about the headache
interview.finding: It hit within seconds, three hours ago, behind his eyes and across his forehead. He calls it the worst pain of his life. He has vomited and feels faint.

interview.prompt: Ask about his eyes
interview.finding: He sees double. His right eyelid is drooping and the sight in that eye has gone dim. Both have got worse in the last hour.

interview.prompt: Ask about the months before, and his medicines
interview.finding: Looking back, he has been tired for months, with a lower sex drive and occasional headaches that he ignored. He takes amlodipine for blood pressure and no blood thinners. He has not hit his head.

exam.prompt: Examine his eyes
exam.finding: His right eyelid droops, and the pupil beneath it is wide. That eye barely moves inward, up or down. With it he can only count fingers. His left eye is normal.

exam.prompt: Bend his neck, and check his temperature
exam.finding: His neck bends freely. He has no fever.

exam.prompt: Check his circulation and the rest of his nerves
exam.finding: He is sweaty, his skin is cool and his pulse is fast. His arms and legs are strong, and his face moves normally.

1.label: Blood tests and scans
1.content:
Sodium: 130, low. Blood sugar: 64, low.
Cortisol, drawn before any steroid: 1.8, far too low for someone this ill.
CT scan of the head: a mass with fresh blood in it, sitting in the pocket of bone that holds the pituitary gland. There is no blood around the brain.
MRI: bleeding into an enlarged pituitary tumor. It bulges upward onto the crossing of the optic nerves and sideways toward the nerves that move the right eye.
Blood count: normal.

0.resident: A thunderclap headache with a paralyzed eye makes me think of the pituitary gland. And look at his blood pressure. If the pituitary has failed, his body cannot make cortisol. He is on his way to a scan.
0.question: What do we give right now?
options: Hydrocortisone into a vein
Mannitol into a vein, for brain swelling
A nicardipine drip, to lower his blood pressure
Nothing yet: do a spinal tap first
Broad antibiotics and acyclovir

terms.meaning: A pea-sized gland under the brain that controls the thyroid, the adrenal glands and the sex glands.
A hormone the adrenal glands make on a signal from the pituitary. Without it, blood pressure and blood sugar fall.
A severe headache that reaches full strength within seconds.

outcomes.story: Blood is drawn, and hydrocortisone is given into a vein with fluids. He goes straight for a CT and an MRI. His blood pressure comes up, and the results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. If his pituitary has stopped signaling, he has no cortisol, and that is what is dropping his pressure. Hydrocortisone costs nothing to give and can save his life.

outcomes.story: You ask for mannitol. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: Mannitol makes the kidneys pass water, and it would drop a pressure that is already low. It is not what he needs.

outcomes.story: You ask for a drip to lower his blood pressure. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: His pressure is 92 over 58. Lowering it further could starve his brain. The problem is that it is too low.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap tray. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Not before a scan. If there is a mass in his head, draining fluid from below can pull the brain downward.

outcomes.story: Antibiotics and an antiviral run in. An hour later his blood pressure is lower and he is drowsy.
outcomes.reply: He has no fever and no stiff neck, so infection is unlikely. What he lacks is cortisol, and he has gone another hour without it. Give the hydrocortisone.

3.resident: A bleed has wiped out his pituitary gland, so several hormones are about to run short. His sodium is 130, his sugar is 64 and his cortisol was 1.8.
3.question: Which missing hormone is the immediate danger?
options: Growth hormone
ACTH, and with it cortisol
The hormones that drive the sex glands
Prolactin
Thyroid hormone

terms.meaning: The pituitary hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol.
A pituitary gland that makes too little of one or more of its hormones.

outcomes.story: You say growth hormone. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: In an adult, missing growth hormone causes problems over years. It never causes an emergency.

outcomes.story: You say cortisol. The resident nods and checks that his next dose of hydrocortisone is written up.
outcomes.reply: Right. Without ACTH the adrenal glands stop making cortisol, and blood pressure, sodium and sugar all fall. It is the one that kills within hours.

outcomes.story: You say the sex hormones. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those explain his months of low sex drive. They matter for his life later, not for his survival tonight.

outcomes.story: You say prolactin. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Too little prolactin causes no illness in a man.

outcomes.story: You say thyroid hormone. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He will need it replaced, but the body holds weeks of thyroid hormone in reserve. Cortisol runs out in hours.

4.resident: His blood pressure is holding on hydrocortisone. But the sight in his right eye is fading, and the eye moves less than it did an hour ago.
4.question: What now?
options: Watch him, and repeat the eye tests from time to time
Call the neurosurgeon urgently, to take the pressure off through the nose
Start cabergoline and send him home
Start a full-dose blood thinner
Radiation to the whole brain

terms.meaning: The place just above the pituitary where the two optic nerves cross.
An operation that reaches the pituitary through the nose and the bone behind it, with no cut on the head.

outcomes.story: He is watched. Three hours later his right eye can make out only light and dark, and the edges of the left eye’s vision are starting to blur.
outcomes.reply: Watching is for sight that is mildly affected and steady. His was getting worse by the hour, and he has lost three more. Nerves crushed too long do not recover. Call the surgeon.
outcomes.alarm: Right eye sees only light · left eye blurring

outcomes.story: The neurosurgeon reviews the scans and takes him to the operating room, to remove the blood and tumor through his nose.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Failing vision is the reason to operate. Taking the pressure off quickly gives his optic nerves the best chance.

outcomes.story: You suggest a tablet and home. The resident stops the discharge.
outcomes.reply: That tablet shrinks one kind of pituitary tumor over weeks. He is losing his sight today, in hospital, with a bleed in his head.

outcomes.story: You write for a blood thinner. The pharmacist calls at once.
outcomes.reply: He has just bled into his pituitary. A blood thinner would make it bleed more.

outcomes.story: You suggest radiation. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Radiation works over months and does nothing for pressure now. He needs the blood taken out.

5.resident: The operation went well. His pituitary gland may never work fully again.
5.question: What follow-up does he need?
options: None, once he is over the illness
Lifelong checks of his pituitary hormones, with replacement of whatever is missing
A yearly eye test and nothing else
Preventive antibiotics, indefinitely
Regular repeat spinal taps

terms.meaning: Taking as a medicine the hormones the body can no longer make, such as hydrocortisone and thyroid hormone.

outcomes.story: You say he needs no follow-up. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Most people are left short of several hormones after this. If he stops hydrocortisone and then gets ill, he could die of it.

outcomes.story: You book him into the hormone clinic and explain his hydrocortisone, including taking extra when he is unwell.
outcomes.reply: Right. Cortisol first, then thyroid and sex hormones, with checks over the years. Some of the gland’s work comes back, and some shortfalls show up later.

outcomes.story: You suggest eye tests alone. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His eyes need following, and so do his hormones. Missing the hormones is what puts his life at risk.

outcomes.story: You suggest antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: This was a bleed, not an infection. He has no need for them.

outcomes.story: You suggest repeat spinal taps. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: They would tell us nothing about his pituitary. Blood tests do that.

differential.resident: His blood tests and scans are in the chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Bleeding around the brain from a burst aneurysm
Pituitary apoplexy: bleeding into a tumor of the pituitary gland
Bacterial meningitis
A clot in the veins behind the eye (cavernous sinus thrombosis)
Migraine with aura
differential.reveal: He has bled into a pituitary tumor that had been growing quietly for months, which is where his tiredness and low sex drive came from. The sudden swelling caused the headache, pressed on the nerves to his right eye and stopped the gland working. A burst aneurysm would put blood around the brain, and his scan shows none. Meningitis brings fever and a stiff neck.

terms.meaning: A sudden bleed into an organ, or loss of its blood supply.
A growth of gland tissue that is not a cancer. In the pituitary it can still press on what lies nearby.

ending.stable: In the neurosurgical unit after surgery to take the pressure off his optic nerves, on hydrocortisone
ending.unstable: In the neurosurgical unit after surgery to take the pressure off his optic nerves, on hydrocortisone
ending.worse: In the neurosurgical unit after surgery, sicker than he needed to be before he got there

endo-046.plainDiagnosis: A sudden bleed into a tumor of the pituitary gland, which cut off his cortisol and threatened his sight (pituitary apoplexy).

science.title: Why a bleed under the brain dropped his blood pressure
science.text: Cortisol is made in the adrenal glands, but only on orders: the pituitary sends ACTH, and the adrenals respond. The bleed destroyed the sender. His adrenal glands were healthy and idle, and without cortisol his blood vessels could not hold their tone.

science.title: Why a swelling there dims vision
science.text: Signals from both eyes travel along the optic nerves, which cross just above the pituitary. A mass pushing up from below squeezes those fibers. Light still reaches the retina, but the signal is blocked on its way to the brain.

sources.title: Rajasekaran et al. (Clin Endocrinol 2011): UK guidelines for the management of pituitary apoplexy
Briet et al. (Endocr Rev 2015): pituitary apoplexy

endo-042.title: Six liters of urine a day, _and a thirst that never ends._

start.alarm: Passing 320 mL of urine an hour · dizzy on standing

endo-042.handoff: A 30-year-old man fractured the base of his skull in a motorcycle crash four days ago. For two days he has been passing huge amounts of pale urine and asking for water constantly. He gets dizzy when he stands.

interview.prompt: Ask about the urine and the thirst
interview.finding: For two days he has passed very large amounts of pale urine, more than six liters in the last day. He is thirsty all the time and keeps asking for water. He feels weak and dizzy when he stands.

interview.prompt: Check what happened in the crash, and since
interview.finding: Four days ago he fractured the base of his skull and bruised the front of his brain. He has been alert and clear-headed throughout.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health and his medicines
interview.finding: He has no diabetes or kidney disease. He takes no water tablets and no lithium. In hospital he has had only acetaminophen and a stool softener.

exam.prompt: Check whether he is dry, and take his blood pressure standing
exam.finding: His mouth is dry, and pinched skin is slow to flatten. His blood pressure falls when he stands, and his pulse speeds up.

exam.prompt: Examine his eyes
exam.finding: His pupils react normally, his eyes move fully and he can see to both sides. He has dark bruising around both eyes from the fracture.

exam.prompt: Feel his belly
exam.finding: It is soft. His bladder is not swollen.

1.label: Blood tests, urine tests and MRI
1.content:
Sodium: 152, high (normal is 135 to 145).
Blood concentration (osmolality): 312, high. His blood is too concentrated.
Urine concentration: 110, very dilute. With blood this concentrated, healthy kidneys would make urine several times stronger.
Blood sugar: normal.
Urine output: 320 mL an hour.
MRI of the pituitary: the bright spot at the back of the gland, which marks its store of water-retaining hormone, is missing.

0.resident: Liters of pale urine and a raging thirst after a head injury. Before we treat it, we need to know why he is losing water.
0.question: Which tests?
options: The concentration of his blood and of his urine, his sodium and his blood sugar
A blood count and blood cultures
Thyroid and cortisol levels only
A urine test with culture
A 24-hour urine collection for protein

terms.meaning: How concentrated a fluid is.
Antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin. The pituitary releases it to tell the kidneys to keep water.

outcomes.story: Blood and urine are sent together, and an MRI of his pituitary is arranged. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Putting the two concentrations side by side shows whether his kidneys are saving water as they should. The sugar rules out the commoner kind of diabetes.

outcomes.story: You request a blood count and cultures. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those look for infection. He has no fever, and infection does not cause six liters of urine.

outcomes.story: You request thyroid and cortisol only. The resident adds to the order.
outcomes.reply: Worth checking after a head injury, but they do not explain the urine. We need the concentrations.

outcomes.story: You request a urine culture. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: An infection makes people pass urine often, in small amounts. He is passing liters.

outcomes.story: You request a 24-hour urine for protein. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That takes a day and looks for leaky kidney filters. His problem is water, and he is drying out now.

3.resident: His kidneys are pouring out water while his blood grows too concentrated. Either the water-retaining hormone is missing, or his kidneys are ignoring it.
3.question: How do we tell which?
options: Stop all his drinks for 24 hours, without checks
Give desmopressin, and measure how his urine concentration changes
Start a thiazide water tablet and see what happens
Give a large bag of saline and recheck his sodium
Measure copeptin alone, and stop there
3.fix: Give a test dose of desmopressin

terms.meaning: A man-made copy of the water-retaining hormone.
Caused by the brain or the pituitary not releasing the hormone.
Caused by the kidneys not responding to the hormone.

outcomes.story: His water jug is taken away. He goes on passing urine at the same rate. Four hours later he is confused, his sodium is 160 and his blood pressure has dropped.
outcomes.reply: His kidneys cannot hold water, so stopping his drinks only dries him out faster. That test is dangerous in someone whose sodium is already high. Give him water, and give the desmopressin.

outcomes.story: A dose of desmopressin is given. Over the next hour his urine output falls, and the urine turns darker. A repeat test shows its concentration has risen from 110 to 480.
outcomes.reply: Right. If the kidneys respond to the hormone when we supply it, the kidneys are fine and the hormone was missing. If nothing changes, the kidneys are the problem.

outcomes.story: You write for a thiazide. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: That is a treatment for the kidney form, and we do not yet know which form he has. Test first.

outcomes.story: You ask for a large bag of saline. The resident changes the order.
outcomes.reply: Saline carries a lot of sodium, and he has too much already. It also does not answer the question.

outcomes.story: You suggest one blood test and no more. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That test can help, but stopping there leaves him untreated. The desmopressin test answers the question and starts the treatment.

4.resident: After desmopressin his urine concentration rose from 110 to 480, and his output fell. The hormone was missing, and his kidneys work.
4.question: How do we treat him from here?
options: High-dose hydrochlorothiazide, indefinitely
Limit his water, and nothing else
Regular desmopressin, with sodium checks and free access to water
Demeclocycline, to block the hormone
A drip of strong salt solution

terms.meaning: Water without salt, by mouth or as a sugar-water drip. It brings a high sodium back down.

outcomes.story: You write for a thiazide. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That helps when the kidneys ignore the hormone. His kidneys respond to it. He needs the hormone replaced.

outcomes.story: His drinks are limited. With nothing replacing the hormone, he keeps losing water. Four hours later his sodium has climbed further, and he is confused and desperately thirsty.
outcomes.reply: Limiting water is the treatment for too much of this hormone. He has too little. He needs the hormone, and as much water as he wants.
outcomes.alarm: Sodium climbing · confused and very thirsty

outcomes.story: Desmopressin is written up twice a day. His water jug stays full, and his sodium is checked every few hours.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Replace the hormone, let his thirst guide his drinking, and watch the sodium. After a head injury this sometimes passes, so we recheck whether he still needs it.

outcomes.story: You write for demeclocycline. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: That drug blocks the hormone’s action. It would cause the very problem he already has.

outcomes.story: You ask for strong salt solution. The pharmacist calls at once.
outcomes.reply: His sodium is already too high. That would push it higher.

differential.resident: His blood tests, urine tests and MRI are in the chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Drinking too much water from habit
Sugar in the urine dragging water out with it
Diabetes insipidus: his kidneys are not holding on to water
SIADH: too much water-retaining hormone
Damaged kidney tubules (acute tubular necrosis)
differential.reveal: It is diabetes insipidus. His blood is too concentrated, and his kidneys are still passing dilute urine, which means the signal to save water is not getting through. Someone who simply drank too much would have a low sodium, not a high one. His sugar is normal. Too much of the hormone would do the reverse: a low sodium and concentrated urine.

terms.meaning: Loss of large amounts of dilute urine because water-retaining hormone is missing or the kidneys ignore it. It has nothing to do with blood sugar.
A high level of sodium in the blood. It usually means too little water.

ending.stable: On the ward on desmopressin, drinking freely, with his sodium coming down slowly
ending.unstable: On the ward on desmopressin, drinking freely, with his sodium coming down slowly
ending.worse: On the ward on desmopressin, after hours of going without the water he needed

endo-042.plainDiagnosis: Loss of the hormone that tells the kidneys to keep water, after a head injury (central diabetes insipidus).

science.title: Why he could not stop passing urine
science.text: The last stretch of the kidney tubule is watertight unless ADH is present. ADH inserts water channels into its wall, and water flows back into the blood. With no ADH the channels stay out, and whatever reaches that stretch leaves as urine.

science.title: Why his thirst worked while his kidneys did not
science.text: Sensors in the brain detect when blood becomes too concentrated. They do two things: trigger thirst, and tell the pituitary to release ADH. The injury cut the second line and spared the first. So he knew he needed water and could not keep it.

sources.title: Christ-Crain et al. (Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019): diabetes insipidus
Refardt, Winzeler and Christ-Crain (Endocrinol Metab Clin North Am 2020): diabetes insipidus, an update

endo-001.title: Up four times a night, _and twelve pounds lighter._

start.alarm: Thirsty for three months · 12 pounds lost

endo-001.handoff: A 54-year-old man has come for a routine physical. For three months he has been drinking water constantly and getting up three or four times a night to pass urine. He has lost 12 pounds without trying.

interview.prompt: Ask about the thirst, the urine and his weight
interview.finding: For three months he has been thirsty all the time and up three or four times a night to pass urine. He has lost 12 pounds without trying, feels tired, and his vision is sometimes blurry.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health and his medicines
interview.finding: He has high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and takes a tablet for each. He has not seen a doctor in four years.

interview.prompt: Ask about his family and how he lives
interview.finding: His mother and his brother have type 2 diabetes. He has a desk job and does little exercise. He eats a lot of fast food, drinks sugary drinks and has two beers most nights.

exam.prompt: Work out his body mass index, and look at his skin
exam.finding: His body mass index is 33, in the obese range. The skin of his armpits and the back of his neck is dark, thickened and velvety.

exam.prompt: Examine his feet
exam.finding: The pulses in his feet are strong. He feels a fine nylon thread on every part of both soles. The skin is unbroken.

exam.prompt: Check his mouth and his breathing
exam.finding: His mouth is slightly dry. He is breathing normally, and his breath has no unusual smell.

1.label: Blood and urine tests
1.content:
HbA1c: 9.2% (diabetes is 6.5% or more). It reflects his average blood sugar over about three months.
Fasting blood sugar: 214, high (normal is under 100).
Blood salts and kidney test: normal.
Urine: a lot of sugar, and no ketones.
LDL cholesterol: 142, high.
Urine protein check: normal.

0.resident: Thirst, passing urine all night and weight loss, in a man whose mother and brother have diabetes. He is comfortable and in no danger today.
0.question: Which test best confirms it?
options: A single finger-prick blood sugar, and nothing else
A hemoglobin A1c
A fasting C-peptide
A glucose tolerance test with insulin levels

terms.meaning: The share of hemoglobin that has sugar stuck to it. It shows the average blood sugar over about three months.
A condition in which blood sugar stays too high because insulin is missing or not working well.

outcomes.story: You prick his finger and stop there. The resident adds a test.
outcomes.reply: One reading shows this moment only, and it shifts with his last meal. We want the average.

outcomes.story: Blood and urine are collected in clinic, with a few tests that will matter if this is diabetes. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The A1c needs no fasting and shows three months of sugar in one number. At 6.5% or above, it is diabetes.

outcomes.story: You request a C-peptide. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That measures how much insulin he still makes. It is useful when the type of diabetes is in doubt. First we need to know whether he has diabetes at all.

outcomes.story: You request a glucose tolerance test with insulin levels. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That takes hours, and the insulin levels add nothing. One blood test answers the question.

3.resident: He has type 2 diabetes. We have talked about food, exercise and weight. His kidneys are healthy.
3.question: Which medicine do we start with?
options: Metformin
Insulin injections several times a day
Glipizide
Empagliflozin alone

terms.meaning: A tablet that lowers blood sugar, mainly by reducing the amount of sugar the liver releases.
A blood sugar that is too low. It causes shaking, sweating and confusion.

outcomes.story: You write for metformin, starting low and building up, to be taken with food. You explain that an upset stomach in the first weeks usually settles.
outcomes.reply: Right. It works, it is cheap, it does not cause weight gain or low sugars, and decades of experience stand behind it.

outcomes.story: You suggest insulin several times a day. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Insulin is for sugars much higher than his, or for people losing weight fast with ketones. He has no ketones and is not that ill.

outcomes.story: You suggest glipizide. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It lowers sugar by forcing out more insulin, so it can cause low sugars and weight gain. It is not where we start.

outcomes.story: You suggest empagliflozin alone. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A good medicine, often added for people with heart or kidney disease. He has neither, and metformin is the usual first step.

4.resident: His sugar has probably been high for years before today. Some damage from diabetes is silent until it is advanced.
4.question: Which checks should be arranged now?
options: An ultrasound of the arteries in his neck
An eye exam with the pupils dilated, and a full foot exam
A CT scan of the arteries of his heart
An ultrasound of his thyroid
4.fix: Book the eye and foot checks

terms.meaning: Damage to the small blood vessels at the back of the eye. It causes no symptoms until late.
Nerve damage. In diabetes it starts in the feet, as numbness.

outcomes.story: You request a neck artery scan. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is not a routine check in diabetes. It is for people with symptoms of a stroke.

outcomes.story: You refer him for an eye exam and record a full foot exam today. He is booked back in three months.
outcomes.reply: Right. High sugar damages the smallest vessels first: in the eyes, the kidneys and the nerves of the feet. In type 2 diabetes we check at diagnosis, because it has often been there for years.

outcomes.story: You request a heart CT. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He has no chest symptoms. Scanning well people exposes them to dye and radiation and changes little. We treat his blood pressure and cholesterol.

outcomes.story: You request a thyroid ultrasound. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nothing about him suggests a thyroid problem, and it is not part of diabetes care.

differential.resident: His blood and urine results are in the chart.
differential.question: What does he have?
options: Type 1 diabetes
Diabetes insipidus
Type 2 diabetes
A rare inherited diabetes of young adults (MODY)
differential.reveal: He has type 2 diabetes. He is middle-aged and carries extra weight, his mother and brother have it, and the dark velvety skin on his neck is a sign that his body resists insulin. There are no ketones, so he still makes insulin. Type 1 usually starts younger, in leaner people, often with ketones. Diabetes insipidus puts no sugar in the urine.

terms.meaning: Cells that respond weakly to insulin, so more of it is needed to move sugar out of the blood.
Dark, velvety skin in the folds of the body. It is a sign of high insulin levels.

ending.stable: Home with metformin, an eye appointment and a visit booked in three months
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

endo-001.plainDiagnosis: High blood sugar because the body no longer responds well to insulin (type 2 diabetes).

science.title: Why his sugar stayed high with insulin present
science.text: Insulin tells muscle and fat to take in sugar, and tells the liver to stop releasing it. His cells have grown deaf to that signal. Sugar stays in the blood, and the liver keeps adding more. Metformin mainly quiets the liver.

science.title: Why high sugar made him thirsty
science.text: The kidney filters sugar and normally takes all of it back. Above a certain level its transporters are full, and the extra sugar stays in the urine. Sugar holds water with it, so he passed more urine, dried out and grew thirsty.

science.title: Why one test showed three months of sugar
science.text: Glucose slowly attaches itself to hemoglobin, with no enzyme involved, and stays attached for the life of the red cell, about three months. The higher the sugar over that time, the larger the share of hemoglobin carrying it.

sources.title: American Diabetes Association (Diabetes Care 2024): pharmacologic approaches to glycemic treatment, Standards of Care in Diabetes 2024
UK Prospective Diabetes Study Group (Lancet 1998): effect of intensive blood-glucose control with metformin on complications in overweight patients with type 2 diabetes (UKPDS 34)

ho-064.title: A fever, _ten days after chemotherapy._

start.alarm: Fever 38.7 · ten days after chemotherapy

ho-064.handoff: A 52-year-old woman is having chemotherapy for breast cancer. Her last treatment was ten days ago. This afternoon she developed a fever of 38.6 °C with chills.

interview.prompt: Ask about the fever
interview.finding: It started this afternoon: 38.6 °C at home, with chills. She feels unwell and tired, and her throat is slightly sore.

interview.prompt: Ask about her chemotherapy
interview.finding: She is on an intensive schedule for breast cancer, and her last dose was ten days ago. Her cancer team told her that her blood counts would be at their lowest about now. She has a port under the skin of her chest for the infusions.

interview.prompt: Ask about symptoms that might show where an infection is
interview.finding: No cough, no burning when she passes urine, no belly pain, no diarrhea and no rash.

exam.prompt: Look in her mouth and throat
exam.finding: The back of her throat is slightly red. There are no ulcers and no pus.

exam.prompt: Look at her port and her skin
exam.finding: The skin over the port is clean, with no redness, tenderness or discharge. There is no rash anywhere.

exam.prompt: Listen to her chest, feel her belly and check around her anus
exam.finding: Her lungs are clear and her heart is fast. Her belly is soft. The skin around her anus is not tender or swollen.

1.label: Blood tests, chest X-ray and urine
1.content:
White blood cells: 0.8, very low.
Neutrophils, the white cells that kill bacteria: 180 (normal is above 1,500, and below 500 is dangerous).
Hemoglobin: 10.4, low. Platelets: 95, low.
Lactate: 1.8, normal.
Chest X-ray: clear. Urine: clear.
Blood cultures: sent, results pending.

0.resident: A fever ten days after chemotherapy, right when her white cells are at their lowest. She looks fairly well. That should not reassure anyone.
0.question: What is the most important thing to do now?
options: Take a blood count and blood cultures, and give antibiotics within the hour
Wait for the neutrophil count to confirm it before giving any antibiotic
Give acetaminophen and watch her for six hours
Get a CT scan of her chest and belly before starting treatment
0.fix: Take cultures and give antibiotics within the hour

terms.meaning: The white blood cells that find and kill bacteria. Chemotherapy wipes them out for a week or two.
The lowest point of the blood counts after a dose of chemotherapy.
Blood samples kept warm to see whether bacteria grow.

outcomes.story: Blood is taken from her arm and from her port, and the count is sent urgently. The first antibiotic will go in as soon as it is chosen. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. With no neutrophils, an infection can go from a fever to shock in hours. The antibiotic goes in within the hour, whatever the count turns out to be.

outcomes.story: The lab is busy, and the count takes ninety minutes. By then she is shaking with chills, and her blood pressure has dropped.
outcomes.reply: We already knew when her last chemotherapy was, and that was enough to act on. Bacteria double every twenty minutes, and she has nothing to stop them. Give the antibiotic now.

outcomes.story: The acetaminophen brings her temperature down, and she is left to rest. Six hours later a nurse finds her confused, with a very low blood pressure.
outcomes.reply: The medicine hid the fever, and the infection carried on underneath. She is now in septic shock. She needed antibiotics six hours ago.

outcomes.story: She waits for the scanner. An hour passes with no antibiotic. Her heart rate climbs and her blood pressure drifts down.
outcomes.reply: A scan can come later if we need to find a source. It must never hold up the first dose. Give the antibiotic.
outcomes.alarm: Heart rate climbing · no antibiotic yet

3.resident: Her neutrophil count is 180. There is no obvious source, which is usual: without white cells, infections make little pus or redness.
3.question: Which antibiotic goes in?
options: Azithromycin tablets
Cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam into a vein, which cover Pseudomonas
Vancomycin alone
Fluconazole alone

terms.meaning: A bacterium that lives in water and soil. It rarely harms healthy people and can kill people without neutrophils within a day.
