Chosen to cover the likely causes before any test has named one.

outcomes.story: You write for azithromycin tablets. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: That misses most of the dangerous bacteria here, and tablets are too slow and too uncertain. She needs a broad antibiotic into a vein.

outcomes.story: Cefepime is run in through her drip, forty minutes after she arrived.
outcomes.reply: Right. The bacteria that kill fastest in this situation come from the gut, and Pseudomonas is the one we must not miss. This covers them.

outcomes.story: You write for vancomycin alone. The resident adds to the order.
outcomes.reply: Vancomycin covers skin bacteria and misses the gut bacteria completely. It is added only if her port or her skin looks infected.

outcomes.story: You write for fluconazole alone. The resident changes the order.
outcomes.reply: That treats yeast. Fungal infection becomes a worry after days of fever on antibiotics, not on day one.

4.resident: The first dose is in, and her blood pressure is holding. A few people with this condition can go home on tablets. She is not one of them.
4.question: What is the main reason to admit her?
options: Her neutrophil count is very low, and it is expected to stay low for days
She has an underactive thyroid
Breast cancer runs in her family
She takes ondansetron at home

terms.meaning: A checklist that sorts patients with this condition into those who are safe at home and those who need hospital care.

outcomes.story: You explain it to her, and she is admitted to the cancer ward.
outcomes.reply: Right. The lower the count and the longer it will last, the higher the risk. Treatment at home is for people whose counts will recover within a few days.

outcomes.story: You point to her thyroid. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A thyroid that is well controlled on tablets makes no difference to this risk.

outcomes.story: You point to her family history. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That bears on why she got cancer. It has nothing to do with tonight’s infection.

outcomes.story: You point to the ondansetron. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: An anti-sickness tablet does not change her risk. Her neutrophil count does.

differential.resident: Her blood count, X-ray and urine results are in the chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A simple cold
Febrile neutropenia: a fever in someone with almost no infection-fighting white cells
A fever caused by her thyroid tablet
A clot around her chest port
differential.reveal: It is febrile neutropenia. Chemotherapy has knocked out her bone marrow, and her neutrophil count of 180 is far below the 500 that marks danger. A fever in that state is treated as a serious bacterial infection until proven otherwise, even when no source can be found. It may turn out to be a cold, but nobody can safely assume so tonight.

terms.meaning: Too few neutrophils in the blood.
The body’s dangerous, whole-body reaction to an infection.

ending.stable: Admitted to the cancer ward, with antibiotics started inside the first hour
ending.unstable: Admitted to the cancer ward, with antibiotics started inside the first hour
ending.worse: Admitted on antibiotics, after a delay that let the infection take hold
ending.critical: In intensive care with septic shock

ho-064.plainDiagnosis: A fever while chemotherapy has wiped out the white cells that fight bacteria (febrile neutropenia).

science.title: Why her counts were lowest on day ten
science.text: Chemotherapy kills cells that are dividing. Cancer cells divide fast, and so do the bone marrow cells that make blood. Neutrophils live only a day or so, and the marrow’s reserve lasts about a week. When it ran out, nothing was coming up to replace them.

science.title: Why finding nothing did not mean nothing was there
science.text: Redness, swelling and pus are produced by neutrophils arriving at an infection. With no neutrophils, an infected lung can look clear on an X-ray, and an infected skin site can look normal. A normal exam is weak evidence when the body cannot make the signs.

sources.title: Freifeld et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2011): clinical practice guideline for the use of antimicrobial agents in neutropenic patients with cancer, 2010 update by the IDSA
Taplitz et al. (J Clin Oncol 2018): outpatient management of fever and neutropenia in adults treated for malignancy, ASCO and IDSA clinical practice guideline update

ho-016.title: Ten minutes into a transfusion, _something is wrong._

start.alarm: Shaking, back pain and red urine · transfusion running

ho-016.handoff: A 55-year-old man broke his pelvis in a car crash two days ago and lost a lot of blood. A blood transfusion was started ten minutes ago. He is now shaking, has severe pain in his back, and says something terrible is happening. His urine has turned red.

interview.prompt: Ask what he is feeling
interview.finding: About ten minutes after the blood started he began shaking with chills. He has severe pain in his back and sides and pain in the arm with the drip. He feels that something terrible is about to happen. His urine has turned dark red.

interview.prompt: Check why he is having blood
interview.finding: He fractured his pelvis in a car crash two days ago and bled. His hemoglobin fell to 6.8 today.

interview.prompt: Ask about his breathing, itching and swelling
interview.finding: He is not short of breath. He has no itching, and his throat does not feel tight.

exam.prompt: Check his airway, his skin and his chest
exam.finding: He breathes without noise or wheeze. His face is not swollen, and he has no hives. His lungs are clear.

exam.prompt: Feel his sides and his drip site, and look at his urine bag
exam.finding: Both sides of his back are tender, and so is the vein the blood is running into. The urine in his catheter bag is red.

exam.prompt: Check his circulation
exam.finding: He is flushed, sweaty and frightened. His pulse is fast, and a pressed fingertip is slow to turn pink again.

1.label: Blood tests, urine and paperwork check
1.content:
Antibody test on his red cells (direct Coombs test): positive.
His plasma: pink, from hemoglobin spilled out of burst red cells.
Paperwork check: he is blood group O. The unit that was hung is group A.
Haptoglobin, a protein that mops up free hemoglobin: used up.
LDH: very high.
Urine: positive for blood on the test strip, with no red cells under the microscope.
Kidney test (creatinine): 1.4 and rising, from 0.9.
Clotting: fibrinogen is falling.

0.resident: Chills, back pain, red urine and a falling blood pressure, minutes after blood was started. The bag is still running.
0.question: What is the single most important thing to do?
options: Slow the transfusion and give acetaminophen
Stop the transfusion now, keep the drip open with saline and call the blood bank
Give adrenaline into the muscle
Give furosemide to protect his kidneys

terms.meaning: Any harmful response to donated blood.
The hospital laboratory that matches donor blood to patients.

outcomes.story: The drip is slowed, and he is given acetaminophen. The blood keeps running. Fifteen minutes later his blood pressure has collapsed, and his urine is the color of cola.
outcomes.reply: Every milliliter of that blood is being destroyed inside him. Slowing it only spreads the harm over a longer time. Stop it.
outcomes.alarm: Blood pressure 76 over 44 · urine dark brown

outcomes.story: You clamp the line. The nurse disconnects the blood, runs saline through new tubing and phones the blood bank. The bag goes back to the lab with fresh samples of his blood and urine. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Stop first, think second. The less of that unit he gets, the better he does. Then the lab can work out what went wrong.

outcomes.story: You reach for adrenaline. The nurse clamps the blood line first.
outcomes.reply: Adrenaline is for an allergic reaction, with hives, wheeze or a swelling throat. He has none of those. And the first step in any reaction is to stop the blood.

outcomes.story: You ask for furosemide. The nurse clamps the blood line first.
outcomes.reply: Protecting his kidneys matters, and fluids do that better. But nothing comes before stopping the blood.

3.resident: The transfusion is stopped. The red cells he was given are bursting, and free hemoglobin is on its way to his kidneys. His blood pressure is low.
3.question: What protects his kidneys now?
options: Plenty of fluid into a vein, to keep his blood pressure up and his urine flowing
Dialysis straight away
High-dose steroids
Limiting his fluids, to avoid fluid on the lungs

terms.meaning: Free hemoglobin in the urine, which turns it red or brown.
Red blood cells bursting open.

outcomes.story: Saline is run in fast, and his urine output is measured every hour. His blood pressure recovers, and his urine starts to clear.
outcomes.reply: Yes. A good flow of urine washes the hemoglobin through before it can clog and poison the kidney tubules. It also holds his blood pressure up.

outcomes.story: You ask for dialysis. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Dialysis is for kidneys that have already failed. His are still working, and fluids are how we keep them that way.

outcomes.story: You ask for steroids. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Steroids do not stop this kind of destruction once it has begun. Fluids are what protect him.

outcomes.story: His fluids are kept low. Two hours later he has passed almost no urine, and his kidney test has climbed.
outcomes.reply: His lungs are clear, and his kidneys are being clogged with hemoglobin. Holding back fluid let it settle. Open the drip.
outcomes.alarm: Almost no urine · kidney test rising

4.resident: The blood bank has the answer: he is group O, and the unit was group A. It was meant for the patient in the next bed.
4.question: What prevents this from happening?
options: Giving acetaminophen and an antihistamine before every transfusion
Using blood with the white cells filtered out
Checking the patient’s identity against the unit at the bedside, every time, before the blood is hung
Washing the red cells before they are given

terms.meaning: Two members of staff confirming the patient’s name, date of birth and wristband against the label on the unit, at the bedside, just before starting.

outcomes.story: You suggest medicines beforehand. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those blunt mild fevers and itching. They do nothing if the wrong blood goes into the wrong person.

outcomes.story: You suggest filtered blood. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Filtering out white cells reduces fever reactions. It does not change the blood group of the red cells.

outcomes.story: You say it plainly. The ward manager starts an incident report, and the event is explained honestly to him.
outcomes.reply: Right. Almost every reaction like this comes from a mix-up of patient or sample, not from a failure of the lab. The check at the bedside is the last chance to catch it.

outcomes.story: You suggest washing the cells. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Washing removes plasma proteins, for patients with severe allergic reactions. The cells would still be the wrong group.

differential.resident: The blood tests, urine result and paperwork check are in his chart.
differential.question: What kind of reaction is this?
options: A fever reaction to the donor’s white cells, with no damage to red cells
An acute hemolytic reaction: his antibodies are destroying the donor red cells because the blood group is wrong
A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)
Too much fluid in his circulation from the transfusion
differential.reveal: He was given blood of the wrong group. He is group O, so his blood carries ready-made antibodies against group A. They attached to the donor cells within seconds and burst them inside his blood vessels. The pink plasma and red urine are the spilled hemoglobin. A simple fever reaction destroys no red cells, and an allergic reaction brings hives and wheeze.

terms.meaning: The four main blood groups: A, B, AB and O, named for the markers on red cells.
A protein made by the immune system that sticks to one specific target.

ending.stable: On the ward on fluids, with his kidneys holding and the mix-up being investigated
ending.unstable: On the ward on fluids, with his kidneys holding and the mix-up being investigated
ending.worse: On the ward on fluids, with his kidneys injured
ending.critical: In intensive care with kidney failure and a clotting disorder

ho-016.plainDiagnosis: Destruction of transfused red cells because the blood group was wrong (acute hemolytic transfusion reaction).

science.title: Why group O blood attacks group A cells
science.text: The A and B genes each add a different sugar to the surface of red cells, and the O version adds none. A person makes antibodies against whichever sugars their own cells lack. Group O lacks both, so it carries antibodies against A and against B from early childhood.

science.title: How antibodies burst a red cell
science.text: Antibodies on the donor cell’s surface set off a chain of blood proteins that ends by punching pores through its membrane. Water rushes in, the cell swells and splits, and its hemoglobin spills into the plasma.

sources.title: Delaney et al. (Lancet 2016): transfusion reactions, prevention, diagnosis, and treatment
Panch, Montemayor-Garcia and Klein (N Engl J Med 2019): hemolytic transfusion reactions

ho-048.title: Bruises everywhere, _and bleeding that will not stop._

start.alarm: Bleeding from gums, nose and vagina · bruises everywhere

ho-048.handoff: A 39-year-old woman has been bruising for days without any injury. Her gums and nose bleed, and she now has heavy vaginal bleeding. She has felt unwell and feverish for two weeks.

interview.prompt: Ask about the bleeding
interview.finding: Bruises have been appearing for several days without any knocks. Her nose and gums bleed, and today she has heavy vaginal bleeding.

interview.prompt: Ask how she has been feeling
interview.finding: For two weeks she has felt more and more unwell, with slight fevers. She is exhausted and gets breathless easily.

interview.prompt: Ask about medicines and anything that could cause bleeding
interview.finding: She has had no injury. She takes no blood thinners and has no liver disease. Her only medicine is a contraceptive pill.

exam.prompt: Look at her skin, her gums and where blood was taken
exam.finding: Bruises and pinpoint red spots cover her chest, back, arms and legs. Her gums are oozing, and so is every site where a needle went in.

exam.prompt: Listen to her heart and lungs, and feel her belly
exam.finding: Her heart is fast, with the soft whoosh of thin blood. Her lungs are clear. Her belly is soft, and her liver and spleen are not enlarged. She is bleeding from the vagina.

exam.prompt: Check how alert she is
exam.finding: She is mildly confused. Her face and limbs move normally, and her neck is not stiff.

1.label: Blood tests, blood film and bone marrow
1.content:
White blood cells: 1.9, low. Hemoglobin: 7.6, low. Platelets: 18, very low.
Clotting times: both prolonged. Fibrinogen, the raw material of clots: 90, low. D-dimer, a product of clots being broken down: very high.
Blood film: abnormal immature white cells packed with granules, some holding bundles of needle-shaped rods.
Bone marrow: full of the same cells.
Genetic test: pieces of chromosomes 15 and 17 have swapped places, fusing two genes (PML-RARA).

0.resident: She is bleeding from several places at once. Low platelets alone do not usually do this. I think her clotting system is being used up faster than it can be made.
0.question: Which pattern of results would show that?
options: Normal clotting times, with only the platelets low
Long clotting times, low fibrinogen, a high D-dimer and falling platelets
One clotting time prolonged, which corrects when normal plasma is added
A high fibrinogen with a normal D-dimer
0.fix: Name the pattern and send the tests

terms.meaning: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: clotting switched on throughout the bloodstream. It uses up platelets and clotting proteins, so the patient bleeds.
The blood protein that is turned into the strands of a clot.
A fragment released when clots are broken down.

outcomes.story: You pick low platelets alone. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That would be a platelet problem only. She oozes from every needle site, which means the clotting proteins are failing too.

outcomes.story: You describe the pattern. Clotting tests, a blood film and an urgent bone marrow sample are sent, and the results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. When clotting runs unchecked, everything is consumed: the clotting times lengthen, fibrinogen and platelets fall, and the debris shows up as D-dimer.

outcomes.story: You pick a single prolonged time that corrects. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That means one clotting protein is missing, as in hemophilia. She is using up all of them.

outcomes.story: You pick a high fibrinogen. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Fibrinogen is consumed in this process, so it falls. And the D-dimer rises as clots are broken down.

3.resident: This is acute promyelocytic leukemia. The leukemia cells themselves are setting off the clotting. People with this disease die of bleeding in the first days, before treatment starts.
3.question: What cannot wait?
options: Nothing. Wait for the full genetic report before any treatment
Start ATRA now, on what the blood film shows, with platelets and clotting proteins by transfusion
Standard leukemia chemotherapy, and nothing else
Platelets alone, and watch

terms.meaning: All-trans retinoic acid, a form of vitamin A given as capsules. It makes these leukemia cells mature, which switches off the clotting.
A concentrate of fibrinogen and other clotting proteins made from donated plasma.

outcomes.story: Treatment is held for the genetic report. Six hours later she has a sudden, severe headache, vomits and becomes hard to rouse. A scan shows bleeding into her brain.
outcomes.reply: This is exactly the death we are trying to prevent. The blood film was enough to start. ATRA is safe to give on suspicion, and every hour without it she was at risk.
outcomes.alarm: Severe headache · hard to rouse · bleeding in the brain

outcomes.story: ATRA is given within the hour, with platelets, cryoprecipitate and plasma. Over the next days her bleeding stops. Then, on day four, she becomes breathless and feverish, and her oxygen level falls.
outcomes.reply: That was the right call, and it stopped the bleeding. Now something new is happening, and it is linked to the treatment.

outcomes.story: You suggest standard chemotherapy alone. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Killing these cells with chemotherapy makes them spill their contents and worsens the bleeding. ATRA makes them mature instead. It has to be there from the start.

outcomes.story: Platelets are given and nothing else. Four hours later she is still oozing, a nosebleed will not stop, and her fibrinogen is lower.
outcomes.reply: Platelets poured into this are used up as fast as they go in. The leukemia cells are driving it, and only ATRA switches them off.

4.resident: Four days into ATRA her bleeding has stopped. Now she has a fever, she is breathless, her oxygen level is 89%, her chest X-ray shows hazy patches and she has gained 3 kg.
4.question: What is happening, and what do we do?
options: Tumor lysis syndrome: give rasburicase only
Differentiation syndrome: start dexamethasone now
Hospital pneumonia: stop ATRA for good and give antibiotics alone
A lung clot: start a full-dose blood thinner

terms.meaning: A reaction to ATRA. As the leukemia cells mature all at once, they release signals that make blood vessels leak fluid into the lungs.
A strong steroid that calms that reaction.

outcomes.story: You say tumor lysis. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Tumor lysis upsets blood salts and the kidneys. It does not fill the lungs with fluid or add 3 kg in days.

outcomes.story: Dexamethasone is given into a vein, with oxygen. Within hours her breathing eases.
outcomes.reply: Right. It comes from the treatment working: the cells are maturing all at once. Steroids settle it, and ATRA is paused only if it is severe.

outcomes.story: ATRA is stopped and antibiotics are started. Three hours later she is fighting for breath, and her oxygen level has fallen further.
outcomes.reply: Antibiotics are reasonable alongside, but this is not an infection, and without steroids it gets worse fast. Stopping ATRA for good would take away her cure. Give dexamethasone.

outcomes.story: You write for a full-dose blood thinner. The pharmacist calls at once.
outcomes.reply: Her platelets are still very low, and she was bleeding four days ago. A blood thinner could kill her.

5.resident: She is through the most dangerous days. Her family asks what her chances are.
5.question: How does this leukemia do, with treatment?
options: It has the worst outlook of all the acute leukemias
It was once the deadliest in the first days, and with prompt treatment it is now among the most curable
The same as every other acute leukemia
It cannot be cured

terms.meaning: No detectable leukemia after treatment.
A medicine used with ATRA. Together they cure most people with this leukemia, often without standard chemotherapy.

outcomes.story: You say it has the worst outlook. The specialist corrects you.
outcomes.reply: That was true decades ago. The early bleeding is still dangerous, but once past it, most people are cured.

outcomes.story: You tell them, and the specialist adds the numbers. Her family is in tears, for a different reason now.
outcomes.reply: Right. ATRA with arsenic cures most people with this leukemia. That is why recognizing it on the first day matters so much.

outcomes.story: You say it is like any other. The specialist corrects you.
outcomes.reply: It behaves differently at both ends: more dangerous in the first days, and far more curable afterward.

outcomes.story: You say it cannot be cured. The specialist corrects you.
outcomes.reply: It is one of the great successes of cancer medicine. Most people treated promptly are cured.

differential.resident: Her blood tests, blood film and bone marrow results are in the chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL)
Chronic myeloid leukemia that has turned aggressive
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
TTP, a clotting disorder of the small blood vessels
differential.reveal: It is acute promyelocytic leukemia. A swap between chromosomes 15 and 17 has fused two genes, and the fused protein stops one kind of white cell from maturing. Those cells pile up, crowd out normal blood, and carry granules that set off clotting all through her bloodstream. The granule-packed cells with bundles of rods are found in no other leukemia.

terms.meaning: A cancer of the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow.
An immature white cell, one step on the way to becoming a neutrophil.

ending.stable: In intensive care with the bleeding stopped, breathing easier, and a leukemia that most people are cured of
ending.unstable: In intensive care with the bleeding stopped, breathing easier, and a leukemia that most people are cured of
ending.worse: In intensive care, recovering more slowly than she needed to
ending.critical: In intensive care on life support, after bleeding into her brain

ho-048.plainDiagnosis: A leukemia whose cells set off clotting throughout the blood, causing severe bleeding (acute promyelocytic leukemia with DIC).

science.title: How a vitamin treats a leukemia
science.text: The fused gene makes a protein that sits on the DNA and keeps the genes for maturing switched off. ATRA binds that protein and changes its shape, so it lets go. The genes switch on, and the leukemia cells grow up into ordinary white cells that live a few days and die.
science.lessonTitle: Follow a gene into a protein

science.title: Why cells that cannot mature are dangerous
science.text: Blood cells normally stop dividing when they mature. A cell stuck at an immature stage never gets that signal, so it keeps dividing. The marrow fills with copies that do no useful work and leave no room for normal cells.

sources.title: Sanz et al. (Blood 2019): management of acute promyelocytic leukemia, updated recommendations from an expert panel of the European LeukemiaNet
Lo-Coco et al. (N Engl J Med 2013): retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide for acute promyelocytic leukemia

rh-008.title: A knee that is hot, swollen _and will not bend._

start.alarm: Hot, swollen knee · fever 38.7

rh-008.handoff: A 60-year-old man has had a hot, swollen, very painful right knee for two days, with fevers and chills. He cannot put weight on it. He had a steroid injection into that knee a few weeks ago.

interview.prompt: Ask about the knee
interview.finding: It came on over two days: severe pain, swelling and heat. He cannot stand on it. He has had fevers, chills and sweats. He did not injure it.

interview.prompt: Ask whether anything has been done to the knee
interview.finding: A few weeks ago he had a cortisone injection into it for arthritis.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health
interview.finding: He has diabetes that is not well controlled, and his kidneys work at reduced strength. He has never had an attack like this. He has had no diarrhea, eye trouble or discharge, and does not inject drugs.

exam.prompt: Look at the knee and feel it
exam.finding: It is tight with fluid, red and hot all round, and too tender to touch. There is a small healed needle mark where the injection went in.

exam.prompt: Try to bend the knee, and ask him to stand
exam.finding: Any movement, by him or by you, causes severe pain. He holds it slightly bent and will not put weight on it.

exam.prompt: Look at the rest of the leg and the other knee
exam.finding: There are no red streaks up the leg. His left knee is normal.

1.label: Joint fluid, blood tests and X-ray
1.content:
Joint fluid: cloudy, with 78,000 white cells (a healthy joint has fewer than 200). Nine in ten are neutrophils.
Joint fluid stain: round bacteria in clusters.
Joint fluid crystals: none. Joint fluid sugar: low.
Blood white cells: 16.4, high. Inflammation markers: both very high.
Uric acid in the blood: normal.
Blood cultures: sent, results pending.
Knee X-ray: a large amount of fluid in the joint. No fracture.

0.resident: One hot, swollen joint with a fever. Until we prove otherwise, there are bacteria in that knee.
0.question: What is the most urgent step?
options: Take blood cultures and start antibiotics, and leave the joint alone for now
Draw fluid from the knee with a needle now, before antibiotics if we can
Get an MRI of the knee first
Start colchicine for a presumed gout attack

terms.meaning: Drawing fluid out of a joint with a needle, after numbing the skin. The fluid is checked for white cells, bacteria and crystals.
Infection inside a joint. It can destroy the joint’s cartilage within days.

outcomes.story: You ask for cultures and antibiotics, and plan to leave the knee. The resident picks up a needle.
outcomes.reply: Blood cultures help. But the answer is in the joint, and tapping it takes five minutes. If antibiotics go in first, the bacteria may never grow in the lab. Tap it, then treat.

outcomes.story: The skin is numbed, and cloudy yellow fluid is drawn from the knee. Blood is sent, and an X-ray is taken. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The fluid tells us whether this is infection or crystals, and which bacteria. Nothing else can.

outcomes.story: He waits two hours for the scanner. The MRI shows fluid in the joint, which you could see from the door. His fever is higher, and the knee is tighter.
outcomes.reply: A scan cannot tell pus from any other fluid. Bacteria have had two more hours inside his joint. Tap the knee.

outcomes.story: He is given colchicine and watched. Four hours later he is shaking with chills, and the knee is no better.
outcomes.reply: Gout can look like this, and so can infection, and infection is the one that destroys a joint. Nobody treats for gout until the fluid has been checked. Tap the knee.

3.resident: The fluid is full of white cells and bacteria. Antibiotics are going in now.
3.question: What else is essential?
options: Strict rest in a splint for six weeks, with no drainage
Urgent drainage of the joint: washing it out, or repeated needle drainage
A steroid injection into the joint, to calm the inflammation
Antibiotic tablets at home, with a visit in two weeks
3.fix: Call for the joint to be washed out

terms.meaning: Flushing a joint with fluid through a keyhole camera or an open cut, to remove pus.
The smooth lining on the ends of bones in a joint. It has no blood supply and does not grow back.

outcomes.story: You suggest a splint and no drainage. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Pus left in a joint keeps eating the cartilage, whatever the antibiotics do. It has to come out.

outcomes.story: The orthopedic surgeon takes him to the operating room and washes out the knee through a keyhole camera. Antibiotics continue through a vein.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Antibiotics and drainage, both. An infected joint is treated like an abscess: the pus is removed.

outcomes.story: You suggest a steroid injection. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Never into an infected joint. Steroids switch off the defenses that are holding the bacteria back.

outcomes.story: He goes home with tablets. Twelve hours later he comes back by ambulance, shaking, with a low blood pressure. The knee is rigid with pus.
outcomes.reply: Tablets could not clear a joint full of pus, and the bacteria have now spread into his blood. He needed a washout and antibiotics through a vein from the start.
outcomes.alarm: Back by ambulance · bacteria in his blood

4.resident: He asks how bacteria got into his knee in the first place.
4.question: What put him most at risk?
options: The recent steroid injection into the joint, and his poorly controlled diabetes
Drinking alcohol now and then
His kidney disease alone
Taking metformin

terms.meaning: Something that makes an illness more likely.

outcomes.story: You explain it to him plainly, without blame.
outcomes.reply: Right. Any needle through the skin can carry bacteria into a joint, though it is rare. High blood sugar weakens the white cells that would normally deal with them.

outcomes.story: You point to alcohol. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: An occasional drink plays almost no part. Look at what went into the joint, and at his sugar.

outcomes.story: You point to his kidneys. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Kidney disease weakens defenses a little. It matters far less than a needle into the joint and a high sugar.

outcomes.story: You point to metformin. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Metformin does not cause infections. His diabetes does, when it is not controlled.

differential.resident: The joint fluid, blood tests and X-ray are in his chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Gout
Septic arthritis: bacteria inside the joint, most likely staph
Reactive arthritis after a gut infection
Pseudogout
differential.reveal: It is septic arthritis. A white cell count that high, nearly all neutrophils, with bacteria visible in the fluid, means infection inside the joint. Round bacteria in clusters are typical of staph, which lives on skin. Gout and pseudogout would show crystals and no bacteria. Reactive arthritis follows an infection elsewhere, and the joint fluid has no bacteria in it.

terms.meaning: A bacterium that lives on skin and is the commonest cause of joint infection.
Extra fluid inside a joint.

ending.stable: Admitted after a washout of the knee, on antibiotics through a vein
ending.unstable: Admitted after a washout of the knee, on antibiotics through a vein
ending.worse: Admitted after a washout of the knee, with more damage to the joint than there needed to be

rh-008.plainDiagnosis: A bacterial infection inside the knee joint (septic arthritis).

science.title: Why an infected joint is ruined so fast
science.text: White cells that rush into the joint release enzymes meant to digest bacteria. The same enzymes digest cartilage. Enzymes are not used up as they work, so as long as pus stays in the joint, the damage continues.

science.title: Why the sugar in his joint fluid was low
science.text: Joint fluid normally holds about as much glucose as blood. Tens of thousands of white cells and a growing colony of bacteria were all burning it, with little oxygen, faster than it could seep in from the blood.

sources.title: Mathews et al. (Lancet 2010): bacterial septic arthritis in adults
Margaretten et al. (JAMA 2007): does this adult patient have septic arthritis?

rh-003.title: Woken at 3 a.m. _by his big toe._

start.alarm: Red, swollen big toe · too tender to touch

rh-003.handoff: A 52-year-old man was woken at 3 a.m. by severe pain in his right big toe. Within hours it was swollen and red, and so tender that he could not bear a bedsheet on it.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain
interview.finding: It woke him at 3 a.m. Within hours the joint was swollen, red and so tender that the weight of a sheet was unbearable. He did not injure it, and he has no fever.

interview.prompt: Ask whether it has happened before, and what came before it
interview.finding: Twice in the past year, in a milder form, clearing up within a week each time. This attack came after a weekend of grilled steak and several beers.

interview.prompt: Ask about his medicines and his family
interview.finding: He takes hydrochlorothiazide, a water tablet, for blood pressure. He drinks four to six beers most weekends. His father had the same kind of joint attacks, and kidney stones.

exam.prompt: Look at the toe and touch it lightly
exam.finding: The joint at the base of his right big toe is swollen, hot and dusky red, with tight, shiny skin. He pulls away from the lightest touch and can barely move it.

exam.prompt: Look for a cut, pus or red streaks
exam.finding: The skin is unbroken. There is no pus, and no red streak runs up the foot.

exam.prompt: Check his other joints
exam.finding: No other joint is warm or swollen.

1.label: Joint fluid, blood tests and X-ray
1.content:
Joint fluid: 28,000 white cells, mostly neutrophils.
Under polarized light: needle-shaped crystals that glow yellow when they line up with the filter.
Joint fluid stain: no bacteria. Culture: pending.
Uric acid in the blood: 6.2, within the normal range.
Blood white cells and kidney test: normal.
Foot X-ray: swelling of the soft tissue only.

0.resident: A red-hot big toe that came on overnight. I think I know what this is. But an infected joint can look identical, and guessing wrong costs him the joint.
0.question: Which test settles it?
options: A blood uric acid level
Fluid drawn from the joint, examined under a microscope for crystals and bacteria
An X-ray of the foot
Blood cultures and a CRP

terms.meaning: Drawing fluid out of a joint with a needle, after numbing the skin. The fluid is checked for white cells, bacteria and crystals.
A waste product of breaking down DNA and some foods. In excess it can form crystals in joints.

outcomes.story: You request a uric acid level. The resident adds a test.
outcomes.reply: During an attack the blood level is often normal, because the uric acid has moved into the joint. And it cannot rule out infection.

outcomes.story: The skin is numbed, and a few drops of fluid are drawn from the joint. Blood and an X-ray are done too. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Seeing the crystals proves it, and the stain and culture rule out bacteria in the same sample.

outcomes.story: You request an X-ray only. The resident adds a test.
outcomes.reply: An X-ray shows swelling and no more. It is normal in early attacks of anything.

outcomes.story: You request blood cultures and a CRP. The resident adds a test.
outcomes.reply: Both can be abnormal with crystals and with infection. Only the joint fluid tells them apart.

3.resident: Crystals, and no bacteria. He is in severe pain now.
3.question: How do we treat this attack?
options: Start high-dose allopurinol straight away
An anti-inflammatory such as indomethacin (or colchicine, or a short course of steroids)
Vancomycin into a vein, and wash out the joint
Probenecid, to make his kidneys pass more uric acid

terms.meaning: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicine, such as indomethacin or naproxen.
A daily tablet that lowers uric acid over weeks. It prevents attacks and does not treat one.

outcomes.story: You write for high-dose allopurinol. The resident changes the order.
outcomes.reply: That lowers uric acid over weeks and does nothing for tonight’s pain. A sudden change in the level can even stir up the attack. Treat the inflammation first.

outcomes.story: He takes the first dose and rests with the foot raised and uncovered. Within the hour the pain is easing.
outcomes.reply: Right. The crystals are already there. What hurts is his immune system’s reaction to them, and an anti-inflammatory turns that down.
outcomes.alarm: Pain easing after the first dose

outcomes.story: You write for vancomycin and a washout. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The fluid showed crystals and no bacteria. He does not need antibiotics or an operation.

outcomes.story: You write for probenecid. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is another long-term medicine. Starting it in the middle of an attack does not help the attack.

4.resident: This is his third attack in a year. Once it has settled, he needs a plan to stop the next one.
4.question: What should the plan be?
options: Change his water tablet to another blood pressure medicine, talk about diet and alcohol, and consider a uric acid-lowering medicine
Indomethacin every day, indefinitely, and nothing else
Drink more alcohol, to dilute the uric acid
Never have a joint tapped again, in case it causes infection

terms.meaning: A kind of water tablet. It makes the kidneys hold on to uric acid, which raises the level in the blood.
Long-term medicine, usually allopurinol, that keeps uric acid low enough for crystals to dissolve.

outcomes.story: You go through it with him: a different blood pressure tablet, less beer and red meat, and a clinic visit to discuss allopurinol.
outcomes.reply: Right. His water tablet has been raising his uric acid all along. With three attacks in a year, he is also someone who should be offered medicine to lower it.

outcomes.story: You suggest daily indomethacin for life. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That treats attacks without preventing them, and years of it can damage the stomach and kidneys.

outcomes.story: You suggest more alcohol. The resident laughs, then corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Alcohol raises uric acid, and beer most of all. He needs less of it.

outcomes.story: You suggest never tapping a joint again. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Done cleanly, it is very safe, and it is the only way to tell crystals from infection. If a joint flares differently next time, it should be tapped.

differential.resident: The joint fluid results are in his chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Pseudogout: calcium crystals in the joint
Septic arthritis
Acute gout: uric acid crystals in the joint
Reactive arthritis
differential.reveal: It is gout. The needle-shaped crystals that glow yellow under polarized light are uric acid, and nothing else looks like them. Pseudogout crystals are stubby and glow blue. An infected joint would show bacteria and usually a far higher white cell count. His normal blood uric acid does not argue against gout, because the level often dips during an attack.

terms.meaning: Attacks of joint inflammation caused by uric acid crystals.
Light filtered to vibrate in one direction. Under it, crystals of different substances show different colors.

ending.better: Home with the pain easing, and a plan to prevent the next attack
ending.stable: Home with the pain easing, and a plan to prevent the next attack
ending.worse: Admitted to hospital

rh-003.plainDiagnosis: Uric acid crystals inflaming the joint at the base of the big toe (acute gout).

science.title: Why the big toe, and why at night
science.text: Uric acid stays dissolved only up to a limit, and the limit falls as temperature falls. The big toe is the coolest joint in the body, and it cools further at night. When the fluid there holds more uric acid than it can keep dissolved, crystals form.

science.title: Why his water tablet made it worse
science.text: The kidney tubule both reabsorbs uric acid and secretes it. Thiazide tablets shift that balance toward keeping it, partly by competing for the same transporters. Less leaves in the urine, and the level in his blood rises.

sources.title: FitzGerald et al. (Arthritis Care Res 2020): 2020 American College of Rheumatology guideline for the management of gout
Dalbeth et al. (Lancet 2021): gout

rh-035.title: Five days of fever, _red eyes and cracked lips._

start.alarm: Fever for five days · very irritable

rh-035.handoff: A 3-year-old boy has had a high fever for five days that medicine barely touches. His eyes are red, his lips are cracked, he has a rash, and today the skin on his fingertips started to peel.

interview.prompt: Ask his parents about the fever
interview.finding: Five days of high fever, up to 39.8 °C. Fever medicine barely brings it down. He is miserable and hardly eating.

interview.prompt: Ask what else they have noticed
interview.finding: Red eyes with no stickiness, very red cracked lips and a bumpy red tongue. A rash over his chest, belly and groin. A lump on the right side of his neck. His hands and feet were puffy and red, and today the skin around his fingertips began to peel.

interview.prompt: Ask about illness around him and his past health
interview.finding: He has always been healthy and has had all his vaccines. He goes to daycare, and nobody there is known to be ill. He has no cough, runny nose or diarrhea, and no blisters or mouth ulcers.

exam.prompt: Look at his eyes and his mouth
exam.finding: The whites of both eyes are red, except for a pale ring around the colored part, and there is no pus. His lips are bright red, dry and split. His tongue is red and bumpy, like a strawberry.

exam.prompt: Feel his neck
exam.finding: There is one tender gland on the right side, nearly 2 cm across.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin, hands and feet
exam.finding: A red, blotchy rash covers his trunk and is strongest in the groin. His palms and soles are red and puffy, and the skin is peeling around his fingernails.

1.label: Blood tests, urine and heart ultrasound
1.content:
White blood cells: 16.8, high. Hemoglobin: 10.4, low.
Platelets: 620, high.
Inflammation markers: both very high.
Liver test: mildly raised. Albumin and sodium: low.
Urine: white cells, with no bacteria growing.
Throat swab for strep: negative. Blood cultures: nothing growing so far.
Heart ultrasound: one of the arteries that feed the heart muscle is wider than it should be. No clot.

0.resident: Five days of fever in a small child, with changes in his eyes, mouth, skin, hands and neck. No single test diagnoses what I am thinking of. It is recognized from a set of findings.
0.question: Which set fits him?
options: Cough, runny nose, sticky red eyes and white spots inside the cheeks
A rough rash like sandpaper, a pale ring around the mouth and pus on the tonsils
Target-shaped skin spots with raw sores in the mouth and eyes
Red eyes without pus, red cracked lips and strawberry tongue, a blotchy rash, red swollen hands and feet that then peel, and a swollen neck gland
Arthritis that moves from joint to joint, with heart inflammation and lumps under the skin
0.fix: Name the pattern and send tests

terms.meaning: An illness of young children in which blood vessels become inflamed throughout the body. The cause is unknown.
Redness of the white of the eye.

outcomes.story: You pick the cough and white spots. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is measles. He has no cough or runny nose, his eyes are not sticky, and he is vaccinated.

outcomes.story: You pick the sandpaper rash. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is scarlet fever, which comes with pus on the tonsils. His throat has none, and his rash is blotchy, not rough.

outcomes.story: You pick target spots and raw sores. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That describes a severe drug reaction. He has had no new medicines and has no sores or blisters.

outcomes.story: You list them, and he has all five. Blood and urine are sent, and a heart ultrasound is arranged for today. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Fever for five days with at least four of those five is Kawasaki disease. The heart scan matters because of what this illness does to the coronary arteries.

outcomes.story: You pick the moving arthritis. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is rheumatic fever, which follows strep in older children. His joints are fine.

3.resident: It is Kawasaki disease, and one of his coronary arteries is already widened. Today is day five. Treatment protects his heart best inside the first ten days.
3.question: What do we give?
options: Immunoglobulin into a vein (IVIG), with aspirin
Ceftriaxone and vancomycin into a vein
Steroids alone
Fever medicine and fluids only
Acyclovir by mouth

terms.meaning: Intravenous immunoglobulin: antibodies pooled from thousands of blood donors, given as one long infusion. It calms the inflammation in his blood vessels.
The arteries that supply the heart muscle.
A weak, ballooned-out section of an artery.

outcomes.story: The infusion is started and runs through the night, with aspirin by mouth. When you see him the next morning, his fever has broken and he is asking for breakfast.
outcomes.reply: Right. Given in time, this cuts the chance of a coronary aneurysm from about one in four to about one in twenty-five. Aspirin is normally avoided in children. Here it is part of the treatment.

outcomes.story: Antibiotics run through the night. In the morning his fever is as high as ever, and every culture is still negative. Day six has begun without treatment.
outcomes.reply: Nothing has grown, because this is not a bacterial infection. Each day of inflammation is another day of injury to his coronary arteries. Give the immunoglobulin.

outcomes.story: You suggest steroids alone. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Steroids are sometimes added for children at the highest risk. They do not replace immunoglobulin, which is the treatment proven to protect the heart.

outcomes.story: He is given fluids and fever medicine. In the morning nothing has changed, except that another day of the ten has gone.
outcomes.reply: The fever would burn out by itself in a couple of weeks. The damage to his arteries would not. He needs the immunoglobulin.

outcomes.story: You suggest acyclovir. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That treats herpes viruses. Nothing here is herpes.

4.resident: His fever is gone and he is playing. His parents ask whether that is the end of it.
4.question: What follow-up does he need?
options: None, now that the fever has gone
Repeat heart ultrasounds over the coming weeks, low-dose aspirin and a heart specialist
A throat swab every year
Steroids for life
Kidney ultrasounds only

terms.meaning: An ultrasound scan of the heart and the vessels around it.
A medicine, such as low-dose aspirin, that makes platelets less sticky, so clots are less likely to form.

outcomes.story: You say no follow-up is needed. The specialist corrects you.
outcomes.reply: A widened coronary artery can keep changing for weeks after the fever is gone. Missing a growing aneurysm could mean a heart attack in a small child.

outcomes.story: You book heart scans at two weeks and at six weeks, and explain the daily low-dose aspirin.
outcomes.reply: Right. We watch the arteries until we know they have settled. The aspirin keeps clots from forming where an artery is widened.

outcomes.story: You suggest yearly throat swabs. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: This has nothing to do with strep. The organ to watch is the heart.

outcomes.story: You suggest lifelong steroids. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The illness burns out. He needs watching, not years of a drug with serious side effects.

outcomes.story: You suggest kidney scans. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His kidneys are not what is at risk. His coronary arteries are.

differential.resident: His blood tests, urine result and heart ultrasound are in the chart.
differential.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Scarlet fever
Measles
Kawasaki disease
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Systemic juvenile arthritis
differential.reveal: It is Kawasaki disease. He has five days of fever with all five features: red eyes without pus, red cracked lips and strawberry tongue, a rash, swollen hands and feet that are starting to peel, and a large neck gland. The very high platelets and the widened coronary artery fit, and no infection has been found. Scarlet fever would show strep, and measles a cough and a runny nose.

terms.meaning: Inflammation of blood vessels.
Small blood cells that start clots. They rise in the second week of this illness.

ending.stable: On the children’s ward with his fever gone, and heart scans booked for the coming weeks
ending.unstable: On the children’s ward with his fever gone, and heart scans booked for the coming weeks
ending.worse: On the children’s ward after a day’s delay in treatment, with heart scans booked
ending.critical: In the children’s intensive care unit

rh-035.plainDiagnosis: An inflammation of blood vessels in a young child that can damage the arteries of the heart (Kawasaki disease).

science.title: Why a widened artery is dangerous
science.text: When a tube widens, the fluid in it slows down, and it can swirl in the wide part. Blood that is slow and swirling is far more likely to clot. In an artery that feeds the heart, a clot cuts off heart muscle.

science.title: How a disease with no test gets diagnosed
science.text: Each of his findings alone is common in childhood infections. Together, with five days of fever, they are rare in anything else. The diagnosis rests on how unlikely the whole pattern is by chance, which is why the criteria ask for at least four of five.

sources.title: McCrindle et al. (Circulation 2017): diagnosis, treatment, and long-term management of Kawasaki disease, a scientific statement from the American Heart Association
Newburger et al. (N Engl J Med 1986): the treatment of Kawasaki syndrome with intravenous gamma globulin

orth-034.title: A broken shin, _and pain that morphine does not touch._

start.alarm: Broken shin · pain rising despite morphine

orth-034.handoff: A 27-year-old man crashed his motorcycle and his left shin hit a curb. The leg is deformed and swollen. He has had morphine, and the pain is still getting worse.

interview.prompt: Ask what happened and about the pain
interview.finding: His shin hit a curb at speed. He cannot stand on it. The pain is severe and still climbing, worse than he expected from a break, and it has spread through the whole calf.

interview.prompt: Ask about other injuries
interview.finding: He wore a helmet and did not hit his head or black out. Nothing hurts in his chest, belly or hips, and the trauma team found no other injury.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health and whether the morphine helped
interview.finding: He is healthy and takes no medicines. The morphine has made no difference. He rates the pain ten out of ten.

exam.prompt: Look at the leg and feel it
exam.finding: The middle of his shin is bent and swollen. The skin is not broken. The calf feels hard as wood, and the bone is extremely tender.

exam.prompt: Gently bend his toes up and down
exam.finding: Moving his toes, even slightly, makes him cry out. The pain is far beyond what the movement should cause.

exam.prompt: Check the feeling, pulses and color of his foot
exam.finding: The skin between his first two toes is going numb. Both foot pulses are there, but you have to press hard to find them. A pressed toenail takes three seconds to turn pink again.

1.label: X-rays
1.content:
X-rays of the left shin, including the knee and ankle: the shin bone (tibia) is broken straight across in the middle, and the two ends are completely out of line.
The thinner bone beside it (fibula) is broken too.
The knee and ankle joints are not involved.
The soft tissue of the whole leg is swollen.

0.resident: The shin is obviously broken. Before we plan anything, we need pictures of it.
0.question: Which imaging comes first?
options: Plain X-rays of the shin that include the knee and the ankle
An MRI of the lower leg
An ultrasound of the calf
A bone scan
0.fix: Get X-rays with the joints above and below

terms.meaning: The shin bone, the larger of the two bones in the lower leg.
Describes a broken bone whose ends have moved out of line.

outcomes.story: A portable X-ray is taken at the bedside, from knee to ankle. The pictures go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. X-rays show the break, and we always include the joint above and the joint below, because a second injury there is easy to miss.

outcomes.story: You request an MRI. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: An MRI takes an hour and adds nothing to a broken shin. Plain X-rays show bone clearly and take minutes.

outcomes.story: You request an ultrasound. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: Ultrasound looks for clots in veins. It does not show a fracture.

outcomes.story: You request a bone scan. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: That is a slow test for hidden problems such as stress fractures or tumors. This break is not hidden.

3.resident: The fracture is bad. But the pain, the rock-hard calf and the numbness are the bigger problem. Pressure is building inside his leg and cutting off its blood supply.
3.question: What do we do right now?
options: Raise the leg above his heart and watch it
Apply ice and a tight compression wrap
Measure the pressure in the leg, and get him ready for emergency surgery to open the compartments
Start a full-dose blood thinner

terms.meaning: A group of muscles wrapped in a tough sheet of tissue that does not stretch. The lower leg has four.
An operation that slits those sheets open along the leg so that the swollen muscle can expand and blood can flow again.

outcomes.story: The leg is propped on pillows above his heart. Two hours later his foot is numb, and he cannot lift his toes.
outcomes.reply: Raising the leg lowers the pressure of the blood arriving, while the pressure inside stays the same, so even less gets through. Muscle and nerve have been dying for two hours. Call the surgeon.
outcomes.alarm: Foot numb · toes will not lift

outcomes.story: The leg is iced and wrapped firmly. Ninety minutes later his foot is pale and numb, and the pain is unbearable.
outcomes.reply: The pressure in that leg is already too high. A tight wrap adds more from outside, and ice narrows the vessels. Take the wrap off, and call the surgeon.

outcomes.story: The leg is laid flat, level with his heart. A needle gauge confirms very high pressure, and the surgeon takes him straight to the operating room. Long cuts are made on both sides of the calf, and the muscle bulges out, dark at first and then pink. His foot warms up.
outcomes.reply: Right. Only opening the compartments lets blood back in. Muscle survives about six hours without it, so the clock started at the crash.
outcomes.alarm: Compartments opened · foot pink and warm

outcomes.story: You write for a blood thinner. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: This is not a clot. It is swelling in a closed space. A blood thinner would add bleeding to the swelling.

4.resident: The pressure is off and his foot is alive. The bone is still in two pieces.
4.question: How should the fracture be fixed for good?
options: A cast from thigh to toes
A frame of pins outside the leg, as the permanent treatment
A removable brace only
A metal rod down the middle of the bone
4.fix: Name the rod down the bone

terms.meaning: A metal rod placed down the hollow center of a long bone and locked with screws at each end.
A frame outside the limb joined to the bone by pins. It usually holds a fracture for a while, until a final repair.

outcomes.story: You suggest a long cast. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A cast cannot hold a break this far out of line, and his leg now has open wounds that need looking after.

outcomes.story: You suggest a frame for good. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A frame is useful for a few days while swelling and wounds settle. As a final treatment it heals this bone less reliably.

outcomes.story: You suggest a brace. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A brace suits a stable break that has stayed in line. His is completely out of line.

outcomes.story: The surgeon plans to pass a rod down the bone once the leg has settled.
outcomes.reply: Right. A rod inside the bone holds it straight, lets him put weight on it early, and heals well.

differential.resident: The X-rays are in his chart. Think about the pain, the hard calf and what happened when you moved his toes.
differential.question: What must not be missed here?
options: A clot in the veins of the leg
Fat from the bone marrow lodging in the lungs
An infected ankle joint
Acute compartment syndrome: pressure building inside the leg and cutting off its blood supply
differential.reveal: He has compartment syndrome. Bleeding and swelling from the fracture are trapped inside the tight sheets that wrap the calf muscles. The pressure has risen high enough to squeeze the small blood vessels shut, so muscle and nerve are being starved. Pain that drugs do not touch, and pain when the toes are moved, are the early signs. The pulses can stay present until very late.

terms.meaning: Too little blood reaching a tissue.
The examiner moving a part of the body while the patient relaxes. Pain on it is an early sign here.

ending.stable: In the recovery room after surgery to release the pressure, with his leg saved
ending.unstable: In the recovery room after surgery to release the pressure, with his leg saved
ending.worse: In the recovery room after surgery, with muscle and nerve damage that came from the wait

orth-034.plainDiagnosis: Dangerous pressure inside the lower leg after a broken shin, cutting off blood to the muscles (acute compartment syndrome).

science.title: Why blood stopped flowing while the pulse was still there
science.text: Blood moves through tissue only if the pressure pushing it in is higher than the pressure around the small vessels. The pulse you feel is in a large artery at high pressure. The capillaries inside the swollen compartment work at a much lower pressure, and they were squeezed shut first.

science.title: Why raising the leg makes it worse
science.text: Pressure in a column of fluid falls with height. Lifting the leg above the heart lowers the arterial pressure reaching it, while the pressure trapped in the compartment does not change. The difference that drives blood in gets smaller.

sources.title: Schmidt (Injury 2017): acute compartment syndrome
von Keudell et al. (Lancet 2015): diagnosis and treatment of acute extremity compartment syndrome

orth-045.title: A limp for three weeks, _and he points to his knee._

start.alarm: Limping for three weeks · knee and groin pain

orth-045.handoff: A 13-year-old boy has had an aching left knee and groin for three weeks, and a limp that is getting worse. He did not injure it. For two days he has found it harder to put weight on that leg.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain and the limp
interview.finding: A dull ache in his left groin and the inner side of his knee for three weeks, with a limp. He points mostly to the knee. It is worse when he is active. There was no fall or injury.

interview.prompt: Ask about fever and other illness
interview.finding: No fever, no night sweats, no weight loss and no rash. He has not been ill, and no other joint hurts.

interview.prompt: Ask his mother about his growth and the family
interview.finding: He has always been big for his age and is well above a healthy weight. He has not started puberty. He is not very active. His mother has type 2 diabetes.

exam.prompt: Watch him walk
exam.finding: He limps, spending as little time as he can on the left leg. The left foot points outward.

exam.prompt: Move his left hip
exam.finding: It will not turn inward and is stiff and sore in other directions. When you bend the hip up, the thigh swings outward by itself, and he cannot stop it.

exam.prompt: Examine his knee, and measure his legs
exam.finding: The knee he points to is normal: no swelling, and it bends fully without pain. The left leg is slightly shorter than the right.

1.label: X-rays of both hips
1.content:
X-rays from the front and with the legs turned out: on the left, the ball of the hip has slipped backward and downward off the neck of the thigh bone.
A line drawn along the top of the neck should cut through the ball. On the left it misses.
The growth plate on the left is widened and irregular.
The right hip is normal.

0.resident: He points to his knee, and his knee is normal. What will not move properly is his hip.
0.question: Which pictures do we need?
options: An MRI of the knee
X-rays of both hips, from the front and with the legs turned out
An ultrasound of the knee
A CT scan of his lower spine

terms.meaning: Pain felt in one place when the problem is somewhere else. Hip problems in children are often felt in the knee.
A layer of soft, growing cartilage near the end of a child’s bone. It is the weakest part.

outcomes.story: He walks to the scanner and waits. The knee MRI is normal. As he walks back, his leg gives way, and now he cannot stand on it.
outcomes.reply: The knee was never the problem, and three hours of walking on that hip have made the real one worse. X-ray both hips, and keep him off his feet.
outcomes.alarm: Cannot put weight on the leg

outcomes.story: He is taken to X-ray in a wheelchair, and both hips are filmed. The pictures go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. In a child with knee pain and a normal knee, look at the hip. And film both sides, because this condition can affect both.

outcomes.story: You request a knee ultrasound. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: His knee has no swelling and moves normally. The stiffness is in the hip.

outcomes.story: You request a CT of his spine. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: His back does not hurt, and his nerves work. Follow the exam: it is the hip that will not turn.

3.resident: The ball of his left hip is slipping off the thigh bone through the growth plate. He walked in here on it.
3.question: What do we do?
options: Encourage weight loss, and arrange physical therapy
No weight on that leg from this moment, and an urgent surgical opinion about pinning it in place
A body cast from chest to ankle for six weeks
A course of steroid tablets
3.fix: Stop weight bearing and call the surgeon

terms.meaning: Putting no weight at all on a leg, using a wheelchair or crutches.
Passing a single screw across the growth plate through a small cut, to stop any more slipping. Nobody tries to push the ball back.

outcomes.story: He goes home walking, with an exercise sheet. The next morning he is carried in. The hip gave way on the stairs, and he cannot move the leg at all.
outcomes.reply: Every step put his body weight across a slipping growth plate. It has now come right off, and the blood supply to the ball of the hip is at risk. He should not have walked out of here.
outcomes.alarm: Hip has slipped further · cannot move the leg

outcomes.story: He stays in the wheelchair, and he and his mother are told why. The orthopedic surgeon sees him and books a screw for the morning.
outcomes.reply: Right. No weight on it, and a screw to hold it where it is. Done early and gently, he keeps a good hip.

outcomes.story: You suggest a body cast. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A cast does not hold the growth plate reliably, and it carries its own harms. A single screw does the job.

outcomes.story: You suggest steroids. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nothing here is inflamed. It is a mechanical slip, and tablets cannot hold a bone in place.

4.resident: His mother asks why this cannot wait a week or two.
4.question: What is the complication everyone is trying to avoid?
options: The hip dislocating again and again
Death of the ball of the hip from loss of its blood supply
Infection of the hip joint
The leg growing too long
4.fix: Explain the risk to the blood supply

terms.meaning: Death of bone because its blood supply has been cut off. In the hip it leads to collapse and early arthritis.

outcomes.story: You say dislocation. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The ball stays in its socket. It is the neck of the thigh bone that moves away from it.

outcomes.story: You explain it to his mother, and she understands why he has to stay.
outcomes.reply: Right. The small vessels that feed the ball of the hip run along the neck and cross the growth plate. A sudden, complete slip can tear or kink them.

outcomes.story: You say infection. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Infection is not a feature of this condition. The danger is to the blood supply.

outcomes.story: You say overgrowth. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: If anything, the leg ends up a little short. The serious risk is the bone dying.

differential.resident: The X-rays of both hips are in his chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Perthes disease: loss of blood supply to the ball of the hip, in a younger child
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis: the ball of the hip has slipped off the thigh bone at the growth plate
An infected hip joint
A brief inflammation of the hip after a viral illness
differential.reveal: He has a slipped capital femoral epiphysis. In early adolescence the growth plate at the top of the thigh bone is at its weakest, and in heavier children the load across it is high. The ball has slid backward off the neck. Perthes disease affects younger children, an infected hip brings fever and severe pain, and a simple inflammation settles within days.

terms.meaning: The end of a long bone, beyond the growth plate. At the hip it is the ball.
The thigh bone.

ending.stable: Admitted and off his feet, with an operation to pin the hip booked for the morning
ending.worse: Admitted for a harder operation, after the hip slipped further

orth-045.plainDiagnosis: The ball of the hip slipping off the thigh bone through the growth plate (slipped capital femoral epiphysis).

science.title: Why his weight mattered
science.text: The growth plate at the hip sits at an angle, so body weight does not only press it together. Part of the force pushes sideways along the plate. The heavier the child and the steeper the angle, the larger that sliding force on the weakest tissue in the bone.
science.lessonTitle: Choose a force or energy model

science.title: Why a hip problem hurt in his knee
science.text: One nerve carries sensation from both the hip joint and the skin on the inner side of the knee. Their signals reach the spinal cord together, and the brain, which seldom hears from the hip, blames the knee.

sources.title: Peck, Voss and Voss (Am Fam Physician 2017): slipped capital femoral epiphysis, diagnosis and management
Loder et al. (J Bone Joint Surg Am 1993): acute slipped capital femoral epiphysis, the importance of physeal stability

orth-009.title: A slip on the ice, _and a wrist bent like a fork._

start.alarm: Swollen, bent wrist after a fall

orth-009.handoff: A 68-year-old woman slipped on an icy sidewalk 45 minutes ago and landed on her outstretched right hand. Her wrist is swollen, very painful and bent out of shape.

interview.prompt: Ask how she fell and whether anything else hurts
interview.finding: She slipped on ice and put her right hand out to break the fall. She did not hit her head or black out. Nothing else hurts.

interview.prompt: Ask about her hand
interview.finding: The wrist is very painful and swollen. Her fingers are not numb and do not tingle. She is right-handed.

interview.prompt: Ask about her bones and her medicines
interview.finding: She has osteoporosis and takes a weekly tablet for it, with calcium and vitamin D. She also takes tablets for blood pressure and her thyroid. Her mother broke a hip. She lives alone and manages by herself.

exam.prompt: Look at the wrist
exam.finding: It is swollen, and seen from the side it is bent upward and back, like the curve of a dinner fork. The skin is not broken.

exam.prompt: Check the blood flow and feeling in her hand
exam.finding: Her hand is warm and pink, and the pulse at the wrist is strong. She can feel a light touch on every finger and on the back of her hand.

exam.prompt: Press on her elbow, her forearm and the base of her thumb
exam.finding: None of them is tender. She can bend and straighten her fingers a little, though it hurts.

1.label: X-rays of the wrist
1.content:
X-rays from the front and the side: the radius, the larger forearm bone, is broken straight across about 2 cm above the wrist joint.
The broken end is tilted and shifted toward the back of the hand, and the bone has shortened.
The tip of the ulna, the other forearm bone, has been pulled off.
The small bones of the wrist are intact, and the break does not reach the joint surface.

0.resident: That wrist is broken, and it is out of line. Before anyone touches it, there are three things to do.
0.question: What comes first?
options: Pull it straight now, with no X-ray and no pain relief
Check and record the feeling and blood flow in her hand, give pain relief and get X-rays
Wrap it and send her home, with a clinic appointment
Get an MRI of the wrist at once
0.fix: Check her hand, treat her pain and get X-rays

terms.meaning: Testing the feeling, movement, pulse and color beyond an injury, to be sure nerves and blood vessels are working.
The nerve that runs through the front of the wrist and supplies feeling to the thumb and the next two fingers.

outcomes.story: You take hold of her wrist. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Not without knowing what the break looks like, and never without pain relief. Check her hand, treat her pain, then look at the X-ray.

outcomes.story: You record that her hand has normal feeling and a strong pulse. She is given pain relief, and X-rays are taken. The pictures go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. If her fingers go numb later, we need to know they were normal at the start. Then pain relief, and pictures before any pulling.

outcomes.story: You wrap it and start a discharge. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: A wrist this bent heals bent unless someone straightens it. She would lose grip and movement in her writing hand.

outcomes.story: You request an MRI. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: Plain X-rays show a broken wrist perfectly well, in minutes.

3.resident: The end of her radius is tilted back and out of place. Nerves and circulation are fine for now.
3.question: What do we do in the emergency department?
options: Numb it, pull it straight, hold it in a splint and repeat the X-ray
Put on a full cast as it lies, without straightening, and send her home
Operate on it here, straight away
A sling only

terms.meaning: Moving a broken bone back into line by pulling and pressing from outside, without an operation.
Local anesthetic injected into the pool of blood around a fracture. It numbs the break within minutes.
A support that holds a limb still and leaves room for swelling, unlike a full cast.

outcomes.story: Local anesthetic is injected into the fracture. The resident pulls the wrist out to length and presses the end back into place, and a molded splint is applied. A repeat X-ray shows the bone in line. Her fingers are checked again and are normal.
outcomes.reply: Right. Restore the shape, hold it with something that allows for swelling, confirm it on X-ray and recheck the hand.

outcomes.story: A snug full cast goes on over the bent wrist. Two hours later, still waiting for her ride, she says her fingers are numb. They are swollen and dusky.
outcomes.reply: A fresh fracture keeps swelling, and a full cast gives it nowhere to go. It is squeezing the nerve and the blood vessels. Split the cast now. And the bone was never straightened.
outcomes.alarm: Fingers numb and dusky in the cast

outcomes.story: You suggest operating here and now. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Most of these are pulled straight and splinted first. If it will not stay in line, surgery is planned properly in an operating room.

outcomes.story: You suggest a sling alone. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A sling rests the arm and holds nothing in place. The break would heal crooked.

4.resident: Her wrist is straight and splinted. She fell from standing height and broke a bone.
4.question: What else should this prompt?
options: Regular MRI scans of the wrist
A review of her osteoporosis treatment, to prevent the next fracture
Six weeks of preventive antibiotics
Permanent rest, with as little activity as possible

terms.meaning: A break from a fall at standing height or less. Healthy bone should withstand it.
Bones that have lost density and strength, so they break easily.

outcomes.story: You suggest MRI scans. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Follow-up X-rays check the healing. The larger question is why the bone broke so easily.

outcomes.story: You arrange a review of her bone treatment and a check of her risk of falling, alongside the fracture clinic.
outcomes.reply: Right. A wrist broken this way often comes a few years before a broken hip. It is a chance to ask whether her treatment is working and how to stop her falling.

outcomes.story: You suggest antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The skin was never broken, so there is nothing to prevent.

outcomes.story: You suggest permanent rest. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Bones weaken with rest. Walking and strength exercises protect them, and they improve balance too.

differential.resident: The X-rays are in her chart.
differential.question: What is this injury?
options: A Smith fracture: a wrist break tilted toward the palm
A Colles fracture: a break of the radius just above the wrist, tilted toward the back of the hand
A break of the scaphoid, a small bone at the base of the thumb
A Galeazzi fracture: a break in the shaft of the radius with a dislocated wrist joint
differential.reveal: It is a Colles fracture, the classic break from landing on an outstretched hand. The end of the radius snaps just above the wrist and tilts toward the back of the hand, which gives the fork shape. A Smith fracture tilts the other way. A scaphoid break is tender at the base of the thumb and causes no deformity.

terms.meaning: The larger of the two forearm bones at the wrist, on the thumb side.
The tilt between the two parts of a broken bone.

ending.stable: Home in a splint with her wrist straightened, and a bone health review booked
ending.worse: Home in a splint after a tight cast had to be cut off, with the feeling in her fingers returning

orth-009.plainDiagnosis: A broken wrist tilted toward the back of the hand, in bone weakened by osteoporosis (Colles fracture).

science.title: Why the bone broke where it did
science.text: Her hand stopped her fall, so the energy of her moving body had to go somewhere in a fraction of a second. It traveled up the arm and broke the bone at its weakest point: the wide, spongy end of the radius, where thinning from osteoporosis is greatest.
science.lessonTitle: Choose a force or energy model

science.title: Why bones thin after menopause
science.text: Bone is constantly dissolved by one kind of cell and rebuilt by another. Estrogen holds the dissolving cells in check. When it falls at menopause, removal runs ahead of rebuilding, and bone is lost year after year.

sources.title: Kamal and Shapiro (J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2022): AAOS/ASSH clinical practice guideline summary, management of distal radius fractures
Mauck and Swigler (Orthop Clin North Am 2018): evidence-based review of distal radius fractures

ur-001.title: It burns, _and she has to go every hour._

start.alarm: Burning when passing urine · two days

ur-001.handoff: A 24-year-old woman has had two days of burning when she passes urine. She needs to go about every hour and never feels empty. She has no fever.

interview.prompt: Ask about the symptoms
interview.finding: For two days it has burned when she passes urine. She goes about every hour and still feels the urge afterward. There is a mild ache low in her belly.

interview.prompt: Ask about fever, back pain and discharge
interview.finding: No fever or chills, no pain in her sides or back, and no vomiting. She has no vaginal discharge or itching.

interview.prompt: Ask about contraception, past infections and allergies
interview.finding: She has one partner and uses a diaphragm with spermicide. She had one infection like this 18 months ago. Sulfa drugs give her hives.

exam.prompt: Press on her belly
exam.finding: It is slightly tender just above the pubic bone and soft everywhere else.

exam.prompt: Tap gently over each kidney, at the back
exam.finding: Neither side is tender.

exam.prompt: Look at the skin of the vulva, and feel the groin
exam.finding: The skin looks normal, with no discharge or sores. No swollen glands in the groin.

1.label: Urine test
1.content:
Urine: cloudy.
Test strip: positive for white cells, and positive for nitrites, a chemical that gut bacteria make.
Under the microscope: 35 white cells per field (normal is fewer than 5), and a few red cells.
Pregnancy test: negative.
Urine culture: not needed for a first simple infection.

0.resident: Burning, going often and feeling the urge all the time, in a healthy young woman with no fever. One quick test in clinic will back up what we suspect.
0.question: Which test?
options: A test strip and microscope check on a clean, midstream urine sample
A urine culture, holding treatment until the result is back
An ultrasound of her kidneys
A CT scan of her belly

terms.meaning: Urine caught partway through passing it, after the first part has rinsed the opening clean.
A chemical that many bacteria make from the nitrate normally in urine. Finding it means bacteria are present.

outcomes.story: She gives a sample, and it is tested in the clinic within minutes. The result goes in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. With symptoms this typical, a positive strip is enough to treat. It takes five minutes.

outcomes.story: You plan to wait for a culture. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A culture takes two days, and she is uncomfortable now. For a first simple infection it is not needed at all.

outcomes.story: You request a kidney ultrasound. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That looks for a blockage. Nothing in her story suggests one.

outcomes.story: You request a CT scan. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Radiation and expense, for a problem a test strip can confirm.
