3.resident: She has a bladder infection. Remember what sulfa drugs do to her.
3.question: Which antibiotic?
options: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for three days
Nitrofurantoin for five days
Ciprofloxacin for three days
Amoxicillin for seven days

terms.meaning: An antibiotic that collects in the urine and works in the bladder.
The treatment to try first, because it works well with the fewest downsides.

outcomes.story: You write for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: It is a good first choice for many people, but it contains a sulfa drug, and those give her hives. Always check the allergy list.

outcomes.story: You write for nitrofurantoin, twice a day for five days, to take with food.
outcomes.reply: Right. It is a first-line choice, it stays effective against most bladder bacteria, and she can take it safely.

outcomes.story: You write for ciprofloxacin. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: It would work, but it is a broad antibiotic with rare, serious side effects. We keep it for infections that need it.

outcomes.story: You write for amoxicillin. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: Too many bladder bacteria resist amoxicillin now. It fails often enough that it is not a first choice.

4.resident: This is her second infection in 18 months. She asks what she can do to avoid another.
4.question: Which advice is best supported?
options: Start a daily preventive antibiotic, indefinitely
Stop all sexual activity for good
Consider a different contraceptive from the diaphragm with spermicide, and drink plenty of fluids
Have a urine culture every month, even when she feels well

terms.meaning: A gel that kills sperm. It also kills the helpful bacteria of the vagina, which lets gut bacteria move in.

outcomes.story: You suggest a daily antibiotic. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is for women with frequent infections, after simpler steps have failed. Two infections in 18 months does not call for it.

outcomes.story: You suggest giving up sex. The resident raises an eyebrow.
outcomes.reply: That is neither reasonable nor necessary. There is a specific risk factor she can change.

outcomes.story: You explain the link, and she says she will think about another method.
outcomes.reply: Right. A diaphragm with spermicide is a known cause of repeat infections. Changing it, and drinking enough to pass urine regularly, are the simple steps.

outcomes.story: You suggest monthly cultures. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Testing urine when she has no symptoms finds harmless bacteria and leads to antibiotics she does not need.

differential.resident: Her urine result is in the chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A kidney infection
Vaginitis
A simple bladder infection (uncomplicated cystitis)
Urethritis from a sexually transmitted infection
differential.reveal: It is a simple bladder infection. She has the three typical symptoms, tenderness over the bladder and urine full of white cells and bacteria. No fever and no pain over the kidneys mean the infection has stayed in the bladder. Vaginitis causes discharge and itching, and a sexually transmitted infection would not usually turn the nitrite test positive.

terms.meaning: Infection of the bladder.
In a healthy, non-pregnant woman with a normal urinary tract.

ending.stable: Home with a five-day course of nitrofurantoin
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

science.title: Why no culture was needed
science.text: A test is worth doing when its result could change the decision. Typical symptoms with a positive strip already make infection very likely, and the first-line antibiotics cover the usual bacteria. A culture would only confirm it, two days later.

science.title: Why drinking and passing urine helps
science.text: Bacteria reach the bladder by climbing the short tube that drains it. Each time the bladder empties, the stream washes most of them back out. A steady flow leaves them less time to multiply and stick to the wall.

sources.title: Gupta et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2011): international clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of acute uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women
Hooton (N Engl J Med 2012): uncomplicated urinary tract infection

ur-059.title: A kick in a soccer game, _and swelling that keeps growing._

start.alarm: Severe pain and swelling after a kick

ur-059.handoff: A 23-year-old man was kicked hard in the scrotum during a soccer game two hours ago. The right side swelled quickly and is extremely painful. He has vomited once.

interview.prompt: Ask what happened
interview.finding: He took a hard kick to the scrotum two hours ago. The pain in his right testicle was immediate and severe, and the swelling came up fast. He felt sick and vomited once. It has not eased at all.

interview.prompt: Ask about fever, urine and earlier problems
interview.finding: No fever and no burning when he passes urine. He has never had testicle pain or swelling before today.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health
interview.finding: He is healthy and takes no medicines. Nobody in his family bleeds easily.

exam.prompt: Look at the scrotum and feel it gently
exam.finding: The right side is very swollen, tight and bruised. The testicle is too tender to examine properly, and its outline is lost in a tense swelling around it.

exam.prompt: Examine the left side
exam.finding: The left testicle is normal in size and position and is not tender.

exam.prompt: Check his penis, groin and belly
exam.finding: There is no blood at the tip of the penis and no bulge in the groin. His belly is soft.

1.label: Ultrasound and blood count
1.content:
Ultrasound with a blood-flow scan: the tough white coat of the right testicle is torn, and tissue from inside is pushing out through the gap.
A large collection of blood surrounds the testicle.
Blood flow to the torn part is reduced or absent.
The left testicle is normal.
Hemoglobin: 13.6, normal.

0.resident: A hard blow, a tense swelling and a testicle I cannot feel properly. We need to see inside.
0.question: Which scan comes first?
options: An MRI of the scrotum
An ultrasound of the scrotum with a blood-flow scan
A CT scan of his belly and pelvis
A dye X-ray of the urethra

terms.meaning: An ultrasound that also shows whether blood is flowing.
The pouch of skin that holds the testicles.

outcomes.story: You request an MRI. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: An MRI can help when the ultrasound is unclear, but it is slow. Ultrasound is at the bedside and answers the question in minutes.

outcomes.story: He is given pain relief, and the ultrasound is done at the bedside. The result goes in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Ultrasound shows whether the testicle’s outer coat is intact, whether blood is reaching it, and how much blood has collected around it.

outcomes.story: You request a CT of his belly. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: CT shows the scrotum poorly and gives radiation to the wrong place. The injury is in front of us.

outcomes.story: You request a dye X-ray of the urethra. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That looks for a torn urethra. He has no blood at the tip of the penis and passes urine normally.

3.resident: The outer coat of the testicle is torn, and its contents are spilling into a pool of blood.
3.question: What is the treatment?
options: A scrotal support, ice and a clinic visit
An emergency operation to clear the blood and stitch the tear
Antibiotics alone
Draw the blood off with a needle, under ultrasound

terms.meaning: The tough white coat around the testicle. It holds the delicate tubes inside under slight pressure.
A collection of blood in the sac around the testicle.

outcomes.story: He goes home with ice and a support. The next morning he is back. The swelling has doubled, the skin is dark purple, and he has a fever.
outcomes.reply: Ice is for a bruise. His testicle is torn open, and overnight the exposed tissue has been dying under a growing pool of blood. He should have gone to the operating room.

outcomes.story: The urologist takes him to the operating room, clears out the blood, trims the tissue that cannot survive and stitches the coat closed.
outcomes.reply: Right. A torn testicle is repaired, and the sooner the better. Nearly all are saved when the repair is early.

outcomes.story: You suggest antibiotics alone. The urologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Antibiotics do not close a tear. The tissue spilling out needs to be put back and covered.

outcomes.story: You suggest drawing the blood off with a needle. The urologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Clotted blood will not come through a needle, and the tear would still be open underneath.

4.resident: He asks why this could not have waited a few days, to see how it settled.
4.question: What does early surgery achieve?
options: It removes any future risk of testicular cancer
It makes it much more likely that the testicle is saved and keeps working
It is the only way to make the diagnosis, since scans cannot suggest it
It stops the other testicle from twisting

terms.meaning: Saving an organ that would otherwise be lost.

outcomes.story: You say it prevents cancer. The urologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Injury and cancer are unrelated, and surgery for one does nothing about the other.

outcomes.story: You explain it to him before he goes to the operating room.
outcomes.reply: Right. Repaired within the first days, most torn testicles survive and go on making hormones and sperm. Left alone, many are lost.

outcomes.story: You say scans cannot show it. The urologist points at the screen.
outcomes.reply: The ultrasound showed the tear clearly. Surgery is the treatment here, not the test.

outcomes.story: You say it protects the other side. The urologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Twisting is a separate problem, with a different cause. This operation is about the injured side.

differential.resident: The ultrasound is in his chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Epididymitis, an infection of the coiled tube behind the testicle
Testicular rupture: the tough outer coat of the testicle has torn
Testicular torsion: the testicle has twisted on its cord
A simple collection of clear fluid (hydrocele)
differential.reveal: The kick tore the outer coat of his right testicle. The tubes that make sperm are pushing out through the tear, and blood has pooled around them. An infection comes on over days, with fever and burning urine. A twisted testicle has an intact coat and no blow to explain it, and a hydrocele is painless.

terms.meaning: A tear through the wall of an organ.
An injury from a blow that does not break the skin.

ending.stable: In the recovery room after surgery, with the testicle repaired
ending.worse: In the recovery room after a late operation, with part of the testicle lost

ur-059.plainDiagnosis: A torn testicle from a direct blow (testicular rupture).

science.title: How ultrasound drew the tear
science.text: The probe sends pulses of sound and listens for echoes. Sound bounces back wherever tissue changes, and the time it takes shows how deep that boundary lies. The testicle’s coat normally shows as an unbroken bright line. In his, the line had a gap.
science.lessonTitle: Read a wave and a logarithmic level

science.title: Why trapped blood threatens what is left
science.text: Blood that leaks into a closed sac cannot escape, so the pressure there rises. Once it is higher than the pressure in the small vessels of the testicle, those vessels are squeezed flat, and tissue that survived the blow loses its supply.

sources.title: Morey et al. (J Urol 2014): urotrauma, AUA guideline
Buckley and McAninch (J Urol 2006): use of ultrasonography for the diagnosis of testicular injuries in blunt scrotal trauma

ur-049.title: A kidney infection _that tablets did not touch._

start.alarm: Fever 39.5 · blood pressure 92 over 56 · confused

ur-049.handoff: A 61-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes has had three days of high fever and severe pain in her right side. Antibiotic tablets started two days ago did nothing. She is now confused, and her blood pressure is low.

interview.prompt: Ask her daughter how the illness has gone
interview.finding: Three days of high fever with shaking chills, severe pain in her right side and vomiting. It burned when she passed urine, and she has been passing very little. She has become more and more confused.

interview.prompt: Ask what treatment she has had
interview.finding: A doctor gave her antibiotic tablets two days ago for a urine infection. She has only got worse.

interview.prompt: Ask about her health
interview.finding: Her diabetes is poorly controlled, and she often misses her insulin. Her kidneys already work at reduced strength, and she has high blood pressure. She has never had kidney stones.

exam.prompt: Check how alert she is, and her circulation
exam.finding: She is drowsy and knows her name but nothing else. Her mouth is dry. Her hands and feet are turning blotchy, and a pressed fingertip is slow to turn pink again.

exam.prompt: Tap over her kidneys, and press on her belly
exam.finding: A light tap over the right kidney makes her cry out, and the muscles there are tight. The right side of her belly is tender, and the rest is soft.

exam.prompt: Listen to her heart and lungs
exam.finding: Her heart is fast. Her lungs are clear.

1.label: Blood tests, urine and CT scan
1.content:
White blood cells: 21.8, very high. Platelets: 96, low.
Blood sugar: 468, very high.
Lactate: 4.6, high. Blood acid level (pH): 7.26, acidic.
Kidney test (creatinine): 3.2, double her usual.
Urine: full of white cells, with rod-shaped bacteria.
CT scan: bubbles of gas inside the right kidney, spreading into its drainage system, with patches where the tissue has been destroyed. No pocket of pus, and no stone blocking the kidney.

0.resident: She is in septic shock from a kidney infection that has not answered to tablets. Fluids and antibiotics through a vein are running. Something about this infection is not ordinary.
0.question: Which scan will show what is going on in that kidney?
options: A plain X-ray of her belly
A kidney ultrasound, and nothing else
A CT scan of her belly and pelvis
An X-ray of her bladder while she passes urine

terms.meaning: Dangerously low blood pressure caused by severe infection.
An infection with something extra that antibiotics alone cannot fix, such as a blockage, an abscess or dead tissue.

outcomes.story: You request a plain X-ray. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: An X-ray might show gas if there is a lot of it, and it would tell us nothing more. We need to see the kidney itself.

outcomes.story: You request an ultrasound only. The resident adds a CT.
outcomes.reply: Ultrasound can show a blocked kidney, but gas scatters the sound and hides everything behind it. CT sees through it.

outcomes.story: She is taken to the scanner with a nurse and a monitor. Her blood results come back while she is there, and everything goes in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. When a kidney infection is not improving, CT looks for the things antibiotics cannot treat: a blockage, an abscess or gas.

outcomes.story: You request a bladder X-ray during urination. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That test looks for urine flowing backward toward the kidneys. It is never done in a patient this ill.

3.resident: There is gas inside her right kidney. Bacteria are fermenting her high blood sugar and destroying the tissue. She is in shock.
3.question: How do we treat this first?
options: Remove the kidney at once, as in every case
Antibiotic tablets, and home once the fever is gone
Fluids, antibiotics through a vein, insulin for her sugar, and a drain placed into the kidney through the skin
Stop the antibiotics and watch how it develops
3.fix: Resuscitate her and drain the kidney

terms.meaning: A thin tube passed through the skin into the kidney, guided by a scan, to let out gas and infected fluid.
Insulin given steadily into a vein, adjusted every hour to bring blood sugar down.

outcomes.story: You say the kidney must come out now. The urologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That used to be the rule. Most patients now do as well or better with a drain first, and they keep the kidney. Removal is for when that fails.

outcomes.story: You suggest tablets and home. The resident stares.
outcomes.reply: She is in intensive care, in shock, with gas in her kidney. Tablets have already failed her once.

outcomes.story: An insulin drip is started, and the radiologist places a drain in her kidney. Gas and cloudy fluid come out. Over the next six hours she does not turn the corner. Her blood pressure needs more and more support, and a repeat scan shows that more of the kidney has been destroyed.
outcomes.reply: That was the right first move, and for most patients it is enough. For her it has not been.
outcomes.alarm: Blood pressure falling despite the drain

outcomes.story: You suggest stopping antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: She would be dead by morning. Nothing here says the antibiotics are wrong. They are not enough alone.

4.resident: She has had a drain and the right antibiotics, and she is still in shock. The repeat scan shows more gas and more of the kidney destroyed.
4.question: What now?
options: An emergency operation to remove the kidney
Switch to antibiotic tablets
High-pressure oxygen treatment, as the answer
Carry on exactly as we are

terms.meaning: An operation to remove a kidney.
Physically removing the place an infection is coming from, when drugs cannot reach it.

outcomes.story: The urologist takes her to the operating room and removes the right kidney. Within hours her blood pressure needs less support.
outcomes.reply: Yes. The kidney had become a mass of dead, infected tissue that nothing could reach. Taking it out removes the source. She can live well on the other one.
outcomes.alarm: Infected kidney removed · blood pressure recovering

outcomes.story: You suggest switching to tablets. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Tablets are for patients who are getting better. She is getting worse on the strongest drugs we have.

outcomes.story: She is taken to the pressure chamber. Three hours later she is back with a lower blood pressure, and her lungs are starting to fail.
outcomes.reply: That treatment has no proven place here, and it cost three hours with the source still inside her. The kidney has to come out.

outcomes.story: Nothing is changed. Four hours later her blood pressure cannot be held, and her other organs are starting to fail.
outcomes.reply: The plan was failing, and repeating it could not work. Dead tissue full of bacteria does not respond to antibiotics. The kidney has to come out.

differential.resident: Her blood tests, urine result and CT scan are in the chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: An ordinary kidney infection
Emphysematous pyelonephritis: a kidney infection in which gas-forming bacteria are destroying the tissue
A kidney cancer with a dead center
A stone blocking the kidney
differential.reveal: It is emphysematous pyelonephritis, a rare and dangerous kidney infection that occurs almost only in people with poorly controlled diabetes. The bacteria are ordinary gut bacteria. In tissue soaked in sugar and short of oxygen, they ferment the sugar and release gas, and the kidney dies around them. An ordinary infection never puts gas in the kidney.

terms.meaning: Containing gas.
Infection of the kidney.

ending.stable: In intensive care after removal of the infected kidney, with her blood pressure recovering
ending.unstable: In intensive care after removal of the infected kidney, with her blood pressure recovering
ending.worse: In intensive care after removal of the infected kidney
ending.critical: In intensive care on life support, after the operation came late

ur-049.plainDiagnosis: A kidney infection in which bacteria make gas and destroy the kidney, in poorly controlled diabetes (emphysematous pyelonephritis).

science.title: Where the gas came from
science.text: With oxygen, cells burn glucose completely. Without it, these bacteria ferment glucose, and their fermentation gives off carbon dioxide and hydrogen. Her blood sugar of 468 gave them an almost unlimited supply.

science.title: Why antibiotics could not reach it
science.text: Years of high sugar narrow and damage small blood vessels, so her kidney was poorly supplied to begin with. Once tissue dies, no blood reaches it at all. Antibiotics and white cells travel in blood, so the infection’s center was out of their reach.

sources.title: Huang and Tseng (Arch Intern Med 2000): emphysematous pyelonephritis, clinicoradiological classification, management, prognosis, and pathogenesis
Somani et al. (J Urol 2008): is percutaneous drainage the new gold standard in the management of emphysematous pyelonephritis? Evidence from a systematic review

ent-042.title: A nosebleed for over an hour, _running down the back of his throat._

start.alarm: Nosebleed for 75 minutes · on a blood thinner

ent-042.handoff: A 70-year-old man has had a heavy nosebleed for 75 minutes. Pinching his nose does not stop it, and blood keeps running down his throat. He takes a blood thinner for an irregular heartbeat.

interview.prompt: Ask about the bleeding
interview.finding: It started without warning 75 minutes ago. He has been spitting and swallowing a lot of blood, and he feels it running down the back of his throat even when he pinches his nose. Nothing hit his nose, and he uses no nasal sprays.

interview.prompt: Ask about his medicines
interview.finding: He takes apixaban, a blood thinner, twice a day for an irregular heartbeat, and he took it this morning. He also takes two blood pressure tablets. He has never had a serious bleed before.

interview.prompt: Ask how he feels, and about his blood pressure
interview.finding: He feels lightheaded when he stands. He has no chest pain and is not short of breath. He ran out of his blood pressure tablets a week ago.

exam.prompt: Look into the front of his nose, after suction and a spray to shrink the lining
exam.finding: There is no bleeding point at the front. Blood is welling up from deep inside.

exam.prompt: Look at the back of his throat
exam.finding: A steady stream of fresh blood is running down the back wall.

exam.prompt: Look at him, and listen to his heart and lungs
exam.finding: He is pale and anxious, and his shirt is stained with blood. His heartbeat is irregular. His lungs are clear.

1.label: Blood tests and first packing
1.content:
Hemoglobin: 10.8, low.
Platelets: 210, normal.
Standard clotting tests: near normal. They do not measure the effect of his blood thinner.
Kidney test (creatinine): 1.3, slightly high.
Both nostrils have been packed at the front. Blood is still running down the back of his throat.

0.resident: He is pale, his heart is fast and he is on a blood thinner. We will spray his nose and pack the front. What else has to happen right now?
0.question: What do you do alongside the packing?
options: Place a line in a vein, send blood tests and a sample to match blood, and watch his heart rate and blood pressure
Bring his blood pressure down to normal fast with a strong drip, before anything else
Give a transfusion of platelets
Send him home to see a nose specialist in clinic
0.fix: Place a line and send bloods

terms.meaning: A blood sample that finds his blood group, so matched blood is ready if he needs it.
Soft material or a small balloon placed in the nose to press on a bleeding vessel.

outcomes.story: A line goes in and blood is sent. His nose is sprayed, and both nostrils are packed at the front. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. A nosebleed like this can cost a lot of blood. We prepare for that while we work on the nose.

outcomes.story: You reach for a blood pressure drip. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: His pressure is high partly from fear and partly from missed tablets. He has also lost blood. Dropping it fast could starve his brain and heart. Stop the bleeding first.

outcomes.story: You ask for platelets. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His platelets are not the problem. His blood thinner blocks a clotting protein, and extra platelets do not change that.

outcomes.story: He is sent home holding a towel to his face. Two hours later an ambulance brings him back. He fainted in his kitchen, and he is still bleeding.
outcomes.reply: Most nosebleeds are harmless. An older man on a blood thinner who has bled for over an hour is the exception. He needed a line, blood tests and monitoring.

3.resident: The bleed is at the back of the nose, where the front packs cannot press on it.
3.question: How do we stop it?
options: Take out all the packing and watch
An emergency operation to tie off the main artery in his neck
Add a pack at the back of the nose, and admit him for monitoring
Repack the front with more gauze
3.fix: Place a posterior pack and admit him

terms.meaning: A balloon or pad passed through the nostril and seated at the very back of the nose, where it presses on the bleeding artery.
The main artery to the back of the nose.

outcomes.story: The packs come out. Blood pours from his nose and mouth, and he coughs and chokes on it. His blood pressure falls.
outcomes.reply: The packs were at least slowing it. He needs more pressure, in the right place. Put a pack at the back.
outcomes.alarm: Bleeding from nose and mouth · pressure falling

outcomes.story: You ask for the artery in his neck to be tied off. The ENT surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is far too big a step. If a pack at the back fails, the next move is to clip or block the small artery inside the nose.

outcomes.story: A balloon is passed through his nostril, inflated at the back of his nose and pulled snug. The front is packed again. The stream down his throat slows, then stops. He is admitted to a monitored bed.
outcomes.reply: Right. The balloon presses on the artery where it enters the back of the nose. He stays in hospital while it is in.

outcomes.story: The front is packed again, tighter. Half an hour later blood is still running down his throat, and he has vomited a bowl of swallowed blood.
outcomes.reply: More of the same pressure in the wrong place cannot work. The bleed is behind the packs. Put a pack at the back.

4.resident: The bleeding is controlled, and he is on a heart monitor with an oxygen probe on his finger. A pack at the back of the nose has its own dangers.
4.question: Which one are we monitoring him for?
options: Permanent loss of his sense of smell
Low oxygen and a slow heart rate from a reflex the pack can set off, and a blocked airway
A sudden rise of pressure inside the eye
A storm of thyroid hormone
4.fix: Explain why he is on a monitor

terms.meaning: An automatic response carried by nerves. Pressure at the back of the nose can slow the breathing and the heart.

outcomes.story: You say he could lose his sense of smell. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The smell nerves are at the roof of the nose, away from the pack. That is not the risk.

outcomes.story: You check that the alarm limits on his monitor are set.
outcomes.reply: Right. Pressure at the back of the nose can slow his breathing and his heart, and a pack that slips can block his airway. That is why he is not going home tonight.

outcomes.story: You say the eye. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A pack in the nose has no way to raise the pressure in the eye.

outcomes.story: You say the thyroid. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The thyroid has nothing to do with a nasal pack.

differential.resident: Both nostrils are packed at the front, and blood is still running down his throat.
differential.question: Where is the bleeding coming from?
options: A small artery high at the front of the nose
The cluster of vessels at the front of the nose, missed by the packs
A bleeding stomach ulcer
The back of the nose (a posterior nosebleed)
differential.reveal: The bleed is at the back of his nose. Packs at the front press on the front, and they would have stopped a bleed there. Blood that keeps running down the throat behind good packs has to be coming from behind them. Bleeds at the back are less common and heavier, and they happen most in older people with high blood pressure or on blood thinners. A stomach ulcer does not send fresh blood down from the nose.

terms.meaning: Toward the back.
A nosebleed.

ending.stable: Admitted to a monitored bed with the bleeding stopped
ending.unstable: Admitted to a monitored bed with the bleeding stopped
ending.worse: Admitted to a monitored bed, weak from blood loss, with the bleeding stopped
ending.critical: In intensive care after heavy blood loss, with the bleeding stopped

ent-042.plainDiagnosis: A nosebleed from the back of the nose, in a man on a blood thinner (posterior epistaxis).

science.title: How a balloon stops an artery
science.text: Blood leaves a torn artery because the pressure inside is higher than the pressure outside. A balloon pressed against the tear raises the outside pressure. When the two match, flow stops, and a clot has time to form.

science.title: Why his blood would not clot
science.text: A clot forms through a chain of enzymes, each switching on the next. Apixaban fits into the active site of one of them, factor Xa, and blocks it. That protects him from a stroke, and it also means a torn vessel takes far longer to seal.

sources.title: Tunkel et al. (Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2020): clinical practice guideline, nosebleed (epistaxis)
Kucik and Clenney (Am Fam Physician 2005): management of epistaxis

ent-011.title: Drooling, _and an empty battery slot in the remote._

start.alarm: Drooling · will not swallow

ent-011.handoff: An 18-month-old girl was found crying and drooling three hours ago. She will not drink, and she gags when she tries to swallow. The battery cover of a small remote was lying open on the floor.

interview.prompt: Ask her parents what happened
interview.finding: She was playing alone near a table where they keep a TV remote and loose watch and hearing-aid batteries. They found her crying and drooling about three hours ago. The battery slot of a small remote was open and empty.

interview.prompt: Ask about swallowing, breathing and vomiting
interview.finding: She pushed away her bottle and a cracker. She gags when she tries to swallow, and she points to her chest. She has not vomited and has no fever. Her breathing has been normal.

interview.prompt: Ask about her health
interview.finding: She is healthy and has had her vaccines. She takes no medicines and has no allergies. She has never choked on anything before.

exam.prompt: Watch her for a minute
exam.finding: She is alert and fussy, and she settles in her mother’s arms. Saliva is pooling in her mouth and running out. She gags when she tries to swallow. Her color is good.

exam.prompt: Listen to her breathing
exam.finding: No noisy breathing and no wheeze. She is not working hard to breathe, and both lungs sound the same.

exam.prompt: Look in her mouth, and feel her neck and belly
exam.finding: Nothing is stuck in her mouth or throat, and there are no burns. Her neck is not swollen. Her belly is soft.

1.label: X-rays of the neck, chest and belly
1.content:
Front view: a round metal disc, 20 mm across, in the upper food pipe at the base of the neck. A faint second ring shows just inside its edge.
Side view: the edge of the disc has a step in it.
No air has leaked around the food pipe.
Lungs: clear.

0.resident: A toddler, loose batteries, sudden drooling. She is breathing comfortably, so we have a moment to find out what she swallowed and where it is.
0.question: What is the most important step right now?
options: Reassure her parents and arrange a clinic visit, since her breathing is fine
X-rays now, from front and side, of her neck, chest and belly
Activated charcoal, to bind what she swallowed
A medicine to make her vomit it up

terms.meaning: A flat, coin-shaped battery from a watch, remote or hearing aid.
The tube that carries food from the throat to the stomach (the esophagus).

outcomes.story: The family goes home. Four hours later they are back. She has a fever, and she has vomited saliva streaked with blood.
outcomes.reply: A child who suddenly drools and cannot swallow has something stuck. If it is a battery, it starts burning within two hours. She needed X-rays the moment she arrived.

outcomes.story: She has X-rays in her mother’s arms within minutes. The pictures go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Metal shows clearly on X-ray. Two views tell us where it is and what it is.

outcomes.story: You ask for charcoal. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Charcoal binds drugs. It does not bind metal. It would also coat her food pipe and hide the view for the surgeon.

outcomes.story: You ask for a medicine to make her vomit. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Never. On the way back up, an object can lodge in the airway, and a battery burns again wherever it touches.

3.resident: The surgeon and the operating room are being called. That takes a few minutes. She can still swallow small sips.
3.question: What can we give her while we wait?
options: Two teaspoons of honey every ten minutes
Large drinks of water to wash it down into her stomach
An acid-blocking medicine into a vein, as the main treatment
Baking soda in water, to neutralize it
3.fix: Give honey while the team gathers

terms.meaning: Thick and slightly acidic. It coats the battery and weakens the burn. Never for babies under 12 months.
The chemical opposite of an acid. Strong alkalis dissolve living tissue.

outcomes.story: She takes the honey from a spoon, two teaspoons at a time, while the operating room is prepared.
outcomes.reply: Right. Honey slows the burn. It does not stop it, and it must never hold up getting the battery out.

outcomes.story: You offer a big cup of water. The resident takes it away.
outcomes.reply: Water will not move a battery that is wedged in place, and she could breathe it in. We also want her stomach empty for the anesthetic.

outcomes.story: You ask for an acid blocker. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That lowers acid in the stomach. The burn here is an alkali made at the battery’s surface, in her food pipe.

outcomes.story: You ask for baking soda. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Baking soda is itself an alkali. The battery is already making alkali, so this would add to the burn.

4.resident: The honey is a stopgap. The battery is still in her food pipe, and it is still burning.
4.question: What is the treatment?
options: Admit her, and repeat the X-ray in 24 hours to see whether it has passed
Book a camera test as an outpatient within 48 hours
Take it out now with a camera, under anesthesia, within two hours
A medicine to relax the lower food pipe so that it passes
4.fix: Call the surgeon for emergency removal

terms.meaning: Passing a thin camera down the throat. Small tools on it can grasp and remove an object.

outcomes.story: She is admitted to wait. By morning she has a high fever and noisy breathing, and a new X-ray shows air around her food pipe.
outcomes.reply: Waiting is for a battery that has reached the stomach in a child with no symptoms. Hers is stuck in the food pipe, and overnight it has burned through the wall. It has to come out now.
outcomes.alarm: High fever · air leaking around the food pipe

outcomes.story: You suggest a camera test within two days. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: In two days the battery could be through the wall and into a major blood vessel. It comes out within two hours.

outcomes.story: Under anesthesia, the surgeon passes a camera down and lifts the battery out. Where it sat there is a ring-shaped burn. A feeding tube is placed, and she is admitted.
outcomes.reply: Right. The battery is the source of the injury, and every minute it stays the burn gets deeper.
outcomes.alarm: Battery out · burn on the wall of the food pipe

outcomes.story: You suggest a medicine to relax the food pipe. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It is stuck at the top, and that medicine works at the bottom. Even if it moved, it would have burned the whole way down.

5.resident: The battery is out. The surgeon tells her parents that the burn can keep getting deeper for days, even now. Suppose a child like her came back two weeks later, vomiting large amounts of blood.
5.question: What would have happened?
options: A small tear in the lining, from vomiting
The burn has worn through into a major blood vessel, such as the aorta
A yeast infection of the food pipe
A stomach ulcer
5.fix: Name the complication to watch for

terms.meaning: The body’s main artery. It runs just behind the food pipe in the chest.
An abnormal opening between two parts of the body that are normally separate.

outcomes.story: You say a small tear. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A tear like that bleeds a little and stops. It would not put a child into shock.

outcomes.story: Her parents are told to bring her straight back for any blood in her vomit or stool, even weeks from now.
outcomes.reply: Right. Burned tissue keeps dying after the battery is out. The aorta lies just behind the food pipe, and an opening between them is the most feared result.

outcomes.story: You say a yeast infection. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That makes swallowing sore. It does not cause heavy bleeding.

outcomes.story: You say a stomach ulcer. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Her injury was in the food pipe, and that is where the danger stays.

differential.resident: Her X-rays are in the chart. Look at the edge of the disc.
differential.question: What has she swallowed?
options: A coin, stuck in the food pipe
A button battery, stuck in the food pipe
Something breathed into the right lung
A lump of food, stuck in the food pipe
differential.reveal: It is a button battery. A coin is one solid piece of metal, so on X-ray it shows as a plain disc with a smooth edge. A battery is built in two layers. From the front the layers show as a ring inside a ring, and from the side as a step. The disc lies behind the windpipe, in the food pipe, and her lungs are clear. Food does not show on X-ray.

terms.meaning: A ring within a ring on X-ray. It is the mark of a button battery.
An object stuck where it does not belong.

ending.stable: Admitted for observation after the battery was removed, with a feeding tube while the burn heals
ending.worse: In intensive care after a late removal, with a deep burn to the food pipe
ending.critical: In intensive care after a late removal, with a hole in the food pipe

ent-011.plainDiagnosis: A swallowed button battery stuck in the food pipe (esophageal button battery).

science.title: Why a battery burns and a coin does not
science.text: A battery drives current through any conductor that joins its two faces. Wet tissue is a conductor. The current splits water at the negative face and produces hydroxide, a strong alkali, right against the lining. A coin has no voltage, so it only blocks.

science.title: What the honey was doing
science.text: Hydroxide raises the pH at the battery’s surface high enough to dissolve tissue. Honey is mildly acidic and thick. It neutralizes some of the hydroxide and puts a layer between the battery and the lining.

sources.title: Litovitz et al. (Pediatrics 2010): emerging battery-ingestion hazard, clinical implications
Anfang et al. (Laryngoscope 2019): pH-neutralizing esophageal irrigations as a novel mitigation strategy for button battery injury

ent-069.title: A teacher _whose voice is gone by the afternoon._

start.alarm: Hoarse for several months

ent-069.handoff: A 38-year-old teacher has been hoarse for several months. By the end of each school day her voice gives out. She also leads a choir, and the season is about to start.

interview.prompt: Ask about her voice
interview.finding: It has been getting hoarse for several months. It tires quickly and gives out by the end of a teaching day. It is worse after heavy use and better after a weekend. Lately it has stayed about the same.

interview.prompt: Ask how she uses her voice
interview.finding: She teaches young children and often raises her voice over the noise. She has no microphone. She also leads a choir. She drinks very little water during the day.

interview.prompt: Ask about other symptoms and habits
interview.finding: No pain, no trouble swallowing, no coughing up blood, no weight loss and no lump in her neck. She has never smoked. She gets mild heartburn now and then.

exam.prompt: Listen to her voice
exam.finding: It is breathy and a little rough, and it does not carry. When she holds a note you can see her straining. Her breathing is quiet.

exam.prompt: Feel her neck
exam.finding: No lumps and no swollen glands. Her voice box is not tender.

exam.prompt: Look in her mouth and throat
exam.finding: No sores or patches. The back of her throat looks mildly irritated. Her palate moves normally.

1.label: Camera view of the voice box
1.content:
Both vocal folds have a small, pale, firm bump. The two bumps sit directly opposite each other, a third of the way back.
Both folds move fully and equally.
When she makes a sound, the bumps meet first and leave a gap in front of and behind them, like an hourglass.
No ulcers, no white patches and no other growths.

0.resident: She has been hoarse for months. Her story sounds like overuse, but a story is not enough for hoarseness that has lasted this long.
0.question: What is the next step?
options: Reassure her, and see her again in six months without examining the voice box
Look at her voice box with a thin camera passed through the nose
A CT scan of her neck first
Start cancer drugs, in case it is cancer of the voice box

terms.meaning: Looking at the voice box with a thin camera, done in clinic in a few minutes.
Two bands of tissue in the voice box that vibrate to make the voice. Also called vocal cords.

outcomes.story: You plan to see her in six months. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Hoarseness that lasts beyond a few weeks needs a look, however harmless it sounds. Occasionally it is something that should not wait.

outcomes.story: The specialist numbs her nose and passes a thin camera through it. Her vocal folds appear on the screen, and the findings go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. It takes a few minutes, and we see the folds directly while she speaks and sings.

outcomes.story: You request a CT scan. The specialist changes it.
outcomes.reply: A CT does not show the surface of the vocal folds or how they move. The camera does.

outcomes.story: You suggest cancer drugs. The specialist stares.
outcomes.reply: Nobody treats a cancer that has not been found. Look first.

3.resident: She has nodules on both vocal folds. They are like calluses, from the folds striking each other too hard and too often.
3.question: What is the first treatment?
options: An operation now to cut both nodules away
Voice therapy with a speech therapist, and better voice habits
Radiation to the voice box
Long-term antibiotics

terms.meaning: Sessions with a speech therapist to learn to produce the voice with less force and strain.
A small, firm bump.

outcomes.story: You suggest surgery now. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Cutting can scar a vocal fold, and a scar changes a voice for good. If her habits stay the same, the nodules would also grow back. Surgery is for the few that therapy does not fix.

outcomes.story: She is booked with a speech therapist for a course of sessions.
outcomes.reply: Right. Remove the cause, and most nodules shrink or disappear without any other treatment.

outcomes.story: You suggest radiation. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Radiation treats cancer. These are harmless calluses.

outcomes.story: You suggest antibiotics. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: There is no infection here. The cause is mechanical.

4.resident: She asks what she can do herself. She has a class of six-year-olds and a choir season ahead.
4.question: What do you tell her?
options: Stop speaking altogether, permanently
Drink water through the day, use a microphone in class, avoid shouting and take voice breaks. Treating her heartburn may help
She must have surgery before she can sing again
Nodules usually turn into cancer, so they need a biopsy whatever happens

terms.meaning: Everyday habits that protect the voice.
A small microphone and speaker, so she does not have to raise her voice.

outcomes.story: You tell her to stop speaking for good. The specialist smiles.
outcomes.reply: A teacher cannot do that, and she does not need to. She needs to use her voice differently.

outcomes.story: She writes the list down and says the school has a microphone nobody uses.
outcomes.reply: Right. Each of those lowers the force on her vocal folds, and they are what keeps the nodules from coming back.

outcomes.story: You tell her she needs surgery before singing. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Most singers with nodules recover with therapy alone.

outcomes.story: You tell her nodules turn into cancer. The specialist corrects you.
outcomes.reply: They do not. Saying so would frighten her for nothing.

differential.resident: The camera findings are in her chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A polyp on one vocal fold
Nodules on both vocal folds
Cancer of the voice box
Swelling of the vocal folds from smoking (Reinke edema)
differential.reveal: She has vocal fold nodules. They are matched bumps on both folds, at the point where the folds strike each other hardest. A polyp is usually single and on one side. Cancer looks irregular or ulcerated, usually in a smoker, and often stops a fold from moving. Smoking-related swelling puffs up the whole length of both folds.

terms.meaning: Not cancer.
On both sides.

ending.stable: Home with a voice therapy referral and a plan for the classroom
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

ent-069.plainDiagnosis: Small calluses on both vocal cords from overusing the voice (vocal fold nodules).

science.title: Why the nodules make her voice breathy
science.text: The voice starts as a vibration. The vocal folds close, air pressure from the lungs pushes them apart, and they spring shut again, hundreds of times a second. Her nodules meet first and hold the folds apart, so air leaks through the gaps without being turned into sound.
science.lessonTitle: Read a wave and a logarithmic level

science.title: How therapy changes a habit
science.text: Shouting over a class is a habit kept going by its result: it works in the moment. Voice therapy replaces it with a different way of producing sound and practices that until it becomes automatic.

sources.title: Stachler et al. (Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018): clinical practice guideline, hoarseness (dysphonia), update

vn-001.title: Slumped at the breakfast table, _unable to speak._

start.alarm: Right side weak · cannot speak · 80 minutes

vn-001.handoff: A 68-year-old man was found by his wife slumped at the breakfast table 80 minutes ago. His face droops on the right, his right side is weak and he cannot speak. He was normal 20 minutes before she found him.

interview.prompt: Ask his wife exactly when he was last normal
interview.finding: At 7:40 he poured his coffee and was fine. At 8:00 she found him slumped, with his face drooping, and he could not answer her. He had no headache, and he did not shake or pass out.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health and medicines
interview.finding: He has high blood pressure, high cholesterol and an irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation. He was prescribed a blood thinner for it and stopped three months ago because of the cost.

interview.prompt: Ask about recent bleeding, surgery or injury
interview.finding: None. He has never had bleeding in his brain, and he has no drug allergies.

exam.prompt: Talk to him
exam.finding: He is awake. He says almost nothing, and he does not follow simple requests.

exam.prompt: Check his face, arms and legs
exam.finding: The right side of his mouth droops, but his forehead still wrinkles on both sides. His right arm falls to the bed within five seconds, and his right leg sags.

exam.prompt: Check his eyes, and feel his pulse
exam.finding: Both eyes are turned to the left. He does not notice things on his right side. His pulse is irregular.

1.label: CT scan, blood tests and heart tracing
1.content:
CT scan of the head: no bleeding. One artery on the left side of the brain shows up brighter than it should, a sign of a clot inside it. The brain around it has barely changed yet.
Blood sugar: 112, normal.
Clotting tests and platelets: normal.
Heart tracing: atrial fibrillation, 88 beats a minute.

0.resident: This looks like a stroke, and we know when it started. His airway and breathing are fine. Every decision from here depends on one test.
0.question: What comes first?
options: A CT scan of his head, as fast as possible
Bring his blood pressure down hard with a drip
An MRI of his brain
Give the clot-dissolving drug now, since the picture is so typical
Start heparin, a blood thinner, as a drip
0.fix: Get a CT of his head

terms.meaning: Sudden loss of brain function because a blood vessel is blocked or has burst.
A fast X-ray scan. It shows fresh bleeding in the brain within minutes.

outcomes.story: He goes straight to the scanner. Blood is drawn on the way, and the results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. A blocked artery and a burst one look the same at the bedside, and their treatments are opposites. The CT tells them apart.

outcomes.story: You reach for a blood pressure drip. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: The brain beyond a blockage is kept alive by that pressure. Drop it hard and more brain dies. We only bring it down a little, and only when we are ready to treat.

outcomes.story: You request an MRI. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: MRI shows an early stroke better, but it takes much longer. CT answers the one question we need right now, in two minutes.

outcomes.story: You ask for the clot-dissolving drug. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: If this is a bleed, that drug would be a disaster. Nobody can tell a clot from a bleed without a scan.

outcomes.story: You ask for heparin. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Heparin does not dissolve a clot that is already there, and in a fresh stroke it causes bleeding.

3.resident: It is 95 minutes since he was last normal. There is no bleeding, his clotting tests are normal, and his pressure is 182 over 98.
3.question: What now?
options: Hold the clot-dissolving drug, because he has atrial fibrillation
Give aspirin and admit him for observation
Bring his pressure just under 185 over 110, then give the clot-dissolving drug
Go straight to removing the clot with a catheter, without the drug
Hold the clot-dissolving drug, because he was once prescribed a blood thinner
3.fix: Treat his pressure, then give the drug

terms.meaning: Dissolving a clot with a drug such as alteplase. In stroke it must start within four and a half hours.
Pulling a clot out of a large artery with a thin tube passed up from the groin or wrist.

outcomes.story: The drug is held, and an hour goes by. His right leg, which could move a little, now lies still.
outcomes.reply: Atrial fibrillation is where his clot came from. It is no reason to hold the drug. He is still inside the time window, so give it now.

outcomes.story: You write for aspirin. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Aspirin does not dissolve a clot. He qualifies for the drug that does, and aspirin is held for a day after it.

outcomes.story: A small dose of labetalol brings his pressure to 172 over 94. The clot-dissolving drug is then run into his vein over an hour. The team also scans his arteries to see whether the clot can be pulled out.
outcomes.reply: Right. He is inside the window, with no bleeding and nothing that rules him out. The sooner it goes in, the more brain it saves.

outcomes.story: You say to skip the drug and go for the catheter. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The catheter team is being called, and he may well need them. The drug goes in first. It starts working now, and it does not hold them up.

outcomes.story: You hold the drug because of his old prescription. The resident checks the chart.
outcomes.reply: He stopped that blood thinner three months ago, and his clotting tests are normal. It is not a barrier.

4.resident: The clot-dissolving drug is running. For the next day, the main danger is bleeding into the damaged brain.
4.question: Where does he go, and how is he watched?
options: Home after four hours, if he is improving
A stroke unit or intensive care, with checks every 15 minutes at first and his pressure kept under 180 over 105 for a day
Start a full-dose blood thinner for his heart rhythm as soon as the drug finishes
Repeat the CT in one hour to confirm the artery has opened, before any monitoring
A general ward, with routine checks every eight hours
4.fix: Admit him to the stroke unit

terms.meaning: A ward where nurses trained in stroke check strength, speech and blood pressure very often.
A quick repeat exam of alertness, speech and strength, done to catch any change early.

outcomes.story: You plan to send him home in four hours. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The risk of bleeding lasts a full day after this drug. Nobody goes home in that time.

outcomes.story: He is moved to the stroke unit. A nurse checks his strength, speech and blood pressure every 15 minutes, and a repeat scan is booked for tomorrow.
outcomes.reply: Right. If he bleeds, the first sign is a change in his exam or a jump in his pressure. Someone has to be watching.
outcomes.alarm: In the stroke unit · checks every 15 minutes

outcomes.story: Heparin is started as the clot-dissolving drug finishes. Six hours later he has a severe headache and is hard to wake. A CT shows bleeding into the stroke.
outcomes.reply: Two drugs that stop clotting, on top of freshly damaged brain. His heart rhythm does need a blood thinner, but only after tomorrow’s scan shows no bleeding, and often days later.
outcomes.alarm: Hard to wake · bleeding into the stroke

outcomes.story: You ask for another CT in an hour. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A plain CT cannot show whether the artery has opened. He is rescanned at 24 hours, or at once if his exam changes.

outcomes.story: He goes to a general ward. At the next round of checks, eight hours later, his pressure is 212 over 116 and he has a new headache. A CT shows a small bleed in the stroke.
outcomes.reply: His pressure climbed for hours with nobody looking. After this drug, pressure must stay under 180 over 105, and that takes checks every few minutes.

differential.resident: The CT and his exam are in the chart. He cannot speak or understand, his right side is weak and his eyes are turned to the left.
differential.question: What is this, and where?
options: A blocked artery to the right side of the brain
A blocked artery to the left side of the brain, the left middle cerebral artery
A blocked artery to the back of the brain on the left
A tiny stroke deep in the left side of the brain
Bleeding deep in the left side of the brain
differential.reveal: A clot is blocking his left middle cerebral artery. Each side of the brain moves the opposite side of the body, so right-sided weakness points to the left. In most people language also sits on the left, which is why he can neither speak nor understand. That artery supplies both areas. A tiny deep stroke causes weakness without loss of language, and the CT showed no bleeding.

terms.meaning: A stroke caused by a blocked artery. Most strokes are of this kind.
Loss of the ability to produce or understand language.

ending.stable: In the stroke unit after clot-dissolving treatment, checked every 15 minutes
ending.unstable: In the stroke unit after clot-dissolving treatment, checked every 15 minutes
ending.worse: In the stroke unit after clot-dissolving treatment and a setback, checked every 15 minutes
ending.critical: In intensive care with bleeding into the stroke

vn-001.plainDiagnosis: A stroke from a clot blocking the main artery to the left side of the brain (left middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke).

science.title: Why minutes matter
science.text: Neurons store almost no fuel. They need a constant supply of oxygen to make ATP, and most of that ATP runs the pumps that keep each cell’s electrical charge. When blood stops, the pumps fail within minutes, and the cells swell and die.

science.title: How a clot is dissolved
science.text: Alteplase is an enzyme. It converts plasminogen, a protein already in the blood, into plasmin. Plasmin cuts the strands of fibrin that hold a clot together. It cannot tell a harmful clot from a useful one, which is why bleeding is the risk.

sources.title: Powers et al. (Stroke 2019): guidelines for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke, 2019 update
NINDS rt-PA Stroke Study Group (N Engl J Med 1995): tissue plasminogen activator for acute ischemic stroke

vn-072.title: Confused and sweating, _and her left arm will not lift._

start.alarm: Confused · sweating · left arm weak

vn-072.handoff: A 63-year-old woman with diabetes became confused and sweaty while cooking dinner 30 minutes ago, and she could not use her left arm. Her husband says she was completely normal before that.

interview.prompt: Ask her husband how it started
interview.finding: She was cooking dinner and was fine. Then, within minutes, she was confused and sweating, and her left arm would not work. She had no headache, did not shake and did not fall.

interview.prompt: Ask about her diabetes and what she has eaten
interview.finding: She has had diabetes for 15 years. She takes a long-acting insulin at night and a fast one with meals. She has started exercising and eating less. Today he thinks she took her mealtime insulin and then skipped lunch.

interview.prompt: Ask about her other health
interview.finding: She has high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and she takes tablets for both. She is not on a blood thinner and has had no recent surgery or bleeding. Her brother had a stroke at 60.

exam.prompt: Talk to her, and touch her skin
exam.finding: She is drowsy and knows her name but nothing else. Her skin is cool and wet with sweat, and her hands are trembling.

exam.prompt: Check her face, arms, legs and speech
exam.finding: The left side of her face droops. Her left arm drifts down when she holds both arms up, and her left leg is a little weak. Her speech is slightly slurred.

exam.prompt: Check her eyes, tongue and pulse
exam.finding: Her pupils are equal and react to light. She has not bitten her tongue. Her pulse is fast and regular.

1.label: Bedside sugar, CT scan and heart tracing
1.content:
Finger-prick blood sugar: 38, dangerously low. Normal is above 70.
Blood sugar from a vein: 41, confirming it.
CT scan of the head, done at the same time: no bleeding and no stroke seen.
Heart tracing: fast, regular rhythm, 108 a minute.

0.resident: Sudden weakness on one side. The stroke team is on the way and the scanner is free. One bedside test has to happen before any of it.
0.question: Which one?
options: A finger-prick blood sugar
A CT scan of her head
A heart tracing
A blood test for heart damage
An ultrasound of the arteries in her neck

terms.meaning: A drop of blood on a test strip. It gives a blood sugar reading in seconds.
Another condition that produces the same sudden weakness or speech trouble as a stroke.

outcomes.story: A nurse pricks her finger while the scanner is readied. She is scanned moments later, and everything goes in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. It takes ten seconds, and it is required before any stroke treatment. A low sugar can copy a stroke exactly.

outcomes.story: You send her to the scanner first. The resident pricks her finger on the way.
outcomes.reply: She needs the CT too. The sugar comes first because it takes ten seconds and can change everything.

outcomes.story: You ask for a heart tracing first. The resident pricks her finger while it is set up.
outcomes.reply: The tracing is worth having, but it will not explain a weak arm. The sugar might.

outcomes.story: You ask for a heart blood test. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That result takes an hour and answers a different question.

outcomes.story: You ask for a neck ultrasound. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That belongs later in a stroke workup, if this turns out to be a stroke.

2.resident: Her sugar is 38, and her head CT is clear. She is drowsy and still weak on the left.
2.question: What is the treatment, right now?
options: The clot-dissolving drug for stroke
Sugar into her vein, then recheck her sugar and her strength
An insulin drip to steady her sugar
An MRI of her brain before any treatment
Sugar tablets by mouth only

terms.meaning: Glucose, the sugar the body runs on, in a strong solution for giving into a vein.
A blood sugar low enough to cause symptoms.

outcomes.story: You ask for the clot-dissolving drug. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: That drug can cause bleeding in the brain. A sugar of 38 explains everything we see. Fix that first and look again.

outcomes.story: A syringe of strong sugar solution is pushed into her vein. Within ten minutes she is awake and asking what happened. The sweating stops, and her left arm lifts as well as her right.
outcomes.reply: That was fast. A brain short of sugar switches off, and it switches back on when the sugar returns.

outcomes.story: You ask for an insulin drip. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Insulin lowers blood sugar. Hers is already dangerously low.

outcomes.story: You ask for an MRI first. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Her brain is running out of fuel while we talk. The sugar takes one minute to give. Scans can wait for that.

outcomes.story: You hand her sugar tablets. The resident takes them back.
outcomes.reply: She is too drowsy to swallow safely and could choke. When someone cannot swallow safely, the sugar goes into a vein.

4.resident: She is back to normal and wants to go home and finish making dinner. Remember which insulins she takes.
4.question: What is the plan?
options: Send her home now, since she has no symptoms
Watch her for several hours, give her a meal, and review her insulin doses before she leaves
Admit her to intensive care on an insulin drip
Start aspirin and clopidogrel to prevent a stroke
Start a blood thinner while she is tested for a source of clots
4.fix: Observe her, feed her and review her insulin

terms.meaning: An insulin that keeps working for about a day after one injection.

outcomes.story: She goes home. Three hours later her husband brings her back. She is confused and sweating again, and her sugar is 44.
outcomes.reply: The sugar we gave lasts less than an hour, and her insulin is still working. She needed a meal and a few hours of watching.

outcomes.story: She eats a sandwich and stays for the evening, with her sugar checked every hour. The diabetes nurse goes through her insulin doses with her.
outcomes.reply: Right. Her doses were set for the way she used to eat. With less food and more exercise they need to come down.

outcomes.story: You ask for an insulin drip. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Too much insulin is what brought her here.

outcomes.story: You write for aspirin and clopidogrel. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those prevent strokes. She has not had one.

outcomes.story: You ask for a blood thinner. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nothing here points to a clot. That would add a bleeding risk and no benefit.

differential.resident: Ten minutes after the sugar, her blood sugar is 122. Her confusion and weakness are gone, and her exam is normal.
differential.question: What was this?
options: A transient ischemic attack, a brief blockage that cleared by itself
A small stroke deep in the brain
A low blood sugar copying a stroke
Weakness after a seizure that nobody saw
A migraine with weakness
differential.reveal: A low blood sugar was copying a stroke. Her sugar was 38, and everything cleared within minutes of correcting it. A brief blockage clears on its own schedule and would not follow the sugar. A true stroke would not reverse with sugar. She had no jerking or bitten tongue to suggest a seizure, and no headache to suggest migraine. The sweating, trembling and fast pulse were the body’s alarm at a low sugar.

terms.meaning: A condition that looks like another one.
A brief blockage of blood flow to part of the brain that clears without lasting damage.

ending.better: Under observation for the evening, fully recovered, with a meal and a new insulin plan
ending.stable: Under observation for the evening, fully recovered, with a meal and a new insulin plan
ending.worse: Admitted overnight after her blood sugar fell a second time at home

vn-072.plainDiagnosis: A low blood sugar that looked like a stroke (hypoglycemia, a stroke mimic).

science.title: Why insulin without lunch dropped her sugar
science.text: Insulin tells muscle and fat to take glucose out of the blood and tells the liver to stop releasing it. A mealtime dose is sized to match the meal. With no meal there was nothing to balance it, and exercise had already made her muscles take up more.

science.title: Where the sweating and trembling came from
science.text: When blood sugar falls, the body answers with adrenaline and other hormones that push it back up. Adrenaline also causes sweating, trembling and a fast pulse. Those are the early warnings of a low sugar, and at a stroke bedside they are a clue.

sources.title: Powers et al. (Stroke 2019): guidelines for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke, 2019 update
Foster and Hart (Stroke 1987): hypoglycemic hemiplegia, two cases and a clinical review

vn-018.title: Four times in one day, _his right arm went dead._

start.alarm: Four spells of arm weakness in 24 hours · normal now

vn-018.handoff: A 64-year-old man has had four spells in 24 hours. Each time his right arm went weak and he could not get his words out, and each time it cleared within 15 minutes. He feels fine now and asks whether he can go home.

interview.prompt: Ask about the spells
interview.finding: Four in the last 24 hours, all the same. His right arm goes weak without warning and he cannot find words. Each lasts 5 to 15 minutes and clears completely. They are coming closer together, and the last one was two hours ago.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health and habits
interview.finding: He has high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and he often skips his tablets. He has smoked for 35 years and still does. He takes no aspirin. His father had a stroke at 60.

interview.prompt: Ask about anything else
interview.finding: He has never had a stroke or been told his heartbeat is irregular. He has not been ill or injured. Between spells he feels normal. He has not seen a doctor in two years.

exam.prompt: Examine his speech, strength and walking
exam.finding: All normal. His speech is fluent, both arms are strong and steady, and he walks normally.

exam.prompt: Listen over the arteries in his neck
exam.finding: On the left there is a whooshing sound with each heartbeat. The right is quiet.

exam.prompt: Listen to his heart
exam.finding: The rhythm is regular, with no extra sounds.

1.label: Scans, blood tests and heart tracing
1.content:
CT scan of the head: no bleeding and no large stroke.
MRI of the brain: one tiny new stroke at the surface of the left side.
Scan of the neck arteries: the left carotid artery is 85% narrowed by a rough, ulcerated plaque.
Blood sugar: 110, normal. LDL cholesterol: 158, high.
Heart tracing: normal, regular rhythm.
Stroke risk score (ABCD2): 6 out of 7, high.

0.resident: He is completely normal now, and he wants to leave. Four identical spells in a day, each one sooner than the last.
0.question: What is this pattern, and what do we do?
options: A harmless inner-ear problem. He can go home and see his own doctor
Warning strokes that are speeding up. Admit him now and scan his brain and neck arteries today
A reaction to stress. Reassure him and send him home
Seizures. Start a seizure medicine and send him home

terms.meaning: A brief blockage of blood flow to part of the brain. The symptoms clear, but a stroke often follows.
Coming more and more often.

outcomes.story: He goes home. That night an ambulance brings him back. His right arm went weak again and he could not speak, and this time it lasted 40 minutes.
outcomes.reply: An inner-ear problem causes spinning. It does not take away an arm and speech. Those spells were warnings, and the stroke they warn of usually comes within days.

outcomes.story: He is admitted and put on a monitor. He has a CT, an MRI and a scan of the arteries in his neck within the hour. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. A TIA is an emergency even when the patient looks perfect. Several in one day, speeding up, is the most urgent kind.

outcomes.story: You suggest it is stress. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Every spell hit the same arm and the same function. A single spot in the brain is losing its blood supply again and again.

outcomes.story: You suggest seizures. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Seizures usually add something, such as jerking or tingling. These spells only take function away. In a 64-year-old smoker with high blood pressure, that is a blood vessel until proven otherwise.

3.resident: The surgeons have been called. Until they operate, we need to keep that plaque from throwing another clot.
3.question: What do we start?
options: Bring his blood pressure down to normal fast, and start a heparin drip
Aspirin with a second antiplatelet drug and a high-dose statin, and leave his blood pressure alone for now
No anti-clotting drugs at all until after surgery
Warfarin
3.fix: Start antiplatelet drugs and a statin

terms.meaning: A drug such as aspirin or clopidogrel that stops platelets from sticking together to start a clot.
A drug that lowers cholesterol and steadies fatty plaques in artery walls.

outcomes.story: A drip brings his pressure down to 118 over 70. Twenty minutes later his right arm goes weak and his words come out jumbled.
outcomes.reply: Blood has to squeeze through a gap 85% closed. Take away the pressure behind it, and the brain beyond goes short. Stop the drip. Heparin is not the standard treatment here either.
outcomes.alarm: Right arm weak again after his pressure was lowered

outcomes.story: He takes aspirin, clopidogrel and a high-dose statin. His blood pressure is watched and left where it is.
outcomes.reply: Right. Clots on a plaque begin with platelets, so we block platelets. The pressure can come down gradually once the artery is fixed.

outcomes.story: You hold all anti-clotting drugs until surgery. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The days before surgery are when a stroke is most likely. Surgeons operate on patients who are taking aspirin all the time.

outcomes.story: You suggest warfarin. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Warfarin is for clots that form in the heart. His form on a plaque, where antiplatelet drugs work better.

4.resident: His left carotid artery is 85% narrowed, and it is causing symptoms. Tablets will not be enough.
4.question: What is the lasting fix, and when?
options: An operation or stent to open the artery, booked for three months from now
An operation or stent to open the artery soon, within about two weeks
Medicines for life, with no procedure
The clot-dissolving drug, now

terms.meaning: An operation that opens the artery in the neck and peels out the plaque.
A small mesh tube placed inside an artery to hold it open.

outcomes.story: You suggest booking it for three months. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His highest risk of a stroke is in the next two weeks. In three months he would have been through the danger with no protection.

outcomes.story: The vascular surgeon sees him that afternoon and puts him on the operating list for this week.
outcomes.reply: Right. Surgery helps most when it is done early, inside the two weeks when a stroke is most likely.

outcomes.story: You suggest medicines alone. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: For a narrowing this tight that is already causing symptoms, removing the plaque prevents many more strokes than tablets do.

outcomes.story: You suggest the clot-dissolving drug. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is for a stroke in progress. Right now he has no symptoms to treat, and the drug carries a real risk of bleeding.

differential.resident: His scans are in the chart. The spells affect his right arm and his speech.
differential.question: What is causing them?
options: Clots thrown from the heart by an irregular rhythm
Bits of clot breaking off the narrowed left carotid artery and lodging in the brain
Disease of the tiny arteries deep in the brain
Low blood flow to the whole brain from dehydration
differential.reveal: Clot is breaking off the rough plaque in his left carotid artery and traveling up into the left side of his brain, the side that controls the right arm and, in most people, speech. Each piece blocks a small branch and then breaks up, so each spell clears. His heart rhythm is normal, which makes the heart an unlikely source. Disease of the tiny deep arteries does not cause trouble with speech like this, and low flow to the whole brain would not pick out one arm.

terms.meaning: One of the two large arteries in the neck that carry blood to the brain.
A piece of clot that travels in the blood and lodges farther along.

ending.stable: Admitted to the stroke unit, with surgery on his neck artery booked for this week
ending.worse: Admitted to the stroke unit after another spell, with surgery on his neck artery booked for this week
ending.critical: In the stroke unit with a completed stroke

vn-018.plainDiagnosis: Repeated warning strokes from a badly narrowed artery in the neck (crescendo TIAs from carotid stenosis).

science.title: What the whooshing sound was
science.text: Blood normally moves through an artery in smooth layers and makes no sound. Forced through a narrow gap, it speeds up and breaks into turbulence. Turbulent flow shakes the artery wall, and a stethoscope picks that up.

science.title: Why his pressure was left alone
science.text: Flow through a vessel depends on the pressure pushing it and on the resistance in the way. A tight narrowing is a large resistance. With the resistance fixed, the only thing keeping flow up is pressure, so lowering it quickly lowers flow to the brain.

sources.title: Kleindorfer et al. (Stroke 2021): guideline for the prevention of stroke in patients with stroke and transient ischemic attack
Rothwell et al. (Lancet 2004): endarterectomy for symptomatic carotid stenosis in relation to clinical subgroups and timing of surgery
Johnston et al. (N Engl J Med 2018): clopidogrel and aspirin in acute ischemic stroke and high-risk TIA

no-001.title: Morning headaches for six weeks, _and now a clumsy right hand._

start.alarm: Headaches for six weeks · weak right hand

no-001.handoff: A 62-year-old accountant has had headaches for six weeks. They are worst in the early morning. For two weeks he has been dropping things with his right hand, and this morning he could not find his words for a few minutes.

interview.prompt: Ask about the headaches
interview.finding: A dull ache all over his head for six weeks. It is worst in the early morning and sometimes wakes him. Twice he has vomited suddenly without feeling sick first. He has had no fever and no injury.

interview.prompt: Ask about his hand and his speech
interview.finding: For two weeks he has dropped things with his right hand, and his handwriting has become unreadable. This morning he could not find words for a few minutes. He has felt foggy for several days.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health
interview.finding: He has high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and he takes a tablet for each. He has smoked for 30 years. He has not lost weight, and he takes no blood thinner. Nobody in his family has had cancer.

exam.prompt: Talk to him, and look into his eyes
exam.finding: He is awake and knows where he is, but his attention drifts. His pupils are equal. The backs of his eyes look normal.

exam.prompt: Test the strength of his arms and legs
exam.finding: His right arm is slightly weak. When he holds both arms out, the right one slowly turns and sinks. His right grip is weak. His left arm and both legs are strong.

exam.prompt: Ask him to write, touch his nose and walk
exam.finding: His writing with the right hand is shaky and hard to read, and his right finger wavers on the way to his nose. He walks steadily.

1.label: CT and MRI of the brain
1.content:
CT scan: a dark, poorly defined area in the left frontal lobe with swelling around it. No bleeding.
MRI with contrast dye: a 4.2 cm mass in the left frontal lobe. Its wall is thick and uneven and lights up with the dye. Its center is dead tissue.
The mass crosses the bridge of fibers that joins the two halves of the brain and spreads into the right side.
A wide zone of swelling surrounds it.
The midline of the brain is pushed 8 mm to the right.

0.resident: Headaches that are worst in the morning, vomiting and a hand that has been getting weaker for two weeks. Something is taking up space inside his skull.
0.question: Which test comes first?
options: A CT scan of his head now, then an MRI with contrast dye
A spinal tap, to measure the pressure and test the fluid
An ultrasound of the arteries in his neck
A brain-wave recording, to look for seizures

terms.meaning: A detailed scan. A dye given into a vein makes abnormal tissue light up.
A needle in the lower back that takes a sample of the fluid around the brain and spine.

outcomes.story: He has a CT within minutes and an MRI within the hour. The pictures go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. CT quickly rules out bleeding, and MRI with dye shows what a mass is made of and how far it reaches.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: If a mass has raised the pressure in his skull, draining fluid from below can pull the brain downward. A scan always comes before a spinal tap.

outcomes.story: You ask for a neck ultrasound. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That looks for narrowed arteries, which cause sudden strokes. His symptoms have crept up over six weeks.

outcomes.story: You ask for a brain-wave recording. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It can show a seizure. It cannot show what is causing his headaches and his weakness. He needs a picture.

3.resident: The neurosurgeon is on the way. The swelling around the mass is causing most of his symptoms, and we can treat that tonight.
3.question: Which medicine do we start?
options: Mannitol into a vein, and a breathing tube, to lower the pressure
Broad antibiotics
Dexamethasone, a steroid, to shrink the swelling around the mass
Heparin, a blood thinner, in case this is a blocked vein

terms.meaning: A strong steroid. It makes leaky tumor vessels less leaky, so the swelling around a tumor goes down.
