Swelling caused by extra fluid in a tissue.

outcomes.story: You ask for mannitol and a breathing tube. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those are for a patient who is going downhill in front of us. He is awake, talking and steady.

outcomes.story: You ask for antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: An abscess can look a little like this, but it has a thin, smooth wall and usually comes with a fever. Nothing here points to infection.

outcomes.story: He is given dexamethasone into a vein and admitted under the neurosurgeons.
outcomes.reply: Right. It does nothing to the tumor itself, but it shrinks the swelling within hours, and most patients feel much better.

outcomes.story: Heparin is started. Four hours later his headache becomes violent and he is hard to wake. A CT shows fresh bleeding inside the mass.
outcomes.reply: A tumor like this is full of fragile new blood vessels, and a blood thinner makes them bleed. Stop the heparin. The swelling is what needs treating.
outcomes.alarm: Hard to wake · bleeding into the mass

4.resident: The scan strongly suggests one diagnosis. Suggesting is not enough to plan months of treatment.
4.question: What is the next step?
options: Radiation to the whole brain, without a tissue sample
An operation to remove as much as is safe, or a biopsy, with the tissue tested under the microscope and for its genes
Start the chemotherapy drug temozolomide on the strength of the scan
A whole-body PET scan to look for a cancer elsewhere, before anything is done

terms.meaning: Taking a small sample of tissue so that a pathologist can name it.
Removing a tumor by surgery.

outcomes.story: You suggest radiation now. The neurosurgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: We do not irradiate a brain without knowing what we are treating. The tissue comes first.

outcomes.story: The neurosurgeon explains the operation to his wife and to him and puts him on the operating list. The tissue will go to the pathology laboratory.
outcomes.reply: Right. Surgery takes pressure off his brain and provides the tissue. The tumor’s genes then decide which treatments follow.

outcomes.story: You suggest starting chemotherapy. The neurosurgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That drug is used after surgery, together with radiation, and how well it works depends on the tumor’s genes. We do not have those yet.

outcomes.story: You ask for a whole-body scan first. The neurosurgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A single mass spreading across the midline like this is almost always a tumor that started in the brain. He needs the operation either way.

differential.resident: The scans are in his chart. The mass has a thick, uneven wall and a dead center, and it has spread across the midline.
differential.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A brain abscess
Glioblastoma, a fast-growing tumor that starts in the brain
A meningioma, a slow-growing tumor of the brain’s covering
A stroke from a blocked artery, a few weeks old
differential.reveal: This is most likely a glioblastoma. It grows fast enough to outrun its blood supply, which leaves a dead center inside a thick, ragged wall. It also spreads along the brain’s own fiber tracts, which is how it crosses to the other side. An abscess has a thin, smooth wall and usually a fever. A meningioma grows from the covering and pushes on the brain from outside. A stroke follows the territory of one artery and does not cross the midline.

terms.meaning: The most common fast-growing cancer that starts in the brain in adults.
The thick bridge of nerve fibers that joins the two halves of the brain.

ending.stable: Admitted under the neurosurgeons on a steroid, on the list for an operation this week
ending.worse: Admitted under the neurosurgeons, more drowsy than when he arrived
ending.critical: In intensive care after bleeding into the tumor, on the list for an operation

no-001.plainDiagnosis: A fast-growing brain tumor, most likely a glioblastoma. Tissue from surgery will confirm it.

science.title: Why the headaches were worst in the morning
science.text: The skull is a closed box filled with brain, blood and fluid. Anything added raises the pressure inside. Lying flat all night lets less blood drain from the head, so the pressure is highest on waking and falls once he is upright.

science.title: Why the center of the mass was dead
science.text: Healthy cells stop at checkpoints before they divide. Cancer cells have lost them and divide without pause. A mass of them can grow faster than new blood vessels can reach it, and the cells in the middle die for lack of oxygen.

science.title: Why the tissue is tested for its genes
science.text: Some glioblastomas have chemically switched off a gene called MGMT, which repairs the kind of DNA damage chemotherapy causes. With that repair gene silent, the drug works better. The gene is still there. It is just not being read.
science.lessonTitle: Follow a gene into a protein

sources.title: Stupp et al. (N Engl J Med 2005): radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma
Louis et al. (Neuro Oncol 2021): the 2021 WHO classification of tumors of the central nervous system, a summary

no-042.title: Back pain for two weeks, _and now his legs are giving way._

start.alarm: Legs weak · cannot pass urine

no-042.handoff: A 67-year-old man with prostate cancer has had severe pain in the middle of his back for two weeks. For two days his legs have felt weak and heavy. He has not been able to pass urine for 12 hours.

interview.prompt: Ask about the back pain
interview.finding: Constant pain in the middle of his back for two weeks, getting worse. It is worst at night and when he lies flat, and painkillers do not help. He has had no fall or injury.

interview.prompt: Ask about his legs and his bladder
interview.finding: Both legs have been weak and heavy for two days. He is numb from the navel down. He has not passed urine for 12 hours, and his belly feels full. He was walking normally until this week.

interview.prompt: Ask about his cancer
interview.finding: Prostate cancer was found three years ago and treated with radiation. His blood marker for it has been rising lately. He has hormone injections for it. He has lost 5 kg in two months without trying.

exam.prompt: Test his legs
exam.finding: Both legs are weak. He can lift them off the bed but not against your hand. They feel stiff, his knee reflexes are jumpy, and both big toes go up when you stroke the soles.

exam.prompt: Test feeling with a pin, working up from his feet
exam.finding: He cannot feel the pin properly anywhere below the navel. Above it, feeling is normal.

exam.prompt: Press along his spine, and feel his lower belly
exam.finding: One spot in the lower part of the mid-back is very tender. His bladder can be felt as a firm swelling up to the navel.

1.label: Blood tests and MRI of the whole spine
1.content:
Hemoglobin: 10.9, low.
Calcium: 11.4, high.
Alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme released by bone: 280, high.
PSA, the blood marker for prostate cancer: 96, very high.
MRI: the T9 and T10 bones, in the middle of the back, no longer show normal marrow. At that level a mass lies in the spinal canal, outside the cord’s covering, and it is squeezing the spinal cord.

0.resident: A man with cancer, back pain that is worse lying down, weak legs and a bladder that will not empty. I do not need a scan to be worried about his spinal cord.
0.question: What do we do right now?
options: Plain X-rays of his mid-back
Give dexamethasone, a steroid, now and get an emergency MRI of his whole spine
Book an MRI as an outpatient within a week
Painkillers and physiotherapy
0.fix: Give the steroid and get the MRI

terms.meaning: The bundle of nerves running down inside the backbone. It carries every signal between the brain and the body.
A strong steroid. It reduces swelling around a tumor within hours.

outcomes.story: You request X-rays. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: X-rays show bone. They do not show the cord or what is pressing on it, and a normal one would not reassure me.

outcomes.story: Dexamethasone goes into his vein within minutes. A catheter drains 700 mL from his bladder. He has an MRI of his whole spine within the hour, and the results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The steroid buys the cord some time, so it goes in before the scan. We image the whole spine because cancer often sits at more than one level.

outcomes.story: He is sent home with an appointment. The next morning his wife calls an ambulance. He cannot lift either leg off the bed.
outcomes.reply: A cord that is being squeezed loses function by the hour, and what is lost may not come back. This could not wait a week. He needs the steroid and the scan now.

outcomes.story: You suggest painkillers and physiotherapy. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A strained back does not cause numbness to the navel or stop the bladder. Those come from the spinal cord.

3.resident: The steroid is in. He is otherwise fit, and the MRI shows the cord compressed at one level only.
3.question: What is the best treatment from here?
options: Radiation alone
Chemotherapy alone
An operation to take the pressure off the cord, followed by radiation
Cement injected into the bone, and nothing else

terms.meaning: Surgery that removes whatever is pressing on the cord or a nerve.
Focused high-energy beams that kill tumor cells over days to weeks.

outcomes.story: You suggest radiation alone. The oncologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is the choice when someone is too unwell for surgery or has many levels involved. In a fit patient with one level, surgery first keeps more people walking.

outcomes.story: You suggest chemotherapy. The oncologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Far too slow. It works over weeks, and his cord is failing over hours.

outcomes.story: The spine surgeon takes him to the operating room that evening, removes the tumor pressing on the cord and fixes the spine with rods. Radiation is planned for when the wound has healed.
outcomes.reply: Right. Surgery frees the cord at once, and radiation then treats whatever tumor is left.
outcomes.alarm: In surgery · pressure taken off the cord

outcomes.story: You suggest cement alone. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Cement strengthens a painful, crumbling bone. It does nothing about a mass inside the canal.

4.resident: His wife asks whether he will walk again.
4.question: What best predicts that?
options: How high his PSA was before treatment
How well his legs were working at the moment treatment started
His high calcium
His age

terms.meaning: The likely course and outcome of an illness.

outcomes.story: You say the PSA. The oncologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The PSA tells us how much cancer there is. It does not tell us what the cord will do.

outcomes.story: You explain it to her, and she nods.
outcomes.reply: Right. People who can still walk when treatment begins usually keep walking. People who have already lost it often do not get it back. That is why hours matter.

outcomes.story: You say the calcium. The oncologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It needs treating, and it tells us the cancer is in his bones. It does not predict walking.

outcomes.story: You say his age. The oncologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Age matters far less than how much function he still has.

differential.resident: His blood tests and MRI are in the chart.
differential.question: What is pressing on his spinal cord, and where did it come from?
options: A deposit of cancer growing inside the spinal cord itself
Cancer cells spread in a thin layer over the surface of the cord
Prostate cancer that has spread to the backbone and grown out of the bone to press on the cord
A separate, slow-growing tumor of the cord’s covering
differential.reveal: His prostate cancer has spread to the bones of his spine. In two of them it has replaced the marrow, grown backward out of the bone and into the canal, and it is now pressing on the cord from outside. This is the usual way cancer injures the spinal cord. The mass is outside the cord and its covering, which rules out a deposit inside the cord. A thin coating of cells would not form a mass, and the diseased bone and very high PSA point to his known cancer.

terms.meaning: A cancer deposit that has spread from where the cancer started.
In the space between the bone of the spine and the tough covering of the cord.

ending.stable: In the recovery room after surgery to free his spinal cord, with radiation planned
ending.unstable: In the recovery room after surgery to free his spinal cord, with radiation planned
ending.worse: In the recovery room after surgery to free his spinal cord. He could not move his legs when it began

no-042.plainDiagnosis: Prostate cancer that has spread to the spine and is pressing on the spinal cord (metastatic spinal cord compression).

science.title: How the exam found the level before the scan
science.text: Each segment of the spinal cord supplies its own band of skin. The band at the navel belongs to the tenth segment in the chest, T10. Signals from below a blockage cannot get past it, so numbness that starts at the navel points to T10.

science.title: What his hormone injections do
science.text: Prostate cancer grows in response to testosterone. The testes make testosterone on a signal from the pituitary, which answers pulses of a hormone from the brain. His injection supplies that hormone constantly. A constant signal makes the pituitary stop responding, and testosterone falls.

sources.title: Patchell et al. (Lancet 2005): direct decompressive surgical resection in the treatment of spinal cord compression caused by metastatic cancer, a randomised trial
Cole and Patchell (Lancet Neurol 2008): metastatic epidural spinal cord compression

no-032.title: The worst headache of his life, _and now he sees double._

start.alarm: Worst headache of his life · double vision · blood pressure 86 over 54

no-032.handoff: A 48-year-old construction worker had a sudden, severe headache four hours ago. He has vomited twice, he sees double and he nearly fainted when he stood up. His blood pressure is 86 over 54.

interview.prompt: Ask about the headache
interview.finding: It came on four hours ago, behind his eyes and across his forehead, and reached full strength within seconds. It is the worst he has ever had. He has vomited twice, and soon afterward he began to see double. He did not hit his head, and his neck is not stiff.

interview.prompt: Ask how he has been over the past year
interview.finding: He has been tired and has lost interest in sex. He feels the cold more, and he shaves less often than he used to. When driving he has noticed he sees less at the sides.

interview.prompt: Ask about dizziness, medicines and habits
interview.finding: He nearly fainted when he stood up today. He has high blood pressure but takes nothing for it, and he is not on a blood thinner. He drinks two or three beers a night.

exam.prompt: Look at his eyes, and ask him to follow your finger
exam.finding: His right eyelid droops. The right eye points down and out, and its pupil is large and slow to react. His left eye moves normally.

exam.prompt: Test his side vision
exam.finding: He cannot see your fingers at the outer edge on either side. Toward the nose, he sees them.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin, and check his neck, arms and legs
exam.finding: He looks ill. His skin is cool and sweaty, and his mouth is dry. His pulse is fast. His neck bends freely, and his arms and legs are strong.

1.label: Blood tests and scans
1.content:
Sodium: 129, low.
Blood sugar: 58, low.
Cortisol, the stress hormone: 2, far too low for someone this ill.
Thyroid hormone: 0.5, low. The pituitary signal that should be driving it up has not risen.
Prolactin, another pituitary hormone: 4, low.
CT scan of the head: a bright mass in and above the bony pocket that holds the pituitary gland.
MRI: a large growth on the pituitary gland with fresh bleeding inside it. It is pushing up on the point where the optic nerves cross.

0.resident: A sudden headache, an eye that will not move and a blood pressure of 86 over 54, in a man who has been running down for a year. Fluids are going in. One drug cannot wait for any test.
0.question: Which one?
options: Hydrocortisone into a vein
Labetalol into a vein, to control his blood pressure
A large dose of thyroid hormone
No drug yet. Do a spinal tap to look for bleeding around the brain

terms.meaning: Cortisol given as a medicine. The body cannot hold its blood pressure during illness without it.
A pea-sized gland under the brain that directs the adrenal, thyroid and sex glands.

outcomes.story: Hydrocortisone and fluids go in. Over 20 minutes his blood pressure comes up and his color improves. Blood is sent, and he is scanned. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. A year of tiredness, feeling cold and losing interest in sex says his pituitary has been failing. If it has now stopped, he has no cortisol. We replace it first and prove it afterward.

outcomes.story: Labetalol goes in. His pressure falls to 70 over 40, and he slumps on the bed, grey and barely answering.
outcomes.reply: Look at the monitor. His pressure was already low, and that drug lowers it. He needs cortisol. Give hydrocortisone now.

outcomes.story: You ask for thyroid hormone. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Thyroid hormone speeds the body up, and the body then needs more cortisol. He has none. Cortisol always goes in first.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Bleeding around the brain is a fair thought for a headache like this, but the first test for it is a CT. And nothing comes before treating his shock.

3.resident: Look at his right eye again. The lid droops, the eye points down and out and the pupil is wide.
3.question: Which structure is being squeezed to cause that?
options: The crossing of the optic nerves
The sixth cranial nerve, which turns the eye outward
The third cranial nerve, which lifts the lid, narrows the pupil and moves the eye up, down and inward
The nerve that carries feeling from the forehead and eye

terms.meaning: Twelve pairs of nerves that leave the brain directly. Three pairs move the eyes.
A space on each side of the pituitary gland through which the nerves to the eye muscles pass.

outcomes.story: You say the optic nerve crossing. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Pressure there explains his lost side vision. It does not move an eye or drop a lid.

outcomes.story: You say the sixth nerve. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: If only that nerve failed, the eye would drift inward, with a normal lid and pupil.

outcomes.story: You recheck him. Over the last two hours his side vision has narrowed further, and his right eye now barely moves.
outcomes.reply: Right. The third nerve runs beside the pituitary. With it knocked out, the two muscles it does not supply pull the eye down and out. And he is getting worse.
outcomes.alarm: Side vision narrowing · right eye barely moves

outcomes.story: You say the nerve of feeling. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That nerve carries sensation only. Squeezing it would cause numbness or pain, not a drooping lid.

4.resident: His blood pressure is holding on hydrocortisone, but his sight and eye movements are getting worse by the hour.
4.question: What is the next step?
options: A clinic appointment with a hormone specialist in two weeks
An urgent neurosurgery review, for an operation through the nose to take the pressure off
Start cabergoline to shrink the growth
Radiation to the whole brain

terms.meaning: An operation on the pituitary done through the nose, with no opening made in the skull.
The point just above the pituitary where the two optic nerves cross.

outcomes.story: No surgeon is called. Twelve hours later, on the ward, he can see nothing to either side and his right eye has stopped moving.
outcomes.reply: Nerves that stay squeezed die. His sight was failing in front of us, and that is the signal to take the pressure off. Call the neurosurgeon now.
outcomes.alarm: Side vision gone in both eyes

outcomes.story: The neurosurgeon reviews the scans and operates that night. Working through the nose, they remove the blood and the growth pressing on the nerves.
outcomes.reply: Right. Vision that is getting worse is the reason to operate. The sooner the pressure comes off, the more sight he keeps.
outcomes.alarm: In surgery · pressure coming off the optic nerves

outcomes.story: You suggest cabergoline. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That shrinks growths that make prolactin, and it takes weeks. His prolactin is low, and he is losing sight today.

outcomes.story: You suggest radiation. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Radiation works over months and does nothing for blood under pressure.

5.resident: After this he will need hormone replacement for life, including cortisol and thyroid hormone. The order they are started in matters.
5.question: Which rule is correct?
options: Always start thyroid hormone first, then add cortisol
Cortisol must be started before thyroid hormone, or together with it
He must also take fludrocortisone, the salt-retaining hormone
Everyone needs desmopressin, the water-retaining hormone, after this

terms.meaning: Taking by mouth or injection the hormones a failed gland no longer makes.

outcomes.story: You say thyroid first. The endocrinologist stops you.
outcomes.reply: That is the classic mistake. Thyroid hormone raises the body’s need for cortisol and clears it faster, and that can tip a patient into collapse.

outcomes.story: The endocrinologist writes his discharge plan in that order.
outcomes.reply: Right. Cortisol first or together, never thyroid alone.

outcomes.story: You say he needs fludrocortisone. The endocrinologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The salt-retaining hormone is controlled by the kidneys, not the pituitary. His adrenal glands still make it.

outcomes.story: You say everyone needs desmopressin. The endocrinologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Only if the back part of the pituitary fails and he passes huge amounts of dilute urine. Most patients do not.

differential.resident: His blood tests and scans are in the chart.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: Bleeding around the brain from a burst aneurysm
Pituitary apoplexy: sudden bleeding into a growth on the pituitary gland
A clot in the vein channel beside the pituitary
Bacterial meningitis
differential.reveal: This is pituitary apoplexy. A growth on his pituitary has been there for months, slowly shutting down his hormones and pressing on his side vision. Today it bled and swelled suddenly. That caused the headache, squeezed the nerve to his right eye and stopped what was left of the gland, so his cortisol fell and his blood pressure with it. A burst aneurysm puts blood around the brain, not inside a pituitary mass. Meningitis brings fever and a stiff neck.

terms.meaning: A sudden bleed into an organ, or a sudden loss of its blood supply.
A growth of gland tissue that is not a cancer.

ending.stable: In the recovery room after surgery through the nose, on hormone replacement
ending.unstable: In the recovery room after surgery through the nose, on hormone replacement
ending.worse: In the recovery room after a late operation, with his side vision gone when it began
ending.critical: In intensive care after surgery, on hormone replacement

no-032.plainDiagnosis: Sudden bleeding into a growth on the pituitary gland, with the gland’s hormones shut down (pituitary apoplexy).

science.title: Why a bleed in the head dropped his blood pressure
science.text: The pituitary releases a hormone, ACTH, that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol. Cortisol keeps blood vessels responsive to adrenaline. When the pituitary stopped, the ACTH signal stopped, cortisol fell and his vessels relaxed.

science.title: Why he lost the outer half of each visual field
science.text: Light from the outer part of each visual field lands on the inner half of each retina. The fibers from those inner halves cross to the other side at one point, directly above the pituitary. Pressure there cuts both sets of crossing fibers at once.

sources.title: Rajasekaran et al. (Clin Endocrinol 2011): UK guidelines for the management of pituitary apoplexy
Briet et al. (Endocr Rev 2015): pituitary apoplexy

pn-014.title: A three-year-old, _seizing for twenty minutes._

start.alarm: Seizing for 22 minutes

pn-014.handoff: A 3-year-old boy with epilepsy has been having a full-body seizure for 22 minutes. Paramedics gave one dose of medicine on the way in, and it did not stop. He has had a fever for two days.

interview.prompt: Ask the paramedics what has happened so far
interview.finding: The seizure began at home about 22 minutes ago and has not stopped. They gave one injection of midazolam into his thigh eight minutes ago, with no effect. His blood sugar was 84, normal.

interview.prompt: Ask his mother about his epilepsy
interview.finding: It was diagnosed a year ago, and he takes levetiracetam twice a day. He missed yesterday’s doses because he could not keep anything down. His seizures usually stop within two minutes.

interview.prompt: Ask his mother about the last few days
interview.finding: Two days of fever and a runny nose, and he has hardly eaten or drunk. He has not hit his head, and he could not have swallowed any medicines or chemicals. His vaccines are up to date.

exam.prompt: Look at him
exam.finding: He does not respond. Both arms and both legs are jerking in rhythm, his eyes are turned to one side, and saliva is pooling in his mouth.

exam.prompt: Check his airway, breathing and circulation
exam.finding: His breathing is noisy. With his jaw lifted and oxygen on, air moves well. His pulses are strong.

exam.prompt: Check his pupils, neck and skin
exam.finding: His pupils react to light. His neck does not seem stiff. His skin is hot and flushed, with no rash and no bruises.

2.label: Blood tests and CT scan
2.content:
Blood sugar: 84, normal.
Sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium: all normal.
Level of his seizure medicine in the blood: too low.
Blood acid level (pH): 7.21, acidic, with a high lactate of 6.5. Both are improving now that the seizure has stopped.
CT scan of the head: no bleeding, no mass and no build-up of fluid.

0.resident: Oxygen is on, his sugar is normal and a line is in his vein. He has been seizing for over 20 minutes, through one dose of midazolam.
0.question: What is the next step, right now?
options: An emergency MRI of his brain, before any more medicine
A second dose of the same class of fast drug, lorazepam, into his vein
Start his usual seizure medicine as a slow drip over an hour, and wait
A spinal tap at once

terms.meaning: A seizure that lasts more than five minutes, or seizures that follow one another without waking in between.
A family of fast-acting calming drugs, such as midazolam and lorazepam. They are the first treatment for a seizure.

outcomes.story: You ask for an MRI. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nobody scans a child who is still convulsing. The longer a seizure runs, the harder it is to stop. Treat first.

outcomes.story: Lorazepam goes into his vein. Five minutes later he is still jerking.
outcomes.reply: That was the right drug, in a full dose. A seizure this long does not always answer to it. We move to the next step without waiting.

outcomes.story: A slow drip is started, and the team waits. Twenty minutes later he is still convulsing, and his lips are turning dusky.
outcomes.reply: A slow drip tops up a level. It does not stop a seizure. He needed a fast drug at once. Give lorazepam now.
outcomes.alarm: Seizing for over 40 minutes · lips dusky

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It cannot be done safely on a convulsing child, and it will not stop the seizure. If we still suspect infection once he is still, we do it then.

1.resident: He has now had two doses of that kind of drug, and he is still seizing.
1.question: What comes next?
options: A third dose of the same kind
A full dose of a different, longer-acting seizure medicine into his vein, such as levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate
A breathing tube at once, with no more seizure medicine
Clobazam by mouth

terms.meaning: The treatment used when the first one has not worked.
A large first dose, given to bring a drug to a working level quickly.

outcomes.story: A third dose goes in. The jerking continues. His breathing slows to a few shallow breaths a minute, and a nurse has to breathe for him with a bag and mask.
outcomes.reply: After two doses, more of that drug rarely stops the seizure. It does stop the breathing. He needs a different drug. Give it now.

outcomes.story: A full dose of levetiracetam runs into his vein over ten minutes. The jerking slows, then stops. He is breathing by himself, deeply asleep. Blood is sent, and he has a CT. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Three drugs are equally good at this step. Levetiracetam makes sense for him because his own level is probably low.

outcomes.story: You ask for a breathing tube and nothing else. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A tube protects his airway, and he may yet need one. It does not stop the seizure in his brain. The drugs used to place it would only hide the jerking.

outcomes.story: You ask for a tablet. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He cannot swallow while he is convulsing, and a tablet takes far too long to work.

4.resident: The seizure has stopped. He is sleepy from the seizure and from three doses of sedating medicine, and he still has a fever.
4.question: What is the plan?
options: Send him home now that the seizure has stopped
Admit him for monitoring, restart his seizure medicine, treat his illness and give his family a rescue plan
Switch him to phenobarbital for life and send him home
Refer him to psychiatry for spells that are not true seizures
4.fix: Admit him and restart his medicine

terms.meaning: A fast seizure drug that parents can give at home, in the nose or cheek, if a seizure lasts too long.

outcomes.story: He goes home, still drowsy. Four hours later the ambulance brings him back. He vomited his evening dose and is seizing again.
outcomes.reply: He was still vomiting, so the cause of this had not been fixed. He also needed watching while the sedating drugs wore off.

outcomes.story: He is admitted to the children’s ward on a monitor. His levetiracetam is given into his vein until he can keep liquids down. His mother is shown how to give a rescue medicine at home.
outcomes.reply: Right. We watch his breathing while he wakes, and we fix what set this off: the missed doses and the fever.

outcomes.story: You suggest changing his medicine for good. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His medicine did not fail. He missed it. One long seizure with a clear trigger is no reason to switch drugs.

outcomes.story: You suggest psychiatry. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He has known epilepsy, his blood turned acidic, and the seizure stopped with a seizure drug. This was real.

differential.resident: The seizure has stopped, and his blood tests and CT are in the chart.
differential.question: What best explains tonight?
options: Bacterial meningitis that has just begun
A prolonged seizure in a child with epilepsy, set off by missed medicine and a fever
Spells that look like seizures but have a psychological cause
A seizure from low blood sugar
differential.reveal: This was a prolonged seizure, called status epilepticus, in a child who already has epilepsy. Two things set it off together: he vomited his medicine for a day, so its level fell, and fever makes seizures more likely. His sugar was normal. He had no stiff neck or rash to suggest meningitis, although the team keeps that in mind until he wakes up normally. Acid in the blood after a long convulsion is expected and clears by itself.

terms.meaning: A tendency to have repeated seizures.
Something that sets off a seizure in a person who is prone to them, such as a missed dose, fever or lack of sleep.

ending.stable: Admitted to the children’s ward, asleep and breathing well, with his seizure medicine restarted
ending.unstable: Admitted to the children’s ward, asleep and breathing well, with his seizure medicine restarted
ending.worse: Admitted to the children’s ward after a longer seizure, with his seizure medicine restarted
ending.critical: In pediatric intensive care, with help for his breathing

pn-014.plainDiagnosis: A seizure that would not stop (status epilepticus), set off by missed epilepsy medicine and a fever.

science.title: How the first drug quiets a seizure
science.text: Nerve cells are calmed by a messenger called GABA. It opens channels that let chloride ions into the cell, and that makes the cell harder to fire. Benzodiazepines make those channels open more often. During a long seizure the cells pull the channels inside, so the drug has less to act on.

science.title: Why his blood turned acidic
science.text: Muscles that convulse without rest use oxygen faster than blood can deliver it. They fall back on breaking down glucose without oxygen, which makes far less ATP and leaves lactate behind. The acid clears once the seizure stops.

sources.title: Glauser et al. (Epilepsy Curr 2016): evidence-based guideline, treatment of convulsive status epilepticus in children and adults
Kapur et al. (N Engl J Med 2019): randomized trial of three anticonvulsant medications for status epilepticus

pn-017.title: A baby with a high fever _who cries harder when he is picked up._

start.alarm: High fever · hard to wake · tight soft spot

pn-017.handoff: An 11-month-old boy has had a high fever for a day. He is feeding poorly, has vomited twice and is getting harder to wake. When his parents pick him up, he arches his back and screams.

interview.prompt: Ask his parents how the illness has gone
interview.finding: He had a cold for two days. Yesterday a high fever started and he became very fussy. He has fed poorly and vomited twice. Today he has been sleepy and floppy, and in the car he was hard to wake.

interview.prompt: Ask what happens when they hold him
interview.finding: Picking him up makes him cry harder, and he arches his back. He has not had a seizure. They have not seen a rash.

interview.prompt: Ask about his vaccines
interview.finding: He is behind. He missed several visits and has not had the vaccines against Hib or pneumococcus, two bacteria that cause meningitis. He goes to daycare. He was born on time and has been healthy.

exam.prompt: Feel the soft spot on his head, and bend his neck gently
exam.finding: The soft spot is full and tight. He resists when you bend his neck, and his knees draw up as you do it.

exam.prompt: Watch how he responds
exam.finding: He looks ill and drowsy. He is hard to settle, and he cries more when he is picked up. He moves both arms and both legs.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin, and check his circulation
exam.finding: On his chest and belly there are a few tiny red-purple dots that do not fade when pressed. His hands and feet are cool, and a pressed fingertip takes three seconds to turn pink again.

1.label: Spinal fluid, blood count and CT scan
1.content:
White cells in the spinal fluid: 3,200, nearly all neutrophils, the cells that fight bacteria. Normal is fewer than 5.
Sugar in the spinal fluid: 22, when his blood sugar is 96. Very low.
Protein in the spinal fluid: 180, high.
Under the microscope: round bacteria in pairs, staining purple.
White cells in the blood: 22,000, high.
CT scan of the head, done before the spinal tap: no mass and no blocked fluid.

0.resident: Fever, a tight soft spot, a stiff neck and a baby who is getting harder to wake. A line is in and fluids are running.
0.question: What is the most important thing to do right now?
options: An MRI of his brain before any treatment
Draw blood cultures and give antibiotics into his vein now, without waiting for the spinal tap
Give acetaminophen by mouth and watch him for six hours
Start the antiviral drug acyclovir alone, and wait for the cultures

terms.meaning: Infection of the membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord.
A blood sample kept warm for days to see whether bacteria grow from it.

outcomes.story: An MRI for a baby needs sedation and takes 90 minutes to arrange. While he waits, with no antibiotic given, he has a seizure.
outcomes.reply: In bacterial meningitis every hour without antibiotics costs brain. No scan comes before the first dose. Give it now.

outcomes.story: Blood cultures are drawn, and the first antibiotics go in within minutes. Because he is so drowsy he has a quick CT, and then a spinal tap. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Antibiotics come first. The spinal tap still shows the infection when it is done soon afterward.

outcomes.story: He is given acetaminophen and watched. Six hours later he is limp and grey. The dots on his skin have spread into purple blotches, and he has had a seizure.
outcomes.reply: This was never a fever to watch. A tight soft spot and a stiff neck in a drowsy baby mean meningitis until proven otherwise. Give antibiotics now.
outcomes.alarm: Seizure · rash spreading · blood pressure 70 over 40

outcomes.story: You ask for acyclovir alone. The resident adds antibiotics.
outcomes.reply: Acyclovir treats the herpes virus. At his age, and without his vaccines, bacteria are the danger, and they need antibiotics now.

3.resident: Antibiotics kill the bacteria. Much of the damage in meningitis comes from the inflammation that follows, so a steroid is sometimes added.
3.question: Which statement about steroids in children with bacterial meningitis is correct?
options: Steroids must never be given to a child with meningitis
Dexamethasone most clearly protects hearing in meningitis caused by Hib, and when it is used it is given with or just before the first antibiotic dose
Steroids should be started only after seven days of antibiotics
In pneumococcal meningitis, steroids replace antibiotics

terms.meaning: A strong steroid that damps down inflammation.
Haemophilus influenzae type b, a bacterium that was a leading cause of childhood meningitis before its vaccine.

outcomes.story: You say steroids are never allowed. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: They are not forbidden. For some bacteria they clearly help.

outcomes.story: The team talks it through with the infectious disease doctor.
outcomes.reply: Right. The proof is strongest for Hib. For pneumococcus in children it is less certain, so it is decided case by case. Timing matters: it has to be on board as the bacteria start to die.

outcomes.story: You say to start after a week. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: By then the inflammation has already done its damage. If a steroid is used, it goes in at the start.

outcomes.story: You say steroids replace antibiotics. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Never. A steroid kills nothing. Antibiotics are the treatment.

4.resident: If he recovers, one long-term problem is common enough that every child is tested for it before going home.
4.question: Which one?
options: Permanent weakness of one side of the body
Hearing loss from damage to the inner ear
A tremor and stiffness like Parkinson disease
Damage to the nerves of the hands and feet

terms.meaning: Hearing loss from damage to the inner ear or its nerve.

outcomes.story: You say weakness of one side. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It can happen, but it is much less common.

outcomes.story: A hearing test is booked for before he leaves hospital.
outcomes.reply: Right. The infection spreads easily to the inner ear. Finding hearing loss early matters, because a baby who cannot hear does not learn to speak.

outcomes.story: You say a tremor. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is not something meningitis leaves behind.

outcomes.story: You say nerve damage in the hands and feet. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Meningitis injures the brain and the inner ear, not the nerves of the limbs.

differential.resident: His spinal fluid results are in the chart.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: Viral meningitis
Bacterial meningitis, caused by pneumococcus
Tuberculous meningitis
Bleeding around the brain
differential.reveal: This is bacterial meningitis. Thousands of neutrophils, a very low sugar and a high protein are the pattern bacteria produce, and the microscope showed the bacteria themselves. Round bacteria in pairs are typical of pneumococcus, one of the two vaccines he missed. A virus leaves the sugar normal and draws a different kind of white cell. Tuberculosis builds up over weeks. Bleeding would fill the fluid with red cells.

terms.meaning: Streptococcus pneumoniae, a bacterium that causes pneumonia, ear infections and meningitis.
A needle in the lower back that takes a sample of the fluid around the brain and spinal cord.

ending.stable: In pediatric intensive care on antibiotics, with a hearing test booked
ending.unstable: In pediatric intensive care on antibiotics, with a hearing test booked
ending.worse: In pediatric intensive care on antibiotics and a seizure medicine
ending.critical: In pediatric intensive care on antibiotics, with drugs to support his blood pressure

pn-017.plainDiagnosis: A bacterial infection of the lining of the brain (pneumococcal meningitis).

science.title: What the microscope showed in minutes
science.text: Bacteria are complete cells with their own walls. A stain that sticks to thick cell walls turns some of them purple, and their shape narrows down the species long before a culture grows. Antibiotics attack parts that bacteria have and viruses lack, which is why they do nothing against a virus.

science.title: Why hearing is at risk
science.text: Sound is turned into nerve signals by hair cells in the inner ear. The fluid around them connects with the fluid around the brain, so infection and inflammation reach them easily. Hair cells that die are not replaced.

sources.title: Tunkel et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2004): practice guidelines for the management of bacterial meningitis
Brouwer et al. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015): corticosteroids for acute bacterial meningitis

pn-016.title: He falls asleep mid-sentence, _and his knees give way when he laughs._

start.alarm: Falls asleep in class · knees buckle with laughter

pn-016.handoff: A 16-year-old boy has been overwhelmingly sleepy in the daytime for six months, although he sleeps eight or nine hours a night. His mother says his knees buckle when he laughs hard.

interview.prompt: Ask about the sleepiness
interview.finding: For six months he has not been able to stay awake in the day, although he sleeps eight or nine hours at night. He falls asleep in class, while texting and in the middle of a sentence. A short nap leaves him fresh for an hour or two.

interview.prompt: Ask his mother about the buckling
interview.finding: When he laughs hard or is startled, his head nods, his jaw goes slack and his knees give way. Once he slid to the floor. He was awake the whole time, heard everything and was normal within seconds.

interview.prompt: Ask about falling asleep, snoring and daily life
interview.finding: As he drifts off he sees vivid, dream-like images, and sometimes he cannot move at all, which frightens him. He does not snore. His grades have dropped, and he nearly crashed the car when he dozed off. He takes no drugs or medicines.

exam.prompt: Watch him during the visit
exam.finding: He is awake and makes sense, but he yawns constantly and his eyelids droop.

exam.prompt: Test his strength, reflexes and walking
exam.finding: All normal. His arms and legs are strong, and he walks steadily, heel to toe.

exam.prompt: Tell him a joke, and look in his throat
exam.finding: He laughs hard. His head drops and his jaw sags for a few seconds, and he hears you the whole time. His tonsils are small, and his jaw is a normal shape.

1.label: Sleep studies and spinal fluid
1.content:
Overnight sleep study: a normal amount of sleep and no pauses in breathing. Dream sleep began unusually soon after he fell asleep.
Daytime nap test, five naps: he fell asleep in 4 minutes on average, when more than 10 is normal. In three of the naps he went straight into dream sleep.
Spinal fluid: hypocretin, a brain chemical that keeps people awake, is low.
Urine drug screen: negative.
Thyroid and iron tests: normal.

0.resident: Before we order anything, think about what his mother described: his knees give way when he laughs, and he stays wide awake throughout.
0.question: What is that called?
options: Drop seizures
Cataplexy
Fainting
Brief blockages of blood flow to the brain

terms.meaning: Sudden, brief loss of muscle strength set off by strong emotion, with the person fully awake.
The slight, constant tension that keeps muscles ready and the body upright.

outcomes.story: You say drop seizures. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those are not set off by laughter, and awareness is usually lost for a moment. He hears everything.

outcomes.story: The specialist books an overnight sleep study with a daytime nap test, and some blood and spinal fluid tests. He comes back to clinic with the results in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Strength that goes with emotion while the mind stays clear is cataplexy. Only one condition causes it, and the tests will confirm it.

outcomes.story: You say fainting. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: In a faint the brain briefly loses its blood supply and the person blacks out. He never does.

outcomes.story: You say blocked blood flow. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That would be extraordinary at sixteen, would not be set off by a joke and would not affect both sides at once.

3.resident: He will take planned short naps and keep regular sleep hours. He also needs a medicine for the daytime sleepiness.
3.question: Which kind of medicine is the first choice?
options: A medicine that promotes wakefulness, such as modafinil, or a stimulant
A sedative of the diazepam family at bedtime
An antipsychotic
A long-acting opioid

terms.meaning: A drug that helps the brain stay awake, taken in the morning.

outcomes.story: He starts a wake-promoting medicine each morning, with two planned 15-minute naps a day.
outcomes.reply: Right. It does not cure the condition, but most people can stay awake through a school day on it. If the buckling stays troublesome, other medicines treat that.

outcomes.story: You suggest a bedtime sedative. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He does not have trouble sleeping. A sedative would leave him sleepier the next day.

outcomes.story: You suggest an antipsychotic. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The images he sees as he falls asleep are dreams starting early. They are not psychosis, and those drugs are sedating.

outcomes.story: You suggest an opioid. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Opioids cause sleepiness and dependence. They have no place here.

4.resident: He is sixteen and has just got his license. He has already had one near miss.
4.question: What is the most important safety advice?
options: Avoid all physical activity for good
Do not drive until the sleepiness is under control, and keep to treatment and naps once he does
Drink less in the evening
Start a strict ketogenic diet

terms.meaning: A sudden, overwhelming need to sleep that cannot be resisted.

outcomes.story: You tell him to give up sports. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He can be as active as he likes. He just needs to know what sets off the buckling.

outcomes.story: He agrees to hand his keys to his mother until the medicine is working.
outcomes.reply: Right. Falling asleep or losing strength at the wheel is the one way this condition kills people. That conversation comes first.

outcomes.story: You tell him to drink less in the evening. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That helps people who wake at night to pass urine. It is not his problem.

outcomes.story: You suggest a ketogenic diet. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That diet is used for some kinds of epilepsy. It does not treat this.

differential.resident: His sleep studies and spinal fluid result are in the chart.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: Obstructive sleep apnea
Narcolepsy with cataplexy (narcolepsy type 1)
Idiopathic hypersomnia, sleepiness with no known cause
Simply not getting enough sleep
differential.reveal: He has narcolepsy type 1. His brain has lost the cells that make hypocretin, the chemical that holds a person steadily awake. Without it, sleep breaks into the day, and pieces of dream sleep appear at the wrong times. The paralysis that belongs to dreaming shows up as buckling when he laughs and as being unable to move at the edge of sleep. Sleep apnea would show pauses in breathing overnight. The other two do not cause cataplexy or a low hypocretin.

terms.meaning: A lifelong condition in which the brain cannot keep sleep and wakefulness apart.
The stage of sleep with vivid dreams, in which the body’s muscles are switched off.

ending.stable: Home with a morning medicine, planned naps and no driving until his sleepiness is controlled
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

pn-016.plainDiagnosis: A condition in which the brain cannot stay steadily awake, with sudden weakness on laughing (narcolepsy type 1).

science.title: One small protein that keeps the brain awake
science.text: Hypocretin is a short chain of amino acids made by a few thousand nerve cells deep in the brain. It works by binding to receptors on other cells. When the cells that make it are lost, nothing else supplies it, and the receptors stay empty.

science.title: Why a drug screen and thyroid test were part of it
science.text: Sleepiness has many causes, including drugs, an underactive thyroid, low iron and poor sleep. A positive nap test means more once each of those has been checked and ruled out. The other tests were controls.

sources.title: Scammell (N Engl J Med 2015): narcolepsy
Maski et al. (J Clin Sleep Med 2021): treatment of central disorders of hypersomnolence, an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

dm-061.title: A rash that is still spreading, _and a swollen face._

start.alarm: Rash over most of his body · swollen face · fever

dm-061.handoff: A 45-year-old man was admitted two days ago for a skin infection of his calf. Over four days a rash has spread from his chest to his limbs and face. His face is puffy, and he has a fever.

interview.prompt: Ask about the rash
interview.finding: Pink spots began on his chest four days ago and spread to his arms, legs and face. It itches. He feels unwell and feverish, and the skin around his eyes and cheeks has swollen. His mouth and eyes are not sore, and nothing has blistered.

interview.prompt: Ask about every medicine and when each was started
interview.finding: Six weeks ago his doctor started allopurinol for gout. He has taken two blood pressure tablets for years. An antibiotic drip was started two days ago for his leg. He has never reacted to a drug before.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health and other symptoms
interview.finding: He has gout, high blood pressure and kidneys that work at about half strength. He is tired, and he has a dull ache under his right ribs. His throat and joints are fine.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin and face
exam.finding: Red spots and small bumps have merged over more than half of his body. They are densest in the skin folds. His eyelids and cheeks are swollen. There are no pus spots.

exam.prompt: Look in his mouth and eyes, and rub the skin gently
exam.finding: The lining of his mouth and his eyes are normal. The skin does not blister or slide when rubbed.

exam.prompt: Feel his neck, armpits and belly
exam.finding: The glands in his neck and armpits are firm and tender. His liver is slightly enlarged and tender.

1.label: Blood tests
1.content:
White cells: 16.8, high.
Eosinophils, the white cells of allergy: 2.4, about five times the upper limit.
Blood film: unusual-looking lymphocytes.
Liver enzymes: AST 188 and ALT 224, about five times normal.
Kidney test (creatinine): 1.9, up from his usual 1.6.
Platelets and hemoglobin: normal.
Inflammation marker (CRP): 62, high.

0.resident: Rashes from drugs are common in hospital, and most are harmless. Something about this one is different.
0.question: Which feature worries you most?
options: The rash looks like measles
A swollen face, fever and tender glands, six weeks after a new drug
The rash itches
The rash is densest in the skin folds

terms.meaning: A rash caused by a medicine.
Small glands that swell when the immune system is active.

outcomes.story: You point to the measles-like pattern. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is the most common pattern of all, and most rashes that look like it are harmless.

outcomes.story: The resident nods and sends a blood count with liver and kidney tests. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. A swollen face, fever and glands mean the whole immune system is reacting. The six-week delay is typical of the dangerous kind.

outcomes.story: You point to the itch. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nearly every drug rash itches. It tells us nothing about how serious this is.

outcomes.story: You point to the skin folds. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Many rashes gather in the folds. The clue is in his face and his glands.

3.resident: Allopurinol is one of the commonest causes of this reaction, and some patients are at much higher risk.
3.question: What put him at risk?
options: His weak kidneys, together with a full starting dose
The beer he drinks
Having gout
His blood pressure tablet

terms.meaning: How quickly the body removes a drug, mostly through the kidneys or the liver.

outcomes.story: You write it in his chart for the team that will treat his gout in future.
outcomes.reply: Right. The kidneys clear the active form of allopurinol. With weak kidneys it builds up, so the dose should start low and rise slowly.

outcomes.story: You say the beer. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Beer can bring on gout. It does not cause this reaction.

outcomes.story: You say the gout. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Gout is why he was given the drug. It does not make him react to it.

outcomes.story: You say his blood pressure tablet. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He has taken that for years without trouble. The new drug is the suspect.

4.resident: His liver and kidneys are inflamed, and the rash is still spreading.
4.question: What is the next step?
options: Continue allopurinol, and add antihistamines for the itch
Swap allopurinol for febuxostat, another gout drug, and watch
Stop allopurinol now, and start steroids by mouth or vein
Stop allopurinol, and start broad antibiotics
4.fix: Stop the drug and start steroids

terms.meaning: A drug such as prednisone that damps down the immune system.
The medicine that set off a reaction.

outcomes.story: Allopurinol is continued. The next morning the whites of his eyes are yellow, he is drowsy and his liver tests have tripled.
outcomes.reply: Every dose fed the reaction, and antihistamines only quieten an itch. The drug has to stop, now and for good.
outcomes.alarm: Eyes turning yellow · liver tests tripled

outcomes.story: You swap one gout drug for another. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Stopping allopurinol is right. Starting a new drug in the middle of a reaction is not. With his liver and kidneys involved, he also needs steroids.

outcomes.story: Allopurinol is stopped and recorded in his chart as a serious allergy. Prednisone is started, and his liver and kidney tests are booked daily.
outcomes.reply: Right. Taking away the cause is the treatment. The steroid protects his organs while the reaction burns out, and it has to be reduced slowly over weeks.

outcomes.story: You ask for broad antibiotics. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Fever and a high white count can look like infection. The eosinophils and the timing say drug reaction. More drugs would only confuse the picture.

5.resident: Most patients recover over weeks. One group of problems can appear months later, and we follow patients for them.
5.question: Which should he be monitored for?
options: Permanent loss of skin color where the rash was
Autoimmune disease, such as thyroid inflammation or type 1 diabetes
Repeated skin infections
Long-lasting hives

terms.meaning: A condition in which the immune system attacks the body’s own tissue.

outcomes.story: You say loss of skin color. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The skin usually heals fully. That is not a known result of this reaction.

outcomes.story: Thyroid blood tests are booked for the months after he goes home.
outcomes.reply: Right. After a reaction like this the immune system can stay unsettled and turn on the thyroid or the pancreas. We check for several months.

outcomes.story: You say skin infections. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That was his reason for coming in. It has nothing to do with the drug reaction.

outcomes.story: You say hives. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Hives are a different, faster kind of allergy. They are not what follows this.

differential.resident: His blood tests are in the chart.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, a drug reaction that blisters the skin and mouth
A drug reaction that covers the skin in tiny pus spots
DRESS syndrome, a drug reaction with rash, high eosinophils and inflamed organs
A staphylococcal infection that makes the skin peel
differential.reveal: This is DRESS syndrome. It starts two to eight weeks after a new drug, later than most drug rashes. The face swells, the glands enlarge and eosinophils flood the blood. The reaction also inflames organs, most often the liver, and his kidneys are affected too. Stevens-Johnson syndrome blisters the skin and the lining of the mouth and eyes, and his are untouched. He has no pus spots and no peeling.

terms.meaning: A white blood cell that multiplies in allergies and some drug reactions.
A set of findings that occur together.

ending.stable: On the ward on steroids, with allopurinol stopped for good and daily blood tests
ending.unstable: On the ward on steroids, with allopurinol stopped for good and daily blood tests
ending.worse: On the ward on steroids, with a badly inflamed liver after another day of allopurinol
ending.critical: In intensive care with liver failure

dm-061.plainDiagnosis: A severe reaction to allopurinol, with a rash and inflamed liver and kidneys (DRESS syndrome).

science.title: What allopurinol was meant to do
science.text: Uric acid is the last product when the body breaks down purines, and one enzyme, xanthine oxidase, makes it. Allopurinol blocks that enzyme, so less uric acid forms and fewer crystals settle in the joints. The reaction he had is unrelated to that action.

science.title: Why a few people react and most do not
science.text: The reaction is far more common in people who inherit one version of an immune gene, called HLA-B*58:01. HLA proteins display fragments to T cells. That version seems to display the drug in a way T cells treat as foreign. A blood test can find it before the drug is started.

sources.title: Kardaun et al. (Br J Dermatol 2013): drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), results from the prospective RegiSCAR study
Husain et al. (J Am Acad Dermatol 2013): DRESS syndrome, part II, management and therapeutics

dm-074.title: Red from head to foot, _and he cannot stop shivering._

start.alarm: Red all over · shivering · temperature 35.4

dm-074.handoff: A 63-year-old man has been admitted with red, scaly skin over almost his whole body. It began two weeks ago. He is shivering under blankets, and his temperature is low.

interview.prompt: Ask about his skin
interview.finding: Redness and scaling began on his chest two weeks ago and now cover almost all of him. It itches badly and feels tight. So much skin is flaking off that his sheets are covered.

interview.prompt: Ask about his skin problems before this, and recent treatment
interview.finding: He has had patches of psoriasis for 20 years, controlled with creams. He ran out a month ago. An urgent-care doctor gave him steroid tablets for a flare, and they were then stopped all at once.

interview.prompt: Ask how he feels in himself
interview.finding: He is cold all the time, even under blankets, and gets shaking chills. He is weak, has eaten little and feels faint when he stands. He lives alone.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin, nails, palms and soles
exam.finding: About nine-tenths of his skin is red, with fine flaking, and it feels thick and tight. His palms and soles are thickened. His nails are pitted and lifting from their beds. The inside of his mouth is normal, and there are no blisters.

exam.prompt: Feel his skin temperature, and watch him
exam.finding: He looks ill and shivers constantly. His chest feels warm, and his hands and feet are cool.

exam.prompt: Check his glands, legs, heart and lungs
exam.finding: The glands in his neck and groin are enlarged and not tender. Both lower legs are swollen and hold a dent when pressed. His heart is fast and regular, and his lungs are clear.

1.label: Blood tests, heart scan and skin sample
1.content:
White cells: 13.8, high.
Sodium 132 and potassium 3.4: both low.
Albumin, the main protein in blood: 2.6, low.
Kidney tests: creatinine 1.4, up from his usual 0.9. He is short of fluid.
Bedside heart scan: the heart is pumping hard and fast, with no fluid around it.
Blood cultures: pending.
Skin sample: thickened skin with the pattern seen in psoriasis.

0.resident: Nearly all of his skin is inflamed. He is cold, and his heart is racing. Before we treat him, work out why.
0.question: What explains his low temperature and fast heart?
options: The blood vessels in his skin have narrowed and are holding heat in
The blood vessels in his skin are wide open, so he is losing heat and fluid, and his heart has to pump harder
Psoriasis has damaged the temperature center in his brain
Steroid creams have shut down his thyroid
0.fix: Explain what the skin is doing

terms.meaning: Redness and inflammation of nearly all of the skin.
Widening of blood vessels.

outcomes.story: You say the vessels have narrowed. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Narrow vessels would make him pale and keep heat in. He is red all over.

outcomes.story: The resident has warm blankets put on him, sends blood, takes a small skin sample and scans his heart at the bedside. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Red skin is skin full of blood. All of that blood is at the surface giving away heat, water leaks out through the damaged surface, and the heart races to keep up.

outcomes.story: You say brain damage. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Psoriasis does not affect the brain. His temperature control is working, which is why he shivers. It is being overwhelmed.

outcomes.story: You say the thyroid. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Creams do not do that, and an underactive thyroid slows the heart.

3.resident: He is cold, dry and short of salts and protein, and his psoriasis is out of control.
3.question: How do we treat him?
options: Send him home with steroid creams and a clinic appointment
Restart high-dose steroid tablets at once
Admit him to a warm room for fluids, salts and skin care, and start a medicine made for psoriasis
Start chemotherapy for a suspected skin lymphoma

terms.meaning: A plain, greasy moisturizer that seals water into the skin.
A fast-acting medicine that calms the immune cells driving psoriasis.

outcomes.story: He goes home with creams. The next morning a neighbor finds him on the floor, cold and confused, and calls an ambulance.
outcomes.reply: He lives alone, and he was already cold with a low blood pressure. This is a skin emergency. He needed a warm room, fluids and a monitor.

outcomes.story: You restart the steroid tablets. The dermatologist stops you.
outcomes.reply: Those tablets are how he got here. They quiet psoriasis and set it up to come back harder. He needs a drug meant for psoriasis.

outcomes.story: He is moved to a warm room. Warmed fluids and potassium run into his vein. His skin is covered in plain ointment under damp wraps, and the dermatologist starts cyclosporine. Three hours later he has stopped shivering.
outcomes.reply: Right. We replace what the skin is losing, which is heat, water, salts and protein, and we treat the psoriasis itself.

outcomes.story: You ask for chemotherapy. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A skin lymphoma can cause red skin all over, but his skin sample shows psoriasis. We treat what the sample shows.

4.resident: He is warmer, and fluids are running. He is not safe yet.
4.question: Which life-threatening problems do we watch for?
options: Infection through the damaged skin, and a heart that cannot keep up
A sudden rise of pressure inside the eye
Inflammation of the pancreas
A collapsed lung

terms.meaning: A dangerous whole-body response to infection.
The heart being unable to pump as much blood as the body needs.

outcomes.story: He stays on a heart monitor, and the nurses check his temperature and his skin every few hours.
outcomes.reply: Right. Skin is a barrier, and his has failed, so bacteria get in. His heart has been running at full speed for two weeks. Those are the two things that kill patients like him.

outcomes.story: You say the eye. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nothing about red skin raises the pressure in the eye.

outcomes.story: You say the pancreas. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: This condition has no link to the pancreas.

outcomes.story: You say a collapsed lung. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His lungs are not involved. Think about what skin normally does, and what happens when it stops.

differential.resident: His skin sample shows psoriasis. He has had it for 20 years, and it has never done this before.
differential.question: What most likely set this off?
options: Stopping a course of steroid tablets suddenly
His cholesterol tablet, atorvastatin
His blood pressure tablet, lisinopril
Drinking alcohol now and then
differential.reveal: This is erythrodermic psoriasis, set off by stopping steroid tablets suddenly. Steroid tablets press psoriasis down hard. When they stop all at once it rebounds, sometimes into this whole-body form. That is why doctors avoid steroid tablets for psoriasis and use creams or other medicines. His cholesterol tablet is not a known trigger, and he has taken the blood pressure tablet for years.

terms.meaning: A long-term immune condition that makes skin cells multiply too fast and form red, scaly patches.
A condition coming back worse than before when a treatment is stopped.

ending.stable: Admitted to a warm room on fluids, skin wraps and a psoriasis medicine, on a heart monitor
ending.unstable: Admitted to a warm room on fluids, skin wraps and a psoriasis medicine, on a heart monitor
ending.worse: Admitted to a warm room on fluids, skin wraps and a psoriasis medicine, on a heart monitor
ending.critical: In intensive care, being rewarmed, on fluids and a psoriasis medicine

dm-074.plainDiagnosis: Psoriasis that spread to cover almost all of his skin (erythrodermic psoriasis), set off by stopping steroid tablets suddenly.

science.title: Why red skin made him cold
science.text: The body loses heat mainly through the skin, and it controls the loss by changing how much blood flows there. Inflammation held every skin vessel open, and the damaged surface let water evaporate freely. He lost heat faster than shivering could make it.

science.title: Why his heart was racing
science.text: Blood pressure depends on how much blood the heart pumps and on the resistance of the vessels. With the skin’s vessels wide open, resistance fell. To hold his pressure the heart had to pump more blood each minute, and it did so with less fluid in the system.

sources.title: Rosenbach et al. (J Am Acad Dermatol 2010): treatment of erythrodermic psoriasis, from the medical board of the National Psoriasis Foundation
Mistry et al. (Adv Skin Wound Care 2015): a review of the diagnosis and management of erythroderma (generalized red skin)

dm-025.title: Pale patches on his back _that would not tan._

start.alarm: Pale patches on his chest and back

dm-025.handoff: A 21-year-old college athlete has pale patches across his chest, shoulders and back. They showed up after a summer in the sun, when the skin around them tanned. He is worried it is something permanent.

interview.prompt: Ask about the patches
interview.finding: He noticed them at the end of the summer. The skin around them tanned, and they stayed pale. They itch a little when he sweats and sometimes look slightly flaky.

interview.prompt: Ask whether this has happened before
interview.finding: Yes, in the last few summers. Each time they faded over the winter. They are not painful and not numb, and he feels well.

interview.prompt: Ask about his health and routine
interview.finding: He is healthy and takes no medicines. He lives somewhere hot and humid, trains every day and sweats heavily. He is afraid it is vitiligo.

exam.prompt: Look at where the patches are, and at their edges
exam.finding: Dozens of small, pale, sharp-edged patches run together across his upper chest, shoulders and upper back. A few are faintly pink-tan. His face and hands are clear.

exam.prompt: Scrape a patch gently with the edge of a glass slide
exam.finding: A fine, powdery scale comes off.

exam.prompt: Test feeling over the patches with a wisp of cotton
exam.finding: He feels it normally everywhere.

1.label: Skin scraping under the microscope
1.content:
Scraping in potassium hydroxide, which dissolves skin cells and leaves any fungus: many short threads mixed with clusters of round yeast cells.
Under ultraviolet light: several patches glow pale yellow-green.
Feeling over the patches: normal.

0.resident: Pale, slightly scaly patches on the upper body that come back every summer. One quick test in clinic will settle it.
0.question: Which test?
options: A skin biopsy with special stains
A scraping of the scale, examined under the microscope
Patch testing for skin allergies
A blood test for sarcoidosis

terms.meaning: A skin scraping mixed with potassium hydroxide, which clears away skin cells so that fungus can be seen.
Flakes of the dead outer layer of skin.

outcomes.story: You ask for a biopsy. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A biopsy leaves a scar and takes a week. A scraping takes five minutes and does not hurt.

outcomes.story: The dermatologist scrapes a patch onto a slide, adds a drop of potassium hydroxide and looks. The room lights go off for an ultraviolet lamp. The findings go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Scale means something is living in the top layer of skin, and the microscope can show what it is.

outcomes.story: You ask for patch testing. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That finds allergies to things that touch the skin. An allergy gives a red, itchy rash where the thing touched, not pale patches.

outcomes.story: You ask for a sarcoidosis blood test. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nothing here suggests it. Start with the simple test on the skin itself.

3.resident: A yeast is overgrowing on his skin. He is otherwise healthy, and it is limited to his upper body.
3.question: What is the first treatment?
options: An antifungal wash or cream, such as selenium sulfide or ketoconazole
Terbinafine tablets
A steroid cream
Acyclovir tablets

terms.meaning: Applied to the skin, not swallowed.
A medicine that kills fungi, including yeasts.

outcomes.story: He is given an antifungal shampoo to lather onto his chest and back, leave on for ten minutes and rinse off, each day for a week.
outcomes.reply: Right. The yeast lives on the surface, so a treatment applied to the surface reaches it, with almost no side effects.

outcomes.story: You suggest terbinafine tablets. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Terbinafine by mouth works for ringworm and nail fungus. It does not work against this yeast. A common mix-up.

outcomes.story: You suggest a steroid cream. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A steroid does not kill yeast, and it can thin the skin. It would make things worse.

outcomes.story: You suggest acyclovir. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That treats herpes viruses. This is a yeast.

4.resident: He has a beach trip in three weeks and wants to know when his skin will look normal.
4.question: What do you tell him?
options: The color will return as soon as the yeast is dead
It rarely comes back, so nothing more is needed
The pale patches can last weeks to months after the yeast is gone, and it often comes back, so a preventive wash now and then helps
He must stay out of the sun for good

terms.meaning: Melanin, the brown coloring made by cells in the skin.
A condition coming back after treatment.

outcomes.story: You promise quick results. The dermatologist corrects you.
outcomes.reply: The yeast dies in a week. The color takes much longer. If he expects it by the beach trip, he will think the treatment failed.

outcomes.story: You say it rarely returns. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: He has had it for several summers already. In heat and sweat it comes back in most people.

outcomes.story: He is disappointed about the trip and glad it is not permanent. He will use the wash once a month through the summer.
outcomes.reply: Right. The treatment has worked even while the patches still show. The skin needs weeks of normal pigment-making to catch up.

outcomes.story: You tell him to avoid the sun for good. The dermatologist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The sun did not cause this. It only made the patches easier to see. He does not need to hide from it.

differential.resident: The microscope and lamp findings are in his chart.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: Vitiligo
Tinea versicolor, an overgrowth of a skin yeast called Malassezia
Ringworm of the body
Pityriasis alba, pale patches linked to dry skin
differential.reveal: This is tinea versicolor. Malassezia is a yeast that lives on everyone’s skin and feeds on skin oil. In heat and sweat it overgrows. The mix of short threads and round yeast under the microscope is its signature, and so is the yellow-green glow. Vitiligo has no scale and no yeast, and its patches are completely white. Ringworm forms rings with a raised, scaly edge.

terms.meaning: A single-celled fungus.
“Of varied color.” The patches can be paler or darker than the skin around them.

ending.stable: Home with an antifungal wash and a plan to repeat it through the summer
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

dm-025.plainDiagnosis: A harmless overgrowth of skin yeast that leaves pale patches (tinea versicolor).

science.title: Why the patches stayed pale
science.text: Skin color comes from melanin, and an enzyme called tyrosinase carries out the key step in making it. As the yeast digests skin oil it releases an acid that blocks tyrosinase. Where the yeast is thick, the skin cannot respond to the sun by making more melanin.

science.title: Why the patches glowed
science.text: Some molecules absorb ultraviolet light, which we cannot see, and give part of that energy back as visible light. Compounds made by this yeast do so in yellow-green. Skin without the yeast does not, so the lamp shows where it is.

sources.title: Renati et al. (BMJ 2015): pityriasis versicolor
Gupta and Foley (J Fungi 2015): antifungal treatment for pityriasis versicolor

oph-027.title: A painful red eye, _and a white spot that grew overnight._

start.alarm: Very painful red eye · vision blurred

oph-027.handoff: A 23-year-old student has had a very painful, red right eye for two days. Light hurts, her vision is blurred and there is thick discharge. She wears contact lenses.

interview.prompt: Ask about the eye
interview.finding: The pain, redness and blur have worsened quickly over two days. Light is unbearable, and it feels as if something is in the eye. A white spot on the eye is clearly larger than yesterday. Nothing hit or scratched it.

interview.prompt: Ask how she looks after her contact lenses
interview.finding: She wears soft lenses every day. She often sleeps in them and swims in them, and she tops up the old solution in the case without replacing it. Two nights ago she fell asleep with them in.

interview.prompt: Ask about her health
interview.finding: She is short-sighted and otherwise healthy. She has no fever, no sore joints and no mouth ulcers. Her left eye is fine.

exam.prompt: Test her vision, and look at both eyes
exam.finding: With the right eye she reads only the large letters, 20/100. That eye is very red, most of all around the cornea, and thick yellow discharge clings to the lashes. The left eye is white and reads 20/20.

exam.prompt: Look at the right cornea through the microscope
exam.finding: In the center is a round, raw patch 3 mm across, with a dense white area in the cornea beneath it. Its edges are soft and blurred, and the cornea around it is hazy.

exam.prompt: Look at the space behind the cornea, and check the pupil
exam.finding: A thin layer of white pus has settled at the bottom of the space between the cornea and the iris. The pupil still reacts to light.

1.label: Scraping and cultures
1.content:
Stain of the corneal scraping: rod-shaped bacteria that stain pink (gram-negative).
Culture from the cornea: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Antibiotics that work against it: fluoroquinolone drops and strengthened aminoglycoside drops.
Culture from her lens case: the same bacterium.
Vision in the right eye: 20/100.

0.resident: A contact lens wearer with an ulcer in the center of the cornea and pus inside the eye. This can cost her the eye.
0.question: What is the most important step right now?
options: Steroid drops to settle the inflammation
Scrape the ulcer for a stain and culture, then start antibiotic drops straight away
Patch the eye, and see her again in a week
Reassure her, and let her keep wearing a lens in the other eye

terms.meaning: The clear window at the front of the eye. It does most of the eye’s focusing.
An open sore in the cornea, usually from infection.

outcomes.story: Steroid drops ease the pain for a night. By morning the white spot has doubled in size, and the layer of pus is deeper.
outcomes.reply: A steroid switches off the eye’s defenses and leaves the bacteria untouched, so the infection runs free. The ulcer needs a scraping and antibiotics now.

outcomes.story: Numbing drops go in. The eye doctor scrapes the edge of the ulcer onto slides and culture plates and scrapes her lens case too. Antibiotic drops start within minutes. The results go in her chart.
