outcomes.reply: Right. We take the sample first, so we learn exactly which bacterium it is, and then treat hard without waiting for the answer.

outcomes.story: You reach for an eye patch. The eye doctor stops you.
outcomes.reply: Never patch an infected eye. A patch makes a warm, dark pocket where bacteria thrive. A week is also far too long. She will be seen every day.

outcomes.story: You reassure her. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: This is an emergency, and lenses are what caused it. No lens goes in either eye until this has healed.

3.resident: The bacterium is Pseudomonas, and we know which antibiotics kill it.
3.question: How do we give them?
options: Amoxicillin by mouth once a day for a week
Antiviral eye drops
A fluoroquinolone or strengthened antibiotic drop every hour, day and night, with a check every day
One injection of vancomycin into the back of the eye

terms.meaning: Applied straight onto the surface, here as eye drops.
Antibiotic eye drops mixed specially at a much higher strength than standard ones.

outcomes.story: She goes home with tablets. The next morning the ulcer is deeper, and the cornea beneath it has thinned.
outcomes.reply: The cornea has no blood vessels, so very little of a tablet reaches it. Amoxicillin does not kill Pseudomonas anyway. She needs drops every hour.

outcomes.story: You ask for antiviral drops. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The culture grew a bacterium. An antiviral does nothing to it.

outcomes.story: She is started on fluoroquinolone drops every hour, day and night, with an alarm set on her phone. She will be seen in clinic every day.
outcomes.reply: Right. Drops put a very high dose of antibiotic exactly where the infection is. For the first days, hourly means through the night as well.

outcomes.story: You ask for an injection into the eye. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Injections are for infection deep inside the eye. Hers is in the cornea, and vancomycin does not kill this bacterium.

4.resident: When this heals she will want to wear lenses again. Her habits are what let it happen.
4.question: What does she need to change?
options: Sleeping in lenses is safe if they are rinsed in tap water
No sleeping, swimming or showering in lenses, fresh solution every time, a new case regularly and clean hands
Switch to colored fashion lenses bought without a prescription
Wear a lens only in the eye that was infected, to rest the other
4.fix: Go through lens care with her

terms.meaning: The liquid that kills germs on contact lenses. It stops working once it has been used.

outcomes.story: You say tap water is fine. The eye doctor stops you.
outcomes.reply: Tap water carries Pseudomonas and an amoeba that is even harder to treat. It never touches a lens.

outcomes.story: She throws her old case in the clinic bin and asks about daily disposable lenses.
outcomes.reply: Right. Sleeping in lenses is the single biggest risk, and old solution in an old case is a culture dish. Every item on that list removes a way in.

outcomes.story: You suggest fashion lenses. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Lenses sold without a fitting cause some of the worst infections we see.

outcomes.story: You suggest a lens in the infected eye only. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That eye will have a scar and is the last place for a lens. Resting one eye was never the problem.

differential.resident: The culture grew Pseudomonas. Her ulcer doubled in size in a day, and its edges look as if they are dissolving.
differential.question: What makes this infection so fast and destructive?
options: It spreads in branching lines across the surface, as a herpes virus does
It grows slowly, with feathery side spots, as a fungus does
It is an amoeba from water, which causes a ring and extreme pain
The bacteria release enzymes and toxins that digest the cornea
differential.reveal: Pseudomonas makes enzymes that cut up collagen, the protein the cornea is built from. That is why the edges of her ulcer look as if they are melting, and why it grows by the hour. Untreated, it can eat through the cornea in days. The other three are real infections of the cornea, and each looks different: herpes draws branching lines, fungus grows slowly, and the amoeba forms a ring.

terms.meaning: Inflammation of the cornea, here from infection.
A bacterium that lives in water and damp places and resists many antibiotics.

ending.stable: Home on antibiotic drops every hour, to be seen in clinic every day
ending.unstable: Home on antibiotic drops every hour, to be seen in clinic every day
ending.worse: Admitted for antibiotic drops every hour, with a deeper ulcer that will leave a scar
ending.critical: Admitted, with the cornea close to breaking open

oph-027.plainDiagnosis: A bacterial infection eating into the cornea, caused by sleeping and swimming in contact lenses (Pseudomonas keratitis).

science.title: What the bacteria were dissolving
science.text: The cornea is clear because its collagen fibers are all the same width and evenly spaced. The enzymes Pseudomonas releases cut collagen into pieces. Where the pattern is broken the cornea turns white, and scar tissue laid down later is never as regular.

science.title: Why sleeping in lenses matters
science.text: The cornea has no blood vessels. It takes its oxygen straight from the air. A lens slows that down, and a closed eyelid over a lens slows it much more. Surface cells short of oxygen break down, and bacteria on the lens get in through the gaps.

sources.title: Lin et al. (Ophthalmology 2019): bacterial keratitis preferred practice pattern
Stapleton and Carnt (Eye 2012): contact lens-related microbial keratitis, how have epidemiology and genetics helped us with pathogenesis and prophylaxis

oph-032.title: A deep ache in one eye, _and he cannot stand the light._

start.alarm: Aching left eye · pain in light

oph-032.handoff: A 34-year-old man has had a deep ache in his left eye for three days. Light is painful, the eye waters and it is red in a ring around the colored part. His vision is slightly blurred.

interview.prompt: Ask about the eye
interview.finding: A dull ache deep in the left eye for three days. Light hurts badly, and the eye waters. The redness sits in a ring around the colored part. There is no sticky discharge and no itch. Nothing went into the eye, and he does not wear contact lenses.

interview.prompt: Ask whether this has happened before
interview.finding: Twice, more mildly. Each time it settled over a couple of weeks.

interview.prompt: Ask about the rest of his health and his family
interview.finding: For months his lower back has been painful and stiff for over an hour each morning, and it eases once he moves around. He put it down to his desk job. His father has a stiff back, and an uncle has inflammatory bowel disease.

exam.prompt: Test his vision, and look at where the redness is
exam.finding: Vision is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left. The redness is deepest in a ring at the edge of the cornea and fades outward. There is no discharge.

exam.prompt: Look at his pupils, and shine a light in the good eye
exam.finding: The left pupil is smaller than the right and slow to react. Light in the right eye makes the left eye hurt.

exam.prompt: Put dye on the cornea, and examine his back
exam.finding: The dye shows no scratch or ulcer. He cannot bend forward fully, and the joints at the base of his spine are tender.

1.label: Microscope examination of the eye
1.content:
Left cornea: clear, with small clumps of cells stuck to its back surface.
Front chamber of the left eye: many white cells floating in the fluid, and the fluid is hazy with protein. No layer of pus.
Left pupil: small and slightly irregular. The iris has begun to stick to the lens behind it.
Eye pressure: 12 left and 15 right, both normal.
Back of both eyes: normal.

0.resident: Most red eyes in clinic are conjunctivitis, an infection of the surface. This one is not.
0.question: Which feature tells you so?
options: A red eye that waters
Slightly blurred vision
A deep ache, pain in light, and redness in a ring around the cornea
It has happened before

terms.meaning: Inflammation of the thin skin over the white of the eye. It feels gritty and sticky more than painful.
Pain on looking at light.

outcomes.story: You point to the watering. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nearly every red eye waters. That does not separate one cause from another.

outcomes.story: You point to the blur. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Discharge across the surface can blur vision a little too. It is not the best clue.

outcomes.story: The eye doctor nods and sits him at the microscope. The findings go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. A surface infection feels gritty. A deep ache and pain in light come from inside the eye, and that ring of redness lies over the inflamed tissue.

outcomes.story: You point to the earlier episodes. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is a useful clue to the cause. Allergic conjunctivitis also comes back, though, so it does not settle the question.

3.resident: Inflammation inside the eye often travels with a disease elsewhere. Think about his back: stiff for an hour every morning, better with movement.
3.question: Which blood test fits that picture?
options: Antinuclear antibody (ANA)
Rheumatoid factor
HLA-B27
ACE level, for sarcoidosis

terms.meaning: An inherited immune marker. It is common in people who get this eye inflammation together with spinal arthritis.
A long-term inflammatory arthritis of the spine and the joints at its base.

outcomes.story: You ask for ANA. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: ANA goes with a quieter, long-lasting eye inflammation in young children with arthritis. That is not his picture.

outcomes.story: You ask for rheumatoid factor. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Rheumatoid arthritis affects the hands and causes a different eye problem. It does not cause a stiff lower back in a young man.

outcomes.story: Blood is sent for HLA-B27, and he is referred to a rheumatologist about his back.
outcomes.reply: Right. Repeated attacks like this in a young man with that kind of back pain point to spinal arthritis. Sometimes the eye doctor is the first to find it.

outcomes.story: You ask for an ACE level. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Sarcoidosis can inflame the eye, but it does not explain his back.

4.resident: The eye needs treating today, before the iris sticks to the lens for good.
4.question: What do we prescribe?
options: Steroid drops, with a drop that widens the pupil and rests the focusing muscle
Antibiotic drops four times a day
Acyclovir tablets and an eye patch
Antihistamine drops

terms.meaning: A drop that relaxes the eye’s focusing muscle and widens the pupil.
Places where the inflamed iris has stuck to the lens behind it.

outcomes.story: He starts steroid drops every hour while awake and a dilating drop twice a day. He will be seen again in two days.
outcomes.reply: Right. The steroid quiets the inflammation. The second drop stops the muscle spasm that causes the ache and keeps the iris moving so that it cannot stick.

outcomes.story: You ask for antibiotic drops. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: There is no infection. This is the immune system inflaming the eye, and antibiotics will not touch it.

outcomes.story: You ask for acyclovir and a patch. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Nothing here looks like herpes, and a patch does nothing for inflammation.

outcomes.story: You ask for antihistamine drops. The eye doctor shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those are for itchy, allergic eyes. His eye aches, and it does not itch.

differential.resident: The microscope findings are in his chart.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: Acute angle-closure glaucoma, a sudden rise in eye pressure
Acute anterior uveitis, inflammation of the iris and the front of the eye
Episcleritis, inflammation of the surface of the white of the eye
A viral infection of the surface of the eye
differential.reveal: This is acute anterior uveitis. White cells and protein floating in the front chamber are inflammation that can be seen directly. The pupil is small because the inflamed iris is in spasm, and it is starting to stick to the lens. In angle-closure glaucoma the pressure is very high and the pupil is fixed half open. His pressure is normal. The other two affect the surface only and leave the inside of the eye clear.

terms.meaning: Inflammation of the middle layer of the eye, which includes the iris.
The fluid-filled space between the cornea and the iris.

ending.stable: Home on steroid and dilating drops, with a review in two days and a rheumatology referral
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

oph-032.plainDiagnosis: Inflammation inside the front of the eye (acute anterior uveitis), probably linked to an inflammatory arthritis of the spine.

science.title: What a positive HLA-B27 would mean
science.text: HLA-B27 is one inherited version of a gene for a protein that shows fragments to the immune system. Most people who carry it stay well, so the test alone diagnoses nothing. In someone with his eye and back symptoms, it makes spinal arthritis much more likely.

science.title: Why the dilating drop blurs his reading
science.text: To focus on something near, a ring of muscle inside the eye tightens and lets the lens grow rounder, which bends light more. The drop relaxes that muscle. The lens stays flat, so near objects are blurred until the drop wears off.

sources.title: Jabs et al. (Am J Ophthalmol 2005): standardization of uveitis nomenclature for reporting clinical data
Agrawal et al. (Indian J Ophthalmol 2010): current approach in diagnosis and management of anterior uveitis

oph-037.title: Headaches every day, _and her vision grays out for seconds._

start.alarm: Daily headaches · vision graying out for seconds

oph-037.handoff: A 31-year-old woman has had a headache every day for six weeks. Several times a day her vision grays out in both eyes for a few seconds. She hears a whooshing in her ears in time with her pulse.

interview.prompt: Ask about the headaches
interview.finding: A dull headache every day for six weeks. It is worse in the morning, when she lies down and when she bends over or strains. She has no fever and no stiff neck, and her arms, legs and speech are normal.

interview.prompt: Ask about her vision and hearing
interview.finding: For a few seconds at a time, everything goes gray or black in both eyes, often when she stands up. It is happening more often. She hears a whoosh in her ears with each heartbeat, sometimes sees double, and feels her side vision has narrowed.

interview.prompt: Ask about her weight and medicines
interview.finding: She has gained about 14 kg in the past year. Three months ago she started isotretinoin for acne. She also takes the contraceptive pill.

exam.prompt: Look at the back of her eyes
exam.finding: In both eyes the optic nerve, where it enters the eye, is swollen. Its edges are blurred, and the blood vessels crossing it are partly buried.

exam.prompt: Test her vision, pupils and side vision
exam.finding: She reads 20/20 with each eye, and her pupils react normally. Her natural blind spots are larger than they should be, and her side vision is slightly narrowed toward the nose.

exam.prompt: Test her eye movements, and bend her neck
exam.finding: Her left eye does not turn fully outward, and she sees double when she looks to the left. Her neck bends freely.

1.label: MRI, vein scan and spinal tap
1.content:
MRI of the brain: no tumor and no blocked fluid. Signs of high pressure: the backs of the eyeballs are flattened, and the sleeves around the optic nerves are stretched.
Scan of the brain’s veins: all open, with no clot.
Spinal tap: opening pressure 32. Normal is 25 or less.
Spinal fluid: normal cells, protein and sugar.

0.resident: Both optic nerves are swollen. That means the pressure inside her skull is high, and we need to know why.
0.question: What is the first test?
options: A spinal tap now, without a scan
An MRI of her brain, with a scan of the brain’s veins
Start acetazolamide, and send her home
A CT scan of her eye sockets only
0.fix: Get an MRI with a vein scan

terms.meaning: Swelling of the optic nerves caused by raised pressure inside the skull.
An MRI that shows the large veins that drain blood from the brain.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap first. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: If a tumor is causing the pressure, draining fluid from below can pull the brain downward. A scan comes first, every time.

outcomes.story: She has an MRI with a scan of the veins. Both are clear, so a spinal tap follows. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Two dangerous things raise the pressure like this: a mass, and a clot in the veins that drain the brain. The scan looks for both. After that the spinal tap is safe.

outcomes.story: You start treatment and plan to send her home. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That treats a diagnosis nobody has made. A tumor or a clot can look exactly like this at the bedside.

outcomes.story: You ask for a CT of her eye sockets. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The problem is behind the eyes, inside the skull. We need to see the brain and its veins.

3.resident: The pressure is high, and nothing structural explains it. She will get help with losing weight, and her acne medicine has to stop, because it can cause this.
3.question: Which medicine comes first?
options: Acetazolamide
Prednisone tablets, long term
Topiramate alone, as the first choice
A blood thinner

terms.meaning: A tablet that slows the production of the fluid around the brain.
A strong acne medicine related to vitamin A. Raised pressure in the skull is a known side effect.

outcomes.story: She starts acetazolamide. Her isotretinoin is stopped, and she is referred to a weight-management clinic.
outcomes.reply: Right. It lowers the pressure by slowing the production of fluid. Weight loss is what lasts: losing even a tenth of her weight often settles this.

outcomes.story: You ask for long-term prednisone. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Steroids cause weight gain, and the pressure rebounds when they stop. Both make this worse.

outcomes.story: You ask for topiramate. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It is sometimes used as a second option. The drug with the best evidence comes first.

outcomes.story: You ask for a blood thinner. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That would be the treatment for a clot in the veins. Her vein scan was clear.

4.resident: Her headaches are what bother her most. They are not the reason she will be followed so closely.
4.question: What are we trying to prevent?
options: Permanent loss of vision from long-standing swelling of the optic nerves
Long-term migraine
Hearing loss from the whooshing
A turned-in eye that stays that way

terms.meaning: A test that maps how far a person can see to each side while looking straight ahead.

outcomes.story: She is booked for a visual field test next week and regular checks with the eye doctors.
outcomes.reply: Right. A swollen optic nerve slowly loses fibers. The loss starts at the edges, where she will not notice it, and it does not come back.

outcomes.story: You say migraine. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The headaches matter to her, and they usually improve. They do not threaten her sight.

outcomes.story: You say hearing loss. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The whooshing is the sound of blood flow under pressure. It fades with treatment and does not damage hearing.

outcomes.story: You say the turned-in eye. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That nerve usually recovers once the pressure falls. The optic nerves do not.

differential.resident: Her scans and spinal tap are in the chart.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: A clot in the veins that drain the brain
A brain tumor pressing on the brain
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: high pressure in the skull with no mass and no clot
Dangerously high blood pressure
differential.reveal: This is idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The pressure of the fluid around her brain is high, the fluid itself is normal, and the scans found no tumor and no clot. It happens mostly in young women who have recently gained weight, and her acne medicine can also cause it. Her blood pressure is normal.

terms.meaning: With no cause that can be found.
Raised pressure inside the skull.

ending.stable: Home on acetazolamide, off her acne medicine, with a visual field test booked
ending.worse: Sent back to the emergency department

oph-037.plainDiagnosis: High pressure in the fluid around the brain with no tumor or clot (idiopathic intracranial hypertension).

science.title: Why the pressure is given as a height
science.text: During a spinal tap the needle is joined to a thin upright tube, and the spinal fluid rises in it until its weight balances the pressure inside. The height of that column is the reading. Hers rose to 32 centimeters, when 25 is the upper limit.

science.title: How the tablet slows fluid production
science.text: The cells that make spinal fluid depend on an enzyme, carbonic anhydrase, which turns carbon dioxide and water into bicarbonate and acid. Moving those ions draws water along with them. Acetazolamide blocks the enzyme, so less fluid is made.

sources.title: Friedman, Liu and Digre (Neurology 2013): revised diagnostic criteria for the pseudotumor cerebri syndrome in adults and children
Wall et al., NORDIC Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension Study Group (JAMA 2014): effect of acetazolamide on visual function in patients with idiopathic intracranial hypertension and mild visual loss

pmr-099.title: She cannot lift her arms _or get up from a chair._

start.alarm: Weak shoulders and hips · three months

pmr-099.handoff: A 48-year-old teacher has grown weaker in her shoulders and hips over three months. She struggles with stairs, with getting up from a low chair and with washing her hair.

interview.prompt: Ask about the weakness
interview.finding: It has crept up over three months, the same on both sides, in her shoulders and hips. Stairs, low chairs, lifting groceries onto a shelf and washing her hair are all hard. Her muscles ache a little, but weakness is the problem.

interview.prompt: Ask about her eyes, swallowing and feeling
interview.finding: Her eyelids do not droop, and she does not see double. She swallows and breathes normally. She has no numbness or tingling. She is no weaker in the evening than in the morning.

interview.prompt: Ask about her health and medicines
interview.finding: She has an underactive thyroid, well controlled on her usual tablet. She does not take a cholesterol medicine. She has had no rash, fever or weight loss. Her sister has rheumatoid arthritis.

exam.prompt: Test her strength
exam.finding: Her shoulders, hips and neck are weak on both sides. Her hands and feet are strong, and her grip is firm. To stand up from the chair she has to push off with her arms.

exam.prompt: Test her reflexes and feeling, and look at her muscles
exam.finding: Reflexes and feeling are normal. Her muscles are not wasted, do not twitch and are not tender.

exam.prompt: Look at her skin, and ask her to look up for a minute
exam.finding: No rash on her eyelids, knuckles or shoulders. Her eyelids stay up for the whole minute.

1.label: Blood tests, muscle test and MRI
1.content:
Creatine kinase, an enzyme that leaks from damaged muscle: 4,200. Normal is under 200.
Aldolase, another muscle enzyme: high.
Liver enzymes: mildly raised. Muscle releases these too.
Thyroid test: normal.
Inflammation marker (ESR): 38, raised.
Antinuclear antibody: positive.
Electrical test of the muscles (EMG): small, brief signals from irritable muscle fibers, the pattern of a muscle disease.
MRI: swelling in the muscles of the shoulders and thighs, the same on both sides.

0.resident: Weakness close to the trunk on both sides, with normal feeling, and no worse at the end of the day. That points at the muscles themselves.
0.question: Which blood test comes first?
options: Antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor
Creatine kinase
Nerve conduction speeds only
A spinal tap

terms.meaning: An enzyme found inside muscle cells. A high blood level means muscle is being damaged.
Close to the trunk: the shoulders, upper arms, hips and thighs.

outcomes.story: You ask for acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That tests for myasthenia gravis. In myasthenia the weakness comes and goes and worsens with use, and it usually starts in the eyelids. Hers is steady.

outcomes.story: Blood is drawn. With the result back, the specialist adds an electrical test of her muscles and an MRI. Everything goes in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. If muscle is the problem, damaged fibers leak this enzyme into the blood. One cheap test tells us whether we are on the right track.

outcomes.story: You ask for nerve conduction speeds alone. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That studies nerves. Her feeling and reflexes are normal, so her nerves are probably fine. Start with the muscle.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Spinal fluid tells us about the nerve roots and the brain. Nothing in her story points there.

3.resident: Her immune system is attacking her own muscle fibers.
3.question: What is the first treatment?
options: High-dose steroids
Pyridostigmine
Immunoglobulin infusions alone, as the first treatment
Plasma exchange

terms.meaning: A drug such as prednisone that damps down the immune system.
A second medicine, such as methotrexate, added so that the steroid dose can be reduced.

outcomes.story: She starts high-dose prednisone, and a second medicine is planned so that the steroid can be reduced later.
outcomes.reply: Right. Steroids quiet the attack on her muscles. They cause trouble over the long run, so we add a second drug early and bring the dose down.

outcomes.story: You ask for pyridostigmine. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That strengthens the signal from nerve to muscle. Her signal is fine. Her muscle is inflamed.

outcomes.story: You ask for immunoglobulin alone. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It is a good extra treatment when steroids are not enough. It is not where we start.

outcomes.story: You ask for plasma exchange. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Trials have not shown it to help in this disease.

4.resident: She asks whether she should rest her muscles until the medicine works, or push hard at the gym to rebuild them.
4.question: What do you advise?
options: Strict bed rest until her strength is back
The hardest weight training she can manage, starting now
A supervised program that starts gently and builds as the inflammation settles
No exercise at all, because activity makes this disease worse

terms.meaning: Moving each joint through its full arc to keep it from stiffening.
Loss of strength and fitness from not using the body.

outcomes.story: You advise bed rest. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Rest costs her the muscle she still has and stiffens her joints. She would end up weaker.

outcomes.story: You advise heavy training now. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Inflamed muscle cannot take maximum loads yet. We build up to that.

outcomes.story: She is booked with a physiotherapist for a program that starts with stretching and light strengthening.
outcomes.reply: Right. Studies show that graded, supervised exercise improves function in this disease and does not make it flare. It is part of the treatment.

outcomes.story: You advise no exercise. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Doctors used to believe that. The evidence says otherwise.

5.resident: One more thing has to be checked in an adult who develops this disease.
5.question: What is it?
options: A hidden cancer
Multiple sclerosis
Diabetes insipidus
Narrowed arteries in the legs

terms.meaning: Testing for a disease before it causes symptoms.

outcomes.story: She is booked for the cancer screening recommended for her age, and she is asked about any new symptoms.
outcomes.reply: Right. Inflammatory muscle diseases sometimes appear alongside a cancer nobody has found yet. We look around the time of diagnosis and keep looking for the first few years.

outcomes.story: You say multiple sclerosis. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is a disease of the brain and spinal cord. It has no link with this one.

outcomes.story: You say diabetes insipidus. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is a hormone problem that causes great thirst. It is unrelated.

outcomes.story: You say narrowed arteries. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Narrowed arteries cause pain on walking. They do not cause this weakness and have no link with it.

differential.resident: Her test results are in the chart. Remember what her skin looked like.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: Dermatomyositis
Polymyositis
Myasthenia gravis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
differential.reveal: This is polymyositis, an immune attack on muscle. It causes weakness close to the trunk on both sides, a very high muscle enzyme, an irritable pattern on the electrical test and swollen muscle on MRI. Dermatomyositis looks the same in the muscles and adds a rash on the eyelids and knuckles, which she does not have. Myasthenia fluctuates and leaves the muscle enzyme normal. ALS damages the nerves that drive muscle and causes wasting and twitching.

terms.meaning: Inflammation of muscle.
Caused by the immune system attacking the body’s own tissue.

ending.stable: Home on steroids, with physiotherapy and cancer screening booked
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

pmr-099.plainDiagnosis: Muscle inflammation caused by her own immune system (polymyositis).

science.title: Why a muscle enzyme was in her blood
science.text: Creatine kinase works inside muscle cells, where it passes phosphate between creatine and ATP to supply quick energy. An intact cell membrane keeps it in. When immune cells damage the fibers it leaks out, and the blood level rises with the damage.

science.title: Why stairs and chairs were the first things to go
science.text: Standing up from a chair or climbing a step means raising the whole body’s weight. The muscles that do it are those of the hips and thighs, working at a poor angle of leverage. Carrying a cup uses a tiny fraction of that force, so hand tasks stay easy.
science.lessonTitle: Choose a force or energy model

sources.title: Dalakas (N Engl J Med 2015): inflammatory muscle diseases
Alexanderson (Curr Rheumatol Rep 2012): exercise in inflammatory myopathies, including inclusion body myositis

pmr-095.title: A school screening, _and a shirt that hangs crooked._

start.alarm: Curve found at school screening · no pain

pmr-095.handoff: A 13-year-old girl was picked up at a school screening for a curve in her back. Her mother has noticed that one shoulder blade sticks out and her clothes hang unevenly. She has no pain.

interview.prompt: Ask how it was noticed, and about pain or weakness
interview.finding: The school nurse noticed it at a screening. Her mother sees one shoulder blade sticking out and shirts hanging crooked. She has no back pain, by day or night. Her legs are strong, with no numbness, and her bladder and bowels are normal.

interview.prompt: Ask about growth
interview.finding: Her periods started six months ago. She has shot up recently, and her shoe size keeps changing.

interview.prompt: Ask about her health, sports and family
interview.finding: She is healthy, takes no medicines and plays volleyball. An aunt wore a back brace as a teenager.

exam.prompt: Look at her standing, then ask her to bend forward and touch her toes
exam.finding: Her right shoulder sits a little higher, and the right shoulder blade sticks out. When she bends forward, the ribs on the right side of her back rise higher than the left.

exam.prompt: Look at the skin over her spine
exam.finding: Normal. There are no birthmarks, no patch of hair and no dimple over the spine.

exam.prompt: Test her strength, feeling, reflexes and walking
exam.finding: All normal.

1.label: Standing X-rays of the spine
1.content:
Front view: the spine curves to the right in the upper back. The angle of the curve, called the Cobb angle, is 28 degrees. Scoliosis means 10 degrees or more.
Side view: normal.
Growth marker on the hip bone (Risser sign): grade 1, on a scale from 0 to 5.
No misshapen bones in the spine.

0.resident: The bend test shows a rib hump. Now the curve needs to be measured.
0.question: What is the next step?
options: An MRI of her whole spine
Standing X-rays of the whole spine, from the front and the side
A bone scan
Send her straight to a spine surgeon

terms.meaning: A sideways curve of the spine, usually with some twisting.
The angle between the most tilted bones at the top and bottom of a curve, measured on an X-ray.

outcomes.story: You ask for an MRI. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: MRI is for curves with warning signs: pain, an abnormal nerve exam or an unusual pattern. She has none.

outcomes.story: She has two X-rays standing up. The specialist measures the curve, and the results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Every decision about scoliosis starts from that one measured angle, taken standing, with gravity acting on the spine.

outcomes.story: You ask for a bone scan. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That looks for infection, tumor or hidden fractures, usually in a child with pain. It cannot measure a curve.

outcomes.story: You send her to a surgeon. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Most curves never need surgery. Nobody can say whether hers will until it is measured.

3.resident: Her curve is 28 degrees, and she has a lot of growing left to do.
3.question: What is the right treatment?
options: A brace around her trunk, to stop the curve growing
Watch only, and repeat the X-ray in four to six months
An operation to fuse the spine
Stop all sports and physical activity

terms.meaning: A fitted plastic shell worn around the trunk under clothes. It holds the curve while the spine grows.
An operation that straightens the curve with rods and joins the bones so that it cannot return.

outcomes.story: She is measured for a brace and booked for an X-ray in four months.
outcomes.reply: Right. A brace will not straighten the curve she has. It keeps the curve from growing while she grows, and it works better the more hours a day she wears it.

outcomes.story: You suggest watching only. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is right for a curve under about 25 degrees, or for a teenager who has finished growing. Hers is past that, and she is still growing fast.

outcomes.story: You suggest fusion. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Surgery is for curves approaching 50 degrees. At 28 the aim is never to get there.

outcomes.story: You tell her to stop sports. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Exercise does not worsen scoliosis. She can keep playing volleyball, and the brace comes off for games.

4.resident: Her parents ask how bad a curve has to be before surgery is advised.
4.question: At about what angle?
options: More than 10 degrees
More than 20 degrees
More than about 45 to 50 degrees
Only beyond 90 degrees

terms.meaning: The level at which the recommended action changes.

outcomes.story: You say 10 degrees. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Ten degrees is only where a curve starts to be called scoliosis. Most of those are simply watched.

outcomes.story: You say 20 degrees. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Curves in the twenties are watched or braced.

outcomes.story: Her parents are relieved to hear how far she is from that number.
outcomes.reply: Right. Curves past about 50 degrees tend to keep growing even in adults, and very large ones can crowd the lungs. That is where surgery is advised.

outcomes.story: You say 90 degrees. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: By then the lungs are already affected. Surgeons act long before that.

differential.resident: Her growth marker is grade 1 out of 5, and her periods began only six months ago.
differential.question: What does that tell you about her curve?
options: Her skeleton is mature, so the curve will hardly change
She has a lot of growing left, so the curve has a real chance of getting worse
Growth has nothing to do with how scoliosis behaves
The curve is certain to need surgery
differential.reveal: She has adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, and she is still growing. A curve gets worse mainly while the spine is growing, so two things predict what happens: how large the curve is now and how much growth is left. Hers is moderate, at 28 degrees, with years of growth ahead. That is the group with the most to gain from treatment. It does not mean surgery is certain, and most braced curves never reach it.

terms.meaning: A marker on a hip X-ray that shows how far the skeleton has matured, from 0 to 5.
With no cause that can be found.

ending.stable: Home, to be fitted with a brace, with volleyball to continue and an X-ray in four months
ending.worse: Sent to the emergency department

pmr-095.plainDiagnosis: A sideways curve of the spine in a teenager who is still growing (adolescent idiopathic scoliosis).

science.title: How a brace holds a curve
science.text: A brace pushes on the trunk at three points: one at the peak of the curve, and one above and one below it on the opposite side. Together they bend the spine back toward straight. Growing bone responds to the loads on it, so the forces have to be there for most of the day.
science.lessonTitle: Choose a force or energy model

science.title: How we know bracing works
science.text: A large trial followed teenagers who wore a brace and others who were only watched. Far more of the braced group stayed below the angle for surgery. Sensors inside the braces recorded the hours worn, and more hours meant better results. A matching dose and response strengthens the case for cause.
science.lessonTitle: Decide what a study can claim

sources.title: Weinstein et al. (N Engl J Med 2013): effects of bracing in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis
Hresko (N Engl J Med 2013): idiopathic scoliosis in adolescents

pmr-073.title: Six weeks after a head injury, _his hip is seizing up._

start.alarm: Right hip stiffening · warm and firm

pmr-073.handoff: A 31-year-old man is on day 40 of rehabilitation after a severe head injury in a motorcycle crash. Over the past week his right hip has become harder and harder to move, and it is warm and firm.

interview.prompt: Ask the therapists what they have noticed
interview.finding: Over the past week his right hip has moved less each day. He grimaces and becomes agitated when they bend it or move it outward. The top of his thigh is newly warm and feels firm deep down.

interview.prompt: Review his hospital stay and medicines
interview.finding: After the crash he spent weeks in intensive care on a breathing machine. He takes a seizure-prevention medicine and has a daily injection to prevent blood clots. He has had no high fevers.

interview.prompt: Ask how the hip is affecting his rehabilitation
interview.finding: He speaks in single words and follows simple requests. He needs a great deal of help to move, and the stiff hip now makes it hard to sit him up and to practice moving from bed to chair.

exam.prompt: Move both hips gently
exam.finding: The right hip bends only partway and then stops firmly. Moving it outward or rotating it is painful and very limited. The left hip moves much more freely.

exam.prompt: Feel around the right hip, and look at the skin
exam.finding: There is a deep, firm, warm swelling at the front and side of the joint. The skin over it is not red or broken, and nothing feels like a pocket of fluid.

exam.prompt: Check his calves, foot pulses and muscle tone
exam.finding: His calves are soft and equal in size, and they are not tender. His foot pulses are normal. Both legs are stiff, with jumpy reflexes, from the brain injury.

1.label: Blood tests, bone scan, X-ray and vein ultrasound
1.content:
Alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme released where bone is being made: 412, high.
White cells: 8.4, normal.
Inflammation markers: mildly raised.
Calcium and phosphate: normal.
Bone scan: strong uptake around the right hip in all three phases.
Hip X-ray: a faint haze in the soft tissue in front of the joint.
Vein ultrasound of the right leg: no clot.

0.resident: A deep, firm, warm swelling at the hip, and a joint that moves less every day, six weeks after a severe brain injury.
0.question: What is the most likely explanation?
options: An infected hip joint
A clot in the main vein of the thigh
An inflamed bursa on the outside of the hip
Heterotopic ossification: new bone forming in the soft tissue around the joint
0.fix: Name the likely problem and test for it

terms.meaning: Bone forming where it does not belong, in muscle and other soft tissue.
How far a joint can move in each direction.

outcomes.story: You say an infected joint. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: An infected joint is worth ruling out, and the blood tests will help. It brings a high fever and a joint too painful to move at all. It does not form a firm mass.

outcomes.story: You say a clot. The specialist adds a vein ultrasound.
outcomes.reply: A clot must be ruled out, because he has been immobile for weeks. It swells the calf and the whole leg, though. It does not stiffen a hip.

outcomes.story: You say bursitis. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That causes tenderness at one spot on the outside of the hip. It does not block the joint’s movement.

outcomes.story: The specialist orders blood tests, a bone scan, a hip X-ray and a vein ultrasound to exclude a clot. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. After a severe brain or spinal cord injury, the tissue around large joints can start making bone. The hip is the commonest site, and this is the usual timing.

3.resident: New bone is being laid down around his hip, and it is still soft and growing.
3.question: Which medicine can limit it?
options: Steroids
Vancomycin into a vein, in case of infection
A bisphosphonate, such as etidronate
Calcium and vitamin D supplements

terms.meaning: A medicine that binds to bone mineral. It slows the hardening of newly formed bone.
The laying down of calcium and phosphate crystals that makes soft new bone hard.

outcomes.story: You ask for steroids. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Steroids are not a treatment for this, and they add risks he does not need.

outcomes.story: You ask for vancomycin. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His white cells are normal, and there is no pus and no fluid in the joint. This is not an infection.

outcomes.story: He is started on etidronate. An anti-inflammatory medicine is another option some teams use.
outcomes.reply: Right. It slows the new bone from hardening while it is still immature. It will not remove bone that has already formed.

outcomes.story: You ask for calcium and vitamin D. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Those supply the very minerals this unwanted bone is built from. His calcium is normal, and he does not need more.

4.resident: His family asks whether a surgeon can simply cut the new bone out.
4.question: When is surgery considered?
options: Now, to stop it from growing
Later, once the bone has matured and gone quiet, if the hip is still limiting him
Never. Surgery has no place in this condition
As soon as the alkaline phosphatase first rises

terms.meaning: Removing tissue by surgery.
Bone that has finished forming and hardening.

outcomes.story: You say to operate now. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Cutting into bone that is still actively forming makes it grow back, often worse than before.

outcomes.story: You explain it to his family, and they agree to wait.
outcomes.reply: Right. Surgeons wait until the blood tests and scans show that the bone has stopped growing. If the hip still blocks sitting or walking then, they remove it.

outcomes.story: You say never. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Mature bone that locks a joint or presses on a nerve can be removed, with good results.

outcomes.story: You say as soon as the blood test rises. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A rising level means the bone is at its most active. That is the worst time to operate.

5.resident: Until then, the therapists need to know how to handle that hip every day.
5.question: What do you tell them?
options: Hold the hip completely still in a cast
Force the hip through its full movement under anesthesia, to break up the bone
Gentle movement every day, stopping at pain
Complete bed rest, with no movement of the leg

terms.meaning: Permanent shortening of the tissues around a joint, which fixes it in one position.

outcomes.story: You say a cast. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Holding it still does not stop the bone, and the joint would stiffen in whatever position we cast it.

outcomes.story: The hip is forced through its range under anesthesia. By the next morning the thigh is more swollen and hot, and the hip moves less than before.
outcomes.reply: Force tears the tissue and makes it bleed, and injured tissue is exactly where this bone forms. That has fed the process. Movement has to be gentle.
outcomes.alarm: Thigh more swollen · hip stiffer than before

outcomes.story: The therapists move his hip gently through whatever range it allows, twice a day, and position him to keep it from stiffening.
outcomes.reply: Right. Gentle movement keeps the range he still has without injuring the tissue. He will need every degree of it to sit and to transfer.

outcomes.story: You say bed rest. The specialist shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Rest adds stiffness, weakness, pressure sores and clots. It takes nothing away from the bone.

differential.resident: New bone is forming around his hip. The X-ray shows only a faint haze, because the new bone has barely begun to harden.
differential.question: Which test picks this up earliest?
options: A three-phase bone scan
A plain X-ray of the hip
A blood calcium level
Drawing fluid from the joint to look for crystals
differential.reveal: A three-phase bone scan finds heterotopic ossification first. A small dose of radioactive tracer is injected, and it collects wherever blood flow is high and bone is being built. That shows up weeks before the new bone holds enough mineral to appear on an X-ray. His blood calcium is normal, as it usually is. Joint fluid is tested for infection or gout, and neither is the problem here.

terms.meaning: A scan that uses a small dose of radioactive tracer to show where bone is being made.
The formation of bone.

ending.stable: On the rehabilitation unit on a bone medicine, with gentle hip movement twice a day
ending.worse: On the rehabilitation unit with a more swollen, stiffer hip, on a bone medicine

pmr-073.plainDiagnosis: New bone forming in the muscles around his hip after a brain injury (heterotopic ossification).

science.title: How a bone scan sees bone being made
science.text: The tracer is a phosphate compound carrying technetium-99m, an unstable atom that gives off gamma rays as it decays. Growing bone takes up phosphate, so the tracer gathers there, and a camera maps the rays. Half of it has decayed within six hours.

science.title: How muscle ends up making bone
science.text: Connective tissue in muscle holds cells that can still become several cell types. Signals released after a major injury switch on the genes of a bone-making cell in some of them. The DNA is the same as before. A different set of genes is being read.
science.lessonTitle: Follow a gene into a protein
